# English

## P1 Why Does Literary Study Need "Theory"?

Every act of reading starts from assumptions: what counts as literature, where meaning is to be found, why criticism exists at all. "Theory" is not a toolkit bolted on top of some natural way of reading; it is a way of bringing those normally invisible assumptions into the open and testing them. The first step towards understanding theory, then, is not to learn any one school's doctrine but to see clearly the starting point that all of them oppose: a way of studying literature that took shape in the nineteenth century and had come to seem self-evident by the middle of the twentieth.

In the six-layer framework, this part sits at "Layer 0", the presuppositions under critique. It answers three questions: why the discipline of English carried a moral and political mission from the very beginning; what tenets that discipline held implicitly in its everyday practice; and what ideas theory, taken as a whole, holds in common. Every later part can be read as a denial, a revision or a fresh defence of some of the tenets set out here.

### How Was English Born as a Substitute for Religion?

**Background:** Until the 1820s, higher education in England was a monopoly of the Church of England. There were only two universities, Oxford and Cambridge; students had to be male and Anglican, the teachers were clergymen forbidden to marry, and the curriculum consisted of classics (Greek and Latin literature), theology and mathematics. Catholics, Jews, Methodists and atheists were shut out, and with them out of the professions and the civil service.

The breakthrough came with University College London, founded in 1826, which awarded degrees to men of any religion or none. English entered the curriculum in 1828 and the first professor of English was appointed in 1829, but the subject was then mainly the study of the English language, with literature serving only as a source of examples; English literature as such was first taught at King's College from 1831. Women came later still: Oxford did not grant women full degrees until 1920, Cambridge not until 1948, whereas the University of London had been awarding degrees to women since 1879.

**Mechanism:** In 1840 **F. D. Maurice**'s inaugural lecture at King's College laid down several founding principles of English literary study. Studying English literature should free people "from the notions and habits which are peculiar to our own age" and connect them with "what is fixed and permanent". Literature was regarded as the property of the middle class and the expression of its values; the middle class embodied the essence of "Englishness" (the aristocracy belonged to an international elite, the poor were busy surviving), so middle-class education should centre on English literature. The political intent was stated bluntly: the "political agitator" will ask what the "nation" means to a man who walks while his neighbour rides in a carriage. Someone educated in English literature would still feel that his national identity was real. In other words, studying English literature could give people a stake in the status quo without any redistribution of wealth.

This logic made literature take over the social functions of religion. The lower classes were going to church less and less, and their rulers feared that, with neither attachment to the nation nor a religion to teach morality and restraint, they would eventually rise up as the French had. Chartism, the movement for universal adult male suffrage, emerged in the 1830s, exactly when the first English courses appeared. The usual account dates the idea of "replacing the cohesive function of religion with a secular vernacular culture" to **Matthew Arnold** in the 1850s and sees it culminating in the *Newbolt Report* of 1921; Maurice's lecture shows that the idea appeared earlier.

**Limitation:** It would be inaccurate to reduce the founding motives of English to "ideological control". Control was one motive, but the reality was a characteristically Victorian mixture: class guilt about social inequality, a sincere wish to improve everyone's lot, a missionary zeal for spreading culture and enlightenment, and a self-interested concern for social stability. *This qualification is itself a methodological lesson: every later theory that "exposes the political function of literature" has to face the objection that it may be oversimplifying motives.*

**The problem of "knowledge content":** Oxford and Cambridge resisted the new subject for a long time, admitting it only in 1894 and 1911 respectively. Oxford's first attempt to establish a chair of English, in 1887, failed largely because of a speech against it by the historian **Edward Freeman**. People said that literary study "cultivates the taste, educates the sympathies, enlarges the mind"; all excellent things, he replied, but "we cannot examine in tastes and sympathies". Examiners needed technical, factual knowledge to test, and if literature were separated from language, literary study would amount to no more than "chatter about Shelley". Freeman won: the Oxford English syllabus of 1894 contained a great deal of historical philology (Old English, Gothic, Middle English and so on). **What exactly the knowledge content of the discipline is has never been fully settled**, and later theory can largely be read as yet another answer to that question.

**The parallel American route:** In the first half of the nineteenth century, humanistic education in American universities consisted entirely of "recitation" in Latin and Greek. When English literature entered the curriculum, it first adopted the `philology` model imported from Germany: analysing grammar, etymology, the sources of images and the classification of figures of speech. The other model was rhetorical: using selected great passages to train recitation and oratory, from which the Harvard composition course developed, dropping its oral component in 1873. The rhetorical mantle passed to the "generalists", who valued appreciation of the whole, but in the wave of professionalisation marked by the founding of the Modern Language Association (MLA) in 1883 they were judged insufficiently systematic. Only after the First World War, with the rise of American literary study, did the New Critics of the 1920s provide, for the first time, a coherent rationale for studying "literature as literature" rather than as language.

**The Cambridge solution and its price:** The Cambridge English faculty was founded last (1911) and carried the least traditional baggage. In the 1920s it was reshaped by three figures:

- **I. A. Richards**'s `Practical Criticism` (1929) isolated the text from history and context and analysed only "the words on the page". Its gain was to put an end to vague, florid impressionistic criticism and to demand precise attention to textual detail.
- **William Empson**'s *Seven Types of Ambiguity* (1930) pushed this word-by-word analysis to its limit. Leavis said it treated poetry with intelligence "as seriously as if it were mathematics"; T. S. Eliot called it "the lemon-squeezer school" of criticism.
- **F. R. Leavis** and Q. D. Leavis founded *Scrutiny* (1932–1953) and extended close reading to the novel. His criticism had two weaknesses. He quoted at length but commented little, assuming that the "competent reader" would naturally see what he saw, so that he was often paraphrasing rather than analysing; and his method was centred on morality, with critical terms that were never defined.

The result of this solution was that literary study, as it grew up, declared itself independent of the study of language, of historical inquiry and of philosophical questions. From the 1930s to the 1960s the consensus of the discipline rested on accepting this threefold separation. **The "theory" project that began in the 1960s was, in substance, an effort to reconnect literary study with the three fields of linguistics, history and philosophy.** This is the clearest thread in the history of the problem: the linguistic thread leads to formalism, structuralism and stylistics (P2–P4); the philosophical thread to phenomenology, deconstruction and the postmodern (P5, P7, P8); the historical thread to Marxism, historicism and the various politics of identity (P9–P15).

**The imperial dimension:** The institutional history of English has another side that the domestic British story tends to leave out. In the late nineteenth century "English" replaced "Classics" as the body of texts used to train young men for the professions: instead of Homer, Aeschylus and Cicero, they read Shakespeare, Milton and Wordsworth. Because Britain was the centre of a global empire, this change turned "English" into a global cultural institution, one that was used to produce a "cultured" and more compliant class of colonial administrators. The local was mistaken for the universal; this theme will be developed in P15.

### Ten Implicit Tenets of Liberal Humanism

**Definition:** `Liberal humanism` is a hostile shorthand that came into currency in the 1970s for the criticism that dominated before theory. "Liberal" roughly means not radical, evasive and non-committal on political questions; "humanism" implies non-Marxist, non-feminist, non-theoretical, and a belief that the "human nature" expressed in great literature is constant and unchanging. In the United States the same thing is often called "formalism" (*here "formalism" means the American close-reading tradition before theory, not the Russian Formalism discussed in P2*). Liberal humanists never call themselves that, but anyone who practises criticism without calling themselves a Marxist, a structuralist or a stylistician is quite likely to be one.

Giving it the name of an "ism" is itself an argument: **there is no way of studying literature that is "theory-free"**; every one of them derives from a set of assumptions, principles or foundational claims, especially when those assumptions are never spoken aloud. The "semi-hidden curriculum" distilled from traditional English studies can be summed up in ten tenets:

1. **Timelessness.** Good literature has timeless significance; it transcends the limitations of its own time and speaks to what is constant in human nature: "not of an age, but for all time" (Ben Jonson on Shakespeare), "news that stays news" (Pound).
2. **Self-sufficiency of the text.** The meaning of a text is contained within it, with no need to place it in the context of socio-political conditions, literary history (influence and generic tradition) or the author's biography.
3. **Close reading detached from context.** To understand a text one must detach it from those contexts and analyse it word by word, without ideological or political presuppositions or any expectations at all: to "see the object as in itself it really is", in Arnold's phrase.
4. **Unchanging human nature.** The same passions, emotions and even situations recur throughout human history, so continuity matters more in literature than innovation; poetry is "what oft was thought, but ne'er so well expressed" (Pope), and it was on grounds of novelty that Johnson dismissed *Tristram Shandy*.
5. **The transcendent subject.** Individuality is a unique "essence" securely possessed by each person; it transcends the influence of circumstance and can develop but cannot be transformed. That is why scenes of characters having a "change of heart" in Dickens's novels are often unsettling. This is what is meant by the `transcendent subject`: the individual as prior to, or beyond, the forces of society, experience and language.
6. **Non-programmatic humane values.** The purpose of literature is to enrich life and propagate humane values, but not in a programmatic way; once literature or criticism becomes overtly political, it slides into propaganda. As Keats put it, "we hate poetry that has a palpable design upon us".
7. **Organic form.** Form and content must be organically fused, each growing necessarily out of the other; imagery that could be detached from the substance is mere "fancy" rather than "imagination" (Coleridge's distinction).
8. **Sincerity lies in the language.** Sincerity (truth to experience, honesty towards oneself, the capacity for empathy) is not a fact or an intention behind the work but something present in its language: in the avoidance of cliché and overstatement, in first-hand, individual description, in the understated expression of feeling. The sincere poet can even make the language seem to "enact" what it describes, abolishing the necessary gap between word and thing.
9. **Showing is better than telling.** Ideas in themselves are worthless in literature unless they are concretely "enacted". This anti-intellectual tendency was especially fervent in Leavis. It contains a self-referential paradox: **"distrust of ideas" is itself an idea**.
10. **Criticism needs no theory.** The task of criticism is to interpret the text and to mediate between text and reader; theories about reading or about the nature of literature only bring in "preconceptions" that stand between reader and text. Behind this lies the `British empiricism` that goes back to **John Locke**: trust only what the senses present, and treat ideas as composed of the imprints that direct sense impressions leave on the mind.

These ten are not a list of parallel slogans but two mutually supporting chains of inference. The first is a **chain about text and value**: timelessness (1) → the text does not depend on context (2) → reading should strip context away (3); and the ground of timelessness lies in an unchanging human nature (4) and in the transcendent essence of the individual (5). The second is a **chain about language and form**: organic unity (7) → sincerity lies in the language (8) → enactment is better than statement (9) → theory becomes an obstacle to reading (10). Tenet 6 links the two: literature has a moral function, but that function must be "above politics". *The impact of later theories on the ten tenets can be mapped roughly as follows: structuralism and deconstruction strike at tenets 2, 3, 7 and 8; psychoanalysis and theories of ideology at tenet 5; Marxism, historicism, feminism and postcolonial criticism at tenets 1, 4 and 6; and all theory together at tenet 10.*

**Reading:** A typical liberal humanist reading of Edgar Allan Poe's *The Oval Portrait* can serve as a baseline for later comparison. The story tells of a painter who paints a portrait of his young bride; as the picture grows ever more lifelike the wife wastes away, and at the moment the last stroke is laid on she dies. A Leavisite reading would focus on the conflict of values between "art" and "life": true value lies in the "lived life" of the unique individual, and an artist who casts himself as a Faustian superman, crossing every boundary and even playing the god who creates and sacrifices life, commits a sin of transgression; the painter in his turret, drawing the life force out of his model, is a degenerate emblem of "art for art's sake". Such a reading has two features. First, it is driven by moral conviction rather than by any systematic critical model. Second, it bypasses form, structure and genre to go straight to content; even when it mentions structure and symbol, they serve only as concrete support for a moral position. This does not make it worthless; the point is simply to mark its features. The same story will be reread by structuralism in P3 and by narratology in P4.

### Two Critical Traditions Before Theory: Text-Led and Idea-Led

The ten tenets may give the impression that British criticism before theory never articulated any theory at all. That is not so. A theoretical tradition was always available, and **historically, critical theory came before criticism of individual works**.

- **Aristotle**'s *Poetics* (4th century BC) defined tragedy, argued that literature puts character first and that character is revealed through action, and tried to identify the necessary stages of a plot. He was also the first "reader-centred" critic: tragedy should arouse pity and fear, and the combination of the two produces `catharsis`, in which these emotions are "exercised" through identification with the hero rather than "purged".
- **Philip Sidney**'s *Defence of Poesy* (c. 1580) developed Ovid's "to teach and delight" and Horace's "speaking picture". Its revolutionary move was to separate literature from other writing by the criterion of "giving delight"; in a religious age suspicious of all fiction and representation, this was a large step.
- **Samuel Johnson**'s *Lives of the Poets* and his Preface to Shakespeare mark the beginning of the British tradition of practical criticism: before him, only sacred texts such as the Bible had received such intensive line-by-line commentary. Extending that scrutiny to works that were not divinely revealed marked an advance of secular humanism.
- The Romantic poets brought a flowering of critical theory. **Wordsworth**'s Preface to *Lyrical Ballads* (1800) demanded that the language of poetry come as close as possible to prose, abandoning traditional poetic diction and compressed syntax, and so raised early the question of how poetic language relates to ordinary language and literature to other writing. **Coleridge**'s *Biographia Literaria* opposed this, arguing that bringing poetic language close to prose would be self-defeating: since literature and other writing have different purposes, and poetry instructs by delighting, the delight must come from the "fictionality" of its language. **Shelley**'s *A Defence of Poetry* (1821) said that poetry "strips the veil of familiarity from the world … it compels us to feel that which we perceive", anticipating the Russian Formalist idea of `defamiliarisation`; his description of the "unconscious" in composition and **Keats**'s "negative capability" (being able to rest "in uncertainties, mysteries, doubts, without any irritable reaching after fact and reason") anticipated Freud's idea of the unconscious.

On this basis one can distinguish two "tracks" in the development of British criticism. **Track One**, running through Johnson and Arnold to T. S. Eliot and Leavis, is led by the text and produced the familiar tradition of close reading. **Track Two**, running through Sidney, Wordsworth, Coleridge and George Eliot to Henry James, is led by ideas and deals with large questions: how literary works are structured, how they affect readers, what the nature of literary language is, how literature relates to politics and gender, what the act of creation is. **Track Two's concerns closely resemble those of theory since the 1960s, so theory is not a foreign invasion of "native" Anglo-American literary study but a dimension that study contained from the start.**

The key figures of Track One and their concepts make up the theoretical sources of liberal humanism:

**Arnold** feared that the decline of religion would leave an increasingly divided society without a shared system of belief, value and imagery, and that literature could fill the gap. He thought the middle class, which bore democratic responsibility, had been corrupted by materialism and philistinism, and that the critic should help it come to know "the best that is known and thought in the world". He stressed the `disinterestedness` of criticism: political detachment, service to no programme of action. His central tool was the `touchstone`: rather than defining any literary quality, it used lines from the masters as a yardstick against which to measure other poetry.

**T. S. Eliot** contributed three widely accepted concepts, all of them flawed. The `dissociation of sensibility` claimed that a split between thought and feeling took place in the seventeenth century, but no historical evidence for it was ever found; it is best taken as a description of the cast of mind of the Metaphysical poets. `Impersonality` set itself against Romantic self-expression: the best parts of a work are those in which the voices of predecessors speak through the poet, and "the man who suffers" should be kept apart from "the mind which creates" (Shelley had held a similar idea). The `objective correlative` held that emotion should be expressed through gesture, action or concrete symbol; this is no more than Plato's ancient distinction between `mimesis` (showing) and `diegesis` (telling). That these concepts stayed in fashion so long shows precisely the theoretical vacuum in which they were put forward.

**Leavis** can be seen as combining Johnson's moralism with Arnold's social vision and anti-theoretical practice. Like Arnold, he thought the appreciation of literature a precondition of social health, distrusted abstract thought and refused the direct politicisation of literature and criticism. The difference was that Arnold took the standing of the past masters for granted, and his view of criticism encouraged the amateur reader to form a direct relationship with great works, whereas Leavis often attacked the reputations of major writers, holding that some of them could not survive close reading. He coined no terms, instead using everyday words such as "life" and "felt experience" as critical terms; his key test was whether a work was on the side of "life" and vitality.

**Empson**'s effect was double. On one hand, his work is the logical extreme of the text-led tradition of Track One. On the other, its underlying view of language is that language is an extremely slippery medium, liable at any moment to erupt with unforeseen meanings; as we move from the first type of ambiguity to the seventh, we draw ever closer to the edge of language, until we seem to glimpse a void of linguistic indeterminacy. This is an anticipation, from within the British tradition, of the poststructuralist view of language; its seventh type of ambiguity ("an irreconcilable conflict of meaning within the text") will be matched in P7 with deconstruction's `aporia`. **Limitation:** placing language in any actual context reduces or removes ambiguity. Spoken on its own, *pain* might be *pane*; in context there is no confusion. The later Empson indeed retreated from the edge of the "linguistic void" by emphasising the biographical context of works.

**Richards**, in the 1920s, gave poems without annotation or authors' names to students and teachers to comment on. The ideal was to strip away all received opinion and cultivate "genuine judgement" based on first-hand impressions, in direct line with Arnold's touchstone. This "Richards moment" established "practical criticism" in Britain and the "New Criticism" in America from the 1930s to the 1970s, and its success was so complete that the discipline fell into a selective amnesia, imagining that Track One was the only tradition there had ever been.

**The prototype of the conflict:** The conflict between liberal humanism and theory did not begin in the 1970s. As early as 1937 the theorist **René Wellek** told Leavis in *Scrutiny* that the close readings of the Romantic poets in his *Revaluations* had been put forward in a theoretical vacuum: "I could wish that you had made your assumptions more explicitly and defended them systematically." Leavis refused. Theory's central demand of liberal humanism is the same as Wellek's, only less politely put: **say what you are doing when you read and criticise literature, and why, so that your method can be evaluated alongside others.** The implied judgement is that once assumptions are made explicit their weaknesses will show, and other approaches will have a chance to take their place.

**Another perspective:** The editors of the anthology place formalism, especially American New Criticism, at the starting point of theory, for reasons consistent with the analysis above: as long as students have been trained in "close reading", they are already formalists, only as unaware of it as Molière's Monsieur Jourdain, who did not know he had been speaking prose all his life. They also describe the formation of this tradition from another direction. Aristotle valued the effect of a work on its audience, whereas Romantic aesthetics shifted attention from the relation between work and audience to genius and to the organic unity inside the work, an aesthetic closer to Plato than to Aristotle. This judgement will return in P5.

### The Common Ground of Theory: Five Recurring Ideas

**Background:** The growth of critical theory after the war came roughly in ten-year waves, each aimed at the liberal humanist consensus established in the 1930s to 1950s. In the 1960s, two approaches that had appeared in the 1930s but had not been absorbed came back to life, Marxist criticism and psychoanalytic criticism; at the same time, linguistic criticism (from the early 1960s) and early feminist criticism (from the late 1960s) mounted direct attacks. In the 1970s structuralism and poststructuralism arrived from France, and by the late 1970s and early 1980s they had brought about a "crisis" or "civil war" in English; their concerns were linguistic and philosophical rather than historical and contextual. The 1980s saw a "turn to history": New Historicism in the United States and cultural materialism in Britain put history, politics and context back at the centre while keeping some insights of the previous decade. The 1990s saw a general flight from grand explanations towards dispersed, eclectic, "special-interest" criticism: postcolonial criticism rejected universally applicable Marxist explanations, postmodernism stressed the fragmentation of contemporary experience, feminism gradually dissolved into a loose federation of gender studies, lesbian and gay literature became a field of its own, and Black feminism (`womanism`) took its place among them. *This model of ten-year waves is itself a simplification; P17 will supplement it with ten concrete events.*

Each approach has its own tradition and history, but several ideas recur and form the common ground of theory. Granting that this is a simplification, it is possible to speak of "theory" as a body of shared assumptions.

**Idea one: basic categories are socially constructed.** Many concepts we usually treat as "givens" of existence, such as gender identity, the individual self, even "literature" itself, are in fact fluid and unstable, dependent on socio-political forces and on changing ways of seeing and thinking. In philosophical terms they are `contingent` (provisional, dependent on circumstance) rather than absolute categories. The position theory attacks is called `essentialism` for short, and most theories describe themselves as `anti-essentialist`. This is the first appearance of the third of the mechanisms that run throughout, **essence ↔ construction**; it will escalate steadily in feminism (P12), queer theory (P13), race studies (P14) and postcolonial criticism (P15), and meet a counter-attack in ecocriticism (P16).

**Idea two: all inquiry is affected by prior ideological commitments.** Disinterested inquiry is impossible: nobody can stand outside the scales and weigh calmly; every researcher has a thumb pressed on one side of them. Every practical procedure presupposes some theoretical standpoint, and to deny this is to treat one's own position as "common sense" and so place it beyond scrutiny. **Objection:** this claim tends to be stated only when rebutting opponents, and it discredits one's own work along with theirs, introducing a `relativism` that disables argument and leaves every commitment without foundation.

**Idea three: language conditions and predetermines what we see.** All reality is constructed through language; nothing is unproblematically "out there". Language does not record reality but shapes and creates it. Meaning is constructed jointly by reader and author and needs the reader's participation to come into being. The theoretical source of this idea is Saussure in P3; its reader dimension is developed in P5.

**Idea four: there is no ultimate reading.** The meaning of a literary work is never fixed but fluid, many-sided and ambiguous; it is the nature of language to generate an endless web of meanings, so texts necessarily contradict themselves, as deconstruction will reveal. Once a work exists it is an independent linguistic structure whose author is always "dead" or "absent"; there is no final arbiter (P7).

**Idea five: distrust of all "totalising" concepts.** The "great work" as a self-sufficient category is suspect, because works always arise from particular socio-political situations, and crowning a work "great" tends to suppress that situation. "Human nature" as a general norm transcending race, gender and class is also suspect, because in practice it is usually `Eurocentric` (taking white European norms as the standard) and `androcentric` (taking male norms and attitudes as the standard); appealing to a generalised, apparently inclusive humanity may well, in practice, marginalise, belittle or even deny the humanity of women and disadvantaged groups.

The five can be compressed into five sentences: **politics is pervasive; language is constitutive; truth is provisional; meaning is contingent; human nature is a myth.** If any later theory feels hard to grasp, going back to these five sentences will often supply the thread: the elusive concept is quite likely a version of one of these positions. *Set against the ten tenets, the five sentences are almost point-by-point counter-propositions: "politics is pervasive" answers non-programmatic humane values (6); "language is constitutive" answers sincerity and enactment (8, 9); "truth is provisional" and "meaning is contingent" answer timelessness and the self-sufficiency of the text (1, 2); "human nature is a myth" answers unchanging human nature and the transcendent subject (4, 5).*

**Two attitudes towards theory itself:** The first attitude (Barry's) stresses that theory is not inherently difficult. The whole edifice rests on a dozen or so ideas that are not complicated in themselves; what is difficult is its language. Many theorists wrote in French, which takes its vocabulary directly from Latin, so English translations are full of long Latinate words. One should therefore adopt a threefold frame of mind: give the difficult surface an initial patience, without concluding too soon that theory is empty jargon; do not assume the fault lies in one's own ability; but, crucially, do not assume that the difficulty of theoretical writing is always the garment of profound thought. It is so only *sometimes*, and the responsibility for judging lies with us. **What we look for in theory is something we can use, not something that uses us; theory should not be given a blank cheque.** Theory's "challenges" and "interrogations" are good things, but in the end they must deliver something. This attitude is the "line of evaluation" that runs through the later parts: each theory will be tested against concrete objections.

The second attitude (that of the anthology's editors) puts more weight on theory's self-doubt. The anthology's cover uses the image of the "No Radio" signs New Yorkers put in their cars (there's no radio here, so don't bother smashing the window) to voice a reservation many people feel about theory: it seems tied to a masterful ideology in which to analyse is to dissect and to dissect is to kill. The editors' reply is that "theory" is itself full of doubt about the ideal of objectivity: some theories do realise the ambition of "the man holding the heart in his hand", but many others side with "the woman lying on the operating table". The two attitudes do not contradict each other: the first demands from outside that theory be clear and deliver results; the second points out from inside that theory already doubts its own urge to master.

**Conclusion:** From its birth the discipline of English carried the mission of replacing religion and binding the nation together (Maurice, Arnold, the *Newbolt Report*), and that mission settled into the ten implicit tenets of liberal humanism. In the 1920s the Cambridge solution gave the discipline, through close reading, a teachable and examinable "knowledge content", at the price of cutting its ties with linguistics, history and philosophy. The five shared ideas of theory refute those tenets almost one by one, and they are also different routes towards restoring those three connections. **The conflict between theory and liberal humanism is therefore not a contest between new and old, or foreign and native, but the continuation of the demand Wellek made in 1937: state the assumptions your reading depends on, and let them be tested.** At the same time, Barry's "line of evaluation" is a reminder that the demand applies to theory too: every theory must also state its assumptions and deliver results that can be tested.

The first systematic challenger of liberal humanism was not politics but language: if the value of literature does not lie in the timeless human nature it expresses, where does it lie? The answer of the two formalisms was that it lies in the particularity of literary language itself.

## P2 What Makes Literature Literature? Two Formalisms

Before the early twentieth century, literary study was concerned with almost everything about literature except its language: the historical background of a work, the life of its author, what the work was "about". Two independent movements changed this: Russian Formalism and American New Criticism. Both made the question "how does literary language differ from ordinary language?" central, and both took the text itself, rather than the author or society, as their object of study; but they gave opposite reasons for why literary language should be studied.

In the six-layer framework this part stands on the border between Layer 0 and Layer 1, and its status is double. Compared with the biographical and moral criticism of P1, it is the first "linguistic turn", moving the source of meaning from author and world to the linguistic organisation of the text. Compared with later theory, New Criticism in turn became the "formalism" mentioned in P1, the American version of liberal humanism. Russian Formalism, by contrast, leads through Jakobson directly to the structuralism of P3.

### Literariness, Device and Defamiliarisation: The Scientific Ambition of Russian Formalism

**Background:** `Russian Formalism` was the work of a group of young scholars in the 1910s and 1920s, centred on the Society for the Study of Poetic Language (Opoyaz), founded in Petrograd in 1916, and the Moscow Linguistic Circle. Its leading figures were **Viktor Shklovsky**, **Boris Eichenbaum**, **Boris Tomashevsky** and **Roman Jakobson**. Its immediate opponents were the Russian Symbolists and their theoretical source, Potebnja: the Symbolists held that literary form was the garment of spiritual meaning, and Potebnja that "poetry is thinking in images". The Formalists were also influenced by philosophies of science such as Husserl's, which sought to isolate the objects of knowledge in their pure state. Their ambition was to move literary study out of the realm of religion and speculation and into the realm of science.

**Definition:** The central proposition was formulated by Jakobson: the object of literary science is not literature but `literariness`, that which makes a given work a literary work. Literary historians had behaved like policemen who, setting out to arrest a suspect, round up everyone at the scene along with any passers-by: environment, psychology, politics, philosophy all went into the net, and the result was not a science of literature but a hotchpotch of home-made disciplines. The history of philosophy, cultural history and psychology may use literary works as second-rate documents, but that is their own business.

**Mechanism one: poetic language versus practical language.** To establish the specificity of literature without recourse to speculative aesthetics, one needs a contrasting system that lies next to literary material but has the opposite function. The Formalists chose linguistics, and from it derived the opposition between "poetic language" and "practical language". Jakubinsky put it like this: if a speaker uses the resources of language for purely practical communicative purposes, those resources (sounds, word forms and so on) have no independent value; they are only means. But there are other linguistic systems in which the practical aim retreats into the background (it need not disappear entirely) and linguistic resources acquire `autonomous value`. Practical language aims at transparency, letting the message pass through as smoothly as possible; poetic language distorts and roughens everyday language, subjecting it to what Jakobson called "organised violence". A meteorologist would say that rainfall on the Iberian Peninsula is concentrated on the central plateau. From a practical point of view the internal rhyme of "*the rain in Spain falls mainly on the plain*" is unnecessary and unpractical, but it is exactly devices of this kind that make poetry an independent linguistic activity whose rules are not subordinate to practical function.

The first consequence is that sound in a poem is not an external, pleasing ornament accompanying the meaning but something of autonomous value. The Symbolist Andrej Belyj heard in two lines of Pushkin a "sound picture" of champagne being poured from bottle into glass; it was precisely this treatment of sound as the "expression" of something behind it that the Formalists opposed. Brik's classificatory study of sound repetitions in Pushkin and Lermontov simply pointed out that repetition in poetry resembles tautology in folklore: it has an aesthetic function in itself, and there is no need to explain what it "means".

The second consequence is of greater theoretical importance. The Formalists freed themselves from the traditional "form–content" pair: form was no longer a container and content no longer a liquid poured into it. **What is specific to art lies not in the elements that make up a work but in the particular way those elements are used.** Form therefore no longer needed to be paired with any other concept. What the Formalists really valued was the `device` (*priem*, also rendered as *technique*): the concrete operations by which the artist handles material. *"Device" is used throughout what follows.*

**Mechanism two: defamiliarisation.** Shklovsky's "Art as Device" (1916) is the manifesto of Formalism. It starts from a law of perception: **once perception becomes habitual, it becomes automatic.** The first time we hold a pen or speak a foreign language feels completely different from the ten-thousandth. In this "algebraic" mode of thought, things are replaced by symbols and we recognise them only by their outlines, as if looking at something inside a sack. Tolstoy recorded in his diary that while cleaning his room he came to the sofa and could not remember whether he had dusted it; if the whole complex life of a person goes on unconsciously, such a life is as if it had never been. Habitualisation devours work, clothes, furniture, one's wife and the fear of war.

**Art exists so that one may recover the sensation of life; it exists to make the stone stony.** The purpose of art is to impart the sensation of things as they are *perceived*, not as they are *known*. The device of art is to make objects `defamiliarised` (*ostranenie*) and forms difficult, increasing the difficulty and length of perception, because the process of perception is an aesthetic end in itself and must be prolonged. It follows that the function of an image is not to make meaning easier to grasp but to create a special perception of the object: to "see" it, not merely to "recognise" it.

**Example: Tolstoy.** Tolstoy makes familiar things strange by not calling them by their names, describing each as if he were seeing it for the first time. In "Shame", flogging is described as stripping people who have broken the law, throwing them to the ground and beating their bottoms with switches; he then asks why this stupid, savage way of causing pain should have been chosen rather than, say, pricking the shoulders with needles or squeezing hands and feet in a vice. Through description and the proposal to "change the form without changing the nature", an accepted institution is made to look absurd. In "Kholstomer" the narrator is a horse, which cannot understand an expression like "my horse": the people who call it "theirs" never ride or feed it, while those who treat it well are the stable hands and the vet; human beings are governed by words rather than deeds, and private property is just a verbal game everyone has agreed to play. After the horse dies, the narrative device does not change, even in the description of its owner's funeral; *this shows that the "motivation" for the point of view has disappeared while the device goes on working by itself.* The opera scene in *War and Peace* is written the same way: "smooth boards", "painted cardboard" with trees on it, "a fat man in silk tights" who began to sing and spread his arms. When Tolstoy described church ritual in the same manner, many people felt insulted; defamiliarisation is not confined to the aesthetic sphere and can just as well unsettle faith and institutions.

**Consequences:** Defamiliarisation is not just Tolstoy's personal style but is found "almost wherever there is form". Three important consequences follow.

First, imagery is not the essence of poetry. The more we know about a literary period, the more we find that images thought to be a poet's own invention were borrowed almost unchanged from predecessors; the work of poetic schools is less the creation of images than their arrangement. Imagery is thus demoted to one device of poetic language among many, alongside parallelism, comparison, repetition, symmetry and hyperbole.

Second, the "principle of economy in art" is overturned. Herbert Spencer had argued that rhythm allows the mind to arrange its attention in advance and so saves effort. Shklovsky's answer was that this confuses the laws of poetic language with those of prose. The rhythm of work songs does automate labour, but poetic rhythm is precisely "disordered rhythm": no column of a Greek temple stands exactly where it should. The crucial point is that if the disordering itself becomes a convention, it loses its force as a means of "roughening".

Third, the boundary between poetic language and prose language shifts. Poetic language is often foreign or archaic; but when Pushkin brought into verse the name of an ordinary country girl, Tatiana, his contemporaries, used to an elevated style, found this "vulgarity" unexpectedly difficult. When literary language seeps into everyday conversation, literature turns in its turn to dialect and the colloquial. Everyday and literary language repeatedly "change places".

*Taken together, these three consequences give a relational definition of literariness: literariness is not an inherent property of certain linguistic features but an effect of deviation relative to the habitual perception of a period. What counts as "strange" depends on what counts as "familiar". This brings Formalism, without its knowing, close to the logic of difference in P3.*

**Prehistory and connections:** The idea of defamiliarisation did not come from nowhere. Shelley's claim that poetry "strips the veil of familiarity from the world", and the aim Coleridge attributed to Wordsworth, "to give the charm of novelty to things of every day … by awakening the mind's attention from the lethargy of custom", are forerunners. Interestingly, when the American New Critic Brooks argued that the language of poetry is the language of paradox, it was this very passage of Coleridge that he quoted; here the two formalisms meet without having planned to.

### Story and Plot, and the Autonomy of Literary Evolution

**Problem:** The theory of defamiliarisation is mainly a local theory of perception. How can it be extended into an analysis of the overall structure of the novel, and how can it explain historical change in literature?

**Mechanism: motivation and device.** The Formalists distinguished between the constructive elements of a work (plot-forming devices such as sequential construction, parallelism, framing and stringing together) and the material it uses (story matter, motifs, characters, themes). The reason for the material's presence in the work was called its `motivation` (*motivirovka*). Old-style scholarship treated only the material as "content" and lumped everything else together as "external form", so critics could say that Turgenev "neglected form" or that Dostoevsky's "form was poor", and excuse it on account of the depth of their ideas. The Formalists reversed this, putting constructive devices first and understanding everything else as motivation.

**Example: *Don Quixote* and *Tristram Shandy*.** Shklovsky saw *Don Quixote* as a point of transition from the story collection of the *Decameron* type to the novel with a single hero. Its structure is one of stringing together, motivated by a journey. In this novel device and motivation have not yet fused; material is often merely inserted rather than permeated, so the constructive procedures stand out with unusual clarity. He even inferred that the plasticity of Don Quixote as a hero was itself produced "under the pressure of constructing the novel": the character is a product of the structure, not the structure a servant of the character. *Tristram Shandy*, by contrast, deliberately "lays bare the device": its awareness of form shows itself through the violation of form, and that awareness is the novel's content. This reading itself turned Sterne's novel back into a "contemporary work".

**Definition: story and plot.** At the end of his study of Sterne, Shklovsky distinguished `fabula` (story: the material of events arranged in the order and duration in which they actually happen) from `syuzhet` (plot: the way they are told in the text, including all the construction of time order, point of view and so on). The plot of *Eugene Onegin* is not the love affair of the hero and Tatiana but the plotting of that material through the introduction of interrupting digressions. **Artistic form is to be explained by laws internal to art, not by motivations drawn from real life.** When an artist delays the action of a novel not by introducing interruptions but simply by rearranging the order of the parts, we become aware of the aesthetic laws governing both kinds of construction. This distinction is the starting point of the whole of narratology in P4. Once it has been made, one can begin to analyse point of view, delayed disclosure, narrative voice and every other device of storytelling: one can study, for instance, the narrative strategies of *The Scarlet Letter* rather than its depiction of Puritanism.

Eichenbaum's own "How Gogol's 'Overcoat' Is Made" combined the problem of plot with `skaz` (construction based on the narrator's oral manner of telling), showing that "The Overcoat" is built from alternating comic narration and sentimental, hyperbolic declamation, which gives it its grotesque quality; the traditional debate over whether Gogol was a "Romantic" or a "realist" becomes irrelevant. In poetry, Brik found "rhythmic-syntactic figures" inseparable from rhythm, proving that rhythm is not something applied to the surface of the sentence, and Tomashevsky proposed the concept of the `dominant`: in a given work one particular rhythmic device dominates and determines the concrete rhythm of the whole. **Verse form understood in this way is not opposed to any "content" outside it; it is the true content of poetic speech.**

**Mechanism: literary evolution.** On one hand the Formalists looked for the invariant patterns, recurring devices and regular relations of literature; on the other they had to explain why literature changes from period to period. Their explanation consisted of two related claims: literary evolution is the result of constantly breaking existing conventions and generating new ones; and literary evolution is the result of the autonomous development of literary devices. The first claim is really the theory of defamiliarisation unfolded in time: new device → defamiliarised perception → the device is imitated and becomes convention → automatisation → yet another new device. The second claim is more radical. The traditional view held that literature merely gives form to thoughts and realities outside it, so that literature changes because the world changes; the Formalists held that devices owe nothing to such motivations and that their evolution has purely literary causes. The comic novel *Don Quixote* mocked the chivalric romances that dominated its day; it appeared not because the world or Cervantes's life had changed but because of evolution internal to literature: the new device of the "problematic hero" was made possible and necessary by the development of the novel form itself.

**Limitation:** The claim that "literary evolution is entirely independent of society and history" is Formalism's strongest and most vulnerable claim. *It explains how change happens (through deviation from convention) but has difficulty explaining why this change rather than another.* Bakhtin, who later shared the Formalists' attention to generic form, nonetheless stressed the social and ideological character of literature; Marxist criticism (P9) rejects this autonomy outright. History gave the Formalists no chance to defend themselves: they were suppressed by the Stalinist regime in the 1920s. Their work was carried to the West by émigrés from Eastern Europe. Jakobson left Russia in 1920 and worked in the Prague Linguistic Circle, which inspired French structuralism in the 1940s and 1950s; René Wellek, Julia Kristeva, Tzvetan Todorov and others brought it into Western Europe and America, where it shaped structuralism, poetics, stylistics and narratology.

### Close Reading, the Intentional Fallacy and the Affective Fallacy: How New Criticism Defined Its Object

**Background:** The leading figures of `New Criticism` were **Cleanth Brooks**, **W. K. Wimsatt**, John Crowe Ransom and Allen Tate. Brooks had studied with I. A. Richards at Cambridge; back in America, a series of his books from *An Approach to Literature* (1936) to *The Well Wrought Urn* (1947) made "close reading" the dominant method in American academia from the 1940s to the end of the 1960s. Unlike the Russian Formalists with their scientific aims, the New Critics were influenced by idealist philosophers such as Croce, and their motive was to refute positivist science, that is, the claim that all truth rests on empirical facts knowable by scientific method. Art offers another kind of truth, reachable only through connotative language (suggestion, metaphor, symbol), which cannot be expressed in the direct, denotative, fact-naming language of science.

**Definition: two fallacies that mark out the object.** New Criticism left two terms designed specifically to separate literary study from biography, psychology and sociology. According to the `intentional fallacy`, meaning lies in the linguistic design of the work, not in the author's statements about his intentions. According to the `affective fallacy`, the subjective effects or emotional responses a work produces in readers are irrelevant to the study of the verbal object itself, because only the objective structure contains the work's meaning. *The two terms come from two essays of the same names written by Wimsatt and Monroe Beardsley (1946, 1949) and later collected in Wimsatt's The Verbal Icon (1954). The classic formulation of the first is that the design or intention of the author is neither available nor desirable as a standard for judging the success of a work of literary art; the second defines the affective fallacy as a confusion between the poem and its results, between what it is and what it does.*

**Argument: Brooks's answer to objections.** Brooks's "The Formalist Critics" (1951) opens with a list of articles of faith: literary criticism is a description and an evaluation of its object; the primary concern of criticism is the problem of unity, the kind of whole the work forms or fails to form and the relation of the parts in building it; formal relations may include logical relations but certainly go beyond them; in a successful work form and content cannot be separated, **form is meaning**; literature is ultimately metaphorical and symbolic; the general and the universal are not seized upon by abstraction but reached through the concrete and particular; literature is not a substitute for religion; "specific moral problems" are the subject matter of literature, but the purpose of literature is not to point a moral.

More important is his response to two kinds of objection. The first says that putting the work at the centre cuts it off from its author's life; the second, that it cuts it off from actual readers, whereas literature is rooted in history. Brooks grants that works are written by particular people for all sorts of motives (for money, for self-expression, for a cause), and that a work is only a potential until it is read, with readers differing enormously in ability, interests and prejudices. His point is a distinction. Speculation about the author's mental processes takes the critic away from the work and into biography and psychology; such studies describe the process of creation rather than the structure of what was created, and apply equally to good and bad works. The study of various readers' responses takes the critic into psychology and the history of taste. These studies are valuable, but they should not be confused with criticism of the work itself.

To criticise the work itself, the formalist critic makes two assumptions. **First, the relevant part of the author's intention is what he actually got into the work**: what counts is "realised intention", not what he consciously meant to do at the time or remembers afterwards. **Second, he assumes an ideal reader**: rather than tracking every possible reading, he looks for a central point of reference from which to focus on the structure of the work. It may be objected that there is no ideal reader and that a critic who sets himself up as one is arrogant. Brooks concedes that no ideal reader exists, but holds that this is a defensible strategy, and one that critics of every persuasion are obliged to adopt. The alternatives are counsels of despair: either one holds that every reading is as good as any other, so denying the possibility of a standard reading, or one takes the lowest common denominator of readings, which means leaving literary criticism for social psychology; and taking the consensus of "qualified readers" merely splits the ideal reader into a panel of ideal readers. *This argument deserves notice: it sketches in advance Fish's "interpretive communities" in P5. The option Brooks treats as a reductio ad absurdum is precisely what reader-response theory would later assert.*

On this basis New Criticism rejects two popular tests of value. The first proves a work's value by the author's "sincerity" or the intensity of his feeling while writing: Hemingway's saying that his latest novel was his best means something for biography but proves nothing about the value of the work. The second takes the reader's response as the measure: A. E. Housman's report that a good line of poetry made the hairs of his beard bristle tells us something about Housman, not about the poem. *This does not contradict tenet 8 of the ten in P1: liberal humanism already held that sincerity lies in the language, not behind the work.*

**Conclusion:** Brooks assigns the critic a modest role. A literary work is a document that can be analysed in terms of the forces that produced it, and also a force that can affect the future; but **reducing a literary work to its causes does not constitute literary criticism, and nor does an estimate of its effects**. Literature can have all sorts of "uses", but all of them ultimately depend on our knowing what a work "means", and that knowledge is fundamental. He also denied that New Criticism was hostile to ideas. In an exchange with Lionel Trilling he agreed that the value of Faulkner and Hemingway lies in the sense they give of "working intensely on the stubborn materials of life", and restated this in structural terms: tension, symbolic development, irony and its resolution. Literature is not the enemy of ideas; it feeds on them, only it does not lay them out neatly but entangles them with the stubborn materials of life.

### Paradox, Irony and the "Concrete Universal": The Metaphysical Commitments of New Criticism

**Problem:** If poetry conveys truths that scientific language cannot name, how exactly does poetic language manage this?

**Thesis: the language of poetry is the language of paradox.** In "The Language of Paradox" (1947) Brooks argued that `paradox` is usually thought of as the language of sophistry, clever rather than profound; yet in a sense paradox is the language appropriate and inevitable to poetry. The truth of the scientist requires a language purged of every trace of paradox, whereas the truth the poet utters seems approachable only in terms of paradox.

**Evidence one: Wordsworth.** Even Wordsworth, who preferred direct statement and distrusted all sophistry, typically built his poems on paradoxical situations. In "It is a beauteous evening" the poet is filled with reverence while the girl beside him is not; yet it is precisely this apparently unmoved girl, with her unconscious sympathy with all of nature, who worships more deeply than the self-conscious poet. In "Composed upon Westminster Bridge" the power of the poem comes neither from noble sentiment nor from vivid imagery (the details are simply heaped together) but from a paradoxical situation: that grimy, feverish London should "wear / The beauty of the morning". The poet has always regarded houses as dead and mechanical; to say now that "the very houses seem asleep" is to say that they are alive. **Only under the appearance of death does the poet see that the city is alive.**

**Mechanism: connotation, analogy and the "tilted plane".** Paradox springs from the nature of the poet's language, in which `connotation` matters as much as `denotation`. The tendency of science is to stabilise its terms, freezing them into strict denotations; the poet's tendency is disruptive. Words continually modify one another, violating their dictionary meanings, and the poet "has to make up his language as he goes". Every subtle emotional state needs metaphor to express it, and metaphors do not lie on the same plane or fit edge to edge: the planes keep tilting, and overlaps, discrepancies and contradictions are inevitable. This does not mean the poet cannot be precise: in Shakespeare's words, he can "by indirections find directions out". The bowl in the game of bowls is weighted off-centre, and the skilled player uses that bias to curve his shot; science uses perfect spheres and can attack directly, but the method of art is always indirect. To demand that the bias be taken off the bowl, that language be used as mere notation, is to confuse the game of poetry with the game of science.

**Reading: Donne's "The Canonization".** In Donne's "The Canonization" the poet treats profane love as if it were divine love: the lovers renounce the world, each making the other's body a hermitage, and so qualify for "canonisation". Modern readers, used to a simple yes or no, can only take paradox as a cheap trick, and so fall into a dilemma: either Donne does not take love seriously, or he does not take sainthood seriously. Neither explanation is right. Donne takes both love and religion seriously, and paradox is his inevitable instrument.

Close reading shows how this is achieved. The poem opens with an indignant rebuff ("For God's sake hold your tongue, and let me love"). The "you" addressed stands for the practical world that thinks love foolish: go to court and look at the king's face, or go into business and look at the face "stamped" on coins. The second stanza ironically piles up stale Petrarchan conceits (winds of sighs, floods of tears) to show that the lovers' passion does the world no harm: "What merchant's ships have my sighs drowned?" In the third stanza the comparisons begin to sharpen: the fly, the taper that dies at its own cost, the eagle and the dove, and at last the phoenix: "we two being one, are it". The tone thereby shifts from ironic bickering to restrained tenderness. "Die" carried a sexual meaning in the seventeenth century, and this does not contradict its other senses but adds to them a layered meaning in which "our death is a more intense life". By the last stanza the lovers who renounced the world have drawn "countries, towns, courts" into each other's eyes, and have become, in fact, the most "worldly" of people.

More crucially, **the poem is both the assertion of the doctrine it maintains and the realisation of that assertion**. The lovers say they can build "pretty rooms" in sonnets, and the poem itself is the "well-wrought urn" that can hold the lovers' ashes no less fittingly than a prince's "half-acre tombs". Donne could have said plainly that love in a cottage is enough, but that would have weakened and distorted what was to be said. **Conclusion:** Brooks's claim is that most of the important things the poet has to say must be said through paradox; this is true of the language of lovers and equally of the language of religion ("he who would save his life must lose it"). Strip away paradox and its two companions, irony and wonder, and Donne's poem falls apart into biological, sociological and economic "facts", and the lovers become Huxley's animals "quietly sweating palm to palm".

Brooks finally connects paradox with Coleridge's definition of the `imagination`, which "reveals itself in the balance or reconciliation of opposite or discordant qualities: of sameness, with difference; of the general, with the concrete; the idea, with the image …". This description is itself a string of paradoxes. Another "urn", Keats's Grecian urn, is equally a model case of this kind of reading. In the "Ode on a Grecian Urn", "Cold Pastoral" and "unheard melodies" suggest life and death at once, the vivid and the static coexisting against nature; this is because the subject of the poem is that art, symbolised by the urn, though it seems lifeless, is more vivid than life itself: dead, and yet immortal. *This opposition of "art and life" will return, in a completely different form, in the structuralist reading of "The Oval Portrait" in P3.*

**Theorisation: Wimsatt's "concrete universal".** In *The Verbal Icon* (1954) Wimsatt raised this practice into a metaphysical thesis. From Aristotle, Plotinus and Hegel to Ransom, critics had said again and again that a literary work is in some special way both intensely individual and intensely universal. This tradition had split into two extremes. The school of Johnson and Reynolds stressed the universal: the poet's business is not to "number the streaks of the tulip" but to give the species. The school of Warton, Blake and Bergson stressed the individual: "to generalize is to be an idiot". **Both extremes lead out of art: the theory of the individual leads to the eccentric, the unintelligible and the author's psychology; the theory of the universal leads to cliché and the "average tulip".**

Wimsatt's solution comes in two steps. The first is to clarify concepts. There are two kinds of "generality": "essential" generality in the sense of logical classification, and "existential" generality in the sense of truth to nature. A "purple cow" is more general than a "tawny cow with a broken horn", but the latter is truer to nature. Moreover, words by their nature generalise; what words convey is never the individual but a more or less concrete generalisation. He also rejected Ransom's model of "argument (universal) + irrelevant local texture (concrete)", seeing it as merely a variant of the theory of "ornamental metaphor".

The second step is the positive answer. A literary work is not simply more individual or more universal than other writing; it is a **complex of detail**, with humane values so intricate that it appears highly individual. This is the `concrete universal`. The first example is character. E. M. Forster's distinction between "flat" and "round" characters is not merely a matter of quantity. Jonson's Bobadil is the type of the braggart soldier, each of his traits just another instance of the same principle; Shakespeare's Falstaff has a special interrelation among his traits, above all the complexity of his self-awareness; one can even argue over whether, when he ran away at Gadshill, he already knew the attackers were the Prince. The second example is metaphor. Behind "my love is like a red, red rose" lies a likeness between two classes, and hence a more general third class; that class has no name and can be expressed only by the metaphor itself. In "The Solitary Reaper" the girl is set beside the nightingale of the Arabian sands and the cuckoo of the Hebrides; this evokes loneliness and mystery, and at the same time, beyond the logic of comparison, suggests the extension of space and communication across the world. A narrative poem too can be seen as a metaphor with its tenor left out.

From this, Wimsatt changed Horace's maxim "simple and unified" to "**complex and unified**": every real poem is complex, and has artistic unity only by virtue of its complexity; newspaper verse has only the unity of an emotion stated abstractly. Further, the "subject matter" of poetry is, broadly, the moral realm, so **complexity of form is maturity of content; unity and maturity are two aspects of one thing**, and rhetorical analysis and evaluation thereby become one. This criticism is "objective" because it relies on a "public psychology" (for instance, that a man may love a woman so much that he gives up an empire) rather than the private psychology of the author or of a single reader. Finally, criticism stands to the poem as 1.414… stands to the square root of two: there is something in the poem that can never be expressed in other words, and criticism can only approach its limit ever more closely.

**Two judgements:** Brooks's articles of faith state explicitly that "literature is not a substitute for religion", drawing a line between himself and Arnold. The anthology's editors judge, by contrast, that New Criticism was in some respects a late Romantic school: its description of figures of speech cannot be separated from a general theory of meaning, and that theory was a polemical response to positive science, full of the values of Christian theology and idealist aesthetics that science had displaced. The two judgements stand side by side. *What Brooks rejects is letting literature take over the social function of religion; what the editors point out is that New Criticism's conception of truth is structurally homologous with religious language. The reading of "The Canonization" itself puts the language of lovers and the language of religion in the same category.*

### The Two Formalisms Compared, and Their Legacy

Russian Formalism and New Criticism had no historical connection, yet in theory they share a root. Both were concerned with the difference between literary and ordinary language, and both restricted their object to the text and its workings rather than the author's life or the socio-historical world literature refers to. They differ as follows:

| Dimension | Russian Formalism | American New Criticism |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Intellectual temper | Scientific and rational, aiming at value-neutral description | Anti-scientific, concerned with the non-rational dimension of art and with evaluation |
| Opponents | Symbolism and "thinking in images"; the hotchpotch of literary history | Positivist science; biographical, impressionistic and history-of-taste criticism |
| Unit of analysis | Whole genres (narrative in the novel, sound in poetry) and recurring devices | The single work, especially the short poem |
| Function of devices | The device is an end in itself: breaking automatism, prolonging perception | The device is a route to the "concrete universal": reconciling opposites, achieving unity |
| Relation to time | Values literary evolution, but assumes it is autonomous | Seeks timeless universal truth |
| Core concepts | Literariness, defamiliarisation, motivation, story/plot, the dominant | Intentional fallacy, affective fallacy, paradox, irony, concrete universal, organic unity |

The crucial difference lies in the fourth row. For the Formalists the value of literature lies in its effect on perception; for New Criticism it lies in giving a truth that cannot be had in any other way. *The first is a relational, historical idea (the strange is strange relative to the familiar); the second is a substantial, transhistorical idea (universal truth resides in the work). This explains why the first leads smoothly to structuralism, while the second will become a target of deconstruction.*

**Legacy and later relations:**

- **Formalism → structuralism.** Jakobson went into exile in Prague and later met Claude Lévi-Strauss in New York; French structuralism shared a methodological interest with Formalist linguistics, treating the whole of culture as made up of the same operating rules as language (P3). Propp, a contemporary folklorist, analysed the sequence of functions in folk tales, the starting point of narratology (P4). Formalism also shaped poetics and stylistics (P4).
- **Formalism → Bakhtin.** Bakhtin shared the Formalists' attention to generic form but stressed the social and ideological character of literature, and extended analysis to uses of language outside literature such as carnival (P9).
- **New Criticism → the long legacy of close reading.** The religious and idealist values of New Criticism have ebbed, leaving close reading of texts and the analysis of the complex workings of literary language. It will reappear in three ways: deconstruction keeps the intensity of close reading but reverses its goal (New Criticism looks for unity beneath apparent disunity, deconstruction for disunity beneath apparent unity, P7); New Historicism applies close reading to non-literary texts (P10); and the new aestheticism reasserts the particularity of the text "after theory" (P17).
- **New Criticism → the bull's-eye for deconstruction.** New Criticism assumed that ideas belong to an ideal order distinct from the material, technical mechanisms of signification, and that poems can embody universal truths. Derrida will show that this is a version of the metaphysical "transcendental signified" (P7).
- **New Criticism → the bull's-eye for political criticism.** The political criticism of the 1970s argued that an exclusive concern with form is itself political: one can certainly study Donne's poems purely in terms of the structure of paradox, but that means ignoring the din of the English Civil War in the background (P9).

**Conclusion:** The two formalisms were the first to move the answer to "where does literary meaning come from?" away from author and world and into the organisation of language. But both confined that organisation within the single text or the single genre. The next question is: if meaning comes from language, how does language itself produce meaning? Saussure's answer will turn attention from the single text to the whole system that contains texts.

## P3 How Does Meaning Arise from a System of Differences? Structuralism

The two formalisms placed the source of meaning in the organisation of literary language, but neither asked how language itself produces meaning. `Structuralism` starts from that question. Forced into a single sentence, it says: **things cannot be understood in isolation; they have to be understood within the larger structures to which they belong.** And those structures are not entities objectively present in the outside world; they are imposed by the way we perceive the world and organise experience. Meaning, accordingly, is not a core or essence inside things but a property "given" to things by the human mind.

This is Layer 1 of the six-layer framework, and the methodological centre of the whole account of theory. It introduces the first of the mechanisms that run throughout, **the logic of relation and difference**. Lacan (P6), Derrida (P7), Foucault (P10, P13), and the analyses of binary oppositions of identity in feminism and race theory (P12–P15) all start from here; Saussure is explained once in full at this point, and later parts only refer back. Structuralism inherits from Russian Formalism both historically and logically: Jakobson is the bridge between them, and the scientific ambition of Formalism is realised in structuralism. The method was developed in France in the 1950s and 1960s by the anthropologist **Claude Lévi-Strauss** and the critic **Roland Barthes**, arrived in Britain in the 1970s, and in the 1980s achieved wide influence, and indeed notoriety, in Britain and America.

### Saussure's Three Propositions: Arbitrary, Relational, Constitutive

**Background:** Nineteenth-century linguistics was mainly historical: it traced the evolution of languages and their family relationships and speculated about the origin of language. The Swiss linguist **Ferdinand de Saussure** (1857–1913) turned instead to the patterns and functions of language in the present, asking how meaning is established and maintained. His *Course in General Linguistics*, compiled from his students' lecture notes, was published in 1916. In his own image, studying language historically is like cutting a plant stem lengthwise, which shows how the fibres run; studying it in the present is like cutting the stem crosswise, which shows how the fibres are arranged on a single plane, a relation that can never be seen in the lengthwise cut. The first is `diachronic` study, the second `synchronic`. The result is a view of the whole language system as an "implicit order": it is present unconsciously in any utterance, and particular utterances are only manifestations of the rules of the system.

**Definition: sign, signifier, signified.** Saussure begins by rejecting the idea of language as a list of names, each word corresponding to a thing it names. That idea presupposes that ideas exist before words, and assumes that linking a name to a thing is a simple operation. What the linguistic sign unites is not a thing and a name but a concept and a `sound-image`. The sound-image is not the physical sound but the psychological imprint the sound leaves on the senses (we can recite a poem to ourselves without moving our lips). Both are psychological, united in the brain by an associative bond. Saussure calls the whole the `sign`, the concept the `signified` and the sound-image the `signifier`:

```latex
\text{sign} = \frac{\text{signified (concept, e.g. "tree")}}{\text{signifier (sound-image, e.g. } arbor\text{)}}
```

The diagram means that the sign is a two-sided psychological entity, concept above and sound-image below, each calling up the other. Its effect is to exclude "things" from the object of linguistics: both sides of the sign are in the mind, and the referent lies outside the diagram. *This point matters enormously for later theory: Lacan will turn the fraction upside down and stress the "bar" between its terms (P6), and Derrida will ask whether the signified can really exist independently of the signifier (P7).*

**Proposition one: the sign is arbitrary.** The bond between signifier and signified is `arbitrary`. There is no inner connection between the idea "sister" and the French sound sequence *s-ö-r*; the same "ox" is *b-ö-f* on one side of a border and *o-k-s* on the other. "Arbitrary" does not mean that individuals can choose signifiers as they please (once a signifier is established in a linguistic community no individual has the power to change it); it means `unmotivated`, having no natural connection with the signified.

**Counter-examples and how they are handled:** Onomatopoeia seems to be a counter-example. But onomatopoeic words are few, and they are themselves conventional approximations (an English dog says *bow-wow*, a French one *oua-oua*). French *fouet* ("whip") and *glas* ("knell") sound highly suggestive, but their Latin sources mean "beech tree" and "trumpet call", and their present sound is an accident of phonetic change. Interjections are the same: the French cry of pain *aïe!* is *ouch!* in English. The principle of arbitrariness is not in itself new (Plato had stated it); what is new is the *emphasis* on it. If language as a sign system rests on arbitrariness, then language is not a reflection of the world and of experience but a system separate from the world. *Strictly speaking, this inference is the structuralists' extension of Saussure: Saussure himself was discussing the relation between signifier and signified, not the relation between language and world.* Saussure also stated a second principle, the `linearity` of the signifier: an auditory signifier unfolds only in time, its elements appearing one after another to form a chain. This looks obvious, but it is the basis of the axis of combination (see the section on Jakobson below).

**Proposition two: meaning is relational.** This is Saussure's most revolutionary argument, and at its core is a distinction between `value` and `signification`. Signification is the vertical relation inside the sign (signifier to signified); value is the horizontal relation between a sign and the other signs in the system. Cut a sheet of paper into pieces: the relation between the front and back of each piece is signification, the relation among the pieces is value. All values have two elements: a dissimilar thing for which it can be *exchanged*, and similar things with which it can be *compared*. The value of a five-franc coin depends both on how much bread it will buy and on how it compares with a one-franc coin or a dollar. A word likewise can be "exchanged" for an idea and compared with other words, and its content is truly fixed only in the second kind of relation.

**Evidence:** French *mouton* and English *sheep* can have the same signification but not the same value, because English uses *mutton* for the meat on the table: *sheep* has a second term beside it that French lacks. French *redouter* ("dread"), *craindre* ("fear") and *avoir peur* ("be afraid") limit each other; if *redouter* did not exist, all its content would pass to its competitors. The French plural and the Sanskrit plural differ in value even where their signification is the same, because Sanskrit has three numbers, singular, dual and plural. French uses *louer* for both "rent from" and "rent to", whereas German has two words, *mieten* and *vermieten*. Hebrew lacks the basic distinction between past, present and future; Slavic languages distinguish perfective and imperfective aspect. **If words stood for pre-existing concepts, they would have exact equivalents from one language to another; they do not.** The conclusion is that concepts are purely differential, defined not positively by their content but negatively by their relations with the other terms of the system.

The same principle applies to the material side of the sign. What matters in a word is not the sound itself but the phonic differences that distinguish it from other words. Phonemes are "opposing, relative and negative entities".
