A French speaker may pronounce *r* as a trilled tongue-tip *r* or even like the *ch* of German *Bach* without disturbing communication, because the French system only requires that it differ from other sounds; in German this would not do, because German treats the two sounds as distinct elements. Writing is the same: one person may write *t* in all sorts of ways, as long as it is not confused with *l* or *d*. "Arbitrary" and "differential" are related qualities: precisely because no sound is naturally suited to express a given concept, a fragment of language can ultimately rest only on its non-coincidence with the rest.

**Conclusion:** From this comes Saussure's most famous sentence: **"in language there are only differences without positive terms."** On the side of the signified and on the side of the signifier alike, language has neither ideas nor sounds that exist before the linguistic system, only conceptual and phonic differences arising from the system. The evidence is that the value of a word can change while its meaning and its sound stay the same, simply because a neighbouring word has changed. In another of his formulations: **language is a form, not a substance.**

**Example: the paradigmatic chain and the train.** A simple example makes the point concrete. English has a set of words related in function and meaning that can be substituted for one another in a sentence: hovel–shed–hut–house–mansion–palace. Remove any one and the meanings of the rest change. A hut and a shed are both small, rough buildings, but a hut is mainly for shelter and a shed mainly for storage; if one of them did not exist, the other would have to carry both meanings. The definition of *mansion* likewise depends on the words either side of it: larger and grander than a house, but not a palace. Pairs of opposites show it even more plainly: "male" largely means "not female", and without "night" there would be no concept of "day". Saussure's own example is the 8.25 express from Geneva to Paris. Every day the locomotive, carriages, driver and passengers are different, and when it runs late it does not even leave at 8.25, yet its identity stays the same, because that identity is entirely relational: it comes between the 7.25 and the 9.25. In the same way a street can be completely rebuilt and still be the same street, because it is not a purely material entity but is fixed by its position relative to other streets.

**Proposition three: language constitutes the world.** Meaning is given to objects by the human mind and is constructed and expressed through language; it is not already contained in things. The same person can be called a "terrorist" or a "freedom fighter"; there is no neutral option, only two descriptions, each of which "constructs" the person in some way. The local tax introduced by the Thatcher government was called the "poll tax" by its opponents (calling up the Middle Ages and the Peasants' Revolt) and the "community charge" by the government (avoiding the word "tax" and borrowing the good name of "community"). Which word a person used revealed their politics at once, and there was no neutral alternative. Colour words are similar: the spectrum is not divided into seven colours; they shade into one another, and we could just as well have had fourteen names. The four seasons too are a way of seeing the year, not an objective fact of nature. *This proposition is the theoretical source of the third shared idea of theory in P1, "language is constitutive".* Austin's `performative utterance` ("I hereby declare this bridge open") is an extreme case of the proposition: the utterance itself is the reality it refers to (P5).

**Extension: semiology.** Saussure imagined a "science that studies the life of signs within society", which he called `semiology`. Language is only one sign system among others, alongside writing, the sign language of the deaf, symbolic rites, forms of politeness and military signals, though it is the most important. This idea turned Saussure's model of language into a transferable model and opened the door to the structuralist analysis of culture.

### Langue and Parole: From the Single Utterance to the System That Contains It

**Definition:** Saussure saw that to make progress amid the profusion of linguistic phenomena one had to isolate a suitable object of study. He distinguished `langue` (language as a system) from `parole` (the concrete act of speaking). To separate them is to separate the social from the individual and the essential from the accidental. Langue is not a function of the speaker but a product the individual absorbs passively; it exists only by virtue of something like a contract among the members of a community, and no individual can create it or modify it alone. Parole is an individual act of will and intelligence. Learning English is not memorising a set of English sentences but mastering a set of rules and norms that make producing and understanding sentences possible; the linguist cares about sentences only as evidence of the underlying system.

**Mechanism: the gap between rule and behaviour.** Jonathan Culler points out that behind the langue/parole distinction lie two more general distinctions: between rules and behaviour, and between the functional and the non-functional. In physical phenomena, laws are simply direct generalisations of behaviour; in social and cultural phenomena, rules always stand at some distance from actual behaviour, **and that distance is precisely the space of meaning**. Suppose a club decrees that "members shall not step on cracks in the pavement". The rule does not necessarily determine behaviour, but it certainly determines meaning: a placing of the foot that meant nothing now means obedience or deviation, that is, an attitude towards the club and its authority. Behaviour can deviate from a norm often without denying that the norm exists: many promises are broken, yet the rule that promises should be kept remains. An observer who had never seen football could describe the players' movements objectively without grasping their meaning: one can kick a ball between two posts anywhere, but one can "score a goal" only within an institutional framework. Lévi-Strauss's formulation is that the concrete acts of individuals are never symbolic in themselves; they are elements out of which a symbolic system, necessarily collective, is built.

**Mechanism: synchronic and diachronic, the chess analogy.** Saussure used chess to explain the relation between a state of language and change in language. The value of a piece depends on its position on the board, just as the value of each term in a language depends on its opposition to other terms; and value also depends on a set of rules fixed before the game begins. Each move shifts only one piece but affects the whole system. From one state of equilibrium to the next, only the state itself matters: a spectator who arrives halfway through understands the present position no worse than one who has watched from the start. The analogy fails at only one point: the player moves pieces intentionally, whereas language premeditates nothing, and its changes are spontaneous and accidental. To make the analogy complete one would have to imagine an unconscious player, and this precisely proves that the synchronic and the diachronic must be kept apart.

**Application: the literary work as "parole".** Structuralists transferred the langue/parole distinction to literature. A single literary work (*Middlemarch*, say) is an act of literary parole, intelligible only within the larger structure (langue) of "the novel" as a genre and system of practices. Faced with Donne's "The Good Morrow", a structuralist's first move is not close reading but to identify the genre it imitates and subverts, the `alba` (the dawn song in which lovers lament their parting at daybreak, a form going back to the twelfth century); the alba in turn presupposes the idea of courtly love, and courtly love presupposes "poetry" as a conventional form of expression. Analysis of this kind takes the critic ever further from the text and into abstract questions of genre, history and philosophy, the exact opposite of the Anglo-American demand to get ever closer to the text. To use a crude image: if the structure containing the work is the "chicken" and the single work the "egg", **the structuralist cares most about the nature of the chicken, the liberal humanist about the details of the egg**. Structuralism thus reopened questions that the "Cambridge revolution" had suppressed for half a century: what does "literary" mean? How does narrative work? What is the structure of a poem? Traditional critics naturally did not welcome the suggestion that attention should turn from the egg to the chicken.

### Is Pure Difference Possible? The Limits of Relational Meaning

**Objection:** The critic Christopher Ricks made a simple and powerful rejoinder: there cannot be only differences; there must be differences *between things*. If this is accepted, the claim that "in language there are only differences without positive terms" needs revising. A similar objection can be made to the train example: the 8.25 has to be something like a train before it can be the 8.25. If a flock of pigeons flew out from under the station canopy, nobody would say "the 8.25 has gone"; a street's identity is largely relational, but a rope stretched between two streets would not be mistaken for a street. (On the other hand, the "train" that turns out on a Sunday to be a replacement bus because of engineering works shows that a "train" sometimes need not be a train after all.)

**Saussure's own qualification:** It is worth noticing that Saussure himself had left room for this objection. He said that the statement "everything in language is negative" holds only when signified and signifier are considered separately; as soon as the sign is considered as a whole, we have something *positive* in its own class. The pairing of a series of phonic differences with a series of conceptual differences is the only type of fact in the institution of language. When we compare two complete signs ("father" and "mother", say), we should no longer speak of "difference" but say that they are "distinct"; between them there is only `opposition`. The whole mechanism of language rests on such oppositions.

*This qualification is crucial. It is by relying on two points, that the sign as a whole is positive and that the system is ordered, that structuralism keeps meaning stable while acknowledging difference. When poststructuralists accuse structuralism of "failing to carry through its own view of language", they are in effect rejecting this qualification: pushing "difference" inside the whole sign, so that the signified itself becomes a signifier (P7). Ricks's objection stands on the same side as Saussure's qualification; Derrida stands on the other.*

### Myth, Kinship and Fashion: How Structuralism Read Culture as Language

**Premise:** Structuralists held that Saussure's model was transferable and could explain every signifying system. Culler sums up this conviction in two basic insights. First, social and cultural phenomena are not simply material objects or events but objects or events with meaning, and hence signs. Second, they have no essences but are defined by a network of internal and external relations. Put the stress on the first and you have semiotics; put it on the second and you have structuralism; but in practice the two cannot be separated. To study signs one has to study the system of relations that makes meaning possible, and only by treating items as signs can one decide which relations are relevant. So if human actions or products have meaning, there must be a system of distinctions and conventions that makes the meaning possible.

**Anthropology: Lévi-Strauss.** During the Second World War Lévi-Strauss met Jakobson, also in exile, in New York, and through him learned of Saussure's ideas. He began to see culture as a form of communication like language: what passes between the members of a culture are tokens, like words, that enact and reproduce the culture's basic assumptions and rules. Structure is like a skeleton and also like a genetic code: it is the principle of a cultural system's stability and coherence, and also the principle of action that lets a culture live in time. In *The Elementary Structures of Kinship* (1949) he argued that primitive cultures maintain peace between groups by treating women as tokens in marriage: intermarriage between families and tribes is a form of communication that creates kinship relations and lowers the chances of conflict. *This argument will be criticised from a feminist standpoint by Gayle Rubin and Luce Irigaray in P12.*

His study of myth found the same kind of fact as Propp's study of folk tales: a bewildering variety of myths tell the same core narratives, and those narratives tend to reconcile contradictions within the culture (for instance, between seeing human beings as creatures of cultivation and peace and seeing them as creatures of hunting and war). He did not read the Oedipus story on its own but set it within the whole cycle of myths connected with Thebes, looking for recurring motifs and contrasts and regrouping them into basic oppositions: animal/human, kin/stranger, husband/son. The various versions of the Oedipus myth all tell of a conflict between the belief that human beings are born from the earth (in many myths those born from the earth have difficulty walking, and "Oedipus" means "swollen foot", while the names of his father Laius and his grandfather Labdacus point to "left-sided" and "lame") and the fact that human beings are born of human beings (which is why the incest taboo is sacred). The function of myth is to offer a reconciliation of the contradiction between nature (sex) and culture (the incest taboo). Taking the linguistic "morpheme" as his model, he also proposed the smallest unit of mythic meaning, the `mytheme`, just as the morpheme is the smallest unit of grammatical meaning (like the past-tense *-ed* added to a verb).

**Semiology: Barthes's *Mythologies*.** In *Mythologies* (1957) Barthes examined France in the 1950s from the standpoint of a cultural anthropologist. His central concept defines `myth` as a `second-order semiological system`: what is a sign (the union of a concept and an image) in the first-order system becomes a mere signifier in the second.

```latex
\underbrace{\frac{\text{concept}}{\frac{\text{signified}_1}{\text{signifier}_1} = \text{meaning (form)}}}_{\text{myth level: signification}}
```

The diagram shows an ordinary sign on the lower level (signifier₁ + signified₁), whose whole is taken over by myth as a new signifier. Barthes calls this whole "meaning" at the level of language and "form" at the level of myth; he calls the signified of myth the "concept", and the relation between the two "signification". Language itself becomes the "object language", and myth is a "metalanguage" in which one speaks about the first. The structure matters because it explains the double function of myth: it points out and it notifies; it makes us understand something and it imposes it on us.

Barthes's two examples show this. A schoolboy reads in his Latin grammar "because my name is lion". The literal meaning of the sentence is simple, but its real signification here is "I am a grammatical example illustrating the rule of agreement of the predicate". The second example is more political. At the barber's, the cover of a copy of *Paris Match* shows a young Black man in French uniform saluting, his eyes uplifted, probably fixed on the tricolour. That is the "meaning" of the picture; but what it signifies to me is that France is a great empire, that all her sons, without colour discrimination, faithfully serve under her flag, and that there is no better answer to the detractors of an alleged colonialism than the zeal shown by this Black man in serving his so-called oppressors.

The short pieces in *Mythologies* apply this method to everyday objects that had never been subjected to intellectual analysis. In Mankiewicz's film *Julius Caesar*, every character wears a fringe over the forehead, whose function is to label "Romanness"; and every face sweats constantly (Vaseline), because sweating signifies inner moral struggle. These signs sit between two extremes: they want to be understood (which is laudable) and they pretend to be spontaneous (which is deceitful); they claim to be at once intentional and irrepressible, artificial and natural. Barthes draws from this an "ethics of signs": signs should either present themselves openly as intellectual, algebraic conventions (as when, in Chinese theatre, a flag stands for a regiment) or be rooted deep in each act of creation; signs that sit between the two make a degraded spectacle. Detergent advertising hides the abrasive function of detergent beneath attractive images of "depth" and "foam", while Persil and Omo are, at one level, exactly the same thing: both belong to the Anglo-Dutch company Unilever. The *Blue Guide* travel books know only "picturesque" mountains and gorges (a bourgeois myth combining nature worship with Puritanism), reduce Spaniards to "types", list only religious monuments and are vague about Franco's regime; they claim to help us see but have become "agents of blindness".

**Reading: *The Family of Man*.** A photographic exhibition brought from the United States to Paris set out to show the universality of everyday life around the world: birth, death, work, knowledge and play happen everywhere in the same way. The myth works in two steps. First it stresses the differences and exoticism of human forms; then from this pluralism it magically draws out a unity: people everywhere are born, work, laugh and die in the same way, the differences are only formal, and beneath them lies a common "nature". Barthes's judgement is that this rests on a very old mystification: **placing Nature at the bottom of History**. All classical humanism assumes that if we scratch a little at the relativity of human institutions and the surface diversity of skin colour, we reach the solid rock of a universal human nature. One might ask the parents of Emmett Till, the Black boy murdered by white men, what they think of "the great family of man". Birth and death are indeed natural facts, but once history is removed there is nothing to say about them; what matters is their historical modes, whether childbirth is easy or not, whether infant mortality is high or low. Work is an entirely historical fact, and to merge the colonial worker and the Western worker into a single gesture is unjust. A progressive humanism must reverse this mystification, constantly discovering history in nature and its "laws" and "limits", **and ultimately establishing nature itself as historical**.

*This is the first appearance of the analysis of "naturalising the historical", and it turns semiology into a critique of ideology. It strikes directly at "unchanging human nature" among the ten tenets of P1, and anticipates the theory of ideology in P9 and cultural studies in P11. The mechanism of essence ↔ construction acquires a concrete operation here: rereading as a sign whatever claims to be "natural".*

**More examples: wrestling and fashion.** Barthes also analysed the difference between boxing and wrestling. Boxing is about restraint and endurance: the boxer does not cry out when hit, the rules cannot be ignored, and the boxer fights as himself. The wrestler roars and postures, theatrically performing pain and triumph and playing larger-than-life villains and heroes. The two sports have different functions in society: boxing demonstrates the stoicism sometimes needed in life, wrestling dramatises the ultimate struggle between good and evil. Fashion too can be read like a language: single garments are combined into an "outfit" according to complex rules of combination (one does not wear evening dress with slippers); many fashions depend on breaking the rules on purpose, but the "statement" made by breaking them presupposes that the rules exist. A nice example: around 1994 fashion favoured exposed seams, crumpled fabric and ill-fitting garments, a style that happened to be called "deconstruction"; but take any one of those features out of the combination and it means only that you have put your jacket on inside out or don't care for ironing. **Each single item has its place in the overall structure, and the structure matters more than the item.**

### Metaphor and Metonymy: Jakobson's Two Poles of Language

**Problem:** Saussure explained how signs acquire value within a system, but how are signs organised in actual speech? Jakobson's answer is that all linguistic activity oscillates between two poles.

**Evidence: aphasia.** Jakobson pointed out that the various aphasias oscillate between two extreme types. One damages the capacity for `selection and substitution` (the `similarity disorder`, in which the patient cannot substitute one word for another); the other damages the capacity for `combination and contexture` (the `contiguity disorder`, in which the patient cannot maintain the hierarchical organisation of linguistic units). The first is cut off from `metaphor`, the second from `metonymy`. Discourse also develops along two semantic lines: one topic can lead to another through similarity (the metaphoric way) or through contiguity (the metonymic way). In normal verbal behaviour both processes are at work, but cultural patterns, personality and style lead to a preference for one or the other.

**Example: the "hut" test.** In a psychological test, children heard a noun and said the first response that came into their heads. To the stimulus word *hut*, some responses were complementary: "burnt out" (a purely narrative context), "is a poor little house". Others were substitutive: the synonyms *cabin* and *hovel*, the antonym *palace*, the metaphors *den* and *burrow*. Metonymic responses were *thatch*, *litter* and *poverty*. *This set of examples matches the paradigmatic chain hovel–palace above exactly: the substitutive responses move along what Saussure called the `paradigmatic axis` (items that can replace one another), the complementary and metonymic responses along the `syntagmatic axis` (items adjacent in the chain). Metaphor and metonymy are condensed expressions of these two axes at the level of rhetoric.*

**Application: literary history and art history.** In verbal art the interplay of the two poles is especially marked. In Russian lyric songs metaphoric constructions predominate; in the heroic epic the metonymic way prevails. That Romanticism and Symbolism are predominantly metaphoric is generally acknowledged; what has been less recognised is that it is the predominance of metonymy that underlies "realism", which lies between them. The realist author follows relations of contiguity, digressing from plot to atmosphere and from characters to their setting in space and time, and favours synecdochic detail: in the scene of Anna Karenina's suicide Tolstoy's attention is focused on her handbag; in *War and Peace* "hair on the upper lip" and "bare shoulders" stand for the female characters who possess them. This oscillation is not confined to verbal art. Cubist painting, which turns the object into a set of synecdoches, is metonymic; Surrealism is metaphoric. Film since Griffith broke with theatrical tradition through the metonymic arrangement of close-ups and set-ups, and Chaplin's films in turn replaced these with metaphoric montage ("filmic similes").

**Extension: dreams and magic.** Jakobson held that the competition between the two poles appears in every symbolic process. In the structure of dreams, the decisive question is whether symbols and temporal sequences are based on contiguity (Freud's metonymic "displacement" and synecdochic "condensation") or on similarity (Freud's "identification" and "symbolism"); Frazer's classification of magic into "homeopathic" magic, based on the law of similarity, and "contagious" magic, based on the law of contact, also corresponds to the two poles. *It is worth noting that Jakobson here places "condensation" on the side of contiguity, whereas Lacan, as P6 will explain, matches condensation with metaphor and displacement with metonymy. Both start from the same bipolar model yet map it differently, which shows that the fit between the model and Freud's concepts is not unique.*

**Reflection: why metonymy has been neglected.** The literature on metaphor is vast; that on metonymy is slight. There are two reasons. First, the researcher's tools are biased towards metaphor: the relation between metalanguage and object language is one of similarity, so metalanguage explains metaphor more readily than metonymy. Second, the objects of study push the same way: poetry focuses on the sign and is governed by similarity (the parallelism of metre, the phonic equivalence of rhyme), practical prose focuses on the referent, and traditionally only the figures of poetry were treated as objects of study.

### Five Codes and Binary Oppositions: The Procedure of Structuralist Reading

**Operations:** Structuralist critics mainly analysed prose narrative, relating the text to some larger containing structure: the conventions of a literary genre, a network of intertextual connections, a hypothesised universal deep structure of narrative, or a complex of recurring patterns and motifs. They also explained literature by analogy with linguistic structures (the mytheme as morpheme, for example), and applied the idea of systematic patterning to the whole of Western culture and even across cultures, treating everything from Greek myth to brands of washing powder as "sign systems".

**Model: Barthes's five codes.** In *S/Z* (1970) Barthes devoted two hundred pages to Balzac's thirty-page story *Sarrasine*, cutting it into 561 `lexias` (units of reading) and classifying them by means of five codes. These five codes were taken as the basic underlying structure of all narrative, just as the grammatical structure of a language generates all its possible sentences:

1. The `proairetic code`: indicates actions ("the ship sailed at midnight").
2. The `hermeneutic code` (also called the code of enigmas): poses questions or puzzles and creates suspense ("he knocked on a certain door near the Rue de Peyrolles": who lives there?).
3. The `cultural code`: points to things outside the text that are regarded as common knowledge ("Agent Angelis was the kind of man who sometimes went to work in odd socks", calling up a stereotype of clumsy incompetence).
4. The `semic code` (also called the connotative code): linked to theme; when organised around a proper name it constitutes "character".
5. The `symbolic code`: also linked to theme, but on a larger scale, made up of the most basic binary oppositions: male/female, night/day, good/evil, art/life. Structuralists held that these oppositions are the fundamental way human beings perceive and organise reality.

**Qualification:** There is a difficulty in treating *S/Z* as a structuralist text: by 1970 Barthes was already in his poststructuralist phase (usually dated from "The Death of the Author" in 1968). It is still regarded as structuralist because it tries to reduce the infinite complexity of the story to the operation of five codes, however playful that attempt may be. More exactly, it straddles the border between the two: the 561 lexias and five codes belong to the "high structuralism" of the 1966 "Introduction to the Structural Analysis of Narratives", while the 93 digressive commentaries scattered among them anticipate the poststructuralism of *The Pleasure of the Text* (1973).

**Reading: "The Oval Portrait" and the symbolic code.** The most basic difference between structuralist and liberal humanist reading is that the former puts comment on structure, symbol and design first, and greatly reduces the emphasis on broad moral significance, and even on interpretation itself. Instead of going straight to content, the structuralist presents a series of parallels, echoes, reflections, contrasts and patterns, schematising the narrative heavily into a kind of "linguistic diagram". What to look for, and where, is roughly this:

| What to look for | Where to look |
| --- | --- |
| Parallels, echoes, reflections/repetitions, contrasts, patterns | Plot, structure, character/motivation, situation/circumstance, language/imagery |

Poe's story itself has a binary structure: the first half is a first-person framing narrative by a wounded officer; the second is the story within the story that he reads in a description of the portrait. The two halves move at very different narrative speeds. The first is leisurely, even sluggish, reflecting the officer's practical, rational mind; the second advances at an increasingly fragmented pace, reflecting the frenzy of artistic creation and the rapid decline of the model's health. The chateau has opposite functions in the two halves: for the officer it is a place of refuge and recovery, for the model a place of danger and destruction. Each half contains a relationship of unequal power (officer and servant, painter and wife), but with different effects. Within the second half, the husband's self-absorbed creative frenzy contrasts with the outgoing passion expected of a new husband: he "already had a bride in his Art"; the marriage is in a sense bigamous, and the weeks spent alone with his bride painting her are a sustained inverted parody of a honeymoon.

A third level of contrast concerns the narrative mechanism. Both narrators are anonymous, and the second half is anonymous throughout (the only named character is the least important, the servant). Barthes encouraged structuralists to ask of a text "who is speaking?" (*qui parle?*), and putting this question to the second half pushes the narrator out of the position of a neutral recorder: the description must come from someone who witnessed everything without intervening. The narrator of the first half may not be innocent either: his long gaze at the portrait parallels the painter's gaze at his wife. There are two intense male gazes in the story, and each has a moment in which the eyes are averted.

All these contrasts are specific to this story. The next simplifying move is like finding the lowest common denominator of a set of numbers: reducing them to more general oppositions, life/art, male/female, light/dark (meaning both physical light and enlightenment versus moral obscurity), seeing/doing, reality/representation. The structuralist argument is that **narrative structure is built on deep oppositions of this kind; they are the skeleton on which all the flesh of narrative hangs**. If only one pair could be kept, it would be art/life. On which side, then, does the story stand? It stands on the side of art: what is described most vividly and passionately is the act of artistic creation, and after it the act of looking at a work of art, not the waste of a young life. The story is "officially" a pious protest against the sacrifice of a young life, but in fact it describes that sacrifice with a loving envy. In D. H. Lawrence's words: **never trust the artist, trust the tale.**

*Compare the liberal humanist reading in P1. Both seize on the opposition of art and life, but by opposite routes and to opposite conclusions. The Leavisite reading starts from moral conviction and finds that the story condemns "art for art's sake"; the structuralist reading starts from the formal patterns of the text and finds that the story structurally favours art, even contradicting the morality it professes. The second discovery, that what a text says and what it does are at odds, already moves quietly towards the temper of deconstruction in P7, although the structuralist is still looking for unifying patterns.*

**Reading: the semic code as a "cloze" exercise.** The semic code works through fine shades of individual words and phrases, and the best way to feel it is the "cloze" exercise used in teaching: delete words from a text and have readers infer from context and overall structure what should go in. The opening of Mervyn Jones's novel *Mr Armitage Isn't Back Yet* presents its hero, Armitage. His weight is given to the "ounce" rather than the "pound", suggesting a man who keeps his life precise and orderly. His watch is "Swiss"; make it a multi-function digital watch, a trendy Swatch, a fob watch or a Mickey Mouse watch and he becomes a gadget freak, a follower of fashion, an old fogey or a joker. The smell of leather in his new car is "luxurious"; make it "sweet", "intoxicating" or "sexy" and he is almost a leather fetishist; "rich" would suggest that his pleasure rises with the price. When the hitch-hiking boy hesitates, he is "puzzled" (suggesting the dignity of a respectable man affronted), not "baffled" or "stunned". The girl smiles "pleasantly"; if she smiled "seductively", his motives would be entirely sexual. She "slid" into the front seat, while the boy merely "got into" the back; swap the two phrases and Armitage is constructed as gay, although the text never says so. The same opening shows the other codes at work too: the hermeneutic code raises questions such as "what will this meeting lead to?" and "are the hitch-hikers as harmless as they seem?"; "he was the kind of man who never kept a car more than a year" appeals to the cultural code, calling up the reader's existing picture of such a man.

### Discourse and Episteme: How Foucault Set Out from Structuralism

**Background:** By the mid-1960s structuralism was the dominant school in French thought, its influence visible in the historian **Michel Foucault**, the psychoanalyst Lacan, the critic Kristeva and the philosopher Althusser. Foucault's works of this period include *The Order of Things* (1966) and *The Archaeology of Knowledge* (1969). They are structuralist in two senses: they move the traditional human knowing subject from the centre of the stage, and they hold that language plays a constitutive role in knowledge.

**Definition: episteme and discursive formation.** Foucault's first important concept is the `episteme`: the conceptual framework through which a period understands the world. Words give us maps for assigning order to nature and society; what counts as knowledge changes over time, and the place of language in knowledge changes with it. In one period the world is seen as a field of analogies between levels; in a later period it is broken down into discrete parts and organised into classificatory tables. His second concept is `discourse` and the `discursive formation`: a coherent set of assumptions and linguistic practices that applies to a field of knowledge, or expresses the beliefs of a social group, or formulates rules and ideals for some kind of behaviour. Modern science is a discursive formation: it has not only a series of discoveries and a body of knowledge but also accepted linguistic forms for describing its methods and findings. When feminists speak of "the discourse of patriarchy", and analyse the discourse of the conduct books that taught women before the modern era how to be "proper", that is "chaste, silent and obedient", they are using this concept (P12).

**Mechanism: physical reality translated into discursive reality.** Many of a culture's assumptions are maintained by linguistic practices that serve both as instruments for knowing the world and as instruments for constructing it. The dominant discourse in the United States gives individual "freedom" enormous privilege; but the material reality of modern life is subject to all kinds of complex constraints (laws allowing the police to search cars without cause, an economic system that requires a great deal of time to be spent working under others' control), and this institutional reality is discursively rendered as "freedom" in the American lexicon. Just as not all women were chaste, silent and obedient, most Americans do not enjoy the pure freedom the dominant word implies. **Knowledge and perception always take place through the mediation of language; unless we can somehow assign order to the world in language, we can know nothing.**

**Method: suspending ready-made unities.** *The Archaeology of Knowledge* first demands a negative task: clearing away every notion that manufactures continuity amid change. "Tradition" reconceives the dispersion of history as forms of the same; "influence" provides an all-too-magical support for transmission and communication; "development" and "evolution" assign scattered events to a single organising principle; "spirit" establishes a community of meaning among the phenomena of a period. Even the divisions between science, literature, philosophy, religion and history should be questioned: "literature" and "politics" are recent categories, and applied to medieval culture they are only retrospective hypotheses. The unities most in need of suspension are the most immediate ones, "the book" and "the oeuvre". The boundaries of a book are never clear: it reaches beyond its title, its first line and its final full stop, caught up in a system of references to other books, other texts, other sentences. **It is a node within a network.**

Once these unities are suspended, what is released is the totality of all actual statements, existing dispersed as events. Describing them differs from linguistic analysis: linguistic analysis asks "according to what rules was this statement constructed?", whereas a statement is always an event, which neither language (*langue*) nor meaning can exhaust. It also differs from the history of ideas, which tries to rediscover behind statements the intention of the speaking subject and his unconscious activity, and to reconstruct "what was being said in what was said". **Discourse analysis does not look beneath what is manifest for the half-silent murmur of another discourse**; it asks why this statement could only be as it is, in what ways it excludes other statements, and how it occupies a place that no other statement could occupy.

When a system of dispersion can be described among a number of statements, and a regularity (an order, correlations, positions, functionings, transformations) can be defined among objects, types of statement, concepts and thematic choices, one speaks of a discursive formation; the conditions to which these elements are subject are called the `rules of formation`. Take psychopathology. Discourse analysis does not try to find out who was mad in a given period or what madness itself is (that would be a "history of the referent"), nor to analyse the meanings of words like "melancholia" or "madness without delirium" (that would be lexical semantics), but to discover how crime became an object of medical expertise and how sexual deviation became a possible object of psychiatric discourse. Discourse is not "a mere intersection of words and things" but a set of practices that systematically form the objects of which they speak.

**Relation and distinction:** Foucault shares two things with structuralism: he denies that authorial intention and psychological synthesis are principles of explanation, and he looks for rules beyond individual control. But his object is not a Saussurean timeless language system; it is statements and practices as events in history, interconnected with technical, economic, social and political events. *Note too that Foucault here explicitly rejects the second of the mechanisms that run throughout, the "manifest/latent" double reading. Psychoanalysis, Marxism and deconstruction all look for repressed meaning beneath the surface; Foucault insists on staying at the level of discourse itself. This difference will reappear in P10 as the divergence between New Historicism and cultural materialism.* Foucault later examined the disciplinary institutions of society from the Middle Ages to modernity in *Discipline and Punish* (1975) (P10), and in *The History of Sexuality* (1976) how different discourses of the body shape sexuality (P13).

**Conclusion:** Structuralism moved the source of meaning from the single text to systems of difference: language, genre, myth, code, discourse. From linguistics it inherited a confident scientific temper, a belief that method, system and reason can establish reliable knowledge; language may construct reality, but it is an ordered system, and recognising this need not lead to despair. Structuralism's two technical offshoots, narratology and stylistics, will turn this confidence into working tools in P4; and when later thinkers ask "if difference has no fixed end-point, can the system still be ordered?", the confidence will collapse in P7.

## P4 How Are Stories Told? Narratology and Stylistics

By the end of P3 structuralism had put forward a general claim: meaning comes from systems of difference, and the individual work is an act of "parole", intelligible only within genres and conventions that function as "langue". The next question is whether this claim can be turned into working tools. If every narrative is built from a limited set of elements combined according to rules, what are those elements and rules? If literary language, like any other language, is made of describable structures, can linguistics supply evidence for literary interpretation? `Narratology` answers the first question, `stylistics` the second.

In the six-layer framework, narratology and stylistics still belong to Layer 1, how texts signify, and they are its most technical part. They inherit three things: from P2, the Russian Formalist distinction between story and plot, together with its scientific ambition; from P3, Saussure's langue/parole model and Barthes's five codes; and, also from P3, Jakobson's poetics, one of the sources of stylistics. The logic of relation and difference appears here as the search for "recurring structures": the narratologist is interested not in this story but in "story" as such, and the meaning of a narrative act, like a Saussurean sign, is determined by its position in a sequence. The road ends at a crack: both narratology and stylistics finally require the reader to make inferences that linguistic structure itself cannot guarantee, and this hands the problem on to P5.

### From Aristotle to Propp: The Deep Content and Surface Functions of Narrative

**Definition: narratology, story and plot.** Narratology is the study of narrative structure: how narrative produces meaning, and what basic mechanisms and procedures are common to all acts of storytelling. It is a branch of structuralism that has gained a degree of independence; rather than reading and interpreting individual stories, it tries to study "story" itself as a concept and a cultural practice. A restaurant menu makes a good way in. The menu does not say "fish and chips" but "fresh-caught, succulent North Sea cod in a light golden batter, served with a generous portion of delicious chips". The catering trade calls such descriptions "narratives", and, worried that customers will take them literally and complain that the batter was brown rather than golden, adds a note at the foot of the menu: "Narratives are for descriptive purposes only and are not to be taken literally." The distinction between the actual meal and the narrative about it is roughly the basic distinction of narratology. The `story` is the actual sequence of events, which has to begin at the beginning, proceed in chronological order and leave nothing out. The `plot` is the same events edited, ordered, packaged and presented as a narrative: it may start in the middle of the chain of events and then go back to fill in what came before, or flash forward to hint at what comes after. The plot is a version of the story and, like the description on the menu, is not to be taken literally.

The distinction has several sets of terms, each school preferring its own: the Russian Formalists' *fabula/syuzhet* (P2), North American narratology's *story/discourse*, Genette's *histoire/récit*; all name the same distinction. The North American use of *discourse* in place of "plot" has a rationale: the issue is not just plot in the narrow sense but all the "packaging" of style, point of view, pacing and so on that produces the overall effect. *Below, "story/plot" is used throughout; where "discourse" appears in connection with Chatman, it refers specifically to the expressive plane of narrative and is not the same concept as Foucault's "discourse" in P3.*

**Model: Aristotle's three elements.** A short history of narratology can be organised around three figures. The first is Aristotle. The *Poetics* identifies "character" and "action" as the basic elements of story and holds that character must be revealed through action, that is, through plot (P1 has already listed him as a source of the text-led tradition). He names three key elements of plot: `hamartia`, the sin or error, which in tragedy often springs from what was later called a "tragic flaw", a fatal defect of character; `anagnorisis`, the moment of recognition in which the hero perceives the truth, often the truth about himself; and `peripeteia`, the reversal of fortune, which in classical tragedy is usually the hero's fall from a height. Aristotle does what all narratologists do: he looks at many different stories (in his case Greek tragedies) and asks what elements they have in common, just as a chemist sees that mountains, lakes and volcanoes are all made of the same limited set of chemical elements. In both cases the skill lies in a trained eye that can see the similarities and uniformities beneath the differences.

**Example: the Brekkies cartoon.** Even the simplest narrative material shows traces of Aristotle's elements. A cartoon on a packet of the British cat food Brekkies is a complete little story. Aristotle concentrates all three elements in the hero, but here they are distributed among different characters; using a theory need not mean following the "manufacturer's instructions" slavishly, and doing it this way anticipates Propp's method. The hamartia is the cat leaving dirty paw prints on the tablecloth, which draws a rebuke ("Oh, Bob, don't!") and brings a peripeteia: the cat falls from favour, a fall marked by its literal descent from the table to the floor. At tea, the visiting aunt is delighted to notice that the replacement tablecloth is the one she gave her niece as a present. She does not know that this tablecloth was not her niece's first choice, but we do, because we occupy the privileged position of having witnessed the whole sequence of events. Here we can see that **the key to storytelling lies not in giving information but in withholding it**: the reader often knows what characters do not, and vice versa, and the narrator holds things back from both. The core mechanism of story is delay, more exactly the delay of information; the Victorian novelist Wilkie Collins said the formula for a successful novel was "make 'em laugh, make 'em cry, make 'em wait". *(This is the same mechanism as Barthes's hermeneutic code in P3, described in another way.)* The anagnorisis is the cat's owner's guilt, off the page: she realises she nearly missed the chance to show gratitude and good manners by using her guest's present when the guest came to tea. This brings a second peripeteia: the cat regains favour, a rise from low to high rather than a fall, marked by the thought bubble "Thank you, Bob", the cat's smug look, and its literal elevation onto the niece's lap.

**Distinction: deep content.** Aristotle's three categories concern, in essence, the underlying theme and moral purpose of a story, and might be called "deep content", because all of them involve "internal events": a moral flaw, the *recognition* of its existence, the *consequences* of its existence. They are easy to discern beneath many narratives and are the generative force of a narrative's moral impact, like psychological "raw ingredients" that are "cooked" into a particular narrative "dish". But actual plots vary endlessly, and describing them needs a different system, one that offers more possible actions and works at a level closer to the surface of the narrative.

**Model: Propp's functions.** The second figure is **Vladimir Propp** (1895–1970; P3 has already mentioned him as a forerunner of Lévi-Strauss). He belonged to neither of the Russian Formalist groups but wrote within the same current of thought that sought to make literary study scientific, and was one of the first structuralists: he tried to map an inner order across a body of texts of many different shapes. *Morphology of the Folktale* was published in Russia in 1928. "Morphology" means "the study of forms", and the book deals only with the structure and plot composition of the tales, not with their history or social meaning. By then the Soviet climate had turned against "formalist" studies of this kind, and the book was forgotten until the 1950s, when structuralists, especially Lévi-Strauss, rediscovered it and used it in their own work on myth; an English translation appeared in 1958.

Propp's method begins with comparison. Compare these events: a tsar gives the hero an eagle, which carries the hero away to another kingdom; an old man gives Sučenko a horse, which carries Sučenko away to another kingdom; a sorcerer gives Ivan a little boat, which takes Ivan to another kingdom; a princess gives Ivan a ring, and young men appearing out of the ring carry Ivan away to another kingdom. There are constants and variables: the names and attributes of the characters change, but their actions, or functions, do not. Baba Jaga, Morozko, a bear, a forest spirit and a mare's head all test and reward the stepdaughter. Tales can therefore be studied according to *the functions of their characters*: what a character "does" is the important question, while "who does it" and "how" are matters of secondary study. The number of functions is extremely small and the number of characters extremely large, which explains the double quality of the tale: on one hand its amazing multiformity, picturesqueness and colour, on the other its no less striking uniformity and repetition.

**Definition: a function is an act of a character, defined from the point of view of its significance for the course of the action.** The definition makes two demands: it must not depend on the character who performs the function (functions are usually named by nouns expressing action, such as "interdiction", "interrogation", "flight"); and it cannot be separated from the act's position in the course of the narration. Ivan marrying a tsar's daughter and a father marrying a widow with two daughters are entirely different things. A hero receiving a hundred roubles from his father and then buying a wise cat with it, and a hero receiving a sum of money as a reward for bravery (at which point the tale ends), are morphologically different elements, even though the act (a transfer of money) is the same. The same act can have different meanings, and vice versa. *This is the narratological version of Saussure's concept of "value" (P3): the meaning of an act is determined not by its "positive content" but by its position and relations in a sequence.*

Propp stated his observations as four theses: (1) the functions of characters are the stable, constant elements of a tale, independent of who fulfils them and how, and form its fundamental components; (2) the number of functions known to the fairy tale is limited; (3) the sequence of functions is always identical; (4) all fairy tales are of one type as regards their structure. The third thesis directly answers Veselovsky and Shklovsky (P2), who held that the order of motifs was accidental, citing as evidence the fact that what witnesses most distort in their testimony is the sequence of events. Propp replied that if witnesses distort the sequence of events their accounts are meaningless; the sequence of events has its own laws: **theft cannot take place before the door is forced**. *This disagreement within Formalism deserves notice: Shklovsky stressed the free combination of devices, Propp the necessity of sequence, and the latter is closer to structuralism's later search for "deep structure".*

From a corpus of a hundred tales Propp concluded that every tale is made up of items selected from a basic stock of thirty-one `functions` (possible actions):

1. One of the members of a family absents himself from home.
2. An interdiction is addressed to the hero.
3. The interdiction is violated.
4. The villain makes an attempt at reconnaissance.
5. The villain receives information about his victim.
6. The villain attempts to deceive his victim in order to take possession of him or of his belongings.
7. The victim submits to deception and thereby unwittingly helps his enemy.
8. The villain causes harm or injury to a member of a family; or (8a) one member of a family either lacks something or desires to have something.
9. Misfortune or lack is made known; the hero is approached with a request or command; he is allowed to go or he is dispatched.
10. The seeker (the hero in "quester" mode) agrees to or decides upon counteraction.
11. The hero leaves home.
12. The hero is tested, interrogated, attacked and so on, which prepares the way for his receiving a magical agent or helper.
13. The hero reacts to the actions of the future donor.
14. The hero acquires the use of a magical agent (an object, an animal and so on).
15. The hero is transferred, delivered or led to the whereabouts of an object of search.
16. The hero and the villain join in direct combat.
17. The hero is branded.
18. The villain is defeated.
19. The initial misfortune or lack is liquidated.
20. The hero returns.
21. The hero is pursued.
22. The hero is rescued from pursuit.
23. The hero, unrecognised, arrives home or in another country.
24. A false hero presents unfounded claims.
25. A difficult task is proposed to the hero.
26. The task is resolved.
27. The hero is recognised.
28. The false hero or villain is exposed.
29. The hero is given a new appearance.
30. The villain is punished.
31. The hero is married and ascends the throne.

No tale contains all thirty-one; each selects some of them, and the functions always appear in the order listed. A tale might, for example, be made up of 5, 7, 14, 18, 30 and 31: the villain receives information about the hero (the victim) (5) and deceives him (7); the hero gets help from a magical animal (14), defeats the villain (18), who is punished (30), and then marries and becomes king (31). But there will be no formula in which 30 comes before 18, since the villain cannot be punished before he has been defeated. The point of the analysis is to show that beneath the "amazing multiformity" of the tales there is an "equally amazing uniformity": they are different dishes cooked from the same set of ingredients.

**Objection: functions counted twice.** Compared with Aristotle, Propp looks at stories at a (literally) more "superficial" level, and since there are more possible kinds of surface event than of underlying motive, he has more variables to work with. Yet a little scrutiny of the list of functions reveals a problem. Functions 6 and 7 are two functions concerning the villain's deception of the victim (the hero), but they involve only *one* action: deception takes two parties, and the deceiver deceiving and the deceived being deceived are the same event seen from different points of view. Nor are 10 and 11 two events: in the first the hero decides to do something, in the second he does it.

**Model: seven spheres of action.** The description of the thirty-one functions and their variants takes up nearly half of Propp's book, while character types get four pages in chapter 6: for Propp, characters are mainly a mechanism for distributing functions through the tale. The functions fall naturally into "spheres" (pursuit, capture and punishment naturally go together, for instance), so the seven `spheres of action` are best seen as *roles* rather than *characters*. This reflects the subordination of character to action, a subordination that also exists in Aristotle's narratology:

1. The villain
2. The donor (provider)
3. The helper
4. The princess (a sought-for person) and her father
5. The dispatcher
6. The hero (seeker or victim)
7. The false hero

With the thirty-one functions and the seven spheres of action, the plot of any folk tale in the whole Russian corpus can be generated, just as mastering the grammar, syntax and vocabulary of English (langue, in Saussure's sense) enables one to generate any possible English utterance (parole).

**Mechanism: merged roles and the realist novel.** Folk tales are relatively simple, but Robert Scholes points out that the flexibility of schemes like this is much increased because one character can play more than one role in a tale (the villain who is also the false hero, the donor who is also the dispatcher), and one role can be taken by several characters (multiple villains); these roles are all the roles a narrative of this kind needs, and they underlie many novels that are otherwise far from the fairy tale. This possible overlap opens Propp's method out from simple material and begins to suggest the complexity of character and motive in the psychological realist novel. In the realist novel the subordination of character to action is reversed, and roles cannot simply be divided into "hero" and "villain": Henry James said he wrote not about good and evil but about "good-and-evil", and in a James story someone trying to help may unwittingly become an obstacle, and may not be sure which he "really" is. Propp's method thus suggests that the simple archetypes of more basic narrative material can be the shadowy deep foundations of complex realist novels: the Cinderella archetype, found in some form in cultures all over the world, lies buried beneath *Mansfield Park* and *Jane Eyre*. *(These two novels will be reread in P15 and P12 respectively, and what they reveal there will no longer be an archetype but structures of empire and gender.)*

**Limitation:** Propp's system lacks everything to do with how narrative is *presented*: point of view, style, pacing. That is the territory of the third figure in the history of narratology.

### Genette's Six Questions: A Grammar of Telling Itself

**Problem:** Aristotle and Propp are both concerned with what is told, the first with deep theme, the second with surface plot; what Propp's system lacks is how narrative is *presented*: perspective, style, pacing. **Gérard Genette**, one of the most prominent narratologists after Barthes, moved the focus in *Narrative Discourse* from the story itself to the process of telling. The categories he discusses can be organised as six basic questions about the act of narration:

1. Is the basic mode of narration "mimetic" or "diegetic"?
2. How is the narrative focalised?
3. Who tells the story?
4. How is time handled in the story?
5. How is the story "packaged"?
6. How are speech and thought represented?

The first five questions are discussed in turn below; the sixth is inseparable from Chatman's theory of narrative transmission and is left until the structure of narrative transmission is discussed.

**Mimesis and diegesis.** `Mimesis` means "showing" or "dramatising": presenting things as a "scene", with a specific setting and dialogue in direct speech. It is a "slow telling" that "stages" what is done and said, creating the illusion that we are seeing and hearing it for ourselves. `Diegesis` means "telling" or "recounting": giving necessary or linking information as efficiently as possible, in a faster, panoramic, summarising way, with no attempt to create the illusion that events are happening before our eyes; the narrator just says what happened rather than showing it as it happens. In actual writing the two alternate, the writer moving between them for strategic reasons: a wholly mimetic novel would be infinitely long, a wholly diegetic one only a few pages long and read like a plot summary. There are "single-scene" short stories written almost entirely in mimetic mode, such as Hemingway's "Hills Like White Elephants": an American man and woman wait for a train at a remote Spanish station, and the words and actions of their waiting reveal a crisis in their relationship; we see only what they do and hear only what they say, nothing more. Novels usually need a *mix* of the two, and "slides" between them:

> For five years Mario walked the same way to work every morning, but he never saw Thelma again. Then one morning, as he came out of the Underground station and began to walk up Charing Cross Road, something very strange happened. It was a bright, sunny day…

The first sentence is diegesis: a rapid summary of a long series of "offstage" events, without passages of which the plot could not be moved on efficiently. The rest is mimesis: after the "fast forward", the author slows down at the next key "scene", giving the weather and the precise location so that we "see" it in our minds. The two need each other and often work together so closely that the seam is hard to locate exactly. *In Chatman this distinction will cross with "process/stasis" and expand into four kinds of narrative statement.*

**Focalisation.** `Focalisation` means the angle or perspective from which a story is told. In `external focalisation` the point of view lies outside the characters depicted and tells us only what can be observed: what characters say and do, what could be seen and heard by someone present. In `internal focalisation` the focus is on what characters think and feel, which could not be known even by someone present. "Thelma got up and called out to Mario" is external focalisation; "Thelma suddenly worried that Mario wouldn't see her and would walk past, unaware, on the other side of Charing Cross Road" is internal focalisation, revealing thoughts that someone standing beside her could not have detected. If a story is mainly focalised through Thelma in this way, she is its `focaliser` (another tradition calls this a "reflector"): she does not tell her own story in the first person, but the reader receives events from her "point of view". Elizabeth Bennet is the focaliser of *Pride and Prejudice*. Sometimes a novelist moves freely in and out of the minds and feelings of several characters, as if knowing everyone's thoughts and feelings; this is `zero focalisation`, which Gerald Prince aptly defines as narration in which "no systematic conceptual or perceptual constraints govern what may be presented". It is characteristic of "traditional" or "classic" narration and is more often called "omniscient narration".

**Who tells.** The author, of course, but not necessarily in the author's own voice or person. One kind of narrator (often going with zero focalisation) is not identified as a separate character with a name and a personal history; it is simply a voice or tone, a "medium of telling" that aims at neutrality and transparency, and can be called a *covert*, *effaced*, *non-intrusive* or *undramatised* narrator. It is not quite accurate to say that this is the author speaking to us directly: authors adopt this tone, pace and level of detail only when narrating fiction, and if we met the author at a party or in a pub talking in this style we could not stand it for more than a few minutes. It is better, then, to regard this disembodied narrator as an "authorial persona" rather than the author. Another kind of narrator is identified as a separate character with a name, a personal history, a gender, a class position, likes and dislikes, who witnessed, heard about or took part in the events narrated; such narrators can be called *overt*, *dramatised* or *intrusive*, like Lockwood in *Wuthering Heights*, Marlow in *Heart of Darkness* or Nick Carraway in *The Great Gatsby*. Of these, the `heterodiegetic` narrator (roughly, "telling of others") is not a character in the story told, like Lockwood; the `homodiegetic` narrator (roughly, "telling of the same") appears as a character in his or her own story, like Jane Eyre. First-person narrators can be heterodiegetic or homodiegetic, since they may be telling someone else's story; omniscient narrators are necessarily heterodiegetic.

**Time.** Narratives often refer backwards and forwards, so that the order of telling does not correspond to the order of happening. A section that goes back to past events is called an `analepsis` (literally "taking back"), one that anticipates future events a `prolepsis` ("taking forward"). In Lawrence's story "The Prussian Officer", a bottle of wine knocked over while a meal is being served hints at the bloodshed that ends the story; the cask of red wine spilt in the street at the start of Dickens's *A Tale of Two Cities* foreshadows the bloodshed the Revolution will bring. These proleptic details show, somewhat crudely, that analepsis and prolepsis are often important in establishing and foregrounding "theme". The beginning is seldom the best place to begin: stories tend to start in the middle (what classical theorists called *in medias res*), using analepsis to sketch what came before and prolepsis to hint at the ending, so drawing the reader in and generating basic narrative momentum. *This is the technical working-out, along the dimension of time, of the story/plot distinction in P2.*

**Packaging: frames and embedding.** Stories are not always presented "directly". A `frame narrative` (also called the "primary narrative") contains an `embedded narrative` (the "secondary narrative"). "Primary" only means that it comes first, not that it is the main one: the main story is usually the secondary narrative. In Henry James's *The Turn of the Screw*, the main story is embedded in a frame in which a group of people sit round the fire in a country house at Christmas telling ghost stories; the story told by one of the guests makes up the body of the novel and is much longer. In Conrad's *Heart of Darkness*, the main story is embedded in a frame in which a group of former merchant seamen tell "yarns" while waiting for the tide to turn. Genette calls embedded narratives "narratives within narratives" (*meta-narratives*), like the tales embedded in the pilgrimage frame of *The Canterbury Tales*. *To avoid confusion with Lyotard's "metanarratives" (grand narratives) in P8, the term "meta-narrative" is not used here; such stories are called "embedded narratives" throughout.*

Frames can be further divided into three kinds: single-ended, double-ended and intrusive. A `single-ended frame` does not return to the framing situation once the embedded story is over: after the story of the governess and the children, *The Turn of the Screw* does not go back to the listeners' reactions by the fire. There are good strategic reasons for this, since once we were back by the fire many of the crucial ambiguities on which the story depends would have to be explained or argued over. A `double-ended frame` reintroduces the framing situation when the embedded story ends: *Heart of Darkness* returns briefly to Marlow's listeners after his story is over. Conrad makes no attempt to "resolve" or illuminate the story's huge moral dilemmas, simply bringing back the imagery that runs through the whole (half-light and the surrounding darkness), using the double-ended frame to reinforce the theme. An `intrusive frame` interrupts the embedded story from time to time to return to the framing situation. In *Heart of Darkness* Marlow breaks off to say, famously, "Of course … you fellows see more than I could then. You see me, whom you know…". This reminds us that all telling is limited by point of view, and shows Conrad's dislike of the traditional narrative stance of zero focalisation: he deliberately chose a narrator whose vision is visibly limited. The intrusion then stresses the darkness and isolation of the listeners ("It had become so pitch dark that we listeners could hardly see one another"). The unnamed figure who later records Marlow's story voices the moral unease it arouses, as if speaking for the reader, and reminds the reader of the alertness and wariness needed ("I listened, I listened on the watch for the sentence, for the word, that would give me the clue"). The intrusive frame thus acts as a kind of `alienation device`, deliberately breaking the narrative's spell and reminding the reader of its moral complexity, so that one does not uncritically sink into it as an adventure story that happens to be set in a colony. *Questions of form and the ethics of colonial narrative meet here; Heart of Darkness will be put back into the context of empire in P15.*

**Reading: a third reading of "The Oval Portrait".** After the liberal humanist reading in P1 and the structuralist reading in P3, Poe's story can be read a third time with a "combined narratology": the story/plot distinction and the categories of Aristotle, Propp and Genette are not applied one after another in order but selectively combined. Using theory effectively is almost always selective rather than exhaustive.

The distinction between plot and story shows up at once: events are told in two "blocks", in reverse chronological order. First come the war, the narrator's wound, his taking refuge in the chateau and his discovery of the portrait; only then the life, many years before, of the woman in the picture. Told in chronological order, the effect would be entirely different and the transition harder to manage; here the officer's picking up the book provides a natural link. These two blocks are the frame narrative and the embedded narrative, what P1 simply called the "story within a story". It is worth noticing that they are unusually balanced (the frame is normally much smaller than the embedded narrative), and that there is an implicit emotional equivalence: the narrator's wound and the details of his processes of perception carry almost as much weight as the tragedy of a young life squandered. Perhaps the first half suggests a whole country being ravaged in the misguided pursuit of some ideal, a large-scale counterpart of what is seen in the embedded narrative. The frame thus gives the theme of the embedded narrative resonance and wider applicability; it is also a delaying device, evoking a mood like an overture before an opera. In a folk tale or fairy tale, generic convention would dispense with the frame and begin directly, "Once upon a time there was a young and gifted painter…". The frame is single-ended: the story does not return at the end to the officer and his servant but stops at its climax, the moment the painter realises his wife is dead. A double-ended frame would blunt this impact, and the narrator would have to make some sort of moral comment, roughly "the human cost of great art is sometimes too high", an inevitable anticlimax.

Propp's material turns out to be unexpectedly productive here. The pathos of the embedded story lies in its fusion of two archetypal fairy-tale motifs. One is the princess captured by an ogre or villain and imprisoned in a tower, or paralysed or entranced by some magical power, then discovered, rescued and married by the hero. The other is the Bluebeard myth, in which the suitor is really a serial monogamist and serial killer, with the bodies of his previous brides hidden in the dungeon. Poe's bridegroom likewise "already had a bride in his Art", and is about to kill his bride. So, by the merging of roles Scholes describes, hero and villain are one and the same character, and the magical power that should enhance life, the hero's artistic gift, becomes its destroyer. This is a free adaptation of Propp's function 14 (the hero acquires a magical agent).

Genette's categories show that both narratives are mainly mimetic, but that mimesis comes in *degrees*. The opening, up to "a remote turret of the building", keeps a certain summarising quality: the servant "ventured to make forcible entrance" into the chateau, a phrase with the summarising touch that usually belongs to telling rather than showing. It is somewhat "diegetised", packaged in "narrator-speak", and we do not really "see" what happened. Did he smash the lock with an axe, put his shoulder to the door again and again, use a broken sundial as a battering ram, or just break a ground-floor window with his rifle butt and climb in? Any of these would give "full mimesis", whereas "forcible entrance" gives only "partial mimesis", keeping the actual method the narrator's secret. The description of the room is closer to full mimesis, but what exactly are its "decorations"? Are the "manifold and multiform armorial trophies" shields, swords, helmets or suits of armour? How many of each, and where? This writing, which might be called "medium mimesis", gives no detail; its task is not to pan slowly round the room like a camera but to give a series of vivid impressions of the room's nature and atmosphere. Only in the paragraph beginning "But the action produced an effect…" does the pace of telling slow further to match the sequence of the officer's impressions, with precise "stage directions" placing us in the officer's position to look with him, and full mimesis is reached. The embedded narrative passes through the same stages, from partial to medium to full mimesis.

The narrators of the two narratives are equally intriguing. The frame narrative is a first-person homodiegetic narration by an overt, dramatised narrator; although we do not know his name, we can infer his personality and background from details. He is educated (he knows the eighteenth-century Gothic novels of Ann Radcliffe, understands painterly techniques such as "vignetting", and is very interested in the processes and stages of perception) and wealthy (he has a personal servant). The narrator of the embedded narrative is more problematic. The little volume on the pillow, which "purported to criticise and describe" the "very numerous" paintings in the house, suggests that he is what we would now call an art critic or connoisseur; beyond that we know nothing. We assume him to be a heterodiegetic narrator, not part of the story he tells; but once the painter "would not suffer any to enter the turret", it is hard to guess where his information comes from. Either he is an omniscient narrator with privileged access to the minds of his subjects, or he had some deeper intimacy with the painter; perhaps he is the painter. The "very spirited modern paintings" in the house, uniform in style, are probably all by the same painter; perhaps each was produced in a similar situation, each at the cost of the model's life, in a compulsively repeated "primal scene" in which art and life struggle for supremacy. *"Compulsive repetition" and "primal scene" are terms from P6; technical speculation in narratology here already leads into psychoanalysis.* Technical speculation about the nature of the narrator thus leads rapidly into the deepest content.

Finally there is the Aristotelian level. The hamartia that drives the whole story is the gifted painter's moral blindness: he raises himself to godlike status, taking on the role of *creating* life, yet can do so only at the *cost* of life; he lacks both *insight* (self-knowledge) and *foresight*, failing to see the inevitable outcome of his creative obsession. Strangely for an artist, he lacks sympathy and imagination, and so cannot represent the real thing, only make a replica, a ghostly hologram from which the essence is wholly absent. The recognition comes too late: it never occurs to him that "she was dying", and there is only the belated perception "she was dead". The peripeteia may apply to both of them. The male figure changes from an artist "of high renown" into a vampiric murderer; the woman, at first apparently the embodiment of vitality itself, becomes a meek, submissive victim, her erotic appeal lying in her languid acquiescence as her life is drained away, the fate of most of Poe's women.

*The comparison of the three readings is clear. The liberal humanist reading starts from moral conviction and finds that the story condemns "art for art's sake"; the structuralist reading starts from binary oppositions and finds that the story structurally favours art; the narratological reading starts from the techniques of telling, arrives likewise at the theme of the conflict between art and life, but finds new possibilities in the uncertainty of the narrator's identity. The closing observation about the fate of Poe's women leaves an opening for the feminist reading of P12.*

**Operations: combined narratology.** This material makes up a basic narratological toolkit. The story/plot distinction reminds us how a narrative is designed and what designs it has on us; Aristotle's categories tune in to the deep psychological fundamentals of narrative; Propp's system supplies data on the surface detail of plot; Genette turns attention to how the story is told and how it achieves its designs. Barthes's five codes (P3) can be added: if Aristotle is mainly concerned with theme, Propp with plot and Genette with narration, Barthes is concerned with the reader, since it is the reader's "decoding" that gives meaning to everything a narrative mobilises. Combined strategically, these systems allow aspects of narrative neglected by one to receive due attention in another. The way narratologists work can then be summed up. They look at individual narratives in search of the recurring structures of all narrative; they move a great deal of critical attention from the "content" of stories to the teller and the telling; they extend and refine categories drawn mainly from short narratives so that they can deal with the complexity of the novel; they counter traditional criticism's emphasis on character and motive by emphasising action and structure; and their pleasure in reading comes more from the kinship among all narratives than from the uniqueness and originality of a few highly prized works. *The last point stands in direct opposition to the liberal humanism of P1, which prizes precisely the "unique".*

**Objection: terminological pedantry.** A notable feature of narratology is that one phenomenon often has different terms coined by different schools, such as "zero focalisation" and "omniscient narration". The terms mostly come from the Greek and Latin layers of the vocabulary (*mimesis*, *diegesis*) and have an evident academic air, whereas the writers who have discussed the theory of writing since the nineteenth century preferred plain words: George Eliot and Henry James said "showing" and "telling", and E. M. Forster in *Aspects of the Novel* (1927) spoke of "flat" and "round" characters, words that openly declare their meaning and make no attempt to impress with technicality or learning. Can this pedantry be defended? One answer is that it reflects the greater distance between narratologists and actual storytelling, since they are usually not creative writers; practitioners of a craft show their everyday familiarity with it precisely by *not* using technical language. An outsider says someone is "a violinist in an orchestra"; he himself will say he "plays fiddle in a band". But these terms are almost never mere empty show; they have an attractive concision and precision, in contrast with the much looser use of terms in poststructuralism (P7).

### The Structure of Narrative Transmission: Narrators and the Recording of Speech and Thought
