**Problem:** Genette's sixth question, how speech and thought are represented, becomes in **Seymour Chatman** the way into a more general question: how is narrative "transmitted" from some source to an audience? Who is speaking, and on what basis does the audience judge who is speaking?

**Definition: the plane of expression and the plane of content.** Chatman starts from an assumption current at the time: narrative is a semi-semiotic structure independent of the language or other medium that conveys it, made up of a `plane of expression` (narrative discourse, "discourse" for short) and a `plane of content` (story). This is Saussure's signifier/signified distinction magnified to the level of narrative (P3). The plane of expression consists of abstract `narrative statements`: a gesture in a ballet, a sequence of shots in a film, a whole paragraph or even a single word in a novel may all realise the same narrative statement, since narrative itself is independent of medium. The basic verb of narrative is DO, or HAPPEN when the subject undergoes rather than acts; as in Aristotle, action is the basic element of narrative. Hence there are two kinds of statement: `process statements`, about actions, and `stasis statements`, about existence (including description). Crossing these is another distinction: whether a statement is presented directly to the audience (who seem to be "overhearing") or mediated by a narrator (who addresses them directly). This is the old distinction between mimesis and diegesis, or in modern terms "showing/telling". Crossing the two distinctions gives four narrative operations:

| Mode of transmission | Process statements | Stasis statements |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Showing (unmediated) | enacts | presents |
| Telling (mediated) | recounts | describes |

Different media are distributed differently across this table. The medium of drama is typically presentational and needs no stasis statements: the characters, props and scenery are there on the stage. Film can add narrational elements through titles and voice-over, and Brecht brought similar devices into the theatre. Literary narrative can be almost purely mimetic, as in a story made up entirely of dialogue.

**Mechanism: narrator, implied author and unreliable narrator.** When does a narrator appear? When the story is made to seem a demonstrable act of communication and the audience feels in some sense "spoken to", a teller has to be assumed; otherwise the audience feels it is witnessing events directly. Apart from scenic arts such as drama and ballet, pure mimesis is an illusion: readers reach events by turning pages and reading words, the author has to make a special effort to sustain the illusion that events are happening before their eyes, and attempts at purely "dramatic" narrative have a history of only a hundred years or so. That the narrator is not the author is by now a commonplace of modern criticism. Beardsley says that unless the author provides a pragmatic context connecting the speaker with himself, the speaker of a work cannot be identified with the author, and the speaker's character and situation can be known only from internal evidence (*this comes from the same source as the intentional fallacy in P2*). Even in such a context it is better to speak of an "authorial" narrator, since this is only one possible narrator among others; otherwise there is no way of explaining the discrepancies between the values of the author known from biography and the values implied in a work, or between different works by the same author. The "Fielding" of *Tom Jones* is not the "Fielding" of *Jonathan Wild* or *Amelia*.

For this reason Chatman adopts Wayne Booth's `implied author`. In writing, the real author creates not an impersonal "man in general" but an implied version of himself, a "second self". It is "implied", that is, constructed or reconstructed by the reader; it is not the narrator but the one who invents the narrator, "the one who stacked the cards in this particular way", who had *these* things happen to *these* characters. The distinction is clearest in the case of the `unreliable narrator`, whose values diverge markedly from those of the implied author: the norms of the work conflict with the narrator's presentation of events, and we come to suspect his sincerity or competence in telling the "truth". There is always an implied author, even when there is no single real author in the usual sense (a ballad composed collectively over a long time, a text generated at random by computer); what establishes its character is the moral and other norms of the work as a whole. Chatman disagrees with Booth on one point. Booth held that works such as Hemingway's "The Killers" have an "implied undramatised narrator"; Chatman thinks there is only an implied author and no narrator at all. Nick, George and Sam are named as soon as they appear, while the two gangsters are at first called just "the two men", and the reader learns their names only when the other characters do. That arrangement is the work of the implied author, not of some narrator. *The concept of the implied author occupies a middle position between the "intentional fallacy" of P2 and the "death of the author" of P7: it grants that a work has a centre of values, but places that centre in an image constituted by the overall form of the work rather than in the mind of a living person.*

**Mechanism: speech acts and the "pretence" of fiction.** Readers judge who is speaking, and whether there is a definite narrator, partly on the basis of the language-philosophical foundations of reported speech, thought and action. The most obvious marks of a narrator are direct intrusions (using "I", "the present author" and so on); other marks are inferential: statements explaining characters' behaviour presuppose an explainer, and general comments on fate or the nature of the world presuppose a commentator. To distinguish precisely between narrators' words and characters' words, Chatman borrowed `speech act theory` (which P5 will discuss in full). According to Austin, a speaker who utters a sentence is doing at least two and possibly three things. He produces a sentence according to the rules of grammar: a `locutionary` act. In saying it, he performs an act that could have been done by non-verbal means, as when saying "Jump in the water" performs an "order", equivalent to pushing the other person towards the water: an `illocutionary` act. And if the other person does jump, he has performed an act of "persuading": a `perlocutionary` act. None of the three determines the others: the same "prediction" can be made as "John will surely go mad" or "John is quite likely to go mad in the end", and it may persuade, deceive, annoy, frighten, amuse or have no effect at all.

On this basis Richard Ohmann proposed an illocutionary definition of literature (here, fictional narrative): a literary work is discourse abstracted from the circumstances and conditions that make illocutionary acts possible, and so has no illocutionary force; or more exactly, only a *pretended* illocutionary force, the reader imagining a speaker and a set of circumstances that make the quasi-speech act felicitous. A novel *imitates* a narrative report, whereas a work like Capote's *In Cold Blood* *is* a narrative report. Of the latter one can ask all the questions implied by Austin's rules (is the speaker entitled to invoke this procedure? Does he really have the thoughts and feelings he reports?), but not of novels and poems.

**Example: the opening of *The Brothers Karamazov*.** The sentences of a narrative thus fall into two broad classes: the narrator's speech acts addressed to his narratee, and the characters' speech acts addressed to one another. The first three sentences of *The Brothers Karamazov* convey a great deal of story information in various forms, but all of them are the narrator's speech acts. From the first sentence several stasis statements can be inferred: there is a man called Alexey Fyodorovich Karamazov; there is a man called Fyodor Pavlovich Karamazov; Alexey is Fyodor's third son; Fyodor is a landowner. At the illocutionary level these are narrative "assertions"; "he was a strange type, despicable and vicious and at the same time senseless" is a "description" or "attribution". "Well known in our district in his own day" and "still remembered among us" look like process statements on the surface, but at the narrative level they are stasis statements: they attribute a quality to Fyodor, just as the word "notorious" might have done. *Chatman stresses here that the basic unit of narrative cannot be identified with the deep structure of the sentence; the surface effect of passive constructions like "was known" and "is remembered" in fact reveals narrative structure better.* The same applies to "as we used to call him" and "he hardly spent a day on his own estate": the habitual past and the negative "hardly" show that repeated actions in narrative tend to characterise rather than advance the plot. "Owing to his gloomy and tragic death", by contrast, states an event.

There is a third kind of speech act, which can be called "generalisation" or "giving an opinion": "this type is fairly common"; "he was one of those … senseless persons who are very well capable of looking after their worldly affairs". The distinction is crucial. **A genuine narrative assertion is an integral part of the story and cannot be questioned, since to question it is to stop the narrative going on and to deny its texture; by convention the author is entitled to posit whatever entities and actions the narrative needs.** An opinion has no such warrant: it points to the narrator's view of the world outside the story, makes an apparent truth claim, and can be challenged on independent grounds. One could imagine a statistical survey of nineteenth-century personality types, but one cannot decide whether Fyodor was vicious, since one cannot claim that he existed. *(What Barthes in S/Z calls the "referential code" or "cultural code", the third of the codes in P3, corresponds to this kind of opinion pointing outwards to reality.)* Characters' speech acts are more varied and refer to other characters and things in the story. In *Pamela*, the heroine writing "forgive me for not writing sooner" is apologising; her parents writing "we must once more warn you against your master's kindness" are warning. Narrators can apologise and warn too (Fielding's narrators often do, and "we intend…" in Book II of *Tom Jones* is a declaration of intent), but only with respect to the narrative itself. The narrator's central speech act is narrating; characters use language to argue, court, do business, promise and lie, all within the boundaries of the story world.

**Counter-example: Beckett's footnote.** In a long list of sick and disabled relatives in *Watt*, Beckett says that Kate was "a fine girl but a bleeder", and adds a footnote: "Haemophilia is, like enlargement of the prostate, an exclusively male disorder. But not in this work." Ohmann analyses this anomaly in terms of the felicity conditions for what Austin calls "stating". To make a statement felicitously, the stater must believe what he says (rule 5) and must not take as the basis of his future words and actions an understanding of the world contrary to it (rule 6). Either the narrator held an improper belief when he stated that Kate was a haemophiliac, or he improperly excused himself afterwards with the footnote; one statement or the other is infelicitous, breaking the contract between author and reader. More fundamentally, behind "stating" lies the overall illocutionary act of storytelling: during the telling, the teller always endorses the fictional world and by convention does not admit that it is fiction. Beckett's narrator admits the discrepancy between the fictional world and the real one, breaking both rules at once; this puts the reader at odds with the text, producing disorientation and comedy, and at a deeper level questions the possibility of constructing narratives, of understanding human action and even of keeping society together. Chatman accepts this analysis, objecting only to Ohmann's calling the anomaly "un-English" (that is, non-linguistic): it is "un-narrative", because the same anomaly can occur in other media. A trick shot in a film of someone flying through the air without any apparatus can be denied by the rest of the film and yet be "true" in a deeper sense of the film; since there are films that use no words, not even titles, the anomaly lies not in language but in discourse. Nor was Beckett simply breaking rules: he was extending them into another kind of discourse, an ironic narrative that "questions the construction of narrative".

**Distinction: direct/indirect and tagged/free.** Analysing the speech acts of narrators and characters presupposes a description of the basic ways in which speech (the outer voice) and thought (the inner voice) are conveyed. The distinction between direct and indirect (*oratio recta*/*oratio obliqua*) has been grammatical common knowledge for centuries. In "'I have to go,' she said" and "She said that she had to go", the reported clause that follows the introducing clause (which Chatman calls the `tag`) changes in tense (*have* → *had*) and person (I → she); the same holds for thought. Over the last hundred years or so another distinction has crossed this one: tagged versus `free` (*erlebte Rede*, *style indirect libre*). A free sentence is one with the tag clause deleted:

| Type | Free | Tagged |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Direct speech | I have to go | "I have to go," she said |
| Direct thought | I have to go | "I have to go," she thought |
| Indirect speech | She had to go | She said that she had to go |
| Indirect thought | She had to go | She thought that she had to go |

The table immediately shows two ambiguities: free direct speech and free direct thought have exactly the same form, and so do free indirect speech and free indirect thought; and a free indirect sentence such as "She had to go" might also come from the narrator. *(A language without tense inflection, such as Chinese, marks the direct/indirect shift mainly through person; that the distinction survives without the change of tense illustrates the point that follows.)* Chatman therefore stresses that narrative discourse, though finally expressed in words, is not the same as linguistic manifestation. The choice between direct and indirect is essentially a choice of discourse, which in realisation happens to involve linguistic choices such as "that" versus zero, "he" versus "I". Quotation marks, ellipses marking a jump in time or place, and the "tear stains" on the letter paper of *Les Liaisons dangereuses* and *Pamela* do not belong to natural language but do belong to discourse; and a process statement such as "John stole the money" can perfectly well be realised by a copular sentence ("John's theft made the headlines"). On this basis he criticised David Lodge for overstressing the place of language in narrative: language is only one of several systems or codes that narrative uses, and they need not be ranked. In James language matters enormously; in Dreiser it is relatively secondary. *This contrasts with the position of stylistics below: stylistics explains effects starting from linguistic facts, whereas Chatman insists that narrative structure has a level independent of linguistic manifestation. Narratology is structuralism, not merely applied linguistics.*

**Example: several versions of Mario and Thelma.** The same distinctions can be demonstrated with a set of very simple sentences. "'What's your name?' Mario asked her. 'Thelma,' she replied" is tagged direct speech. Writing just "'Thelma.'" is untagged direct speech, which easily becomes confusing when more than two people are talking or the exchange is not question-and-answer, so selective tagging is common: "'What's your name?' Mario asked. 'Thelma.'" The difference looks slight, but every tag inserted reminds the reader of the narrator's presence, blunting the edge of mimesis and pushing "showing" back towards "telling". "He asked her what her name was, and she told him it was Thelma" is tagged indirect speech: it gives a report rather than the actual words (what he actually said was "What's your name?", not "What's her name?"), and the tag merges with the speech, introducing a formal distance between reader and event. `Free indirect speech` reduces this distance a little: "What was her name? It was Thelma." It suits internally focalised narrative especially well, because it is easy to "slide" from here into the speaker's thoughts and feelings: "Thelma, was it? Not a name to launch a thousand ships. More the kind of name you'd get in a suburban house with lace curtains." These reflections on the name clearly belong to the man asking, not to an omniscient narrator; and the narrative can just as easily move from here in the other direction, giving outward actions and reactions.

Genette's own terms are more general, envisaging three levels at increasing distance from the original words:

1. `Mimetic speech`: "I have to go," I said to her.
2. `Transposed speech`: I told her that I had to go.
3. `Narratised speech`: I informed her of my need to leave.

Transposed speech is not quite the same as free indirect speech: it is indirect but not free, since it carries the tag "I told her". The fundamental difference between transposed and narratised speech is that the former lets us infer the form of the original words ("I have to go"), while the latter conveys only the substance of what was said, not its wording (the original might have been "I must go", "I've got to go" or "I've no choice but to go"). Narratised speech thus turns living speech into a narrated event, putting the greatest possible distance between the reader and the direct impact and tone of the words. *Genette and Chatman think in different directions: Genette arranges a scale by distance from the original words, while Chatman treats "direct/indirect" and "tagged/free" as features that can be freely combined.*

**Mechanism: a spectrum from "transcript" to narrator.** This feature-based approach is a general methodological principle of Chatman's: the discussion rests on the idea that *features* of discourse combine freely, not on homogeneous, fixed genres. Differences between narratives are explained by different mixtures of independent features, without multiplying categories endlessly or forcing individual cases into normative types. On this basis he criticised Stanzel, who classified narrative situations as "authorial", "first-person" and "figural" and then explained mixed forms by intermediate positions on a circle. These categories are not parallel: what first-person narrative refers to in the first person is the *narrator*, whereas what "authorial" narrative refers to in the third person is the *character*; the narrator of *Tom Jones* calls himself "I" and Tom "he". Person in itself is therefore not a strong distinguishing feature. Molly Bloom and Ishmael both say "I", but *Ulysses* and *Moby-Dick* cannot be put in one class, because Molly is not a narrator; at this point *Ulysses* has no narrator at all. It is better to treat the narrator itself as a feature, and ask to what extent a statement or a work presupposes its existence. At the negative pole (pure mimesis) are statements claiming to transcribe characters' behaviour directly, strictly possible only when the behaviour is verbal; at the positive pole (pure diegesis) is discourse in which the narrator, in his own voice and using "I", offers not the story itself but his *views* about the story. Even a tag such as "he said" is not a strong mark of mediation; it is no more conspicuous than marking a change of speaker by a new paragraph. Mediation begins to show only when the tag uses an interpretive verb such as "he guessed" or "he implied". Likewise, "John flopped into the chair" or "John lounged about" does not just imitate an action in words; it at least implies a comment on the action. Even a neutral "sat" means a more loaded word has been avoided, and a sentence adverb ("Obviously, John was tired") necessarily contains a speaker's judgement.

The spectrum begins at the least mediated end. In `written records`, epistolary and diary novels, the implied author is reduced to a collector of documents and need not even turn speech into writing. The implied reader of a diary is usually the writer, and diarists, like letter writers, do not know what will happen next. Roquentin in Sartre's *Nausea* is often not recording events at all, and narrative mostly appears as illustration: he feels something cold in his hand with a kind of "personality", opens his hand and sees that it is only a doorknob. Bresson's film *Diary of a Country Priest* exploits the possibilities of this convention in cinema, with a voice-over reading the diary while the images show the actions it records. Sometimes the voice-over says he must write down at once what is happening and breaks off, while the image cuts straight to the action, and the audience is momentarily lost: has the action suddenly run ahead of the diary, or is this an unmarked flashback? Only context can decide.

In `recorded speech` the implied author is merely a stenographer. In a dramatic monologue one character speaks to a silent listener. Dorothy Parker's "Lady with a Lamp" consists entirely of an unnamed woman talking to her friend Mona, who has had a breakdown; ostensibly she is comforting her, but in fact she makes her steadily worse. Mona's replies never appear and can only be inferred from what the speaker says (at one point the speaker concedes that she would deserve a scolding too, which implies that Mona has just protested). Keeping the victim silent throughout supports the speaker's moral and psychological obtuseness, even her unconscious malice: **the content finds a direct formal correlative in the technique**. Dialogue is the most common case, but narratives that rely wholly or mainly on recorded speech require more inference, or at least a special kind: the reader has to interpret the illocutionary force of the characters' words more than usual, as if supplying the appropriate tag verbs at a metatextual level: "complained", "argued", "pleaded". In Hemingway's "Hills Like White Elephants", the girl looks at the distant hills and says, "They look like white elephants." The man says, "I've never seen one," and drinks his beer. She says, "No, you wouldn't have." He says, "I might have. Just because you say I wouldn't have doesn't prove anything." The girl is first of all *poeticising*. The man's words, in another context, would be an *admission of ignorance*; here, as a response to her poeticising, they are more like a *rejection* of her fancy, with a touch of smugness. She then *disparages* him; he *defends himself* and *challenges her right to judge him*. **These inferences about speech acts, like all inferences in reading, rest on everyday knowledge of the world and everyday expectations about human behaviour in one's own society**, which may be precisely why narratives of pure recorded speech find it hard to cross deep cultural boundaries.

`Soliloquy` is often used to describe Woolf's *The Waves* and Faulkner's *As I Lay Dying*. Soliloquy in drama has two necessary features: the character really is speaking, and he is alone on stage, or others present show that they cannot hear. *The Waves* has the tags "he (she) said" and quotation marks, while *As I Lay Dying* identifies speakers with play-script name headings; in both books the other characters never respond directly, so these are not dramatic monologues. Soliloquy can only appear in tagged form, because it must be clearly identified as speech rather than thought. *As I Lay Dying* gives only names, without saying whether the words are spoken or thought, and so is more ambiguous; perhaps its words are neither naturally spoken nor naturally thought by the characters but attributed to them in some supernaturalistic way.

`Records of thought and feeling` first require a distinction between two kinds of mental activity: those that involve language (one may say to oneself "I must buy milk and bread") and those that do not (walking past a garden, one does not say to oneself "the roses are red"). The first appear in narrative as unmediated thought in the strict sense; the second must be turned into words by someone, which raises the question of who does the turning. Film can simply show red roses, but literature is a verbal art. "Elizabeth almost stared at her.—'Can this be Mr. Darcy!' thought she" in *Pride and Prejudice* is tagged direct thought: the implied author has become a mind reader as well as a stenographer, but still offers no interpretation. Remove the quotation marks and the tag and we get `free direct thought`, commonly called `interior monologue` or `stream of consciousness`. Its features are: the character refers to himself in the first person; predicates are in the present tense; the diction is appropriate to the character; references to the character's experience carry only such explanation as the character would need in thinking them; and there is no presupposed audience other than the thinker himself.

**Reading: Bloom's breakfast.** The passage at the start of the first chapter of the second part of *Ulysses*, with Bloom preparing breakfast in the kitchen, is often cited as a standard example of "stream of consciousness", but sentence-by-sentence analysis shows that it only gradually approaches free direct thought. The first four sentences are narrated in the conventional way by an invisible narrator, whose presence shows only in his use of the third person for the character and the past tense for actions. He also summarises the character's habits ("he liked") and turns into words feelings Bloom may never have verbalised (kidneys that "gave to his palate a fine tang of faintly scented urine"). The truncated syntax of sentences five to seven hints at a shift, and only with sentence eight, "Another slice of bread and butter: three, four: right", does the passage turn into free thought. What makes it so is not the truncated syntax itself but the fact that "right" cannot be attributed to the narrator: only Bloom would assess whether he is doing it right. Because the tense has been deleted, one cannot tell whether this is free direct or free indirect thought. Sentence nine keeps the past tense ("She didn't like her plate full") and can be identified as free indirect thought; only sentence twenty, "Just how she stalks over my writingtable", in the present tense, is unambiguously free direct thought. The conclusion: **fewer than half the sentences need to use free direct thought to create a strong "stream of consciousness" effect**. Truncated syntax and free association may accompany the style, but the only *necessary* conditions are first-person self-reference and the present tense, which must be presupposed even when they are deleted.

**Reading: the "community" of Mrs Dalloway.** Sustained free indirect style often has a different effect: more sympathy, or agreement of views, between narrator and character. The first sentence of *Mrs Dalloway*, "Mrs Dalloway said she would buy the flowers herself", is tagged indirect speech. The second, "For Lucy had her work cut out for her", can be attributed equally to the narrator ("You see, dear reader, Lucy had her work cut out for her"), to Mrs Dalloway's thoughts, or to what she said; the possibilities hang suspended in the sentence, creating a special closeness of narrator to character's mind, a kind of communal form: "all parties (the narrator included) know that Lucy has her work cut out for her". The first sentence does not say whom she is speaking to, which suggests that she is used to always having an audience (at the least, servants and attendants). The narrative structure thus confirms from the outset the fundamental difference between the two novels: Mrs Dalloway is a society hostess closely surrounded by society, with even a sympathetic narrator at her side, whereas Stephen Dedalus and Bloom are loners living on the margins of society and in conflict with it, whose narrators are distant, objective and at times ironic. Sympathy is not, however, the only aesthetic product of free indirect style. Dorrit Cohn points out that imitation has two directions, merging with its object or keeping a distance from it and becoming satire, so "narrated monologue" can be lyrical or ironic. A passage in *Madame Bovary* that slides from direct narration into free indirect style (Emma sitting on Charles's knee to explain the promissory note) suggests how ordinary and frequent her deceiving of Charles has become, to the point of "you know how it's done in petty-bourgeois circles".

**Conclusion:** Free indirect style offers a middle ground of consciousness between full immersion in a character's consciousness, "stream of consciousness", and the Jamesian observation in which the narrator keeps a relative distance from a "central consciousness". Chatman's analysis has two consequences. First, the distinctions between narrator, implied author and unreliable narrator show that "who is speaking" is never a fact given directly on the surface of the text but something inferred according to convention. Second, from the narrative assertions of *The Brothers Karamazov* to the illocutions of "Hills Like White Elephants", part of narrative meaning can be fixed only with the help of speech act theory and the reader's social knowledge. At its most refined, narratology already cannot do without a theory of the receiver.

### From Rhetoric to Stylistics: Can Linguistics Supply Evidence for Literary Interpretation?

**Definition:** `Stylistics` is a critical approach that uses the methods and findings of linguistics (the scientific study of language and its structures, not the learning of particular languages) to analyse literary texts. It developed in the twentieth century, with the aim of showing how the technical linguistic features of a literary work, such as the grammatical structure of its sentences, contribute to its overall meaning and effect.

**Background: does it count as theory?** Most introductions to theory say nothing about stylistics, apparently assuming it is not theory. The ground for this exclusion is presumably that its theoretical position has much in common with liberal humanism. Both have a strong empirical bent, preferring detailed linguistic analysis of particular canonical texts to establishing general theoretical positions; both keep clear of the eclecticism that cross-breeds Marxism, feminism, structuralism and poststructuralism; and both generally reject the idea of the "floating signifier", that the meanings established by language are inherently fluid, indeterminate and constantly slipping. Yet they are not natural allies: in the 1960s stylistics clashed fiercely with liberal humanism, at least a decade before the full-scale conflict between theory and liberal humanism. Compared with other theories, stylistics also resisted the "relativism" that pervades other theoretical discourse. Elsewhere there is uncertainty everywhere, critics carefully avoid "totalising claims", and it is accepted that there are only partial points of view and no panorama; **stylistics keeps a positivist stance, believing that a disinterested researcher can accumulate knowledge through empirical study of external phenomena.** There is good reason to think stylistics distinctive, but no reason to think it has no theory: much of its practice is the product of a particular theory of how literary language works.

Stylistics is also not confined to literature; it applies equally to expository prose, political speeches, advertising and so on. It therefore assumes that literary language is not a "special case" but can be analysed like any other language, to show precisely how effects are produced. It grants literary language no mysterious quality: literary language is not sacred, merely data to which method can be applied.

**History: from rhetoric, philology and linguistics to stylistics.** In a sense stylistics is a modern version of ancient rhetoric. Rhetoric taught how to organise arguments, use figures of speech effectively, and arrange and vary speech or writing for maximum impact. In the Middle Ages it trained people for the church, law, politics and diplomacy; cut off from these professional purposes it degenerated into a dry, mechanical study of the surface features of language, identifying and classifying figures, whose pedantry (its love of grand labels, for instance) Chaucer, Shakespeare and others often mocked. In the nineteenth century this rhetoric was gradually absorbed into the kind of linguistics then called `philology`, which was almost entirely historical (precisely the kind Saussure took leave of in P3). The twentieth century turned to studying how language is constituted as a system; a "reborn" rhetoric appeared before the First World War, and a new interest in literary style and its effects can be seen in the Russian Formalists of the 1920s and in Jakobson, leader of the Prague Linguistic Circle.

In 1958 Indiana University held a "Conference on Style", whose proceedings were published in 1960 as *Style in Language* (edited by Thomas Sebeok). Jakobson's "Closing Statement" seemed to announce a takeover of literature by linguistics:

> Poetics deals primarily with problems of verbal structure … Since linguistics is the global science of verbal structure, poetics may be regarded as an integral part of linguistics.

("Poetics" here means literary study in general.) The thrust of the volume was that linguistics offered a more objective way of studying literature, and it produced what Roger Fowler called a "confrontation" between the study of language and the study of literature. Fowler's *Essays on Style and Language* (1966) tried to repair the "unnecessary split" between "language" and "literature" and instead widened it. Helen Vendler, reviewing it in *Essays in Criticism*, said that linguistics had great potential, but that present-day linguists were simply not well enough educated in reading poetry and were dealing with documents whose basic sense and value they were not equipped to absorb. Fowler's rejoinder led to a famous controversy between him and the journal's editor, F. W. Bateson, which once again hardened the language/literature polarity. By the 1980s the defect Vendler pointed to, that linguistics could analyse only isolated phrases and sentences, had been made good by `discourse analysis`, and linguistics became able to analyse whole works. Non-linguists began to take notice of linguistic papers, linguists recognised the need to take in non-linguistic material, and a "new stylistics" is said to have emerged: somewhat eclectic (absorbing the results of feminism, structuralism and poststructuralism), and less inclined to claim that it alone studies literature objectively.

**Objection: the break of the "new stylistics" has been exaggerated.** Claims of superiority on both sides in fact continued. In *Linguistic Criticism* (1986) Fowler still called linguistic criticism "an objective description of the text" and traditional criticism "amateur commentary" using "casual descriptive jargon"; his arguments of the 1980s almost repeated those he had used against Bateson in the 1960s ("there is no such thing as one linguistics … vague talk about 'linguistics' is useless"). Conversely, not all stylistics in the 1960s was exclusivist: Fowler stressed even then that being a linguist was not in itself enough to deal with poetry, and that literature, though language, has, like other distinctively formed texts, its own particular context, which linguist and critic alike must study. In the mid-1980s Fabb and Durant could still say that literary criticism "often proceeds without any systematic or even explicit examination of its methods and assumptions". It is fair to say, then, that stylistics today is more open than in the past, but the clean break with a hard-line past implied by the term "new stylistics" is overstated. On the other hand, for a long time the main threat to the values of traditional criticism was felt to be structuralism and poststructuralism rather than stylistics, and most of liberal humanism's polemical fire was aimed at them.

**Another account: stylistics as a revival of rhetoric.** The anthology's editors tell the same history within the longer tradition of rhetoric. Greece and Rome saw language as an important feature of social and political life; training in right thinking took the form of training in the effective use of language, and logic was studied together with rhetoric. The rise of the modern positivist model of science and the refinement of abstract mathematical logic severed philosophy from rhetoric, and rhetoric sank to a minor place in the humanities (Kenneth Burke in the 1930s was one of the few who still insisted on its importance for understanding social action and literary form). The twentieth-century intellectual revolution that restored the importance of the study of language began in linguistics and spread to anthropology, philosophy, and the literary criticism of Russian Formalism and French structuralism; Cassirer, Heidegger, Wittgenstein and Austin all argued that language is central to human experience and social institutions, and rhetoric regained the interest of literary scholars. Today the study of literary language called "stylistics" has merged with the study of language use in other fields such as medicine and economics, attending to **how language embeds schemes for understanding the world in particular ways**; its key assumption is that language shapes people's perception of the world. *The two accounts put the weight differently. Barry's stylistics is a positivist science modelled on linguistics, seeking objectivity and keeping its distance from the relativism of "theory"; the editors' stylistics is the modern form of rhetoric and pragmatics, concerned precisely with the construction of reality by language, and stands with "language constitutes the world" in P3 and with speech act theory in P5.*

**Distinction: stylistics and ordinary close reading.** Stylistic analysis tries to offer commentary that is objective, scientific, based on concrete quantifiable data and systematically applied; to stylisticians, ordinary "close reading" is more or less impressionistic, intuitive and haphazard. To a casual observer the difference between the two may look superficial, but there are at least three points of difference. First, close reading stresses the *difference* between literary language and the language of the speech community at large, and tends to isolate the literary text as a pure aesthetic object or "verbal icon" (P2) whose language works by its own rules; stylistics stresses the *connections* between literary and everyday language. This continues an old argument. Wordsworth held that poetic language is most effective when it is plainest and closest to the language "really used by men"; Coleridge held that the effect of poetic language depends on the poet's heightening and intensifying it, through patterning, compression, repetition and so on, so that it moves away from the patterns of everyday speech. *The Russian Formalist distinction between poetic and practical language (P2) stands on Coleridge's side; stylistics inherits Wordsworth's.* Second, stylistics uses specialised terms derived from linguistics, such as `transitivity`, `under-lexicalisation`, `collocation` and `cohesion`, which have no general currency outside their own field; close reading uses terms that are slightly bookish but belong to ordinary language: "nuance", "irony", "ambiguity", "paradox", "ambivalence". Third, stylistics claims greater scientific objectivity and stresses that its methods can be learned and applied by anyone, so part of its aim is a double "demystification", of literature and of criticism. Of literature, it shows the continuity between literary language and other forms of written communication; of criticism, it offers publicly available procedures, against close reading's insistence that the critic must cultivate "tact" and "sensitivity" and avoid explicit method (Leavis was famously unwilling to describe his critical method). If, as many believe, the feelings expressed in a poem are uniquely embodied in the verbal form the poet chose, there are strict limits to what critical inquiry can add; stylistics rejects this inference.

**Mechanism: the three ambitions of stylistics.** First, **to provide "hard" data for existing "intuitions"**. Readers feel that Hemingway's style is plain and distinctive; the stylistician asks what "plain" actually means. Hemingway usually avoids adjectives and adverbs: where another writer might write "Smith ran resolutely through the heavy rain", Hemingway would cut "resolutely" and "heavy" and write just "Smith ran through the rain", letting those implications emerge implicitly, in the belief that this has more impact. A stylistician might count that "73 per cent of the nouns and verbs in this story have no adjectival or adverbial modification" and compare a writer whose style is generally felt to be less plain (with, say, 30 per cent). The result gives no new information about Hemingway, since every reader quickly sees that plainness is his most striking quality, but it states precisely how that plainness is achieved and sustained in language.

Second, **to propose new readings based on linguistic evidence**. Colin MacCabe argues that Falstaff in Shakespeare's history plays has a certain gender ambiguity. Falstaff often mentions his great belly and complains that it makes bravery difficult, but the word he uses is not *stomach* but *womb* ("My womb, my womb, my womb undoes me"). When the plays were written, *womb* was in the middle of a semantic shift: its old meaning was "belly" in general, applicable to men and women alike, while it was acquiring its modern sense, restricted to the female organ. Since both meanings were possible at the time, Falstaff's use of the word suggests a corresponding ambivalence of gender in him. Only a reader with specialist knowledge of semantic change would notice this; other readers would consult the notes and conclude that this is merely an archaic sense with no bearing on characterisation. **Objection:** the argument assumes that a word undergoing semantic change carries traces of both meanings every time it is used, but it is more likely that each use takes only one. *Disinterested* is changing today too, but each use means either "impartial" or "uninterested", never both. The more general problem is how to regard evidence that only professional linguists can detect, below the threshold of perception of all other readers. How did these meanings get into the text: did the author plant them deliberately? Probably not. If, apart from contemporary texts, the existence of such a body of readers could not have been foreseen at all, in what sense are these meanings "there"?

Third, **to establish general arguments about how literary meaning is produced**. Linguists hold that literary effects are produced at the levels of form and content simultaneously. In Hardy's *Tess of the d'Urbervilles*, Tess's subjection to Alec's social and physical superiority is expressed not only in what is said but in the grammatical structure of the "seduction" (or "rape") scene: Alec (or some attribute of his) is often the subject of sentences and Tess the object, as in sentences where he touches her or his fingers sink into her. If this argument is accepted, powerful literary effects are `overdetermined`: content is subtly reinforced by grammatical structure, overall discourse structure, choice of words, imagery and so on; **no level of language is neutral**, and syntax, morphemes and phonemes are all implicated in literary meaning. **Objection:** as a general argument this seems to turn authors into intuitive geniuses who instinctively "know" the contents of modern linguistics.

*The problem common to the three ambitions is already visible: the first only confirms what is known, the second relies on evidence only experts can see, the third needs dubious assumptions about authors' capacities. All of them have to build a bridge between linguistic fact and meaning; whether that bridge can be built is the problem of the "hermeneutic gap".*

**Operations:** Stylistic critics describe the technical aspects of a text's language (grammatical structure, for example) and then use this data in interpretation. Sometimes the aim is simply to supply objective linguistic data for an existing reading or intuition; sometimes it is to establish a new reading, which may be based solely or mainly on linguistic data and may challenge established readings. These technical accounts of how meaning is produced in literature belong to an overall project: to show that literature has no mysterious, ineffable core beyond analysis, but belongs to a common "universe of discourse" and uses the same techniques and resources as other language. To this end stylistics often sets literature beside other discourses, comparing for instance the linguistic devices of poetry and advertising, and moves from "sentence grammar" to "text grammar", examining how a text as a whole achieves (or fails to achieve) its aims, to amuse, to create suspense or to persuade, and which linguistic features contribute to them.

### Figures, Tropes and Modes of Persuasion: The Toolkit of Classical Rhetoric

**Background:** The technical vocabulary of stylistics comes from modern linguistics, but the question it asks, which arrangements of language produce effects, had already been systematised in classical rhetoric. Edward Corbett's *Classical Rhetoric for the Modern Student* (1965) was one of the landmarks of the revival of rhetoric in the second half of the twentieth century.

**Definition: figures are not ornament.** It is fair to regard `figures of speech` as "the graces of language", "the dress of thought", "embellishment"; they do give prose "style". But it is a mistake to regard ornament as their chief or only function. Aristotle and Longinus both pointed to the persuasive function of figures; Quintilian most explicitly linked figures with the three appeals of argument, `logos` (rational argument), `pathos` (emotion) and `ethos` (character), seeing figures as one more means of making an argument credible, stirring the emotions and winning approval for the advocate. Sister Miriam Joseph reclassified the more than two hundred figures distinguished by Tudor rhetoricians into four groups, grammar, logos, pathos and ethos, and showed convincingly that all three Renaissance schools of rhetoric linked figures closely with the invention of `topics` (the "places" where arguments are found); metaphor, for instance, involves the topic of similarity.

Corbett adopts Quintilian's definition of *figura*: any deviation, in thought or expression, from the ordinary and simple manner of speaking, like the different postures a body takes in sitting, lying or looking back. Figures fall into two main classes. `Schemes` (Greek *schema*, form) depart from the ordinary pattern of arrangement of words; `tropes` (Greek *tropein*, to turn) depart from the ordinary meaning of words. Both involve some kind of *transference*: tropes transfer meaning, schemes transfer order. When Shakespeare's Antony says "Brutus is an honourable man", he uses the trope of irony, transferring the ordinary meaning of "honourable" into another; if he said "Honourable is the man who gives his life for his country", he would be using the scheme of inversion. *This distinction corresponds roughly to Jakobson's two poles in P3: schemes operate on the syntagmatic axis (the arrangement of words), tropes on the paradigmatic axis (the substitution of words). This is an auxiliary analogy, not an argument of Corbett's own.*

The main classes and examples can be summarised as follows:

| Class | Figures | Definition and examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Schemes of balance | Parallelism, isocolon, antithesis | Like things expressed in like grammatical structures, equal length strengthening the symmetry: "Contempt is the proper punishment of affectation, and detestation the just consequence of hypocrisy" (Johnson) |
| Schemes of inversion | Anastrophe, parenthesis, apposition | Natural word order altered for emphasis; a parenthetical element interrupts the syntax and diverts the train of thought |
| Schemes of omission | Ellipsis, asyndeton, polysyndeton | "I came, I saw, I conquered" has a hurried rhythm; Hemingway's strings of "and" suggest the continuousness of experience |
| Schemes of repetition | Alliteration, assonance, anaphora, epistrophe, epanalepsis, anadiplosis, climax, antimetabole, chiasmus, polyptoton | "We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds…" (Churchill); "Ask not what your country can do for you; ask what you can do for your country" (Kennedy) |
| Tropes of comparison | Metaphor, simile, allegory, parable | "David was a lion in battle" / "like a lion" |
| Tropes of substitution | Synecdoche (part for whole), metonymy (attribute or associated word for the thing meant) | "Sail" for ship; "the crown" for royal power, "the bottle" for drink |
| Other tropes | Puns of various kinds, anthimeria, periphrasis, personification, hyperbole, litotes, rhetorical question, irony | "He lost his hat and his temper"; "the thunder would not peace at my bidding" in *King Lear* |

Corbett notes in particular that metonymy and synecdoche are so close as to be almost the same trope; the eighteenth-century rhetorician George Campbell doubted whether distinguishing them was worth the trouble. *This echoes Jakobson's placing of both at the pole of contiguity (P3).* He also warns that terminology is not an end in itself: just as one can speak one's mother tongue without knowing the names of the parts of speech, one can use and respond to figurative language without knowing the names of the figures; naming is only a convenience for classification and discussion.

**Mechanism: Lanham's "tacit persuasion".** Richard Lanham asked a more fundamental question: why do repetition and crossing do so much to persuade? He borrowed the pattern game theorists call "tacit bargaining". Two parachutists dropped behind enemy lines become separated with no agreed meeting place; one lands in a meadow, the other in a forest, and the map shows a bridge. Most people guess that the other will guess that they will go to the bridge. The bridge is not at the centre of the map, but, like a crossroads, it offers a "natural" focal point; if both had grown up in the area and often visited a pool in the woods, the answer would be different. The shape of certain social situations itself suggests a "logical" or "fair" outcome. Something similar happens in verbal style: patterns of sound or sight themselves carry a *non-logical* persuasive power, which Lanham calls `tacit persuasion patterns`.

There are only a few basic patterns. **Chiasmus (ABBA)** has the force of a kind of "verbal judo": it keeps the opponent's wording and reverses its meaning, using the opponent's strength to overcome him. The New Testament repeatedly uses chiasmus to express the fundamental reciprocity of its ethics ("the first shall be last, and the last first"; "Judge not, that ye be not judged"), pointing to Christian ethics' hundred-and-eighty-degree reversal of worldly values. The professional footballer's maxim about injury, "if you're hurt you don't play, and if you play you're not hurt", uses the X shape to mark out two mutually exclusive roles and rule out a middle position (playing and then blaming a poor performance on injury). Churchill in 1942 said: "Now this is not the end. It is not even the beginning of the end. But it is, perhaps, the end of the beginning", a measured consolation. On Watergate, Attorney General Mitchell said "When the going gets tough, the tough get going", which sounds rousing; but as John Dean saw, the same logic of reversal also suggests the opposite: when things get tough, the smart get going on the first bus out of town. The two meanings are flatly opposed, yet both rely on the persuasive force created by the same symmetrical geometry.

**Repetition (ABAB)** is double isocolon. A sentence to the effect that fighting against what is wrong does not by itself make you right, or the basketball coach John Wooden's "Don't let what you cannot do interfere with what you can do": equal length means equal value, the two members are parallel while their meanings cross, and the current of paradox starts to flow. This is the form of the maxim. **Climax** extends ABAB upwards or downwards. Churchill on the pilots of the Battle of Britain: "Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few". The first two terms are alike and linked by alliteration, while the third forms an opposed climax. **Enumeration** creates a world of equal integers that allows systematic search and arrangement. In Shaw's *Man and Superman*, Don Juan lists for the Devil's friends a long string of paired adjectives ("They are not beautiful: they are only decorated. They are not clean: they are only shaved and starched…"). Once a list has begun, its tacit logic is accepted: that experience can be fully described by contrasting adjectives. When the Commander, who is present, admires "your flow of words", he is looking *at* the list as a list rather than through it; praising the way an opponent's argument is expressed is the best way to belittle the argument. The list depends on a "fraudulent conversion" from number to infinity, from quantity to quality: list enough, and you seem to have grasped the essence.

**Reading: *Euphues*.** The classic home of tacit persuasion patterns is John Lyly's *Euphues* (1578). Its plot is ordinary: the prodigal hero goes to Naples, takes his best friend's sweetheart, is jilted by her and goes home repentant. But one sentence, "When parents have more care how to leave their children wealthy than wise, and are more desirous to have them maintain the name than the nature of a gentleman … it is no marvel that the son, being left rich by his father's will, become retchless by his own will", piles up alliteration, isocolon, diacope, hidden rhyme and chiasmus. Crossing the contrast of goods and godliness throws up the central moral of the sermon: those poor in goods are rich in godliness, and vice versa. The theme is stale, and Lyly has nothing new to say; he lets the tacit persuasion patterns generate meaning for him. Vernon Lee once called syntax the mould left by long-repeated acts of thought; Lyly reverses the observation: **thought becomes the mould left by endlessly repeated patterns of persuasion**. Modern readers dislike this compulsive patterning, and dislike still more the direction of its intellectual current, from pattern to thought rather than the other way round. Since the plain style that followed the scientific revolution rejected such patterning, we have believed that "thought comes first" and words merely dress it. For most of Western educational history before that, the opposite view prevailed: verbal patterns were tools for thinking and were taught as part of thinking.

*This conclusion builds a bridge between "language constitutes the world" in P3 and the level of rhetoric: thought does not come first and then seek expression; the forms available take part in generating thought. It also anticipates the problem of P5: since the persuasive power of patterns depends on the audience's "tacit" agreement, part of meaning necessarily happens in the receiver.*

### The Hermeneutic Gap: The Leap from Linguistic Fact to Literary Meaning

**Problem:** The ambitions of stylistics rest on an implicit premise: that there are objectively establishable connections between linguistic features and interpretation. In "What Is Stylistics and Why Are They Saying Such Terrible Things About It?" **Stanley Fish** pointed out that there is always a gap between the linguistic features identified in a text and the stylistician's interpretation of them, which can be called the `hermeneutic gap`. Someone notes, for instance, that a passage uses many passive constructions ("I have been told that…"): that is a linguistic fact. He then says that these passives show the text to be evasive: that is interpretation. The difficulty is establishing a connection between the two. Are people who use the passive usually evading something, concealing who told them, say, and even concealing the concealment? If the passive is evasive only *sometimes*, what conditions make it so? *(This very paragraph uses passives, "are identified", "have been told"; are they evasive?)* In reading a stylistic analysis, the key is to locate the moment at which the critic moves from describing linguistic data to interpreting it, the moment the gap opens, and to judge whether it has been convincingly crossed.

**Example: transitivity and Benjy's mind.** Traditional grammar says that a verb is transitive when the action has a definite "goal" or "object" ("she shut the door": the action of shutting "passes across" to the door), and intransitive otherwise ("she vanished"). `Transitivity`, as an abstract notion of the range of possible verb patterns, comes from the work of the linguist M. A. K. Halliday in the 1960s and 1970s. `Under-lexicalisation` is Roger Fowler's term for "a lack of a set of words adequate to express a particular concept": calling a tool whose name we don't know "that thing", or saying "the thing you hold" when we have forgotten the word "handle".

The opening of Faulkner's *The Sound and the Fury* is narrated from the perspective of Benjy, who is thirty-three but has the mind of a small child, watching golf through a fence. He sees "them" hitting, walking towards the flag, taking the flag out and putting it back; "he" hits and "the other" hits; we are never told what is hit. Fowler writes that there is a consistent oddity in the transitivity: there are hardly any transitive verbs with objects, intransitive verbs predominate overwhelmingly, and the only transitive verb, "hit", is used repeatedly without an object, ungrammatically. That is the data. Then he takes the step from description to interpretation: this oddity means that "Benjy has little conception of actions and their effects on objects". The conclusion is perhaps a little too specific, but readers do notice that something is odd about Benjy's language and register it as an oddity of his mind. Fowler's implicit argument is that it is significant that the author chose to disturb *this* linguistic feature, since in theory disturbing any feature of language could convey mental disorder. Benjy's under-lexicalisation shows in his frequent use of descriptive circumlocutions in place of the correct word: he never says "golf", and he calls a bush a "flower tree". The interpretation: this shows that the character cannot perceive the world in the socially sanctioned way most people do. Through analysis of the language associated with the character, the stylistician thereby shows the degree of his isolation.

**Example: collocation and cohesion.** `Collocation` means "the habitual or expected co-occurrence of words". Words often occur in combinations with a certain predictability, even when they are not fixed phrases. Complete without thinking "a box of …", "a black …", "an unexpected …": most people write "a box of chocolates" or "a box of matches", "a black cat", "an unexpected visitor"; twenty people will certainly not give twenty different answers. This is how each word in discourse progressively narrows the range of words that can follow. A common feature of poetry is the breaking of habitual collocations, so that words that do not normally go together suddenly meet. Analysing Auden's "The Capital", Ronald Carter notes that the poet avoids an expected collocation such as "wait patiently" and has the idle rich of the great city wait "expensively" for miracles, and that he calls the quarters where political exiles gather and plot their return to power "villages" qualified by a word of malice, whereas the usual collocates of "village" are "friendly", "picturesque", "sleepy". Carter's general point is that such "collocational clashes" mark the "thematically loaded" parts of a poem and deserve further exploration.

`Cohesion` means the lexical devices that operate across sentence boundaries, linking grammatically independent sentences into continuous discourse. Without cohesion a text goes in jerks like an old-fashioned children's reader: "This is Mandy. Mandy is my friend. Mandy and I go to the cinema together." Substituting pronouns (`pronominalisation`) removes the jerkiness: "This is Mandy. She is my friend. We go to the cinema together." Modern writers have been very interested in the effects of distorting cohesive patterns. The opening of a short story by Donald Barthelme keeps repeating the full names "Edward" and "Pia" where pronouns would be expected, so that a sequence of brief, flat sentences reports Edward looking at his beard, the couple going to Sweden, Pia finding a cheque, putting it in her coat pocket, being pregnant and vomiting every day in London. The effect also comes from the incongruity of grammatically continuous discourse framing content that is logically, conceptually and emotionally distorted and fragmented; the simple language and short sentences give the tone of a children's reader, while the subject matter is distinctly adult and traumatic. **In cases like this, it is legitimate to use linguistic techniques to explore how a particular use of language creates a particular literary effect.**

**Conclusion: what the gap means.** These examples show both the real contribution and the real limits of stylistics. It can state precisely how an effect is achieved in language (Hemingway's plainness, Benjy's isolation, Barthelme's incongruity), and in this respect it is indeed more testable than impressionistic close reading. But in every example, the step from "transitive verbs without objects" to "no conception of action", from "collocational clash" to "thematically loaded", from "passive voice" to "evasiveness" is not guaranteed by the linguistic data themselves; it needs a reader who is already interpreting. MacCabe's *womb* pushes the problem to an extreme: if only professional linguists can "see" a meaning, does that meaning exist in the text, or in the interpretive capacity of a certain class of reader? **The hermeneutic gap shows that meaning cannot be deduced from linguistic fact but is always conferred on linguistic fact by an act of interpretation.** Fish, who identified the gap, later went further: he would argue that formal features themselves are products of interpretive strategies, not the starting points of interpretation (P5).

**Conclusion:** Narratology and stylistics pushed structuralism's scientific ambition to its most operational point: functions, focalisation, levels of narration, the representation of speech, transitivity and figures of speech are all tools that can be learned and publicly tested. But at their respective edges they meet the same problem. Chatman has to borrow Austin's speech act theory to explain the narrator's "assertions" and the "pretence" of fiction; the dialogue of "Hills Like White Elephants" means something only when the reader infers its illocutionary force from everyday social knowledge; Lanham's tacit persuasion depends on the audience's tacit agreement; and every interpretation in stylistics has to cross a gap that linguistic fact cannot cross by itself. The place where meaning is produced thus moves from the structure of the text towards the people who receive it. What readers actually do in the production of meaning is the question of P5.

## P5 What Do Readers Do in the Production of Meaning? Rhetoric, Phenomenology and Reader Response

The two threads of P4 end up pointing to the same place. To explain "who is speaking", narratology had to borrow speech act theory and admit that a dialogue like "Hills Like White Elephants" means something only when readers use everyday social knowledge to infer its illocutionary force; every interpretation in stylistics had to cross a hermeneutic gap that linguistic fact cannot cross by itself. The question becomes: if meaning cannot be deduced from the text, how is it produced at the receiving end? Is the reader a consumer of meaning, a collaborator, or a producer? And who is the reader: a universal mind, a consciousness in history, a member of a community, or a class position?

The anthology's editors state at the outset that what is brought together here are two sides of reading: the production of verbal acts called rhetoric, and the reception of those acts in reading and interpretation. The dialogical structure of the literary text demands attention to both: rhetoric organises language for readers; it invites and solicits their response. In the six-layer framework this is the reader dimension of Layer 1, and its chain runs: Austin → Fish → interpretive communities → Bourdieu. It inherits "language constitutes the world" from P3 (where the performative utterance was already mentioned) and the analysis of speech acts and the hermeneutic gap from P4, and it stands in direct opposition to the New Criticism of P2: New Criticism declared the "affective fallacy" out of bounds, while reader theorists treat readers' responses and interpretations as the source of meaning. The fifth of the mechanisms that run throughout, the `shifting boundary between text and context`, here becomes a theme for the first time: the boundary of the text will be pushed outwards again and again, until "the text" itself becomes a function of reading practices. *(Foucault's remark in P3 that a book "is a node within a network" already anticipated this.)*

**Background: how the audience was forgotten and rediscovered.** Aristotle was one of the first critics to notice that the effects of a literary work are as striking as its causes: the success of tragedy lies less in formal perfection than in the emotional transformation it works on the audience. The turns of the tragic plot are also turns in the audience's feelings; spectators move with the hero from blindness to recognition, a turn at once cognitive and a matter of emotional sympathy. *(This is the other side of "recognition" in P4: narratology treats it as an element of plot; here it is the audience's experience.)* Later aesthetics, especially Romantic aesthetics, pushed the connection between work and audience aside, stressing the writer's genius in uniting ideal and real, universal and concrete within the work; attention shifted from the psychological and emotional link between work and audience to the inner harmony or organic unity of the work itself. These theories were Platonic rather than Aristotelian. *(The "organic unity" and "concrete universal" of New Criticism in P2 are heirs of this tradition.)* Two schools of thought brought the audience back into theory. One was the historical school of the eighteenth century, which held that to understand older texts one had to reconstruct the context in which they were first written; whom a work was written for determined in part how it should be interpreted in retrospect. The other was the philosophy of Kant.

### The A Priori Structures of the Mind: Why Kant and Husserl Turned to the Observer

**Problem:** Why does a theory of reading need to start from epistemology? Because once part of the form of an object is held to come from the knower, one has to ask which part, and how. This is the philosophical prehistory of reader theory.

**Definition: appearance and the thing in itself.** In the *Critique of Pure Reason* (1781) **Immanuel Kant** argued that the mind is an active constructor of our knowledge of the world. Earlier philosophers had noticed the role of experience (the mind's empirical sensations of objects) in forming concepts, but had failed to account for the mind's own `a priori` operations, which take place before experience and make experience possible. The central claim of the Transcendental Aesthetic is that all our intuition is nothing but the representation of `appearance`; the things we intuit are not in themselves what we intuit them as being; and if we removed the subject, or even only the subjective constitution of the senses, the whole constitution and all the relations of objects in space and time, and indeed space and time themselves, would vanish. What objects may be apart from our receptivity, the `thing in itself`, remains wholly unknown to us; we know only our own way of perceiving them, a way shared by every human being but not necessarily by every being. **Space and time are the pure forms of this way of perceiving; sensation is its matter.** The former can be known a priori, before any actual perception, and is called `pure intuition`; the latter makes knowledge a posteriori, empirical intuition. Even if we raised our intuition to the highest degree of clarity, we would come no closer to the constitution of objects in themselves; we would only know our own receptivity more completely.

**Mechanism: the difference is transcendental, not logical.** Kant here opposes the philosophy of Leibniz and Wolff, which treated the difference between the sensible and the intellectual as merely logical: sensible representations are confused intellectual ones, containing the properties of things in themselves, which we simply fail to distinguish clearly. Kant thought this sent all inquiry into knowledge in the wrong direction. The difference is plainly `transcendental`: it concerns not clarity and confusion but origin and content. It is not that through sensibility we know things in themselves only confusedly; we do not know them in any way at all. The rainbow illustrates the point. In the everyday sense the rainbow is appearance and the rain the thing in itself; but raise the question to the transcendental level and we find that not only the raindrops are appearances, but their round shape, and even the space in which they fall, are not things in themselves but modifications or basic forms of our sensible intuition.

**Evidence: geometry.** Kant's argument is that geometrical propositions are synthetic a priori and are known with necessary certainty. Take the proposition "two straight lines cannot enclose a space" and try to derive it from the concepts of "straight line" and "two": it is futile. You have to turn to intuition, and this intuition cannot be empirical, since experience never yields necessity and universality. So there must be a faculty of a priori intuition, and this subjective condition must at the same time be the universal a priori condition under which external objects are possible; otherwise you could not say that what lies in you as the subjective condition of constructing a triangle must necessarily belong to the triangle itself. It follows that space and time, as the necessary conditions of all outer and inner experience, are merely subjective conditions of all our intuition, and that relative to these conditions all objects are mere appearances.

**Distinction: appearance ≠ illusion.** Kant takes care to clarify that saying objects are appearances is not saying they are illusions: in appearance, objects and their properties are always regarded as something actually given; it is only that, in the relation between the given object and the subject, these properties depend on the subject's mode of intuition. It is precisely by taking these forms of representation for objective realities that one turns everything into illusion, as "the good Berkeley" reduced bodies to mere illusion. One more detail deserves notice: everything in our knowledge that belongs to intuition contains nothing but relations (positions in an intuition, changes of position, laws according to which change is determined), and a thing in itself cannot be known through mere relations. *This sentence echoes, across the distance, Saussure's "in language there are only differences" in P3: both limit what can be known to relations and leave "the thing itself" outside the system. The difference is that Kant's relations are guaranteed by universal forms of the mind, Saussure's by an arbitrary social system.*

**Application: what an audience brings to *King Lear*.** For literary criticism, one consequence of Kant's argument is that the mind comes to literature already prepared to follow the logic of a narrative or a verse form, to form judgements, to assign or derive meaning. There may be an object called *King Lear* existing independently in the world, but its being constructed as an ordered narrative presupposes certain capacities in the audience: they must be able to recognise the play's temporal structure as a unity, and perceive this display of literary signs as a coherent order. The editors divide these a priori operations into two kinds. One is universal, having to do with following the logic of a temporal narrative and recognising the spatial positions of characters from scene to scene. The other is more socially and historically specific, and so variable: varying with gender (some women might find Goneril more attractive than Cordelia), or with geography (in a country that has suffered under tyrants, Lear's downfall might be a happy rather than a tragic resolution). *"Socially and historically specific a priori judgements" is almost a contradiction in Kant's terms: what makes the a priori a priori is its universality and necessity. The editors' extension marks exactly the direction of the whole movement of reader theory: historicising and socialising Kant's transcendental forms step by step, until Bourdieu rewrites them as embodied class schemes.*

**Definition: the natural standpoint and the horizon of consciousness.** Kant's inquiry into how the mind shapes knowledge was continued in the early twentieth century by **Edmund Husserl**. His *Ideas* (1913), a general introduction to pure phenomenology, made consciousness and its operations its object, and became the source of the phenomenological literary criticism of the mid-century, which studied the movements of consciousness in literary texts. Husserl begins from the `natural standpoint`, with a series of simple first-person meditations. I am aware of a world spread out endlessly in space and endlessly becoming in time; I discover it immediately and intuitively, I experience it; things are "simply there for me", whether or not I pay them particular attention. Around what is actually perceived lies a fringe of the *co-present*, more or less clear or dim, distinct or obscure, forming a continuous ring around the field of perception; beyond that lies a dimly apprehended, indeterminate depth or fringe of reality, which I can penetrate to varying degrees with the beam of attention, but a hazy `horizon` that can never be fully outlined necessarily remains. Time is the same: every waking "now" has its temporal horizon stretching endlessly in both directions.

More importantly, this world is not for me merely a world of facts; it is there with the same immediacy as a *world of values*, a *world of goods*, a *practical world*. Without further effort on my part, the things before me carry not only qualities appropriate to their positive nature but value characters such as beautiful or ugly, agreeable or disagreeable; they stand there as things for use: the book on the desk, the drinking glass, the vase, the piano. The people around me are "friends" or "enemies", "servants" or "superiors", "strangers" or "relatives". Others are ego-subjects like me; I grasp their surrounding worlds and mine objectively as one and the same world, which affects each consciousness differently. Each sees things appear differently from his own place, and yet we come to an understanding with our neighbours and jointly posit an objective spatio-temporal world of fact. Husserl calls all this the `general thesis of the natural standpoint`: the world is always there, and every doubt and rejection leaves this thesis untouched, at most striking "illusions" and "hallucinations" out of it. *The anthology's extract is titled "The Thesis of the Natural Standpoint and Its Suspension", and it stops at the threshold of that suspension: Husserl will put the thesis in brackets and turn to describing conscious experience itself; every experience in the "stream of experience" that can be grasped in reflection has an essence that can be intuited.*

**Conclusion: why the observer cannot be bypassed.** Kant and Husserl reach the same conclusion from different directions: **the object known is already an object constituted by the forms or acts of consciousness of the knower.** For Kant, what constitutes the object is the universal forms of space and time; for Husserl, the world is given within the horizon of consciousness and always already carries value and practical characters. For literature, this means that any description of a work must include how the work is grasped by a consciousness. But both imagine this consciousness as structurally the same in everyone: Kant's forms are shared by all, and Husserl seeks pure ideas possible only in consciousness. This leaves the next question: is the observer also in history?

### The Historicity of Interpretation: From Phenomenology to Hermeneutics

**Mechanism: a compromise between historicism and Kantianism.** The anthology's editors describe the shift from phenomenology to hermeneutics as a compromise between the two schools mentioned above. Other philosophers in the same tradition, especially Heidegger and Gadamer, found a compromise between the historicist position and the Kantian one: knowledge takes place in time and history, and cannot attain the transcendence that Husserl in particular longed for. **All knowledge is interpretation, the carrying of meaning from one moment of history to another, and this carrying always affects what is known through the categories and assumptions of the later moment.** In *Truth and Method* Gadamer even held that, for this reason, all knowledge is necessarily tinged with error. *A three-way relation can be seen here. The historical school wanted to recover a text's meaning by reconstructing its original context and audience; the New Criticism of P2 dismissed context and audience alike as fallacies, leaving only the text; hermeneutics both grants the importance of context and denies the possibility of reconstructing a pure original context, because the reconstructor also stands in history. Husserl's "horizon" here acquires temporal depth: the horizon of the one who understands is itself historical.*

**Background: phenomenological criticism.** The leap from these philosophical conclusions to an understanding of the role of the reader's cognition in the work of art was made by Georges Poulet and Roman Ingarden. Poulet's phenomenological literary criticism, especially *The Metamorphoses of the Circle* (1961), carried the importance of the reader's experience of the literary work into American criticism; Ingarden's *The Cognition of the Literary Work of Art* argued for an essential connection between the work of the audience and the work itself. The American critic most responsible for spreading the idea that the reader's experience matters as much as the intrinsic qualities of the work was Stanley Fish, discussed in detail below.
