The feared father and the desired lover are then *condensed* into a single dream image. The two devices have a double aim. One is to disguise repressed fears and wishes so that they can get past the `censorship` that normally prevents them from surfacing, like someone barred from a club who gets in by dressing up as someone else. The other is to work this material up into something that can be represented in a dream, that is, into images, symbols and metaphors, since dreams do not "say" things but "show" them. **It is precisely at this point that dreams are very like literature**, and this is the fundamental reason literary criticism is interested in Freudian interpretation. *(The popular "Freudian" interpretation that reads every tower and ladder as a phallic symbol was a joke even in Freud's lifetime; actual Freudian interpretation is often extremely ingenious rather than simple.)*

**Example: the dream of the botanical monograph.** One of Freud's own dreams: "I had written a monograph on a certain plant. The book lay before me and I was at the moment turning over a folded coloured plate. Bound up in each copy there was a dried specimen of the plant, as though it had been taken from a herbarium." The morning before, he had seen in a bookshop window a new book on the genus *Cyclamen*, evidently a *monograph* on the plant. Cyclamens were his wife's favourite flowers, and he reproached himself for so seldom remembering to bring her flowers; "bringing flowers" reminded him of a woman whose husband had forgotten to give her flowers on her birthday, an anecdote he had used to show that forgetting is often determined by an unconscious purpose. He had indeed written something like a "monograph on a plant": a paper on the coca plant, which had drawn Karl Koller's attention to the anaesthetic properties of cocaine, an application Freud himself had not pursued to the end. The word "botanical" connected with Professor Gärtner (whose name means "gardener"), his wife's "blooming" looks, a woman patient called Flora, and the woman who had been forgotten on her birthday; "monograph" touched on the one-sidedness of his studies and the costliness of his favourite hobbies. All the chains of association finally led to an interrupted conversation of the previous evening with the eye surgeon Königstein. The meaning of the dream then emerged: it was a *self-justification*, a plea for his own rights: "after all, I am the man who wrote the valuable and memorable paper (on cocaine)", "I may allow myself this".

**Mechanism: nodal points and overdetermination.** This dream shows the structure of condensation. "Botanical" and "monograph" found their way into the content of the dream because they had copious contacts with most of the dream-thoughts, forming `nodal points` upon which a great number of dream-thoughts converged, and so having several meanings in interpretation. In other words, every element of the dream is `overdetermined`, represented many times over in the dream-thoughts. *(The term was later borrowed by Althusser to describe the structure of social contradictions; see P9.)* Another of Freud's examples is the "beautiful dream" of a patient suffering from claustrophobia. He was driving with a large party to X Street, where there was an unpretentious inn in which a play was being performed; he was now audience, now actor; afterwards there was a quarrel between the people upstairs and the people downstairs; finally he climbed laboriously up a slope, and only at the top did it become easy. "Inn" connected with a small hotel near that street where he had once stayed for the sake of an actress, and, through a poem by Uhland and the lines in *Faust* about "a lovely apple tree, two lovely apples", with women's breasts: for an infant, the wet-nurse's breast is an inn. The climb that turns from hard to easy reverses the opening scene of Daudet's *Sapho*, where a young man carries his mistress upstairs and she grows heavier the higher he goes; "upstairs/downstairs" reverses the actual social standing of himself and his brother (in Vienna, saying someone is "on the ground floor" meant his family had come down in the world). A single dream image points at once to a recently abandoned mistress, a childhood wet-nurse and an adult social anxiety. Condensation can even work on a single word. Freud dreamed the sentence "This is written in a positively norekdal style"; the strange word parodies German superlatives such as *kolossal* and *pyramidal*, and is put together from the names Nora and Ekdal, characters in two of Ibsen's plays (*A Doll's House* and *The Wild Duck*).

**Mechanism: displacement and the transference of psychical intensities.** Displacement reveals another relation: the elements most prominent in the manifest content of a dream do not necessarily play the same part in the dream-thoughts, and conversely the essence of the dream-thoughts may not be represented in the dream at all. The dream and the dream-thoughts "are differently centred". Freud's explanation is that a psychical force is at work in the dream-work which, on the one hand, strips elements of high psychical value of their intensity and, on the other, by means of overdetermination, creates new values from elements of low value: this is the "transference and displacement of psychical intensities". Its condition is that the elements that enter the dream must escape the censorship imposed by resistance.

**Definition: manifest and latent content.** From this follows the most important distinction in psychoanalysis: between the `manifest content` of the dream (what the dream itself presents) and its `latent content` (the dream-thoughts). They are like two versions of the same subject matter in two languages: the dream-content is a transcript of the dream-thoughts into another mode of expression, written in a kind of "pictographic script" whose characters must be translated one by one into the language of the dream-thoughts; reading the characters according to their pictorial value rather than their symbolic relation would be a mistake. Freud's image is the `rebus`. A picture showing a house with a boat on its roof, a single letter of the alphabet, a running figure whose head has been conjured away, and so on, is absurd as a landscape painting: a boat has no business on a roof, a headless man cannot run, letters do not occur in nature. But replace each element by the syllable or word it can somehow represent, and the elements may form a poetical phrase of the greatest beauty and significance. **A dream is a rebus, and earlier interpreters of dreams erred in treating the rebus as a pictorial composition.** *This image is the direct starting point of Lacan's "the unconscious is structured like a language": Freud himself demanded that dreams be taken "to the letter".*

**Example: *aliquis*.** *The Psychopathology of Everyday Life* (subtitled "Forgetting, Slips of the Tongue, Bungled Actions, Superstitions and Errors") studies the `parapraxis`, popularly the "Freudian slip". Its premise is that when a wish, fear or memory is hard to face, we may clear it from consciousness by repression, but it does not disappear; like radioactive material buried on the seabed, it stays active in the unconscious, constantly seeking a way back into consciousness, and it always succeeds. In Freud's famous phrase, **"the repressed always returns"**. Slips of the tongue and pen, forgotten names, and "accidents" such as unwrapping a sweet, putting the wrapper in one's mouth and throwing the sweet away, are signs of repressed material finding its way back. On holiday Freud met a young scholar, Jewish like himself, and they talked about the antisemitism that might hold back their careers. The young man passionately quoted the line Virgil gives to Dido when Aeneas abandons her, *Exoriare aliquis nostris ex ossibus ultor* ("Let someone arise from my bones as an avenger"), but left out *aliquis* ("someone"). Freud corrected the quotation, and the young man, who had read Freud's work, challenged him to explain the forgetting. Freud told him to direct his attention to the forgotten word and say "candidly and uncritically" whatever occurred to him. The associations ran: words of similar sound, *relics*, *liquefying*, *fluidity*, *fluid*; Simon of Trent, whose relics he had seen a few years before; an Italian newspaper article entitled "What St Augustine Says Concerning Women"; St Januarius, whose blood is kept in a phial in a church in Naples and miraculously liquefies on a certain holy day, and "people get very agitated if it's delayed". Freud pointed out that both saints, Januarius and Augustine, have names closely bound up with the calendar (*Januarius* and January, *Augustine* and August). The young man, embarrassed, said that he had suddenly thought of a young lady from whom he might hear a piece of news that would be awkward for them both. Freud asked: "That her periods have stopped?" and explained how he knew: think of the calendar saints, the blood that starts to flow on a particular day, the agitation when the event fails to take place. Saying *aliquis* would have reminded him of this anxiety again, so his unconscious protected him by deleting the word from his conscious memory. *(Whether this example is credible will be tested in the discussion of evidence.)*

**Mechanism: symptoms and defences.** Neurotic symptoms work like dreams: they displace unconscious desires, anxieties or drive energy onto expressive activities or obsessive thoughts, performing various "translation procedures" on unconscious material. `Compromise formation` constructs an indirect expression that both releases unacceptable drive energy and respects the commands of repression; someone brought up in a religious setting that strictly forbids sexual activity might, for instance, perform the forbidden sexual act in a ritualised form, appearing to observe the norm while obtaining satisfaction. `Inversion` turns a desire or impulse into its opposite: someone who feels intense hostility towards a cold, distant mother might turn this feeling into a fantasy that all women are themselves hostile and so unworthy of his love. Dreams contain inversion too. A woman dreams that she cannot prepare a smoked-salmon supper for a friend; the dream has nothing to do with food but points to a wish not to help her friend grow plumper and more attractive to her own husband, who had remarked that very day that he found the friend attractive for her plumpness. *(The dream fulfils a wish in the guise of a wish not fulfilled.)* Other important terms include: `fixation`, in which anxiety about entering the adult world keeps some people at an earlier stage of development, still drawing satisfaction from early forms of emotional and sexual activity; `splitting`, dividing an object of anxiety in two, one bearing all the negative feeling and the other embodying all the positive, as when a child directs all its hostility at one parent and idealises the other; `introjection`, taking something of another person into oneself, creating an ideal of that person within; and `projection`, throwing out something inside oneself (usually a negative desire or hostility) so that it appears to be a characteristic of someone else. These can be grouped together as `defence mechanisms`, psychical procedures for avoiding painful admissions. In the same family are `transference`, in which the patient redirects towards the analyst feelings recalled in analysis (past hostility or resentment towards a parental figure, for instance, reactivated but aimed at the analyst), and the `screen memory`, a trivial, irrelevant memory whose function is to screen out a more important one.

**Conclusion:** At the heart of Freud's model is a double structure full of tension: the repressed does not disappear; it can return only in disguise, in dreams, slips and symptoms. The means of disguise (displacement, condensation, inversion, considerations of representability) are essentially "rhetorical": they turn abstract ideas and feelings into concrete images. **Dreams, like literature, make no explicit statements, but convey meaning indirectly through the concrete embodiments of time, place and character.** This analogy is both the strength of psychoanalytic criticism and its risk: since meaning is never stated, deciding which latent content is the "real" one always involves the interpreter's judgement.

### Oedipus, Drives and Repetition: Freud's Theory of Sexuality

**Background: repression and civilisation.** Freud held that much of our mental life derives from biological drives, and that the highest achievements and ideals of civilisation are inseparable from instinctual impulses that seek pleasure, constancy and the release of excitation and energy. Every child, growing up first into a family and then into society, learns to repress these drives and the conscious desires they give rise to, shaping aggressive and sexual impulses, and the initial grandiose sense of self, to fit the demands of living with others. **Repression is the necessary condition of civilisation, the transformation of animal instinct into civilised behaviour; but repression also produces in each of us a second self, a stranger within ourselves.**

**Mechanism: primary and secondary processes.** Freud spent his life studying the boundary and the dynamic movement between the conscious ego and the unconscious, which he later called the id. The id is the seat of psychic energy, made up of sexual `libido` and other instincts such as aggression, driving the organism to grow, develop and finally die. This `primary process` is entirely irrational: it cannot distinguish images from things, reasonable objects from unreasonable or socially unacceptable ones. The `secondary process`, located in the ego and the super-ego (conscience), brings reason, order, logic and social acceptability to the realm of the drives. Repressed drives can never be wholly pacified. They appear in dreams; when the rational part of the mind fails to handle them, they appear in the apparently irrational behaviour of neurosis (phobias, groundless anxieties, compulsions); and when conscious control breaks down altogether and drives and unconscious contents are expressed directly, without the mediation of consciousness, we enter the realm of psychosis or schizophrenia. **Distinction:** neurosis still maintains a relation to external reality; in psychosis that relation is completely broken.

**Definition: infantile sexuality and the stages of the libido.** The idea of `infantile sexuality` is that sexuality does not begin with physical maturity at puberty but in infancy, especially through the infant's relation to the mother. In classical Freudian theory the libido focuses in turn on three stages: the `oral`, the `anal` and the `phallic`. Sexual energy is far from merely genital; it can also be oral or anal, and it can be displaced onto `fetish` objects, substitutes that replace an object of early desire so as to avoid anxiety or respond to trauma. **Example:** in a famous case, an obsessional neurotic known as the "Wolf Man" (because he dreamed of wolves in a tree staring at him) developed a sexually invested fondness for military uniforms and discipline in response to early traumatic experiences concerning sexual identity; anxiety led him to turn his sexual drive away from human objects towards fetishistic substitutes.

**Definition: the Oedipus complex.** At the centre of Freud's theory of sexuality is the so-called `Oedipus complex`, which he believed all children go through as a rite of passage into adult gender identity. All boys have an early attachment to the mother which is sexual in nature; the male infant develops a desire to eliminate the father and become the mother's sexual partner. Only the father's intervention, separating mother and child, prevents incest; **all civilisation is founded on the prohibition expressed by the father's intervention.** The boy learns to give up his first, "pre-Oedipal" desires and attachments, identifying instead with the father (no longer wanting to be the father who is with the mother), learning to desire women other than the mother, and becoming an adult heterosexual male, Freud's implicit norm. Freudians see many intergenerational conflicts as having an Oedipal colouring, treating professional rivalry, for example, as a re-enactment of siblings competing for parental favour. For girls, the anthology's introduction gives a formulation symmetrical with the boy's: the girl experiences an early desire for the father, which also takes the form of a desire to *be* the mother, to replace her as the father's sexual object; but she too learns to give up this desire, identifies with the mother and seeks an object outside the family. *This symmetrical model was Freud's original assumption; the extension of psychoanalysis to gender will show that Freud later overturned it himself, and that Chodorow rebuilt the theory of gender from that revision.* **Limitation:** as the very concept of the Oedipus complex suggests, Freud's theory often carries a deep androcentric bias; as was usual at the time, Freud was mainly concerned with the boy's Oedipal trajectory, which is why it is called Oedipus and not Clytemnestra or Medea.

**Mechanism: identification, wanting to be and wanting to have.** The key process in the formation of gender is `identification`: shaping the ego by internalising the image or model of an external object, establishing an equation between oneself and that object. *Group Psychology and the Analysis of the Ego* (1921) gives its clearest formulation. Identification is the earliest expression of an emotional tie with another person, and it plays a part in the early history of the Oedipus complex. A little boy shows a special interest in his father; he would like to grow like him and be like him, and take his place everywhere; he takes his father as his ideal. This behaviour has nothing to do with a passive or feminine attitude towards the father. At the same time, or a little later, he begins to develop a true `object-cathexis` towards his mother according to the attachment type. The two ties exist side by side for a while, until the irresistible advance towards a unification of mental life brings them together, and the Oedipus complex arises. Freud gives a concise formula: in identification with the father, the father is what one would like to *be*; in choosing the father as an object, he is what one would like to *have*. The first tie attaches to the subject of the ego, the second to its object, which is why identification is possible before any sexual object choice has been made. **Example: identification in symptoms.** A little girl develops the same painful symptom as her mother, the same tormenting cough. If this identification comes from the Oedipus complex, it signifies a hostile wish to take her mother's place, and the symptom expresses her object-love for her father. A third, particularly frequent and important kind of symptom formation leaves any object relation to the person copied entirely out of account. In a boarding school, a girl receives a letter from someone with whom she is secretly in love; it arouses her jealousy, and she reacts with a fit of hysterics; some of her friends who know about it catch the fit by "mental infection". The mechanism is identification based on the possibility of, or wish for, "putting oneself in the same situation": the other girls would also like a secret love affair, and under the influence of a sense of guilt they accept the suffering that goes with it too. It would be wrong to think they took on the symptom out of sympathy; **on the contrary, sympathy arises out of identification.** Freud's summary: first, identification is the original form of emotional tie with an object; second, in a regressive way it can become a substitute for a libidinal object tie, as it were by the introjection of the object into the ego; third, it may arise with any new perception of a common quality shared with some other person who is not an object of the sexual instinct.

**Another assessment: is the castration complex credible?** In their headnote to this selection, the anthology's editors pass a sharp judgement on one of Freud's central concepts: "castration" and the "castration complex" are "very dubious notions", which wrongly turn historically specific, local cultural anecdotes about threatening children into principles of psychology and anthropology. In a more sociological explanation already hinted at in Freud, so-called "castration anxiety" can be seen as a misreading or misnaming of an anxiety any young person feels on entering adult sexual life: an anxiety about loss, and more about whether one can meet the social ideals of adult sexual identity. One way of attaining adult identity is to identify with father or mother and try to emulate them. *This judgement points in the same direction as Barry's charge of a "deep androcentric bias" in Freud, but places the problem differently: Barry points to a bias, while the editors offer a de-biologised alternative explanation, rewriting Freud's theory as a theory of identification and social ideals.*

**Mechanism: narcissism and the ego ideal.** "On Narcissism" (1914) deals with another kind of internalisation. People are unwilling to give up the narcissistic perfection of childhood, when they were their own ideal; when the admonitions of others and the awakening of their own critical judgement prevent them from keeping it, they try to regain it in the new form of an `ego ideal`: **what they project before them as their ideal is the substitute for the lost narcissism of their childhood.** There is an important distinction here. `Sublimation` concerns object-libido and refers to the instinct's turning towards an aim remote from sexual satisfaction; the emphasis is on deflection from sexuality. `Idealisation` concerns the object, which, without any change in its nature, is enlarged and exalted in the subject's mind. A person who has exchanged his narcissism for homage to a high ego ideal has not necessarily succeeded in sublimating his libidinal instincts: the ideal can demand sublimation but cannot enforce it, and it is precisely in neurotics that the gap between the formation of the ego ideal and the degree of sublimation is widest. The psychical agency that watches the actual ego and measures it by the ideal is what we call `conscience`. The "delusion of being watched" presents this power in regressive form and reveals its origin: conscience first embodied the criticism of the parents (conveyed through the *voice*), to which was later added the criticism of teachers and society. *The editors point out that this anticipates post-Freudian developments: the object-relations school will reinterpret the ego ideal as an internalisation modelled on the parents, and Lacan will rewrite it as the "ideal ego" of the mirror stage.*

**Mechanism: beyond the pleasure principle.** Libido is part of a more general drive that the later Freud called `Eros`, roughly the life instinct; its opposite is `Thanatos`, roughly the death instinct, a concept that is of course contested. *Beyond the Pleasure Principle* (1920) is Freud's attempt to face the recognition that something more than the pursuit of pleasure seems to be at work in the mind and in life. **Example: *fort/da*.** A boy of one and a half was not precocious in intellect and could say only a few words, but he was praised as a "good boy": he did not disturb his parents at night, conscientiously obeyed orders not to touch certain things, and above all never cried when his mother left him for a few hours, although he was greatly attached to her. He had a disturbing habit of throwing any small objects he could get hold of into a corner or under the bed, while uttering a long-drawn-out "o-o-o-o" with an expression of interest and satisfaction, which his mother and the observer agreed stood for the German *fort* ("gone"). One day he had a wooden reel with a piece of string tied round it. It never occurred to him to pull it along the floor behind him and play at its being a carriage; instead he held the reel by the string and very skilfully threw it over the edge of his curtained cot so that it disappeared, saying "o-o-o-o"; then he pulled it out again by the string and hailed its reappearance with a joyful *da* ("there"). The complete game was disappearance and return. **Reading:** the game is related to the child's great "cultural achievement", the instinctual renunciation of allowing his mother to go away without protesting; he compensated himself by staging, with objects within reach, their disappearance and return. The question is this: his mother's departure cannot have been agreeable or even indifferent to him, so how does repeating this distressing experience as a game fit with the `pleasure principle`? Freud considered two answers. First, at the outset the child was in a passive situation, overpowered by the experience; by repeating it as a game, unpleasurable though it was, he took on an active part, which might be attributed to an instinct for mastery acting independently of whether the memory was pleasurable. Second, throwing the object away so that it was "gone" might satisfy an impulse suppressed in actual life, to revenge himself on his mother for going away: "All right, then, go away! I don't need you. I'm sending you away myself." A year later the same child, when angry with a toy, would throw it to the floor exclaiming "Go to the front!" He had heard that his absent father was "at the front", was far from regretting it, and made it quite clear that he did not want to be disturbed in his sole possession of his mother. Freud admitted that no certain conclusion can be drawn from a single case. He added an observation important for literary theory: the artistic play and artistic imitation of adults differ from children's play in being aimed at an audience; they do not spare the audience (in tragedy, for instance) the most painful experiences, yet can be felt as highly enjoyable. This proves that even under the dominance of the pleasure principle there are ways enough of making what is in itself unpleasurable a subject to be recollected and worked over in the mind. *This puts the question of tragic pleasure from Aristotle at the start of P5 back into the "economics" of psychoanalysis.*

**Mechanism: the compulsion to repeat.** The more crucial evidence comes from treatment. The patient cannot remember the whole of what is repressed, and what he cannot remember may be precisely the essential part; he is obliged to *repeat* the repressed material as a present experience, instead of *remembering* it as something belonging to the past, as the physician would like. This is the `compulsion to repeat`. The repressed itself offers no resistance to treatment; its only effort is to break through the pressure weighing on it into consciousness. Resistance comes from the ego, which operates under the pleasure principle and seeks to avoid the unpleasure that the liberation of the repressed would bring. Most of what is re-experienced under the compulsion to repeat causes the ego unpleasure, but this does not contradict the pleasure principle: unpleasure for one system is simultaneously satisfaction for the other. **The new and remarkable fact is that the compulsion to repeat also recalls from the past experiences that include no possibility of pleasure, and that can never, even long ago, have brought satisfaction to instinctual impulses.** The early efflorescence of infantile sexual life is doomed to extinction and comes to an end in the most distressing circumstances; loss of love and failure leave a permanent injury to self-regard, a "narcissistic scar". Patients repeat all these unwanted situations and painful emotions in the `transference` with great ingenuity: they contrive to break off the treatment while it is still incomplete, contrive to feel scorned once more, oblige the physician to treat them coldly and harshly. The same compulsion appears in the lives of some normal people, who give the impression of being pursued by a malignant fate or possessed by some "daemonic" power; but psychoanalysis has always held that their fate is for the most part arranged by themselves and determined by early infantile influences. There is the benefactor abandoned in anger by each of his protégés; the man whose every friendship ends in betrayal by his friend; the man who time after time raises someone into a position of authority and then overthrows him himself; the lover whose every love affair passes through the same phases and reaches the same conclusion. Still more impressive are cases of passive experience: a woman married three husbands in succession, each of whom fell ill soon after the wedding and had to be nursed by her on his deathbed. The most moving poetic picture of such a fate is in Tasso's *Gerusalemme liberata*. The hero Tancred unwittingly kills his beloved Clorinda in a duel while she is disguised in the armour of an enemy knight. After her burial he makes his way into a magic forest that terrifies the Crusaders; he slashes with his sword at a tall tree, blood streams from the cut, and the voice of Clorinda, whose soul is imprisoned in the tree, complains that he has wounded his beloved once again. Freud thus finds courage to assume that **there really does exist in the mind a compulsion to repeat which overrides the pleasure principle**, and connects with it the dreams of traumatic neurosis and the impulse that leads children to play; but he also cautions that the effects of a pure compulsion to repeat can rarely be observed, since it is always interwoven with other motives.

**Implication:** Repetition thereby becomes a central category of psychoanalytic reading. The narratological reading of "The Oval Portrait" in P4 already speculated that the stylistically uniform paintings in the house might all be by the same painter, each made at the cost of the model's life, in a compulsively repeated "primal scene" in which art and life struggle for supremacy. This is one route from narrative technique to the compulsion to repeat. "The Uncanny" will show that repetition is itself a source of aesthetic effect; trauma theory will move the cause of repetition from repressed wishes to unassimilated reality.

### The Uncanny: The Stranger in the Most Familiar

**Problem:** "The Uncanny" (1919) is one of Freud's best-known literary essays, partly a reading of E. T. A. Hoffmann's horror story "The Sandman", and it can be said to have founded psychoanalytic literary criticism as a genre. Critics often use "uncanny" to discuss things that seem to slip outside normal perception or normal assumptions; in Freud it refers to the effects of the unconscious, which startle us precisely because we do not know the unconscious is at work, and so produce the feeling of the "uncanny". The question is: what kind of thing frightens us in this particular way?

**Definition: starting from the meaning of the word.** `The uncanny` (*das Unheimliche*, literally "unhomely") is obviously the opposite of *heimlich* and *heimisch* ("familiar", "native", "belonging to the home"), and one is tempted to conclude that the uncanny is frightening precisely because it is unknown and unfamiliar. But not everything new and unfamiliar is frightening; the relation cannot be reversed. **Ernst Jentsch**, who had studied the question before, did not get beyond the equation "uncanny ≈ novel and unfamiliar"; he attributed the essential factor in the feeling of uncanniness to *intellectual uncertainty*: the uncanny is always something one does not know one's way about in, and the better oriented one is in one's environment, the less readily one has the impression of uncanniness. Freud thought this definition incomplete. He first consulted dictionaries of other languages, with little result (Latin *locus suspectus*, "a suspicious place"; English "haunted (house)"; Arabic and Hebrew words for "daemonic"), and so returned to German. Sanders's dictionary of 1860 showed that *heimlich* belongs to two sets of ideas, not contradictory but very different: on the one hand what belongs to the home, is not strange, familiar, tame, intimate, comfortable; on the other what is concealed and kept out of sight, kept secret from others. Grimm's dictionary showed further that from the idea of "belonging to the home" developed the idea of "something withdrawn from the eyes of strangers", hence hidden, secret; applied to knowledge, mystical, allegorical; and further still, the idea of "something hidden and dangerous" gave *heimlich* the meaning usually ascribed to *unheimlich*: "At times I feel like a man who walks in the night and believes in ghosts; every corner is heimlich and full of terrors for him." **Conclusion:** *heimlich* is a word whose meaning develops in the direction of ambivalence until it finally coincides with its opposite; **unheimlich is in some way a sub-species of heimlich**. Schelling's definition then comes into view: the uncanny is everything that ought to have remained secret and hidden but has come to light. *(Note the method of this argument: before offering a psychological explanation, Freud finds a "coincidence of opposites" in the history of language. Lacan would later say that every third page of Freud's collected works refers to philology, and this is a typical example.)*

**Reading: "The Sandman".** One good example Jentsch gives is doubt whether an apparently animate being is really alive, or conversely whether a lifeless object might not in fact be animate: waxwork figures, ingeniously constructed dolls and automata. He held that one of the most successful devices for creating uncanny effects in storytelling is to leave the reader uncertain whether a particular figure is a human being or an automaton, without focusing attention directly on the uncertainty, lest the reader clear it up and the effect dissipate; Hoffmann used the device repeatedly. Freud agreed with the observation but held that the theme of the doll Olympia, who appears to be alive, is by no means the most important element in "The Sandman"; Hoffmann even treats the Olympia episode with a touch of satire, mocking the young man's idealisation of his beloved. The theme of the story is what gives it its name and recurs at every critical moment: the Sandman who tears out children's eyes. The student Nathaniel cannot shake off childhood memories bound up with the mysterious and terrible death of his beloved father. On certain evenings his mother would send the children to bed early, warning them that "the Sandman is coming", and he would always hear the heavy tread of a visitor with whom his father spent the evening. His mother denied that there was a Sandman, saying it was only a figure of speech; but his nurse told him that the Sandman was a wicked man who came when children would not go to bed and threw handfuls of sand in their eyes so that they jumped out of their heads bleeding, then put the eyes in a sack and carried them off to the half-moon to feed his children, who had hooked beaks. Nathaniel hid in his father's study and recognised the visitor as the lawyer Coppelius, whom all the children feared, and identified him with the Sandman. His father and the guest were at work over a brazier; Coppelius cried out "Here with your eyes!", the eavesdropping child screamed and gave himself away, and Coppelius seized him and was about to drop red-hot coals into his eyes when his father begged for them to be spared. A year later, on another visit of the Sandman, the father was killed in an explosion in his study, and Coppelius vanished. As a student, Nathaniel believed he recognised this childhood phantom of horror in an itinerant Italian optician, Giuseppe Coppola, who offered him barometers: "Don't want barometer? Don't want barometer? Also got fine eyes, fine eyes!" He bought a pocket spyglass, used it to look into Professor Spalanzani's house opposite, and fell madly in love with the professor's beautiful but strangely silent and motionless "daughter" Olympia, so completely that he forgot his clever and sensible fiancée Clara. But Olympia was an automaton whose clockwork Spalanzani had made and whose eyes the Sandman Coppola had put in. Nathaniel came upon the two "masters" quarrelling over their work: the optician carried off the eyeless wooden doll, and Spalanzani picked Olympia's bleeding eyes up from the floor and threw them at Nathaniel's breast, saying that Coppola had stolen them from him. Nathaniel went mad again. After his recovery he was reconciled with Clara and meant to marry her. One day the two climbed the high tower of the town hall, leaving Clara's brother below; Nathaniel looked down into the street through Coppola's spyglass, went mad once more and tried to throw the girl into the abyss; her brother rescued her. Among the crowd gathered below appeared the lawyer Coppelius, suddenly returned, who laughed and said: "Wait a bit; he'll come down of himself." Nathaniel saw Coppelius, gave a wild shriek, "Yes! 'Fine eyes, fine eyes!'", and flung himself over the parapet.

**Mechanism: why intellectual uncertainty is not enough.** This summary shows that the feeling of the uncanny attaches directly to the figure of the Sandman, that is, to the idea of *being robbed of one's eyes*. Hoffmann does create a certain uncertainty at the beginning: he deliberately does not let us know whether we are being taken into the real world or a purely fantastic one. But this uncertainty disappears as the story proceeds: the ending makes it clear that Coppola the optician really is Coppelius the lawyer, and so the Sandman. We now know that we are not looking at the products of a madman's imagination, and this knowledge does nothing to lessen the uncanny impression. **The theory of intellectual uncertainty therefore cannot explain it.** Psychoanalytic experience, on the other hand, shows that injury to or loss of the eyes is a terrible fear for children; the study of dreams, fantasies and myths shows that anxiety about one's eyes, the fear of going blind, is often a substitute for the fear of castration. The self-blinding of the mythical criminal Oedipus is only a mitigated form of the punishment of castration. A rationalist might object that the eyes are so precious that it is natural for a corresponding fear to guard them. Freud's reply is a textual argument: why, then, did Hoffmann bind the anxiety about eyes so closely to the father's death? Why does the Sandman always appear as a disturber of love, separating Nathaniel from his fiancée and her brother (his best friend), destroying his second object of love, Olympia, and driving him to suicide just as he is about to marry Clara? These features become intelligible only when the fear of castration is substituted for the fear about the eyes. Freud also notes in a footnote that Nathaniel's father and Coppelius are the two halves into which ambivalence splits the father-imago of childhood (one threatens to blind him, the other intercedes for him), and that Olympia's two "fathers", Spalanzani and Coppola, are a new version of this pair; Olympia is a dissociated complex of Nathaniel's own, confronting him as a person, and his senseless compulsive love for her may rightly be called narcissistic. He even adds that Hoffmann was the child of an unhappy marriage, whose father left the family when he was three and never returned. *(Note the mixture of evidence here: patterns within the text, clinical experience, mythological analogy and the author's biography are all called on together. The evidential force of such a mixture is exactly the problem Freudian criticism has to face.)*

**Mechanism: the double, repetition and the omnipotence of thoughts.** Freud then extends the infantile factor to other uncanny phenomena. Living dolls do not arouse fear in children, who may even *wish* their dolls to come alive (a woman patient said that at the age of eight she still believed her dolls would come to life if she looked at them in a certain extremely concentrated way), so the source of the uncanny here is an infantile wish or belief. The second theme is the `double` (*Doppelgänger*). **Otto Rank** had already examined the connections of the double with mirror images, shadows, guardian spirits, belief in the soul and the fear of death: the double was originally an insurance against the destruction of the ego, an "energetic denial of the power of death", and the "immortal" soul was probably the first double of the body. These ideas sprang from the unbounded self-love of `primary narcissism` in the minds of children and primitive peoples; once this stage is surmounted, the double reverses its aspect and turns from an assurance of immortality into an uncanny harbinger of death. Its uncanniness can only come from the fact that the double is a creation of a very early mental stage, long since surmounted, in which it wore a friendlier aspect, just as the gods of a religion turn into demons after its fall. *(The double's second meaning connects with "conscience" in "On Narcissism": the agency in the ego that observes and criticises the self, isolated in the "delusion of being watched", can also be experienced as a double.)* The third theme is the involuntary repetition of the same thing. Freud tells of an experience of his own. Strolling one hot summer afternoon through the deserted streets of an unfamiliar provincial town in Italy, he found himself in a quarter whose windows were full of painted women, and hurried away at the next turning; after wandering about for a while he found himself back in the same street, left again, and came back a third time, at which point a feeling he could only call uncanny came over him. Another example is the number 62. That one's cloakroom ticket is number 62 and one's cabin on a ship is number 62 is of no consequence; but if the number crops up again and again within a short time, one can hardly help attributing a secret meaning to it, even taking it as an indication of the span of life allotted to one. Freud here refers to another work about to be published: there is in the unconscious a `compulsion to repeat`, proceeding from the instinctual impulses and probably inherent in the very nature of the instincts, powerful enough to override the pleasure principle. That work is *Beyond the Pleasure Principle*. **Whatever reminds us of this inner compulsion to repeat is perceived as uncanny.** Finally, the fear of the "evil eye" and the unease felt when wishes are fulfilled one after another (like the guest in "The Ring of Polycrates" who leaves in horror because his host is too fortunate) can be traced to what Freud calls the `omnipotence of thoughts`: an archaic, animistic conception of the universe that narcissistically overvalues subjective mental processes. Each of us has passed through a phase of individual development corresponding to the animistic stage of primitive peoples, and each retains traces of it; everything that strikes us as uncanny fulfils the condition of stirring those animistic remnants.

**Conclusion: the return of the repressed.** Freud himself reduced the gist of the study to two points. First, if psychoanalytic theory is right in holding that every affect, whatever its quality, is transformed by repression into morbid anxiety, then among such anxieties there must be a class that can be shown to come from something repressed which *recurs*; this class of anxiety is the uncanny. Second, if this really is the secret nature of the uncanny, we can understand why linguistic usage extended *das Heimliche* into its opposite, *das Unheimliche*: **the uncanny is in reality nothing new or alien, but something long familiar and established in the mind, which has become estranged only through the process of repression.** This also explains Schelling's definition. The uncanny is thus the aesthetic version of the central proposition of psychoanalysis: the repressed does not disappear; it returns in an unfamiliar guise. This is the literal meaning of the title of the anthology's introduction, "Strangers to Ourselves". *(The `defamiliarisation` of Russian Formalism in P2 is an artistic device for making the familiar strange; the uncanny is the strangeness the familiar already contains. The contrast shows how differently formalism and psychoanalysis understand the "familiar": for the first it is the automatisation of perception, for the second the product of repression.)*

### What Can Freudian Criticism Do, and Where Is Its Evidence?

**Mechanism: why literature is like dreams.** The fundamental reason Freudian interpretation has always attracted literary critics is that the unconscious, like a poem, novel or play, cannot speak directly and explicitly, but only through images, symbols, emblems and metaphors; literature likewise does not deal in direct statements about life but shows and expresses experience through imagery, symbol and metaphor. The anthology's editors stress one qualification of this analogy: the rules Freud worked out for interpreting dreams apply equally to literature. Literature does not translate the unconscious directly into symbols that "stand for" unconscious meanings; it displaces unconscious desires, drives and motives into images that may bear no resemblance to their origins yet still allow them release or expression. As fiction, literature can even be said to enact this process of "representation by indirection" itself. Language matters because latent connections show themselves only in language: in "The Uncanny" the fear of castration appears not as a literal image but as a metaphorical substitute, "losing one's eyes", which can be interpreted because language (the semantic history of *heimlich*) displays the hidden connection.

**Operations: what Freudian critics do.** A recognisable set of critical operations follows. Freudian critics give the distinction between conscious and unconscious a central place in interpretation: they associate the "manifest" content of a work with the former and the "latent" content with the latter, privileging the latter as what the work is "really" about, and aim to prise the two apart. They therefore attend closely to unconscious motives and feelings, whether the author's or those of the characters depicted. They show the presence in literary works of classic psychoanalytic symptoms, conditions or stages, such as the oral, anal and phallic stages of infantile emotional and sexual development. They apply psychoanalytic concepts wholesale to literary history: **Harold Bloom**'s *The Anxiety of Influence* sees each generation of poets' struggle for identity under the "threat" of their predecessors' greatness as an enactment of the Oedipus complex. Finally, they establish a "psychological" context for literary works at the expense of social or historical context, putting the individual "psychodrama" above the "social drama" of class conflict: conflicts between generations or between siblings, or between competing desires within one person, seem far more important than conflicts between social classes. *The last of these marks in advance the boundary between psychoanalysis and the Marxist criticism of P9: the two share the "manifest/latent" structure, but locate the "latent" content in the psychodrama of the family and the class structure of society respectively.*

**Reading: *Hamlet*.** This example has become a cliché, and it embodies the first three operations at once. Hamlet's father has been murdered by his own brother, Hamlet's uncle, who then marries Hamlet's mother. The father's ghost tells Hamlet to avenge him by killing his uncle. There is no obvious difficulty in this, yet Hamlet delays and makes excuses for most of the play. Why? He is not especially squeamish, since he kills other people in the play; what the ghost reveals only confirms suspicions he already had, and he gathers other external evidence besides. Critics argued over the question for a long time without agreed result. Psychoanalysis offers a neat solution: **Hamlet cannot avenge the crime because he himself harbours a guilty wish to commit the same crime**. He has an Oedipus complex, a repressed sexual desire for his mother and the consequent wish to be rid of his father; his uncle has merely done what Hamlet secretly wanted to do himself. The view was first sketched by Freud in *The Interpretation of Dreams* (1900): Hamlet cannot take vengeance on the man who did away with his father and took his father's place with his mother, because that man shows him the repressed wishes of his own childhood realised, and so the loathing that should drive him to revenge is replaced by self-reproach and scruples of conscience. Psychoanalytic critics cite the closet scene, in which Hamlet shows an unusually intense awareness of his mother's sexuality. Freud also linked Hamlet's situation in the play with Shakespeare himself, citing the view that the play was written after the death of Shakespeare's father in 1601 and noting that Shakespeare's son, who died young, was called Hamnet, a name identical with Hamlet. But it is still the character Hamlet, not the author Shakespeare, who is diagnosed with the Oedipal conflict. Freud's sketch was later developed by his British colleague **Ernest Jones** in *Hamlet and Oedipus* (1949); Joyce's *Ulysses* (1922) contains a famous sustained parody of this psychoanalytic-biographical view of *Hamlet*. *Hamlet will be reread in Lacan's seminars and by other theories later; the reading here is a point of comparison.*

**Reading: Pinter's *The Homecoming*.** Harold Pinter's *The Homecoming* embodies the third operation, and the classic Freudian condition it shows is `mother fixation`. The play centres on an all-male family in the East End of London: a domineering father and two grown-up sons. The mother died many years before but is revered by the widower and his sons. A third son, who has emigrated to America and become a university professor, comes home on a visit with his wife (the literal meaning of the title). During the visit the father and the younger brothers hit on the idea of having their brother's wife work as a prostitute from a flat in Soho, living on her earnings. The brother agrees, and the wife, hearing the proposal, calmly accepts it, first negotiating the most favourable financial terms and making it clear that she will in many ways be mistress of this new household. The husband returns alone to America and their three children (all boys). The events are so bizarre that the play is often performed as a kind of surreal farce. In an article of 1991, "Pinter's Freudian Homecoming", M. W. Rowe proposed that the underlying explanation can be found in Freud's paper "On the Universal Tendency to Debasement in the Sphere of Love". **Mechanism:** men with a mother fixation feel excessive reverence for the mother and are attracted only to women like her; but for that very reason the shadow of the incest taboo makes it difficult or impossible for them to express sexual feeling towards such women. Their only way out is to have sex with women unlike the mother, whom they therefore despise; to become sexually aroused they must degrade the object of their love, since if she were not degraded she would resemble the mother and could not, in their minds, be a sexual partner. Women are thus polarised into idealised mother figures and whores. Excessive reverence for the mother is usually much diluted by adolescence, but if the mother dies before the child reaches adolescence, as in the play's family, a harmful, idealised mother image persists and overshadows every possible sexual partner. When the younger brothers propose the prostitution scheme, the husband accepts because, to make sex with his wife possible, he has always seen or fantasised her in exactly this way. The surface bizarreness of the plot thus becomes the enactment of a central character's repressed desires.

**Objection: is *aliquis* credible?** Since psychoanalytic interpretations are not explicit statements, they inevitably involve an element of "judgement", and so often provoke controversy. This is easiest to test on the *aliquis* example. Freud's process of deduction is logically impressive, but it should also be noted that the word *aliquis* may have been easy to forget simply because the quotation makes sense without it ("let an avenger arise from our bones"). There are three more general problems. First, should there be an upper limit to the number of associative steps allowed between a slip and its explanation? Without such a limit, the chain of associations seems capable of being stretched to almost any interpretive end-point. Second, what fails to convince may be not the number of steps but their nature. Third, the example seems to require the unconscious to *foresee* the course of conscious thought: it must see in advance that any word suggesting liquid would arouse the fear of pregnancy, and pre-emptively delete the Latin word *aliquis* from consciousness. On the other hand, the example has an attractive complexity, far from the banality of what is popularly called "Freudian" interpretation: the young man's anxiety seems to pervade his whole mind rather than being locked in one compartment, and so it may surface anywhere, which is psychologically quite plausible. *But Barry himself admits that this may only mean he likes its very intricacy.* Freud himself anticipated a related objection in *The Interpretation of Dreams*: new trains of thought arising in the course of analysis may have played no part in forming the dream. He grants this only in part. Some trains of thought do appear for the first time in analysis, but these new connections are made only between thoughts already connected in other ways in the dream-thoughts; he calls them "loop-lines" or "short circuits". *This answer presupposes the existence of the dream-thoughts, which can be reached only through the analysis itself, and the circularity of the evidence thereby comes into view.*

**Objection: the Dora case.** Since the 1980s distrust of Freud has grown greatly, partly because of his largely negative view of women: his belief that female sexuality rests on narcissism, masochism and passivity, and that women are inherently afflicted by an inferiority complex called "penis envy". Influential studies seem to show that these views were sustained by misreading or even distorting the evidence his patients gave him, for instance by treating accounts of childhood sexual abuse as fantasy rather than reality. *This connects with a remark Freud makes in analysing the "beautiful dream": analysis gives only the content of a thought and leaves us to decide its reality; in dreams, real and imagined events at first sight have equal validity. It is in this gap that assigning something to "fantasy" or to "reality" becomes a decision prejudice can sway; trauma theory will tip the balance back towards reality.* Freud's misreading shows in the case usually known as "Dora" (formally *Fragment of an Analysis of a Case of Hysteria*), which feminist critics and others have read as a psychoanalysis of Freud himself. In the autumn of 1900 Dora, aged eighteen, was brought to Freud for treatment by her father, after her parents found a note in which she threatened suicide, the climax of a period of withdrawal and difficulty. Dora broke off the treatment before it reached any conclusion, which is why Freud called it a "fragment". The family situation was this. Dora's wealthy parents were unhappily married but close friends of another couple, Herr and Frau K. A sexual relationship developed between Dora's father and Frau K. and lasted several years; Herr K. knew of it, and the three adults seem to have had a tacit arrangement in which, in return, Dora would be "available" to Herr K. He made advances to her twice. The first time was in his office when she was fourteen: in an evident state of excitement he suddenly embraced her and began to kiss her, and she felt a violent disgust and ran away. Freud thought this reaction neurotic: in his view "this was surely just the situation to call up a distinct feeling of sexual excitement in a girl of fourteen", since, as he says in a footnote, Herr K. was "still quite young and of prepossessing appearance". The second time she was sixteen, and they were walking by a lake; Herr K. "had the audacity to make her a proposal", and she slapped his face and walked off. Freud was puzzled by the "brutal form" of her refusal and again saw it as neurotic. When Dora told her father, he asked Herr K. for an explanation; Herr K. denied that the episode had happened, and her father believed him rather than her.

**Reading: the jewel-case dream.** The body of the analysis is Freud's interpretation of two dreams Dora told him, one of them recurrent, first dreamed while they were staying at the lakeside house where Herr K. made his improper proposal: "A house was on fire. My father was standing beside my bed and woke me up. I dressed quickly. Mother wanted to stop and save her jewel-case; but Father said: 'I refuse to let myself and my two children be burnt for the sake of your jewel-case.' We hurried downstairs, and as soon as I was outside I woke up." Freud points out that the immediate cause of the dream was her father's saying, when they arrived at the wooden cottage, that he was afraid of fire; that afternoon Dora had woken from a nap on the sofa to find Herr K. standing beside her, so that in the dream her father and Herr K. have changed places; years before she had overheard her parents quarrelling badly over jewellery; and "jewel-case" is a colloquial German term for the female genitals. According to Freud's interpretation, then, the dream expresses Dora's repressed wish to give Herr K. what he wanted (her "jewel-case"); the fire stands for her own repressed passion; and the substitution of her father for Herr K. expresses a wish that her earlier Oedipal love for her father would protect her from yielding to the temptation of Herr K.'s advances. Freud also saw a remnant of this Oedipus complex in Dora's resentment of her father's relationship with Frau K., her successful rival for her father's love. **Conclusion:** facing the united male force of her father, Herr K. and Freud, Dora seems to have had no chance; the case study shows **Freud and psychoanalysis at their weakest**. The problem is not only insufficient evidence but that the interpretive framework itself redescribes a girl's reasonable refusal of sexual harassment as repressed desire: when every reaction (refusal included) can be read as evidence of its opposite, the mechanism of `inversion` in the dream-work turns from a tool of interpretation into an unfalsifiable talisman. *(The last sentence is an auxiliary judgement.)* The relation between psychoanalysis and feminism will be discussed further in P12.

### The Object-Relations School: The Pre-Oedipal Period and the Formation of the Self

**Background: two forks.** Psychoanalytic theory after Freud divided into two branches: `object relations theory` and the `neo-Freudianism` represented by Lacan. The first tends towards a model that has almost no need of instincts, concentrating on how the self interacts with its social world, especially the first world of primary carers such as the mother. The second holds that instinctual drives and the unconscious are more fundamental to psychoanalytic work than the ego, which is merely an illusion that can never fully know or master the unconscious. Both forks start from Freud's concept of `identification`, but they lead in opposite directions. The anthology's editors point to this genealogy in their headnotes to both "On Narcissism" and *Group Psychology*. Constructions such as the ego ideal were later described by theorists as "internalisations" or "introjections" modelled on external objects such as the parents; they were no longer seen as expressions of libido but as representations the self establishes within itself to secure the benefits of relations with others. The child's capacity to internalise representations of its carers and of others in its social surroundings is the core of later object relations theory, which seeks to explain *the social character of the self*: how the self is constructed by relations with others.

**Definition:** The object-relations school took shape in Britain and the United States after the Second World War and is associated with the names of **Melanie Klein**, **D. W. Winnicott**, **Margaret Mahler** and others. It is less concerned with the battle between the ego and the instinctual drives (some of these theorists rejected the idea altogether) and more with how, in the `pre-Oedipal period`, the child's relations with its objects, especially with the mother, shape personality. The "object" here means the person, or part of a person, in which desire and feeling are invested, not an inanimate thing. The outline of self-identity is given or shaped by this primary relationship: whether it is distant, cold and frustrating, or overwhelming and engulfing. Whether the child succeeds in separating from its original unity with the mother is decisive for later personality.

**Distinction: three differences from Freud.** First, unlike Freud, object relations theorists see the ego as the main part of personality, or even the whole of it. Second, they hold that how the self in the pre-Oedipal stage constructs for itself an inner world of introjected fantasy objects, and how it projects destructive feelings onto the world, matter more than the later Oedipal stage as the passage into adult gender identity. Third, they do not agree among themselves in their assessment of this early relationship. Some hold that the original separation from the mother is a primary frustration that can never be healed, whose pattern governs a lifetime of longing; Mahler sees the relation to the mother more positively, as a "beacon" that lets the child venture into the world out of an original state of `symbiosis`; Klein holds that the child constructs a world for itself through fantasies which, by means of introjection and projection and of `splitting` between good and bad inner objects, allow it to distinguish its destructive feelings from its loving ones. For the child the mother is made up of "part objects", such as the breast or the face. Eventually the child learns `reparation`: restoring whole objects and good relations, which its own destructive impulses have split apart in the process of separation, individuation and growth.

**Objection: an overly optimistic view of "adaptation".** The main criticism of object relations theory is that it sometimes paints too optimistic a picture: the "adaptation" of a "self", whose very coherence is questionable, to an unproblematic "environment". This criticism links up with Lacan's position: for Lacan, the unified self presupposed by object relations theory is an illusion; a whole self, transparent to itself and defined by a healthy ego, is impossible. It is only the ego's delusion, and the delusion of ego psychology. *There is an easy confusion here. The editors' criticism is aimed at the normativity implicit in the theoretical picture of "adaptation", as if the aim of therapy were to fit the individual smoothly into existing society; it does not deny the influence of early relations on personality. Chodorow shows precisely that the object-relations framework can be used to reveal how social structures are reproduced through the division of mothering, not to justify them.*

**Example: Theweleit's *Male Fantasies*.** Despite these problems, object relations theory also inspired pioneering studies, the best known being **Klaus Theweleit**'s *Male Fantasies*. It studies representations of violence against women in the literature written by German veterans of the First World War, who later became leading supporters of Nazism, and interprets them as expressions of hostility towards the mother. These works are marked by images of fear of women perceived as too powerful, a fear displaced into anxiety that the boundaries of the self will be swamped by the "red flood" of Bolshevism. Nazism was Germany's response to the political threat of communist revolution: it set up a rigid social order equivalent to the psychological defences these men built to protect themselves from personal dissolution, which Theweleit calls `body armor`. In his view, the relation to the mother determined these men's psychological identity more than the relation to the father, who is often a marginal figure in these works. What the works present is not an ego doing battle with a paternal super-ego or with pleasure-seeking unconscious impulses and encountering repression, but a self that was never fully formed and never achieved a healthy relation to the world, rooted in the abusive child-rearing practices of German society at the time. This is what explains the enormous representational violence the works inflict on women who might be seen as equally maternal and equally threatening to the self's identity. Theweleit also sees women, communists and Jews as external equivalents in one and the same psychological configuration: all stand for inner impulses that threaten boundaries and must be violently expelled or disciplined.

**Reading: from Oedipal to pre-Oedipal.** The editors sum up what this shift means for literary criticism with a contrast. Freud and many early psychoanalytic critics were concerned with the primary anxiety of patriarchal culture: the boy's fear in moving from asexual childhood to sexual adulthood, a trajectory that necessarily passes through the sexual relationship between his mother and father. The whole of Nathaniel Hawthorne's fiction can be read in this light as an Oedipal conflict between sons and threatening fathers, such as the relationship between the Reverend Dimmesdale and Chillingworth in *The Scarlet Letter*. When object relations theory turned attention to the pre-Oedipal realm, later psychoanalytic criticism likewise attended more to the relational dynamics of psychosexual development, and to the child's relation to the mother in a patriarchal culture that assigns the work of child-rearing to women. *This shift connects directly with the feminist criticism of P12: the question is no longer only how "the law of the father" forms the male subject, but who raises children, and how.*

**Conclusion:** The object-relations school developed Freud's theory of identification into a theory of *how the self is constructed in relationships*, and moved the theoretical centre of gravity from the Oedipal to the pre-Oedipal period, from father to mother. It gave literary criticism tools for reading violence, boundary anxiety and the reproduction of gender (Theweleit, Chodorow), at the price of a dubious normative premise: a whole self that can "adapt" healthily to its environment. It is exactly at this point that Lacan gives his sharpest rebuttal: the unity of the self is itself a misrecognition.

### The Mirror Stage and the Imaginary: The Ego as Misrecognition

**Background:** **Jacques Lacan** (1901–1981) first took a medical degree, trained in psychiatry in the 1920s and studied paranoia in the 1930s, writing his doctoral thesis on a patient called Aimée; his famous theory of the "mirror stage" was first presented at a conference in 1936. He was then influenced in turn by the figures who dominated Parisian intellectual life: the anthropologist Lévi-Strauss and the linguists Saussure and Jakobson. Only in the 1950s did he begin to challenge the orthodoxy of his discipline. At a conference in Vienna in 1955 he called for a neo-Freudianism that would go "back to basics"; but by this he did not mean rethinking the "conscious personality" (the ego) and explaining its behaviour through an understanding of the workings of the unconscious, which many took to be the whole point of Freudianism, but re-emphasising the unconscious itself as "the core of our being". These unorthodox views led to his expulsion from the International Psychoanalytical Association, and in 1964 he founded his own Freudian School in Paris; part of his training seminars was published as *Écrits* (1966). The anthology's editors call *Écrits* the most influential work of structuralist psychoanalysis. It is a rebuke to ego psychology and a return to Freud's belief in the power of the unconscious, yet it also rewrites Freud in important ways: **it inserts the self into culture**; we are all shaped by the symbolic order into which we are born, which determines our gender identity and our place in the family. *Lacan's writing is notoriously obscure. His seminars were not group discussions but long lectures to graduate students, with something of performance, improvisation and an initiation rite in which information is passed on in code; Lacan himself said that the only teaching worthy of the name is one that can be grasped only in its own way. With texts of this kind, rereading one closely pays better than skimming many.*

**Example: the infant before the mirror.** "The Mirror Stage as Formative of the Function of the I as Revealed in Psychoanalytic Experience" (1949) starts from a fact of comparative psychology. For a time the human infant is outdone by the chimpanzee in instrumental intelligence, yet it can already recognise its own image in a mirror, a recognition shown in the illuminative mimicry of what Köhler called the "Aha-Erlebnis". For the monkey, once the image has been mastered and found empty, the behaviour stops there; the infant, by contrast, immediately goes through a series of playful gestures in which it experiences the relation between the movements assumed in the image and the reflected environment, and between this virtual complex and the reality it duplicates, its own body and the persons and things around it. This event can take place from the age of six months. The infant cannot yet walk, or even stand up, and is held tightly by some support, human or artificial (what the French call a *trotte-bébé*); yet in a flutter of jubilant activity it overcomes the obstruction of the support and fixes its attitude in a slightly leaning-forward position, so as to hold the image in its gaze. Lacan holds that this activity keeps the meaning he gives it until the age of eighteen months.

**Mechanism: identification with a whole external image.** The mirror stage is to be understood as an `identification` (the concept from Freud's *Group Psychology*), the transformation that takes place in the subject when it *assumes* an image; analytic theory uses the ancient term `imago` for such an image. The jubilant assumption of its specular image by the infant, still sunk in motor incapacity and nursling dependence, displays in exemplary fashion a symbolic matrix in which the I is precipitated in a primordial form, *before* it is objectified in the dialectic of identification with the other, and *before* language restores to it, in the universal, its function as subject. This form may be called the `Ideal-I`, and it is also the source of all later secondary identifications. **The point is that this form situates the agency of the ego, before its social determination, in a fictional direction**, which will always remain irreducible for the individual. The reason is this: the total form of the body, by which the subject anticipates in a mirage the maturation of its power, is given to it only as a `Gestalt`, that is, in an exteriority in which the form is more constituent than constituted. It appears to the subject in a size that fixes it and in a symmetry that inverts it, in contrast to the turbulent movements the subject feels animating itself. This Gestalt symbolises the mental permanence of the I, and at the same time prefigures its *alienating* destination.

**Evidence:** Lacan's evidence for the "formative effect" of the Gestalt comes from biology and ethology. It is a necessary condition for the maturation of the female pigeon's gonad that it should see another member of its species, of either sex; and it is enough merely to place the pigeon within the field of reflection of a mirror. The transition of the migratory locust from the solitary to the gregarious form within a generation can be brought about by exposing the individual, at a certain stage, to the purely visual action of a similar image. Lacan also cites Roger Caillois's studies of mimicry, and mocks the ludicrous attempt to attribute these phenomena to a supposedly supreme "law of adaptation". *It is worth noting that this evidence is all analogical: it shows that images can have a formative effect on organisms, but cannot directly prove that the human infant's ego is formed in this way.*

**Mechanism: prematurity and the fragmented body.** The human case is special because man's relation to nature is altered by a certain dehiscence at the heart of the organism: the unease and motor unco-ordination of the neonatal months reveal a primordial discord, and the anatomical incompleteness of the pyramidal system and the presence of certain humoral residues of the maternal organism confirm the fact of the *specific prematurity of birth* in man (what embryologists call "foetalisation"). So **the mirror stage is a drama whose internal thrust is precipitated from insufficiency to anticipation**: for the subject caught up in the lure of spatial identification it manufactures a succession of fantasies, extending from a `fragmented body` (*corps morcelé*) image to a form of its totality that Lacan calls "orthopaedic", and finally to the assumption of the *armour of an alienating identity*, which will mark with its rigid structure the subject's entire mental development. The fragmented body often appears in dreams when analysis reaches a certain level of aggressive disintegration in the individual: disjointed limbs, organs growing wings and taking up arms for intestinal persecutions, the very images Bosch fixed in painting. Correspondingly, the formation of the I is symbolised in dreams by a fortress or a stadium, surrounded by marshes and rubbish tips, in which the subject struggles to reach the lofty, remote inner castle; and the mechanisms of obsessional neurosis (inversion, isolation, reduplication, cancellation and displacement) are themselves like the structure of fortifications.

**Mechanism: from the mirror to the social.** The moment at which the mirror stage comes to an end inaugurates, through identification with the imago of the *counterpart* and the drama of primordial jealousy (shown by the Charlotte Bühler school in the infant's "transitivism": the child who hits another says it has been hit, the child who sees another fall cries), the dialectic that will henceforth link the I to socially elaborated situations. It is this moment that decisively turns the whole of human knowledge towards mediation through *the desire of the other*, constitutes its objects in an abstract equivalence through the co-operation of others, and turns the I into an apparatus for which every instinctual thrust constitutes a danger, even if it corresponds to a natural maturation. *(The parenthetical explanation of "transitivism" is an auxiliary gloss.)*

**Distinction: Lacan's opponents.** The theory has definite targets. One is ego psychology. Lacan's experience taught him not to regard the ego as centred on the "perception–consciousness system" or as organised by the "reality principle", which he saw as a scientific prejudice most hostile to the dialectic of knowledge, but to start from the function of *misrecognition* (*méconnaissance*), which characterises the ego in all its structures. The other is existentialism: Sartre's philosophy of "being and nothingness" grasps negativity only within the limits of a self-sufficiency of consciousness, and that self-sufficiency, one of its premises, is precisely bound up with the misrecognitions that constitute the ego and the illusion of autonomy in which it trusts. **The ego is not the core of the subject but the subject's imaginary identification with an external image; its unity is a misrecognition.** *A footnote in Beyond the Pleasure Principle acquires a strange resonance here. The child who played fort/da discovered his reflection in a full-length mirror during the hours of his mother's absence and crouched down so that the image was "gone"; when his mother came back, he greeted her with "Baby o-o-o-o!". Making one's image disappear and assuming one's image in the mirror are two sides of one structure.*

**Distinction: the place of the Imaginary, two formulations.** On the relation between `the Imaginary` and `the Symbolic`, Barry and the editors put things somewhat differently, and the two formulations are worth setting side by side. In Barry's summary, the Imaginary is the realm *before* the mirror stage: before any sense of self emerges, the child lives in a world where there is no distinction between self and other, and an idealised identification with the mother. The mirror stage, between six and eighteen months, lets the child see itself in the mirror and begin to conceive of itself as a unified being separate from the rest of the world. At this point the child enters the system of language, a system essentially concerned with `lack` and `separation`, since language names what is absent and replaces it with a linguistic sign. This stage also marks the beginning of socialisation, with its prohibitions and restraints associated with the figure of the father, and the new order the child thereby enters is the Symbolic. In the editors' account the order is different. The child is at first a set of fragmented drives, perceptions and attachments, which only *coalesce* into an imaginary identity in the mirror stage. The Imaginary is therefore not the chaos before the mirror but the psychological realm established by mirror identification, marked by narcissistic unity and longing for a lost wholeness; the headnote calls this longing, and the consciousness it gives rise to, the Imaginary, "the narcissistic part of the activity of the ego". The arrival of language and the establishment of the Symbolic then shatter the Imaginary: to learn to name a thing is to accept separation from it; the presence of the word is the absence of the thing. *Lacan's own text is closer to the editors' formulation: mirror identification comes "before" the dialectical identification with others and before language, and the imaginary "Ideal-I" is precipitated precisely in the mirror. What the two formulations share remains constant: the Imaginary concerns images, identification and the illusion of wholeness; the Symbolic concerns language, law and separation.*

**Implication: Barry's literary extension.** Between the literary poles of realist and anti-realist texts, Barry matches the Symbolic with the world of realist literature, a patriarchal world of order and logic; the anti-realist text represents the Imaginary, in which language exceeds itself, exceeds logic and grammar, as poetic language often does. The contrast between Imaginary and Symbolic can even be likened to that between poetry and prose. In practice the two realms, and the two languages, must always coexist, so a Lacanian critical stance favours texts in which the Imaginary keeps breaking into the Symbolic, such as "metafiction" or "magic realism" that undermines and questions its own realism. The work of the English novelist B. S. Johnson is a good example: characters interrogate the author, disputing his account of their motives or his handling of the plot they are in.
