Such novels turn abstract ideas such as "the constructedness and instability of the subject", "the subject as a linguistic construct" and "language as a self-contained universe of discourse" into something visible in the texture of the fiction. *This correspondence is Barry's extension; the editors make no such match. French feminism's use of the distinction between Imaginary and Symbolic (P12, especially Kristeva's "semiotic/symbolic") will rewrite it in another way.*

**Limitation:** The evidential basis of the mirror-stage theory itself deserves questioning: from an observable behaviour (the infant's jubilant response to its reflection), with the help of ethological analogies, it derives universal conclusions about the nature of the ego. A systematic critique can be found in the chapter "The Mirror Stage: A Critical Reflection" in Raymond Tallis's *Not Saussure: A Critique of Post-Saussurean Literary Theory* (1988); the objection asks whether the mirror stage is an empirical discovery or a metaphor taken for a discovery. *One argument often made is that for most of human history and in most cultures mirrors were not common, so a universal developmental stage dependent on mirrors is hard to sustain; and if the "mirror" can also be the face and gaze of a carer, the theory loses the very observable evidence it appeals to. The "rouge test" of developmental psychology also shows that infants usually do not recognise themselves in a mirror until between eighteen months and two years, later than the six months Lacan speaks of.*

### Why Is the Unconscious Structured Like a Language?

**Problem:** The mirror stage explains how the ego is formed, but not yet how language "restores to the subject its function as subject". "The Instance of the Letter in the Unconscious, or Reason since Freud" (1957; Barry cites it under the translated title "The insistence of the letter") is Lacan's most important text for literary studies, a lecture given to philosophy students rather than trainee psychiatrists. It opens with an oath of allegiance to the reign of the study of language: how could today's psychoanalyst fail to realise that his realm of truth is in fact the word? In examining the unconscious the analyst always both uses and examines language; Freudian psychiatry is entirely a science of speech. The unconscious is not the chaotic, disorderly heap of material it was once thought to be, but an ordered network as complex as the structure of language: **"what the psychoanalytic experience discovers in the unconscious is the whole structure of language."** This is Lacan's most famous slogan: `the unconscious is structured like a language`. It means rethinking the idea that the unconscious is merely the seat of the instincts.

**Definition: the letter.** By "letter" Lacan means something to be taken "to the letter": the *material support* that concrete discourse borrows from language. The definition presupposes that language is not to be confused with the various psychical and somatic functions that serve it in the speaking subject, since language and its structure exist before each subject enters it at a certain moment in its mental development. The subject, if he can appear to be the slave of language, is still more the slave of a discourse in whose universal movement his place is already inscribed at birth, if only by virtue of his proper name. Accordingly, the dualism of nature and culture in anthropology is giving way to a trinity of nature, society and culture, the last term of which could well be reduced to language. *This is exactly the direction anticipated by Lévi-Strauss's structures of kinship in P3.*

**Mechanism: the algorithm S/s.** Lacan locates the birth of the science of language in a founding algorithm:

> S / s

It reads "signifier over signified", "over" corresponding to the bar separating the two levels. It establishes signifier and signified as two distinct orders, separated initially by *a barrier resisting signification*. *This notation is a deliberate inversion of Saussure's diagram in P3. Saussure put the concept (signified) above and the sound-image (signifier) below, with an ellipse and two arrows showing that each calls up the other; Lacan puts the signifier on top, removes the ellipse and arrows, and shifts the emphasis to the bar itself: the signifier does not represent the signified but governs it.* It follows that any signification can be sustained only by reference to another signification; as long as we cling to the illusion that the signifier's function is to represent the signified, we cannot inquire further into the nature of language.

**Example: two doors and a train.** Lacan first reproduces the classic but faulty illustration (the word "tree" over a drawing of a tree), and then replaces it with another: two identical doors, one marked LADIES, the other GENTLEMEN. The simple juxtaposition of two nouns, terms that should complement each other, produces an unexpected meaning: the law of urinary segregation that Western man observes in public life. The signifier has entered the signified in material form. He then tells a childhood memory. A train arrives at a station; a little boy and a little girl, brother and sister, sit facing each other by the window, watching the buildings along the platform slide past. "Look," says the brother, "we're at Ladies!" "Idiot!" replies his sister, "can't you see we're at Gentlemen?" **Reading:** the rails materialise the bar of Saussure's algorithm; each child, from his or her own position, sees a different signifier, and the meaning of the same "place" splits into two irreconcilable "fatherlands". *Barry sums the illustration up as "the same signifier can have different signifieds"; Lacan's formulation points rather the other way: the same image (the door) is given different meanings by different signifiers above it, the signified being determined beneath the signifier. Both summaries stress that there is no fixed one-to-one correspondence between signifier and signified.* From this follows the inference most crucial for poststructuralism: if signifiers relate only to signifiers, language is detached from external reality and becomes an independent realm (see P3, P7).

**Mechanism: the signifying chain and the sliding of the signified.** The structure of the signifier is "articulated": its units can be reduced, on the one hand, to ultimate differential elements (the `phoneme`, which is not a phonetic constant but the synchronic system of differential oppositions needed to discriminate sounds in a given language), and on the other hand combine according to the laws of a closed order. Lacan calls this topological structure the `signifying chain`: "rings of a necklace that is a ring in another necklace made of rings". The signifier always anticipates meaning by unfolding its dimension before it. A sentence interrupted at the significant point ("I shall never…", "All the same it is…") does not lack meaning; its meaning is all the more oppressive for making us wait. **Meaning "insists" in the signifying chain, but none of its elements "consists" in the signification of which it is capable at that moment.** We are thus forced to accept the notion of an `incessant sliding of the signified under the signifier`. Clinical experience runs counter to this linearity, so Lacan proposes the schema of the `points de capiton` (upholstery buttons, which fix the stuffing to the fabric) to show how, in dialogue, signifiers temporarily pin meaning down. He also points out that the "linearity" Saussure regarded as constitutive of the chain of discourse is necessary but not sufficient: one need only listen to poetry to hear a polyphony, all discourse aligned along the several staves of a score; from each signifying unit hangs "vertically" a whole articulation of relevant contexts. Take "tree": it can call up the strength and majesty of oak and plane, in a biblical context raise the shadow of the cross on a barren hill, and be reduced to the capital Y, the sign of dichotomy; *arbre* ("tree") and *barre* ("bar") are anagrams; and the line in Valéry's "Au Platane", "No! says the Tree, it says No! in the shower of sparks of its superb head", demands precisely these harmonics of the tree.

**Mechanism: metonymy and metaphor.** The signifier acts on the signified along two "slopes". `Metonymy` is based on the word-to-word connection. Lacan analyses the example endlessly repeated in rhetoric textbooks, "thirty sails". If understood as part for whole, it tells us almost nothing about the size of the fleet, since a ship having only one sail is the least likely case; **the connection between ship and sail exists only in the signifier, and metonymy rests on this word-to-word connection.** The formula of `metaphor` is "one word for another". Surrealist poetry shows that any conjunction of two signifiers can constitute a metaphor, provided the signified images are far enough apart to produce a poetic spark. But Lacan stresses that the creative spark of metaphor does not spring from two images equally actualised; it flashes between two signifiers, one of which has replaced the other in the signifying chain, the occulted signifier remaining present through its (metonymic) connection with the rest of the chain. His example is the line from Hugo's "Booz endormi", "His sheaf was neither miserly nor spiteful". Miserliness and spite are properties of Booz; "his sheaf" has replaced him in the place where he should be praised, and Booz himself is thereby swept into the "outer darkness". Yet he is resurrected around the figure, because the sheaf is an image of abundant growth that announces the old man's coming paternity in a sacred context: the spark of metaphor flashes between "a man's proper name" and "the signifier that metaphorically abolishes him", and here realises the signification of `paternity`. *Barry's summary is more popular: metonymy is part for whole, "twenty sails" for twenty ships; metaphor, as in "the ship ploughed the waves", condenses two images, the ship cleaving the waves and the plough cleaving the soil, into one. The difference deserves notice: Barry's part/whole understanding is exactly what Lacan uses "thirty sails" to question. For Lacan, the ground of metonymy lies not in an actual relation between things but in the connection between signifiers.*

**Mechanism: the dream-work as rhetoric.** Lacan then returns to Freud. Every third page of Freud's collected works refers to philology, and the closer he comes to the unconscious, the greater the proportion of linguistic analysis. *The Interpretation of Dreams* announces at the outset that the dream is a rebus and demands that it be taken "to the letter", that is, in the literal or phonematic structure in which the signifier is articulated. Freud takes the example of Egyptian hieroglyphs: in a text, the frequency of a vulture (*aleph*) or a chick (*vau*) indicates a form of the verb "to be" or a plural, and to conclude from this that the text has anything to do with these birds would be a ridiculous joke. What the analyst does, therefore, is not "decoding" but "deciphering". This yields a set of correspondences. What Freud calls the general precondition of the dream, `distortion` (*Entstellung*), is the sliding of the signified under the signifier. `Condensation` (*Verdichtung*) is the structure of the superimposition of signifiers, the field of metaphor; the German word itself condenses *Dichtung* ("poetry"), showing that the mechanism is naturally akin to poetry. `Displacement` (*Verschiebung*) is closer to the veering of signification seen in metonymy, and from the start it is presented as the unconscious's best means of foiling the censor. The only difference between the dream-work and the homologous functions in discourse is a condition imposed on the signifying material: `considerations of representability` (*Rücksicht auf Darstellbarkeit*). In formula:

> Condensation ≈ metaphor (one signifier replaces another, the replaced one sinking beneath the bar); displacement ≈ metonymy (sliding along the signifying chain from one word to the next)

*Recall P3: Jakobson put both condensation and displacement on the side of contiguity (the first as synecdoche, the second as metonymy), whereas Lacan reassigns condensation to metaphor. The two start from the same bipolar model and connect it differently, which shows that the correspondence between the model and Freud's concepts is not unique.* The claim has an evidential dimension too: whenever the unconscious is discussed, the proportion of linguistic analysis rises, because puns, allusions and every kind of wordplay are often precisely the mechanisms by which unconscious contents appear. Freud's *aliquis* is an example.

**Mechanism: the symptom is a metaphor, desire is a metonymy.** The double mechanism of metaphor is the mechanism by which the `symptom`, in the analytic sense, is determined: between the enigmatic signifier of sexual trauma and the term that replaces it in an actual signifying chain, a spark flies that fixes in the symptom a signification inaccessible to the conscious subject. Desire, on the other hand, is a metonymy: caught in the rails, it is eternally stretching forth towards the desire for "something else". Lacan cites a case from Freud's paper on fetishism (1927): a patient needed a certain "shine on the nose" (*Glanz auf der Nase*) in order to obtain sexual satisfaction; analysis showed that his early English-speaking childhood had displaced his curiosity about the mother's lack of a phallus, a "lack of being", into "a glance at the nose": in the forgotten language of his childhood it was *glance*, not *Glanz*. *This example pushes "the unconscious is structured like a language" to its most literal point: the determinant of the symptom is not a resemblance between images but the similar sound of two signifiers in two languages.* The editors sum up this structure as a drama on either side of a bar. On entering the Symbolic, the original desire for the mother is repressed; the mother's body is "barred", and desire for it is placed beneath the bar of the signifier and enters the unconscious. The small o (the first object, the other) becomes the capital O (the `Other` of the symbolic unconscious), which takes on meaning as what one cannot have, as that whose absence determines the form of all later desire. This bar can never be crossed; a lifetime of desire is an attempt to come to terms with this separation, with our `lack-of-being` (*manque-à-être*). What lies on the other side of the bar can enter consciousness only in the form of substitutes, so all desire is essentially metaphorical; and since no metaphor can embody what we ultimately desire, we are condemned to slide along a signifying chain in which each signifier is a metonymy, a part standing for the whole we (always) miss. They never reach `the Real`, the ever-absent cause of desire, the undifferentiated state of nature, which the headnote also describes as the realm of drives, instincts and unconscious processes.

**Conclusion: I am where I do not think.** The question of the subject is thereby posed anew: is the place I occupy as subject of the signifier concentric or eccentric to the place I occupy as subject of the signified? The question is not whether the way I speak of myself conforms to what I am, but whether I am the one of whom I speak. The philosophical `cogito` lies at the centre of a mirage that makes modern man so sure of being himself even in his doubts about himself. Lacan's answer inverts Descartes: **"I think where I am not, therefore I am where I do not think."** Barry simplifies this to "I am where I do not think", that is, in the unconscious, where my true self lies, and draws out what Lacan calls "the radical eccentricity of the self to itself" and the question: who is this other to whom I am more attached than to myself, since at the heart of my assent to my own identity it is still he who agitates me? Correspondingly, when Freud introduced the ego into his doctrine, he defined it by the resistances proper to it; Lacan holds that these resistances are imaginary in nature, the ego resisting the messages of the unconscious with its imaginary inertia. The various defence mechanisms psychoanalysts describe are only the reverse side of the mechanisms of the unconscious: periphrasis, hyperbaton, ellipsis, suspension, anticipation, retraction, negation, digression, irony. They are what Quintilian called "figures of thought". **The unconscious is neither primordial nor instinctual; what it knows of the elementary is only the elements of the signifier.** Freud's three classic works on the unconscious, *The Interpretation of Dreams*, *The Psychopathology of Everyday Life* and *Jokes and Their Relation to the Unconscious*, are nothing but a web of examples woven from formulas of connection and substitution. Lacan even held that what provoked resistance to psychoanalysis from the start was not its emphasis on sex (sex has always been a principal subject of literature) but its being so "intellectual". Freud's maxim *Wo Es war, soll Ich werden* is usually translated "Where id was, there ego shall be", that is, the colonisation of the unconscious by reason; Lacan reads it as "I must come to the place where that was", and uses it against an ego psychology that would turn psychoanalysis into a sociological hymn to the "autonomous ego".

**Implication: character and realism.** The appeal of this argument for literary criticism comes from the relentless logic of its consequences. If the unconscious is "the kernel of our being", and the unconscious is linguistic, and language is a system complete before we enter it, then the idea of a unique, separate self is deconstructed; the self is merely an effect of language, and the liberal humanist tenets of P1 (unchanging human nature, the unique self) are shaken. Two things are shaken with them. One is the idea of `character`: since the subject is no longer a stable mixture of conscious elements, characters in novels cannot be treated as people but should be held in suspension, seen as clusters of signifiers gathered round a proper name. The other is literary realism: since language is radically detached from any referent in the world, the basic assumption of the realist novel, that it "presents the real world to us", cannot stand, and is replaced by a preference for the experimental, fragmented, densely allusive texts of modernism and postmodernism, in which fiction plays with the devices of fiction and alludes to other fictions, just as Saussure's signifiers relate and interact only with each other rather than depicting a world. **A wholly new reading strategy and a wholly new set of literary preferences are thereby demanded at once.**

### "The Purloined Letter": From the Author's Psyche to the Unconscious of the Text

Lacan's three texts with the greatest influence on literary studies are "The Instance of the Letter in the Unconscious" (1957), the seminar on Edgar Allan Poe's "The Purloined Letter", and the seminar on *Hamlet*, "Desire and the Interpretation of Desire in *Hamlet*". The last two happen to give the same texts a second reading within psychoanalysis: in Freud and Jones, *Hamlet* is the Oedipus complex of a character; in Lacan it becomes a problem in the structure of desire. In Bonaparte, Poe is the author's symptom; in Lacan, the text's own unconscious. The second case is taken as the example here, since it shows most clearly the gulf between the two kinds of psychoanalytic criticism.

**Example: the story.** Poe's pioneering detective story has an archetypal quality that makes it particularly suited to psychoanalytic interpretation: there is no depth of characterisation, and the characters are moved by the author like chess pieces in a ritual battle of bluff, double bluff and stratagem; their names are simply the Queen, the King, the Minister, the Prefect of Police and the detective Dupin. The plot falls into four stages. First, the Minister is talking to the Queen in her apartment when the King suddenly comes in; the Minister notices the Queen's anxiety that the King should not see a letter lying on the table, but she cannot hide it, since that would only draw the King's attention. While the two are distracted, the Minister takes the letter, leaving in its place a similar-looking letter from his own pocket. Second, the Queen discovers the theft and knows who did it; while the Minister is out, she has the Prefect of Police and his men search his residence, and despite the most thorough and scientific methods they find nothing. Third, in despair she asks Dupin for help. Dupin visits the Minister and reasons: carrying the letter on his person would be too risky, but the letter's usefulness lies in its being producible at any moment, so it cannot be hidden outside the house; and if it were *hidden* in the house the search would certainly have found it, so it must be in the house but not hidden. Sure enough, he sees the letter casually stuck among a bundle of letters above the mantelpiece. Fourth, he visits again, arranges a disturbance in the street, and replaces the real letter with a fake one. The letter goes back to the Queen; the Minister, not knowing that he no longer has it, is eventually brought down; and a note inside the fake letter shows that this is Dupin's revenge for an injury the Minister had done him in an earlier love affair.

**Distinction: two readings.** The traditional Freudian approach to Poe, represented by **Marie Bonaparte**, a disciple of Freud in the 1930s, read this story, like all Poe's work, as a symptom of the author's neurotic inner life: she went beyond the text to the author, diagnosing mother fixation and necrophilia in Poe on the basis of the stories' content. Lacan says nothing at all about the author's personal psychology; he treats the text as a metaphor that illuminates the nature of the unconscious, of psychoanalysis and of language. His reading can be reduced to three correspondences. First, **the stolen letter is a symbol of the unconscious itself.** We know nothing of the letter's contents in the story; we see only how it affects every character's actions. Likewise, the contents of the unconscious are by definition unknowable, but everything we do is affected by it; we can guess the general nature of its contents by observing its effects, just as we can infer the general nature of the letter's contents from the anxiety it causes. Freud's researches led to confident assertions about the exact nature of the unconscious's contents; Lacan is deeply sceptical about the possibility of such certainty. Like the letter, the fragments that might make our inner mental world meaningful have been stolen, and we must learn to function without them: **using the code without the key**. Second, **Dupin's investigation enacts the process of psychoanalysis.** The analyst uses repetition and substitution: he has the patient put painful repressed memories into words, so that the original event is repeated in verbal form, and the verbal account replaces the repressed memory in the unconscious with something in consciousness; once made conscious and spoken, the memory loses its power. Dupin's investigation likewise turns on repetition and substitution: in stealing the letter from the Minister he repeats the Minister's theft of it from the Queen, and both thefts are accomplished by substitution, a fake letter put in place of the real one. *(Note that "repetition" here no longer means the same as the "compulsion to repeat" of Beyond the Pleasure Principle: it is no longer the blind return of the repressed but the transfer of a structural position between characters. The Queen, the Minister and Dupin occupy in turn the position of "holder of the letter", and that position determines their behaviour.)* Third, **the letter whose contents are unknown embodies the nature of language.** Language involves an endless play of signifiers but no simple link with any signified content outside language; the signified is always lost or stolen. Likewise, throughout the story we see the letter's significance but never learn exactly what it signifies; it is an instance of signification itself, not a sign of any particular thing. It can be said, then, that all words are purloined letters: we have the signifiers, the "verbal envelopes" of concepts, but the envelopes cannot be opened, and the signified is always hidden.

**Operations: what Lacanian critics do.** Like Freudian critics, Lacanian critics attend closely to unconscious motives and feelings, but instead of excavating those of the author or characters, they look for the motives of *the text itself*, revealing the contradictory undercurrents of meaning that exist beneath the text's "consciousness" like an unconscious. This is also another way of defining the process of "deconstruction" (P7). They show Lacanian symptoms or stages in works, such as the mirror stage or the sovereignty of the unconscious; treat texts within a series of broader Lacanian orientations, such as lack or desire; and see texts as demonstrations of Lacan's views of language and the unconscious, especially the general elusiveness of the signified and the centrality of the unconscious. In practice this leads to a preference for anti-realist texts that challenge the conventions of literary representation. Lacan's reading of "The Purloined Letter" belongs to the last of these operations: what Lacan finds in the story is evidence for his own views of language and of the psychoanalytic process.

**Example: *A Farewell to Arms*.** The anthology's editors borrow Ben Stoltzfus's reading to show another kind of Lacanian reading. The title of Hemingway's novel depends on a pun. A wounded soldier falls in love with a nurse, who finally dies in childbirth (the child too is stillborn); *arms* are both bodily "arms" (the sexual embrace) and military "arms" (the guns that wound the hero). He hopes to escape from the army into the arms of the maternal Catherine, but in the end has to bid farewell to her arms. The novel thus traces the developmental path Lacan describes: the boy must give up the imaginary moment of shared, satisfied desire with the mother, accept separation, and enter the symbolic order. The forked meaning of *arms* marks a split in the narrating subject (throughout the novel the narrator keeps shifting from "we" to "I"), and this split testifies to the division within all human subjectivity: between the conscious ego and the unconscious that determines it, between the desiring self and the ultimate impossibility of desire's satisfaction (a return to the mother's arms). The imaginary identification (self/mother) must be given up, and separation, the doubleness of meaning in which one can have only metaphors and never the real thing or full satisfaction, must be accepted.

**Reading: Poe's third appearance.** The structuralism of P3 read "The Oval Portrait" with Barthes's codes and binary oppositions; the narratology of P4 asked about its frame and narrator, and in speculation touched on "compulsive repetition" and the "primal scene". The division of labour among the three readings is now clear: structuralism asks *how* the text organises meaning; narratology asks *who* tells it and where the information comes from; psychoanalysis asks *what* in the text cannot be said and yet keeps returning. A Bonaparte-style reading would attribute the theme of art devouring life in "The Oval Portrait" to Poe's own necrophilia; a Lacanian reading would see the portrait itself, a signifier that draws the life out of the model and announces her death at the moment of its completion, as an allegory of the priority of the "letter" over what it signifies. *(The last sentence is an extension following Lacan's logic, not an existing reading.)*

**Conclusion:** The distance between Bonaparte and Lacan shows that two kinds of criticism both descended from Freud have almost nothing in common. The first treats the text as a window onto the author's inner life, and **the end-point of interpretation is a person**; the second treats the text as a demonstration of structure, and **the end-point of interpretation is a position**: letter, signifier and unconscious are all defined by their position in a chain rather than by their content. This is the result of the first mechanism, the logic of relation and difference, being transferred from language to the subject.

### Race, Gender and Trauma: The Expanding Frontiers of Psychoanalysis

The universal claims of classical psychoanalysis (that the Oedipus complex is every child's necessary passage to adult gender identity, that neurosis originates in infantile experience within the family) were tested in the second half of the twentieth century from three directions: race in the colonial situation, gender in the division of mothering, and trauma in war and violence. None of the three simply abandoned psychoanalysis; each asked under what conditions its models hold and under what conditions they fail. Only the skeleton of their arguments is given here; they are developed in full in P14–P15, P12 and P15 respectively.

**Frantz Fanon** trained in medicine and psychiatry and later joined the Algerian revolution against French colonial rule; *Black Skin, White Masks* (1952) combines psychological insight with concern for the effects of domination on the conquered. His starting point is a premise of psychoanalysis itself: the task of psychoanalysis is to understand patterns of behaviour within the specific group that is the family; in Europe the structure of the family is closely bound to the structure of the nation, and the individual assimilates the authority of the state to the authority of the parents who shaped his childhood, perceiving the present in the manner of the past. **Mechanism: the break between family and society.** But with people of colour the situation is the reverse: **a normal Black child, having grown up within a normal family, will become abnormal on the slightest contact with the white world.** Freud said that every neurosis originates in specific experiences (*Erlebnisse*) repressed into the unconscious; yet a Black man who has passed the baccalauréat and gone to the Sorbonne to study philosophy is already on guard before any conflictual elements have gathered around him, something that cannot be understood without recourse to Jung's disturbing hypothesis of a "collective unconscious". Fanon's answer is `collective catharsis`: every society must have a channel through which accumulated aggressive energy can be released, and games in children's institutions, comic strips and adventure stories are such channels; and in these channels "the devil" and "the savage" are always embodied by Black people. Black schoolchildren in the Antilles recite "our ancestors the Gauls" in class, identifying themselves with the explorer, the bringer of civilisation, the white man who brings truth to savages, an all-white truth. Fanon proposes an experiment: watch a Tarzan film in the Antilles and again in Europe. In the Antilles the young Black man in fact identifies with Tarzan against the Black characters; in a European cinema this is much harder, since the rest of the audience automatically identifies him with the savages on the screen. The Antillean family thus has virtually no connection with the French, European structure; the individual must choose between family and European society, and the individual who "climbs up" into white society throws the structure of the family back into the id.

**Distinction: complexes in consciousness.** Fanon thereby modifies the concept of the unconscious itself: **the racial drama is played out in the open, and the Black man has no time to "make it unconscious"**; the white man succeeds in this to some extent because a new element appears: guilt. The Black man's inferiority complex, superiority complex or feeling of equality are *conscious*. He even asserts that the Oedipus complex is far from coming into being among Black people. Malinowski would attribute this to matriarchal structures, but Fanon holds that every neurosis, every abnormal manifestation in the Antillean, is the product of his cultural situation. *In a footnote he answers Lacan's remark on the "richness" of the Oedipus complex: even if the boy must kill the father, the father must still consent to be killed.* The Black man becomes a `phobogenic object`, a stimulus to anxiety; on contact with the white world a "sensitising action" takes place, and if the psychic structure is weak, the ego collapses: the Black man no longer acts as an "actional" person, and the goal of his behaviour becomes the Other (in the guise of the white man). *Here the connection with Lacan's terms is direct: Lacan says desire is always constituted through the Other; Fanon shows that in the colonial situation this Other has a definite skin colour.* The race constructionism of P14 and Bhabha's "mimicry" in P15 will both draw a psychological dimension from here.

**Nancy Chodorow**'s *The Reproduction of Mothering* (1978) is the representative work of feminist psychoanalysis, applying the object-relations perspective to gender. Her starting point is Freud's own revision. Freud first believed that the female and male Oedipus complexes were symmetrical: the girl discovers at around three that she has no penis, believes she has been castrated, and so turns to her father, the mother becoming her rival. This is exactly the symmetrical formulation given in the anthology's introduction. But Jeanne Lampl-de Groot reported cases of two girls with a "negative Oedipus complex", who cathected their mothers and regarded their fathers as rivals. Freud reviewed his own clinical experience and agreed: daughters, like sons, are entirely attached to the mother at the beginning of life; the child is originally not bisexual but "matrisexual". He described the surprise of this discovery with a famous comparison: it was like discovering the Minoan-Mycenaean civilisation behind the civilisation of Greece. The pre-Oedipal mother–daughter relationship thus demanded a reformulation of the whole of psychoanalytic theory; few analysts today still regard the Oedipus complex as the "nucleus" of neurosis.

**Mechanism: mothering and ego boundaries.** Chodorow's argument is that girls' pre-Oedipal love for the mother and preoccupation with pre-Oedipal issues are prolonged in ways that boys' are not, because women mother; specifically, because mothers are the same gender as their daughters and of a different gender from their sons. She stresses that this is not a biological claim. Because mothers were themselves girls, they tend not to experience infant daughters as separate from themselves in the way they experience infant sons, whom they experience as a male opposite, so that their cathexis of sons takes on the quality of object-cathexis of a sexual other earlier. As a result, **girls experience themselves as less separate than boys, have more permeable ego boundaries, and define themselves more in relation to others.** Separation and individuation thus become particularly female developmental issues, and as long as women perform the primary nurturing functions, the structure is reproduced from generation to generation. **The problem of evidence:** Chodorow admits that it is hard to prove that mothers treat pre-Oedipal boys and girls differently. Maccoby and Jacklin's authoritative review of the psychological literature of observation and experiment found the results so inconsistent that selective citation could support almost any hypothesis; but among the studies that did report sex differences, the direction of the differences tended to be consistent. She therefore turns to clinical material. The psychotic mothers described by Fliess inflicted their pathology mainly on daughters, being "unsymbiotic" when the daughter needed symbiosis and then, when she began to differentiate, treating her as interchangeable with themselves and so keeping her unindividuated. Enid Balint described the feeling of an "empty self", of not being acknowledged as having a separate reality and the agency to interpret the world in one's own way, which she thought women more prone to, citing her patient Sarah: the mother's "empathy" was false, responding to her assumptions about what the baby should feel rather than to what the baby actually felt. The cases of Christine Olden and Klaus Angel showed the difference between "overidentification" and "symbiosis/pseudo-symbiosis". None of these authors connected their findings with gender, but the examples they chose are not accidental. *The evidential structure of this argument deserves comparison with the problem of evidence in Freudian criticism: when quantitative studies are inconsistent, the theory turns to the "interpretive" evidence of clinical cases, exactly the kind of evidence exposed by aliquis and the Dora case.* P12 will put Chodorow back into the history of feminism and psychoanalysis, from rejection to rereading.

**Bessel A. van der Kolk** and **Alexander C. McFarlane**'s "The Black Hole of Trauma" (1996) takes psychoanalysis to another of its frontiers. **Background:** experiencing trauma is part of being human, and history is written in blood; most people exposed to terrible experiences survive without developing psychiatric disorders, but trauma can also so alter a person's psychological, biological and social equilibrium that the memory of one event contaminates all other experience. The establishment of the diagnostic category of `post-traumatic stress disorder` (*PTSD*) was seen by victims as an acknowledgement and validation of their suffering: in an important sense an experience does not really exist until it can be named and placed in a larger category. In the biblical myth, Adam's first task in paradise was to name the animals.

**Distinction: reality and neurosis.** Unlike other psychological disorders, the core problem of trauma is *reality*. They quote Cathy Caruth: **"it is not a pathology of falsehood or displacement of meaning, but of history itself."** This stands in sharp contrast to Freud's model of disguise. Psychoanalysis held that the essence of neurosis is the pathological persistence of defence mechanisms erected against unacceptable unconscious wishes; character "hardens" into "armour" against the outside world, and the neurotic reacts to the present as if reliving the past. Before the concept of PTSD was accepted, clinical thinking attended only to secondary psychological elaboration and neglected the reality driving these repetitions. In PTSD, by contrast, **the primary symptoms are not symbolic or defensive, nor driven by secondary gain**; the core is the inability to integrate the reality of particular experiences, and the resulting repeated reliving of the trauma in images, behaviours, feelings, physiological states and interpersonal relationships. They also stress, however, that what makes an event traumatic is the victim's subjective assessment of how threatened and helpless they were; the meaning of the event is as fundamental as the event itself, and that meaning keeps evolving long after the trauma is over. One woman who had been raped reinterpreted the rape as a life-threatening attack, and developed full PTSD, only months later, on learning that her attacker had murdered another victim.

**Mechanism: time failing to heal the wound.** Post-traumatic syndromes result from "the failure of time to heal all wounds": traumatic memories are not integrated into the individual's past but exist apart from previous schemes, that is, `dissociated`. Ordinarily, memories of particular events are remembered as stories, which change over time and no longer arouse intense emotions and sensations; in PTSD the past is relived with immediate sensory and emotional intensity, as if the event were happening again. A longitudinal study of two hundred Harvard undergraduates who served in the Second World War found that, when they were interviewed again forty-five years later, those without PTSD had substantially changed their original accounts, the most intense horrors having faded, whereas the memories of the few with PTSD had not been altered by time. **Being able to transform memory is the norm; in PTSD the full impact of the experience does not fade with time.** More than a century ago Charcot called traumatic memories "parasites of the mind"; they are often not coherent stories but sensory fragments that cannot be made sense of. The authors also describe a group of behaviours not mentioned in the diagnostic criteria: `compulsive re-exposure` to situations reminiscent of the trauma, in harm to others (many violent criminals were physically or sexually abused as children), self-destruction (cutting, self-starvation) and revictimisation. *This is the clinical counterpart of what Freud called the "compulsion to repeat" and "daemonic" fate, but the weight of explanation has moved from repressed wishes to unintegrated real events.* Finally, they warn against "fixation on the diagnosis": the intrusion/numbing/arousal framework of PTSD is far from adequate to describe people's complex responses to overwhelming experience.

**Conclusion:** Each of the three extensions modifies one premise of psychoanalysis. Fanon shows that the continuity between family and society, the social premise of the Oedipal model, breaks down in the colonial situation, and the boundary of the unconscious shifts with it. Chodorow shows that the father-centred Oedipal narrative obscures the pre-Oedipal mother–daughter relation determined by the social division of labour, so that gender difference is *reproduced* rather than given. Trauma research shows that not every symptom is a disguise awaiting interpretation; some repetitions point not to a latent meaning but to a history that cannot be narrated. **The second mechanism, the "manifest/latent" double reading, here meets its first frontier: sometimes beneath the surface there is no repressed wish, only a reality not yet integrated.**

**Conclusion:** From Freud to Lacan, the subject loses its sovereignty over itself step by step. Freud split the mind into conscious and unconscious; the repressed can return only in the disguises of condensation, displacement and inversion, and the compulsion to repeat even overrides the pleasure principle; "the uncanny" shows that what frightens us most is precisely what is most familiar but has become strange through repression. The object-relations school traced the formation of the self back to the pre-Oedipal relation with the mother, but was accused for this of an overly optimistic theory of "adaptation". Lacan combined Freud with Saussure: the ego is an imaginary misrecognition of a whole external image in the mirror stage; the subject is assigned its place by a symbolic order that exists before it; and the unconscious is structured like a language, condensation being metaphor and displacement metonymy, the signified sliding incessantly under the signifier, desire forever pointing elsewhere along the chain of metonymy. For literary criticism the consequence of this path is a series of shifts in the object of interpretation: from the author's neurosis (Bonaparte's Poe), to the character's unconscious (Freud and Jones's Hamlet), to the unconscious of the text itself (Lacan's "Purloined Letter"). **The source of meaning moves from the language system and the reader to the division within the speaker, and the basic units of liberal humanism, "author", "character" and "self", are all redescribed as effects of the signifier.** The limits of this path are equally clear: the problem of evidence in Freudian interpretation and the bias of the Dora case; the androcentric Oedipal model and the "very dubious" concept of castration; the adaptationism of the object-relations school; the obscurity of Lacan's texts and Tallis's critique of the mirror stage; and trauma research's challenge to the idea that "every symptom is symbolic".

But Lacan's argument rests on a premise not yet questioned to the end. He treats the sliding of the signified and the endless extension of the signifying chain as the structure of *the unconscious*; but if this is the structure of *language itself*, then not only the subject but every system of meaning, including the ordered system of differences on which structuralism was founded, loses a centre that could bring the sliding to a halt. Lacan has already applied Saussure to the subject; deconstruction will push both to the extreme together. Layer 3's "who speaks?" and Layer 2's "can meaning be stable?" converge here, flowing together into the "death of the author". This is the question of P7.

## P7 When Structure Loses Its Centre, Can Meaning Still Be Stable? Poststructuralism and Deconstruction

P6 closed with a question: if what Lacan called "the incessant sliding of the signified under the signifier" describes not just the unconscious but language itself, is there still a centre where meaning can come to rest? Poststructuralism answers this question head on. In the six-layer framework it is the first part of Layer 2, whether meaning can be stable, and also the point where Layer 3 meets Layer 2: the question "who speaks?" will be posed again in the "death of the author". It inherits three things. First, Saussure from P3: a sign's identity is constituted by its differences from other signs, and poststructuralism will ask whether the system can still be ordered if difference has no fixed end-point (Ricks's objection to structuralism and Foucault's rejection of the manifest/latent distinction in P3 already anticipated this question). Second, Lacan from P6: the sliding signified and the divided subject. Third, the New Criticism of P2: the "organic unity" it trusted will become the most direct opposite of deconstructive reading, and yet the two show a surprising technical continuity.

Several of the mechanisms that run throughout are pushed to their limits here. The first mechanism, the `logic of relation and difference`, is radicalised: difference is no longer just the organising principle of a language system but the condition under which all presence, identity and substance are produced. The second, `manifest/latent double reading`, becomes "the unconscious of the text": deconstructive reading looks not for an author's hidden intention but for the contradictions a text exposes without knowing it. The third, `essence ↔ construction`, acquires a philosophical foundation: the authentic is itself an artefact. The fifth, the `shifting boundary between text and context`, reaches its limit in the famous phrase "there is nothing outside the text", at least on one reading. The argument therefore follows a clear route: first the philosophical genealogy before Derrida (Nietzsche, Heidegger, Bataille); then the differences between structuralism and poststructuralism and the turning point of 1966; at the theoretical core, différance and the trace, the logic of the supplement and "nothing outside the text", and Barthes's "death of the author"; and finally the turn to practice: how deconstruction reads at the three levels of word, text and language, and its real relation to the tradition of close reading.

### Nietzsche and Heidegger: Truth as Metaphor, Identity as Difference

**Background: the confidence of positivism and its first crack.** In the first half of the nineteenth century `positivism` was so dominant that few doubted the mind could attain purely factual, scientific knowledge of the world. Doubt about this certainty began at the end of the century, and ironically it used science's own observations about perception. In his early essay "On Truth and Lies in a Nonmoral Sense" (1873), **Friedrich Nietzsche** (1844–1900) argued that the intellect, as a means for the preservation of the individual, unfolds its principal powers precisely in `dissimulation`. Nature conceals most things from man, even his own body (the convolutions of the intestines, the rushing of the blood, the delicate vibrations of the fibres), so as to lock him in a proud, deceptive knowledge: nature threw away the key. If anyone could peer out through a crack in the chamber of consciousness, he would find that man, indifferent to his own ignorance, rests on the merciless, the greedy, the murderous, "as if hanging in dreams on the back of a tiger".

**Mechanism: two metaphors.** Are the conventions of language, then, products of knowledge, of the love of truth? Do names and things coincide? Nietzsche says no. What is a word? The expression of a nerve stimulus in sounds. To infer from the nerve stimulus a cause outside us is already a false and unjustified application of the principle of causality; how dare we say "the stone is hard", as if "hard" were known to us otherwise than as a wholly subjective stimulation? German makes the tree masculine (*der Baum*) and the plant feminine (*die Pflanze*): what arbitrary metaphors! We say "snake", a name that fits only its winding, and so could equally well apply to a worm: what arbitrary demarcations! The many languages placed side by side show that truth or adequate expression does not matter to words; otherwise there would not be so many languages. Nietzsche breaks the process into two leaps. A nerve stimulus is transferred into a perceptual image: first metaphor. The image is then imitated in a sound: second metaphor. "And each time there is a complete overleaping of one sphere, right into the middle of an entirely new and different one." Between subject and object there is no causality, no correctness, no expression, but at most an aesthetic relation: a suggestive transference, a stammering translation into a completely foreign tongue.

**Mechanism: the concept equates the unequal.** Every word immediately becomes a concept, not because it is meant to recall the unique, wholly individualised original experience, but because it must fit countless more or less similar cases at once, which means cases never equal and so altogether unequal. **Every concept originates through our equating what is unequal.** Just as no leaf is ever wholly equal to another, the concept "leaf" is formed by arbitrarily dropping individual differences and forgetting distinguishing qualities; it then awakens the idea that there is in nature, besides the leaves, something called "the leaf", a primal form on which all leaves are woven, drawn, measured and coloured, but by clumsy hands, so that no copy turns out a faithful likeness of the original. *This is a reversal of Plato's theory of Forms: it is not that the Form precedes the particulars, but that the omissions of language produce the illusion of the Form. Saussure said in P3 that language divides up a continuum; Nietzsche gives the genealogical version of the same insight: the division is not only arbitrary but paid for by forgetting differences.*

**Definition: truth as a forgotten metaphor.** From this comes Nietzsche's most famous definition: "What, then, is truth? A mobile army of metaphors, metonyms and anthropomorphisms: in short, a sum of human relations which have been poetically and rhetorically intensified, transferred and embellished, and which after long use seem firm, canonical and obligatory to a people. Truths are illusions which we have forgotten are illusions; metaphors which have become worn out and drained of sensuous force; coins which have lost their embossing and are now considered as metal and no longer as coins." The key here is `forgetting`. The obligation society imposes in order to exist is to be "truthful", that is, to use the usual metaphors; in moral terms, "to lie according to a fixed convention, to lie with the herd in a style binding upon all". Man forgets that he does so, and **it is precisely through this unconsciousness, this forgetting, that he arrives at his sense of truth**. Setting himself against the "liar", whom no one trusts and everyone excludes, he demonstrates to himself the venerability, reliability and usefulness of truth. As a "rational" being he dissolves concrete metaphors into schemata, and so builds a pyramidal order of castes and degrees, a new world of laws, privileges, subordinations and boundaries. Every perceptual metaphor is individual and unique and so knows how to escape all classification; the great edifice of concepts has the rigid regularity of a Roman columbarium. Anyone touched by this coldness will hardly believe that the concept, as bony, cubical and interchangeable as a die, is nothing but "the residue of a metaphor".

**Example: the columbarium, the bush and the camel.** Nietzsche's rhetoric is itself a demonstration of this view. Man is a genius of construction, piling up an infinitely complicated dome of concepts on shifting foundations, as if on running water; he is more admirable than the bee, which builds with wax gathered from nature, whereas man builds with concepts he must first make within himself. But this is not because he is driven to truth. If someone hides something behind a bush and then looks for it in the same place and finds it, there is not much to boast of in this seeking and finding; yet this is how matters stand with seeking and finding "truth" in the realm of reason. If I define the mammal and then, having inspected a camel, declare "look, a mammal", I have indeed brought a truth to light, but it is of limited value. It is anthropomorphic through and through and contains not a single point that would be "true in itself", real and universally valid apart from man. The seeker after such truths seeks at bottom only the metamorphosis of the world into man, treating the whole world as the infinitely prolonged echo of one original sound, man. *Here one can hear the earliest and most radical version of the first shared idea of theory in P1, "basic categories are socially constructed".*

**Mechanism: the will to power and "making equal".** Nietzsche's unfinished *The Will to Power* (notebooks of 1885–1886) pushes this etymological critique into a power theory of knowledge. The anthology's editors summarise: Nietzsche held that the fundamental drive of all life is a desire for mastery, and that when we know the world we master its reality, flowing in time and manifold in space, by fixing identities with words. The fragments read like a series of axioms. The essential feature of our thinking is fitting new material into old schemas (the "Procrustes' bed"), "making" the new "equal"; all thought, judgement and perception, as comparison, presuppose "positing as equal", and earlier still "making equal", a process no different from the amoeba's incorporation of the matter it appropriates; **"the will to equality is the will to power"**. Logic is conditioned by the assumption that identical cases exist, and so can be carried through only after a fundamental *falsification* of all events: logic does not spring from the will to truth. The inventive force that devised categories served our needs: for security, for quick understanding by means of signs and sounds, for means of abbreviation. "Substance", "subject", "object", "being" and "becoming" have nothing to do with metaphysical truths. "It is the powerful who made the names of things into law, and among the powerful it is the greatest artists in abstraction who created the categories." A morality, a way of life tested over a long time, finally enters consciousness as a law, becomes credible, unshakeable, holy and true, and "it is part of its development that its origin should be forgotten; that is a sign that it has become master". The categories of reason may likewise have prevailed by groping and through their relative utility, and then been taken as a priori, beyond experience and irrefutable. Even the law of contradiction, which Aristotle held to be the most certain of principles, is no exception: either it asserts something about being, as if we already knew this from elsewhere; or it means that opposite attributes *should* not be ascribed to it, in which case logic is an imperative, not for knowing the true but for positing and arranging a world that shall be called true by us.

**Conclusion: the fiction of the subject and the retreat of the "true world".** Nietzsche draws a chain of consequences from this. Once we understand that the "subject" is not something that produces effects but only a fiction, the reality of things (which was invented on the model of the subject and projected onto the chaos of sensations) also disappears; so does the "thing in itself", since it is at bottom the conception of a "subject in itself"; so the opposition between "thing in itself" and "appearance" no longer holds, and the concept of "appearance" disappears with it. Permanence, self-identity and being inhere neither in the subject nor in the object; they are only complexes of events that seem relatively durable. Oppositions such as rest/motion and firm/loose do not exist in themselves; they are differences of degree that look like oppositions from a certain perspective: **"There are no opposites: only from those of logic do we derive the concept of opposites, and falsely transfer it to things."** "Truth" is therefore not something there to be found but something that must be created; it is the name of a process, of a will to overcoming that has in itself no end, another word for "will to power". Man seeks a "true world" that does not contradict itself, does not deceive and does not change because he has derived suffering from change and contradiction; belief in being is only a consequence, the real prime mover being mistrust of becoming. The will to truth is thus "the impotence of the will to create": how far one can do without meaning in things, how far one can endure living in a meaningless world, is the measure of the strength of one's will. The editors point out that Nietzsche's scepticism about a separate realm of the spirit continues in poststructuralism's questioning of the secular versions of this transcendent ideal: **when poststructuralists declare that there is no `transcendental signified`, they are echoing Nietzsche's claim that the world has no theological origin or purpose**.

**Mechanism: Heidegger and "difference as such".** Together with Nietzsche, **Martin Heidegger** (1889–1976) played a key role in shaping Derrida's philosophy of deconstruction. His *Being and Time* (1927) placed philosophy in the world of existence, displacing centuries of purely rationalist concern. His essay *Identity and Difference* (1957) works out the necessity of difference for any determination of identity. Metaphysics thinks the Being of beings in the greatest generality and the highest totality; it presupposes Being as the ground that gives reasons, so all metaphysics is "fathoming the ground", reasoning that accounts for the ground. But whether we speak of "the Being of beings" or "the beings of Being", each time we are dealing with a difference. When we try to form an idea of it, we are at once tempted to take difference as a relation our thinking adds to Being and beings, so that difference is reduced to a distinction, a product of the human understanding. But if difference is an addition, to what is it added? To beings; yet "beings" means nothing other than "what is", which is to say that we have already placed the so-called addition under "Being". Wherever we try to introduce difference as an addition, we already find Being and beings in difference. **Difference is not added afterwards; it is the place where Being and beings appear**; it is everywhere, and precisely for that reason unnoticed. Heidegger's project is to show that the essence of the `onto-theo-logical constitution` of metaphysics derives from this matter, met at the beginning of the history of metaphysics, running through all its epochs, yet everywhere concealed and therefore forgotten, a forgetting from which we ourselves cannot escape. *Nietzsche says truth is a forgotten metaphor; Heidegger says metaphysics is founded on the forgetting of difference. "Forgetting" is the key word linking both to Derrida, who in "Différance" will explicitly place his concept after Heidegger's "ontological difference".*

**Definition: heterology.** The third forerunner came from outside academic philosophy. **Georges Bataille**, an independent scholar who never held an academic post, was inspired by Mauss's *The Gift* (1925) to develop an idea of economy based on "unreserved expenditure" (holding nothing back, seeking no return); Derrida and other poststructuralists saw in it an anticipation of their own idea that the excess of differential relations overflows the limits of meaning and truth. Bataille's writing of 1930 divides social facts into two polarised impulses: `appropriation` and `excretion`. Appropriation is marked by `homogeneity` (static equilibrium) between the appropriator and the object as final result: man appropriates not only food but clothing, furniture, dwellings and instruments of production, and finally land divided into parcels; appropriation is achieved through a homogeneity (identity), of a more or less conventional kind, between possessor and possessed. Excretion results from `heterogeneity` and may move towards ever greater heterogeneity, releasing impulses ever more contradictory, its representative being sacrificial consumption, whose primitive form is the orgy. A more fundamental homogenisation takes place in knowledge: everywhere in the external world man substitutes classifying series of concepts for objects that are a priori unthinkable, and the representations of the world in philosophy, science and common sense are as far from what we could imagine a priori as the public square of a capital is from a high mountain region. This appropriation reaches its terminal phase in the sense of excretion only when the irreducible waste products of its operation are determined. `Heterology` is the deliberate taking up of this terminal process, hitherto regarded as the abortion and shame of human thought. It is not "the science of the heterogeneous", since the heterogeneous is by definition outside scientific knowledge, which applies only to homogeneous elements; it opposes any homogeneous representation of the world, that is, any philosophical system, and leads to a complete reversal of the philosophical process, philosophy ceasing to be an instrument of appropriation and serving excretion instead.

**Mechanism: the kinship of the sacred and waste.** Bataille noticed a strange kinship: a culture's "waste" and its "sacred" are both regarded as wholly outside normal life. Just as in the sociology of religion *mana* and taboo are particular applications of a more general form, the sacred, so the sacred itself can be seen as a restricted form of the heterogeneous. The heterogeneous world includes everything resulting from *unproductive* expenditure, everything rejected by homogeneous society as waste *or* as superior transcendent value: the excreta of the human body and analogous matter (rubbish, vermin), parts of the body, persons, words or acts with suggestive erotic value, unconscious processes such as dreams and neuroses, and the numerous social forms homogeneous society cannot assimilate (mobs, warriors, aristocratic and impoverished classes, violent individuals who refuse the rule: madmen, leaders, poets and so on). Heterogeneous elements provoke affective reactions of varying intensity, now attraction, now repulsion, and the repulsive can become attractive and vice versa. Heterogeneous reality is not of the same order as homogeneous reality. Homogeneous reality presents itself with the abstract, neutral aspect of strictly defined and identified objects; it is solid reality. Heterogeneous reality is a force or shock, passing from one object to another as a charge, a value, in which the part can have the same value as the whole. The structure of knowledge of homogeneous reality is science; knowledge of heterogeneous reality is found in the mystical thinking of primitives and in dreams, and "it is identical to the structure of the *unconscious*". *The "value passing from one object to a neighbouring one" described here is exactly displacement in Freud's dream-work in P6; Bataille's own notes cite The Interpretation of Dreams.* In a note Bataille points out that the Latin *sacer* carries the double meaning "filthy" and "sacred", so that the most expressive equivalent of the abstract term "heterology" is "scatology". *A word that carries two opposite meanings at once is a structure deconstruction will meet again and again; pharmakon and guest/host/hostis below are variants of it.*

**Example: laughter.** Bataille pushes this logic into philosophy itself. Philosophy, unlike science and common sense, must positively consider the waste products of intellectual appropriation, but it usually considers them only in abstract total forms (nothingness, infinity, the absolute) to which it cannot itself give positive content; its speculations come down in the end to "adequately" identifying the infinite world with the finite, the unknowable with the known. Once the heterogeneous is made purely objective, it is incorporated into a homogeneous intellectual system, and its excretory character is hypocritically abolished. So "when the effort of rational comprehension ends in contradiction, the practice of intellectual scatology requires the excretion of unassimilable elements", which is a vulgar way of saying that **a burst of laughter is the only imaginable and definitively terminal result of philosophical speculation, and not the means**.

**Conclusion:** The three forerunners prepared deconstruction from three directions. Nietzsche showed that truth is a forgotten metaphor, the concept an equating of the unequal and logic an imperative of the will to power, so drawing the foundations of philosophy back into rhetoric. Heidegger showed that difference is not a relation added to identity but the condition under which identity appears, and that the history of metaphysics is the history of the forgetting of this difference. Bataille showed that a homogeneous system always produces waste it cannot assimilate, and that this waste occupies the same place as the sacred. Superimpose the three and you have Derrida's basic gesture: **in any system that claims to be complete, self-sufficient and self-present, look for the difference it must forget, suppress or exclude**. When this gesture appeared in France in the 1960s, it first took the form of a divergence from structuralism.

### Four Differences Between Structuralism and Poststructuralism

**Problem: continuation or revolt?** Is `poststructuralism` a continuation and development of structuralism, or a revolt against it? In an important sense it is the latter, since one very effective way to revolt is to accuse one's predecessors of lacking the courage of their convictions. The signature view of structuralism is that language does not merely reflect or record the world but shapes it, so that how we see is what we see (P3). Poststructuralists hold that the consequence of this belief is that we enter a radically uncertain universe, since we cannot reach any fixed landmark beyond the processing of language, and so have no definite standard by which to measure anything. Barry's image: sitting in a stationary train with another train standing between you and the distant platform, when that train moves you may feel that you are the one moving, until it has gone and you see the fixed platform again. Poststructuralism amounts to saying that if we take seriously what the structuralists say about language, the fixed platform is gone for ever. Or another image: in space, without gravity, there is no up or down. This situation without intellectual reference points is what poststructuralists call the `decentred universe`, in which by definition we cannot know where we are, because every concept that previously defined a centre (and therefore a margin) has been "deconstructed". **A way in: anxiety about language.** This concern may seem remote at first; doesn't language work perfectly well in everyday life? But as soon as we go beyond casual conversation with acquaintances and peers (writing to the bank, writing an essay, making conversation with strangers at a party, writing a letter of condolence), almost everyone worries that language will express something we did not intend, leave the wrong impression, betray our ignorance, coldness or confusion. Even phrases like "if you see what I mean" and "so to speak" reveal that we are not really in control of the system of language. Magnified, these anxieties share a source with the radical linguistic scepticism characteristic of deconstruction.

**Distinction: four differences.** The theoretical differences between the two can be summed up in four points:

- **Origins.** Structuralism derives ultimately from linguistics, which has always been confident about the possibility of establishing objective knowledge: observe accurately, collect data systematically, reason logically, and reliable conclusions about language and the world follow. Structuralism inherited this confident scientific outlook. Poststructuralism derives ultimately from philosophy, which has always stressed the difficulty of attaining reliable knowledge; Nietzsche's dictum "there are no facts, only interpretations" sums up the view. Poststructuralism inherited and intensified this habit of scepticism, regarding any confidence in scientific method as naive, and even taking a kind of masochistic intellectual pleasure in "knowing for certain that we cannot know anything for certain", while being fully aware of the irony and paradox involved.
- **Tone and style.** Structuralist writing tends towards abstraction and generalisation, aiming at a detached "scientific coolness"; Barthes's "Introduction to the Structural Analysis of Narratives" (1966) proceeds in orderly steps, with diagrams, in a neutral, anonymous style. Poststructuralist writing is more emotional; its tone is often urgent and excited, its style flamboyant and self-consciously showy. Titles may contain puns and allusions; the central thread of the argument is often built on a pun or wordplay, and often seizes on some "material" aspect of language, such as a metaphor the author uses or the etymology of a word.
- **Attitude to language.** Structuralists accept that the world is constructed through language, but decide to live with the fact, continuing to think and perceive through language: language is, after all, an ordered rather than a chaotic system, and awareness of our dependence on it need not lead to intellectual despair. Poststructuralism insists more "fundamentalistically" on the consequences of the view that reality itself is in effect textual, and develops an almost fatal anxiety about the possibility of any knowledge through language. It speaks of language with an almost obsessive liquid imagery: signs drift away from what they refer to, meaning is fluid, constantly "slipping" and "spilling", and cannot be carried carefully in containers called words from "giver" to "receiver". Meaning cannot be planted in fixed positions like a row of potatoes, only scattered at random, like a sower walking along and flinging seed in wide sweeps: `dissemination`.
- **Programme.** Structuralism questions the ways we structure and categorise reality, urging us to break free of habitual modes of perception and classification, but believes that a more reliable view can be reached in this way. Poststructuralism is more radical: it distrusts the very notion of reason, distrusts the idea of the human being as an independent entity, and prefers the "dissolved" or "constructed" subject, in which what we take to be an individual is really the product of social and linguistic forces, not an essence but merely a "textual fabric". Its fire of scepticism burns away the intellectual foundations on which Western civilisation was built.

**Background: 1966 and the event of "decentring".** Poststructuralism emerged in France in the late 1960s. The anthology's editors date its beginning to Paris around 1967: structuralism, which had dominated French intellectual life for most of the 1960s, was replaced by the new thinking of Derrida, Kristeva, Deleuze, Irigaray, Cixous, Lyotard and Baudrillard. The three books Derrida published in 1967 (*Writing and Difference*, a collection of essays on philosophy and literature; *Of Grammatology*, a long critical reading of Lévi-Strauss, Saussure and Rousseau; and *Speech and Phenomena*, a "deconstruction" of Husserl's *Logical Investigations*) in effect brought structuralism to an end. The editors also note that the concept of difference Derrida found in Nietzsche, Heidegger and Saussure reminded him of the pre-Socratic philosophers, who stood outside the dominant tradition of Plato and Aristotle. Aristotle understood knowledge as the analysis of objects by their essences, and Plato invented a realm of Forms beyond physical reality; the pre-Socratics, by contrast, were concerned with the spatio-temporal processes that weave all material things together, the "interweaving" (*sumplokē*) of being, stressing change rather than rest, the blending of things rather than their separateness. Barry dates the beginning to Derrida's 1966 lecture "Structure, Sign and Play in the Discourse of the Human Sciences". In this lecture Derrida saw a particular "event" of modernity that constituted a radical break with past ways of thinking, and loosely connected it with the philosophy of Nietzsche and Heidegger and with Freud's psychoanalysis: the `decentring` of our intellectual universe. Previously it was taken for granted that everything had a norm or centre. The Renaissance slogan was "man is the measure of all things", and the norms of white Western man in dress, behaviour, architecture and intellectual outlook provided a firm centre, from which deviations and variations could be identified as "other" and marginal. In the twentieth century these centres were destroyed or eroded. Sometimes it was historical events: the First World War destroyed the illusion of steady material progress, and the Holocaust destroyed the idea of Europe as the source and centre of human civilisation. Sometimes it was scientific discoveries: relativity destroyed time and space as fixed central absolutes. Sometimes it was intellectual or artistic revolutions: the modernist art of the first three decades of the century rejected such central absolutes as harmony in music, chronological sequence in narrative, and the representation of the visible world in the visual arts. In the resulting universe there are no absolutes or fixed points, only `free play`. In the lecture Derrida embraces this decentred universe as a liberation, and calls on us not to be among "those who turn their eyes away in the face of the as yet unnameable which is proclaiming itself"; Barry sees this quasi-religious appeal as typical of the apocalyptic tone common in poststructuralist writing. Along these lines, deconstructive reading tends to turn literary texts into emblems of the decentred universe: texts previously seen as unified works of art are shown to be fragmented, self-divided and centreless, and always end up representing the "monstrosities" foretold at the end of "Structure, Sign and Play".

**Example: Hyppolite's question.** The lecture was given in October 1966 at an international symposium at Johns Hopkins University, "The Languages of Criticism and the Sciences of Man". The symposium was organised jointly with the "sciences of man" section of the École Pratique des Hautes Études in Paris, the cradle of structuralism; the term "sciences of man" referred to a new field linking the humanities and social sciences (anthropology, philosophy, literature, linguistics, psychology, history and so on), exactly the network of disciplines pooling resources under the structuralist banner. The symposium celebrated the arrival and establishment of structuralism, and leading figures such as René Girard, Georges Poulet, Lucien Goldmann, Tzvetan Todorov and Barthes attended; but it also marked a move beyond the complete dominance of linguistics, since it was already recognised that linguistics could not really deliver on its promise of a "universal model for understanding all human phenomena". *(This is the second of Barry's "ten events" in the history of theory, the first being the Indiana conference of 1958 in P4; all of them will be strung together into a timeline in P17.)* Derrida's impact lay in announcing his doubts about the triumph of structuralism and opening the new phase of "poststructuralism". But Barry thinks the characteristic weakness of his method already showed in the discussion after the lecture. Jean Hyppolite, questioning from a structuralist perspective, kept asking: can there be a structure without a referent? The former "centres" of our thought ("man", "God", "truth" and so on) have been decentred and erased, leaving only structures such as "difference": neither A nor B, only the difference between them. Language is a game with a rule-governed structure, but we do not ask what the game is for, what ultimate purpose it serves. One cannot, he said, think a structure without a centre. Barry illustrates the problem with football: a match is governed by an elaborate structure of rules and conventions, but what lies behind the rules? The excitement of playing and watching? The trophy the winners receive? The glory of victory? Or the sublimated sense of triumph over life's adversities that victory brings? Something must surely lie behind the structure. Derrida did not answer, but deflected the question in what later became an all too automatic way: "I don't know where I am going." Pressed further on what a structure is, he said the concept of structure "is no longer satisfying", so "what I have said can be understood as a criticism of structuralism". Someone accused him of always talking about the "non-centre", when without the concept of a centre perception cannot be explained, "since perception is precisely the way in which the world appears centred to me". Derrida denied that he had ever denied the existence of the centre, adding: **"I believe that the centre is a function, not a being, a reality, but a function."** Yet in the end he denied the existence of perception: "I don't believe that anything like perception exists … I don't believe that there is any perception." **Objection:** in Barry's view this closed off a "moderate" understanding of poststructuralism, as a system that merely stresses the constructedness of everything, that "perception is always conception"; and the exchange seems to show Derrida being pushed into a more extreme formulation than he intended, which he could never afterwards retract. *(This improvised answer later resurfaced in an unexpected way in the Sokal affair of 1996; see P17.)*

**Another judgement:** Barry and the editors present the temper of this divergence differently.
