**Objection: Lyotard's counter-attack.** The word "postmodernism" was in use as early as the 1930s, but its current meaning and vogue can be said to begin with **Jean-François Lyotard**'s *The Postmodern Condition: A Report on Knowledge* (1979). The anthology's editors add that Lyotard borrowed the word from American culture, where it had been used to describe a self-reflexive writing that broke with standard literary conventions; almost at once "postmodernism" came to be applied both to the contemporary era and to poststructuralism. Lyotard's essay "Answering the Question: What Is Postmodernism?", first published in 1982 and included as an appendix to the book in 1984, entered this debate about the Enlightenment in a somewhat oblique way, aiming chiefly at Habermas. Barry points out that Lyotard's opening move in effect turned the debate into a contest to prove that the opponent is the real conservative (a common trump card in the writing of cultural polemic): "From every direction we are being urged to put an end to experimentation." He has read a "thinker of repute" defending modernity against those he calls the neoconservatives; for Lyotard, Habermas is just one voice in a chorus calling for an end to "artistic experimentation", calling for "order … unity, identity, security", in a word, to "liquidate the heritage of the avant-gardes". The Enlightenment project Habermas wants to continue is, for Lyotard, just another self-authorising, "all-embracing", "totalising" explanation of things, like Christianity, Marxism or the myth of scientific progress.

**Definition: metanarratives and "incredulity".** These `metanarratives` (also called `grand narratives`) claim to explain everything and to offer comfort, but are really illusions fostered in order to smother difference, opposition and plurality. Lyotard's own definition is more precise. Science has always been in conflict with narratives; judged by the yardstick of science, most narratives prove to be fables. But to the extent that science does not restrict itself to stating useful regularities and seeks the truth, it is obliged to legitimate the rules of its own game, and so produces a discourse of legitimation with respect to its own status, called philosophy. He uses the term "modern" to designate any science that legitimates itself with reference to such a metadiscourse, making an explicit appeal to some grand narrative, such as **the dialectics of Spirit, the hermeneutics of meaning, the emancipation of the rational or working subject, or the creation of wealth**. For example, the rule of consensus between sender and addressee of a statement with truth-value is deemed acceptable if it is cast in terms of a possible unanimity between rational minds: this is the Enlightenment narrative, in which the hero of knowledge works towards a good ethico-political end, universal peace. Hence: **"Simplifying to the extreme, I define postmodern as incredulity toward metanarratives."** This incredulity is undoubtedly a product of progress in the sciences, but that progress in turn presupposes it. The narrative function is losing its functors: its great hero, its great dangers, its great voyages, its great goal. It is being dispersed in clouds of narrative language elements, but also denotative, prescriptive, descriptive and so on, each cloud carrying its own pragmatic valencies specific to its kind; each of us lives at the intersection of many of these. The society of the future therefore falls less within the province of a Newtonian anthropology (such as structuralism or systems theory) than of a pragmatics of language particles: there are many different `language games`, which give rise to institutions only in patches ("local determinism"). *The phrase "Newtonian anthropology" shows that Lyotard counts structuralism (P3, P4) too as a metanarrative kind of knowledge, one that assumes elements are commensurable and the whole determinable.*

**Mechanism: two narratives of legitimation.** Lyotard distinguishes two main versions of the narrative of legitimation in the history of modern knowledge, one more political, the other more philosophical. The subject of the first is humanity as the hero of liberty: all peoples have a right to science, and if the social subject is not already the subject of scientific knowledge, it is because priests and tyrants have forbidden it; this narrative leans towards a policy of primary education, of which the educational policy of the French Third Republic is an example. In this version knowledge finds its validity not within itself but in a practical subject, humanity; the principle that moves the people is not the self-legitimation of knowledge but the self-grounding of freedom. This gives priority to the language game Kant called imperative and we now call prescriptive: what matters is not merely to legitimate denotative statements such as "the earth revolves around the sun" but prescriptive ones such as "Carthage must be destroyed" or "the minimum wage must be set at x dollars". Knowledge is no longer the subject but in the service of the subject; a scientist who judges the state's policy unjust may refuse to lend it scholarly support, which reintroduces the critical function of knowledge. Lyotard makes two remarks on this. First, Marxism has wavered between the two models: the party takes the place of the university, the proletariat that of the people or of humanity, dialectical materialism that of speculative idealism; the result may be Stalinism, in which the sciences figure only as citations of the metanarrative of "the march towards socialism". But it can also develop, along the lines of the second version, into a form of critical knowledge, declaring that science has no legitimacy except in giving the empirical subject (the proletariat) the means of emancipation from alienation and repression; this is roughly the position of the Frankfurt School. Second, Heidegger's address of 27 May 1933 on assuming the rectorship of the University of Freiburg is an unhappy episode in the history of legitimation: speculative science becomes the questioning of Being, and this questioning is the "destiny" of the German people, called a "historical-spiritual people"; inserting the narratives of race and labour into the narrative of the spirit in order to legitimate knowledge and its institutions was theoretically inconsistent, but sufficient to find disastrous echoes in the political sphere. *An editors' note at this point adds that Heidegger became rector only after joining the Nazi Party as the law required, and publicly supported National Socialism. This is a necessary reminder for understanding the genealogy of forerunners in P7, and it stands in distant counterpoint to the affair of de Man's wartime articles that Barry records.*

**Mechanism: delegitimation.** In contemporary post-industrial society and postmodern culture, the grand narrative has lost its credibility, regardless of the mode of unification it uses, speculative narrative or narrative of emancipation. One may attribute this to the blossoming of technology since the Second World War (which shifted emphasis from the ends of action to its means), or to the redeployment of advanced liberal capitalism after its retreat under the protection of Keynesianism during 1930–1960; but Lyotard thinks such searches for causes will always be disappointing, and that the seeds of "delegitimation" and nihilism must first be found within the grand narratives of the nineteenth century. Take the narrative of emancipation. The difference between a denotative statement with cognitive value and a prescriptive statement with practical value is a difference of relevance, and therefore of competence: nothing proves that if a statement describing a real situation is true, a prescriptive statement based upon it will be just. **There is no inference, in the sense of propositional logic, between "the door is closed" and "open the door"**; they belong to two autonomous sets of rules. The splitting of reason into theoretical and practical reason had the effect of indirectly attacking the legitimacy of scientific discourse: it revealed that science is a language game with its own rules, with no special calling to supervise the game of practice (nor the game of aesthetics), and so the game of science is put on a par with the others. More importantly, it is incapable of legitimating itself. The social subject itself seems to dissolve in this dissemination of language games: the social bond is linguistic, but it is not woven of a single thread. Wittgenstein writes: "Our language can be seen as an ancient city: a maze of little streets and squares, of old and new houses, and of houses with additions from various periods; and this surrounded by a multitude of new boroughs with straight regular streets and uniform houses." And he asks, with the old sorites paradox, how many houses or streets it takes before a town begins to be a town. Lyotard adds that thirty-five years later one could add to the new suburbs of this city the languages of machines, the matrices of game theory, new systems of musical notation, the notations of non-denotative logics, the language of the genetic code …

**Implication: the mourning is complete.** One can take a pessimistic view of this splintering: nobody speaks all these languages, they have no universal metalanguage, the project of the system-subject has failed, the goal of emancipation has nothing to do with science, and we are all stuck in the positivism of this or that discipline. Turn-of-the-century Vienna grew up on this pessimism: not only artists such as Musil, Kraus, Hofmannsthal, Loos, Schoenberg and Broch, but also the philosophers Mach and Wittgenstein. *This is the very epicentre of what Barry calls the modernist earthquake, and Loos's "ornament is crime" is the manifesto of modernist austere aesthetics.* But Lyotard says: **"We may say today that the mourning process has been completed."** Wittgenstein's strength lay in not opting for the positivism developed by the Vienna Circle, but in outlining, in his investigation of language games, a kind of legitimation not based on performativity. Most people have lost the nostalgia for the lost narrative, but it in no way follows that they are reduced to barbarity: what saves them from it is their knowledge that legitimation can come only from their own linguistic practice and communicational interaction.

**Mechanism: performativity and terror.** After the metanarratives, where can legitimacy reside? One dangerous answer is `performativity`, the best possible input/output ratio. Decision-makers try to manage these social clouds according to input/output matrices, following a logic that implies the commensurability of elements and the determinability of the whole; they allocate our lives for the growth of power. In matters of social justice and of scientific truth alike, the legitimation of that power is based on optimising the system's performance, its efficiency, and applying this criterion to all our games necessarily entails a certain level of terror, whether soft or hard: **"be operational (that is, commensurable) or disappear."** Capitalism solves the problem of funding research in its own way: scientists, technicians and instruments are purchased not to find truth but to augment power. Since performativity increases the ability to produce proof, it also increases the ability to be right; conversely, the probability that an order will be pronounced just increases with its chances of being implemented. This leads Luhmann to suppose that in post-industrial societies the normativity of laws is replaced by the performativity of procedures. Power thus legitimates itself: it legitimates science and law on the basis of their efficiency, and legitimates efficiency on the basis of science and law; the general computerisation of society may bring exactly this "context control", since the performativity of a statement increases in proportion to the amount of information about its referent one has at one's disposal. And when efficiency is obtained by "say this or do this, or else you will never speak again", we enter the realm of terror, and the social bond is destroyed. *This 1979 analysis reads with particular force today, in a situation where research funding, information storage and "performativity" stand side by side. It also anticipates the question of Foucault's "power/knowledge" in P10.*

**Conclusion: paralogy, not consensus.** Does legitimacy then reside in consensus reached through discussion, as Habermas thinks? Lyotard's answer is no: **such consensus does violence to the heterogeneity of language games, and invention is always born of dissension.** Postmodern knowledge is not simply a tool of the authorities; it refines our sensitivity to differences and reinforces our ability to tolerate the incommensurable; its principle is not the `homology` of experts but the `paralogy` of inventors. Barry's summary is that grand narratives are no longer tenable, and the most we can hope for is a series of "mini-narratives", provisional, contingent, temporary and relative, which provide a basis for the actions of particular groups in particular local circumstances; postmodernity thus "deconstructs" the basic aims of the Enlightenment, "the idea of a unitary end of history and of a subject".

**Another judgement:** The two books present Lyotard with clearly different emphases. Barry places Lyotard in a polemic: against Habermas, throwing the label "conservative" back at him, concluding with mini-narratives; this is a Lyotard of cultural history. The anthology's editors select from *The Postmodern Condition* the analyses of the legitimation of knowledge, of the denotative/prescriptive distinction and of performativity, and stress in their introduction that Lyotard saw the world as a rhetorical field of competing little narratives, in which people strive to make their narratives more persuasive and so make their views and interests prevail; this is a Lyotard of the sociology of knowledge and political philosophy. *The first shows how "postmodern" became a camp label; the second shows why it still has explanatory power in the analysis of the institutions of knowledge.*

**Example: *Waiting for Godot*.** The example of postmodernist criticism Barry gives is a direct application of Lyotard's ideas: Jeffrey Nealon's "Samuel Beckett and the Postmodern: Language Games, Play and *Waiting for Godot*". Nealon first explains the "language game", which derives from Wittgenstein: when we claim that something is true, we measure it not against some external absolute standard but against internal rules and criteria that operate only within a designated field, just as "knight to king's rook four" may be a winning move in chess but carries no weight in a football match or an argument about whose turn it is to do the washing-up. For Nealon, Vladimir and Estragon are playing such language games without realising their full significance: such language games are all we have, there is no transcendent reality behind them, they are self-validating, and they provide the social identity we seek. On his account, what constitutes the two men's social bond is the playing of their discourse, not any agreed meaning of it, so that waiting for Godot to legitimate their society was unnecessary from the start. They want the guarantee and absolute validation of some "grand narrative", which in the play is linked with the Christian idea of salvation. Lucky's "thinking" monologue at the end of Act One is a parody of the "totalising" metadiscourses of philosophy and religion, a practical demonstration of the "language game of truth": if Godot did come, what could he offer but this kind of pretentious and pedantic gibberish? The two are happy and creative when they forget Godot, but they keep coming back to him. Barry's reading is that **they are stuck in the "modernist" phase, experiencing fragmentation with nostalgia and anxiety; at times they seem about to make the "breakthrough" to a postmodern attitude, but in the end they fail to do so.** He suggests applying the same reading to other "waiting" plays: Pinter's *The Dumb Waiter*, or Chekhov's *Three Sisters*, where the three sisters wait in vain for some outside force to transform their provincial lives. The ideals each of them longs for can be seen as personal "metanarratives", and Moscow, that glittering mixture of memory and desire, constitutes for them a kind of hyperreality or simulacrum.

**Operations: what postmodernist critics actually do.** When these ideas are applied to literature, the commonest practice of postmodernist criticism is to find postmodernist themes, tendencies and attitudes in twentieth-century literary works and explore their implications; Nealon's reading of *Godot* belongs mainly here, and derives directly from Lyotard. Adjacent to this is attention to "the disappearance of the real": critics foreground novels that can be said to embody this condition, seeing a fluid postmodern identity, for example, in a mixture of genres such as the thriller, the detective story, the mythic epic and the realist psychological novel; this dimension comes from Baudrillard. A third practice is to foreground the "intertextual elements" in literature (parody, pastiche and allusion), forms in which texts refer to other texts much more than to a secure external reality; this extends into criticism the concepts of intertextuality and "text" from P3 and P7. The remaining three practices are connected with the difference in mood and style between modernism and postmodernism: foregrounding irony in Eco's sense (the modernist tries to destroy the past, while the postmodernist realises that the past must be revisited, but "with irony"); foregrounding "narcissistic" elements in narrative technique, where the novel focuses on and discusses its own aims and processes, thereby "denaturalising" its content; and challenging the distinction between high and low culture, foregrounding texts that are a mixture of the two. *If one sorts these six practices by their sources, it becomes clear that "postmodernist criticism" is less a method than a set of thematic concerns.*

### Rhizomes and Little Narratives: The Social Version of Decentring

**Background: from Nietzsche to *A Thousand Plateaus*.** Lyotard applied decentring to the legitimation of knowledge; **Gilles Deleuze** and **Félix Guattari** applied it to models of history and the world. Deleuze's book on Nietzsche, *Nietzsche and Philosophy* (1962), helped launch the interest in Nietzsche that culminated in the emergence of poststructuralism at the end of the 1960s; his *The Logic of Sense* (1969) explored the reverse side of structuralism, the realm of nonsense that underlies the rules of linguistic order. His two books with Guattari are *Anti-Oedipus* (1972), a critique of Freudian psychoanalysis, and *A Thousand Plateaus: Capitalism and Schizophrenia* (1980). The latter describes a conflict between two modes of social organisation, corresponding to two models of reality: one `arborescent`, favouring order and hierarchy; the other `rhizome`-like, favouring the undoing of all order and hierarchy. A rhizome is a plant stem that spreads sideways underground and proliferates unpredictably. History alternates between moments of fixity and power (`territorialization`) and moments when fixed orders break down and are transformed (`deterritorialization`). *P7 began by citing the editors' judgement that Deleuze's shift from the arborescent to the rhizome and Lyotard's shift from grand narratives to little narratives both bear the mark of Derrida's turn from substance, presence and identity to différance.*

**Mechanism: a book is an assemblage, not a meaning.** The opening of *A Thousand Plateaus* dissolves the authors: "The two of us wrote *Anti-Oedipus* together. Since each of us was several, there was already quite a crowd." Why keep their own names? Out of habit, purely out of habit; just as everyone knows that "the sun rises" is only a manner of speaking, yet still says it. The aim is not to reach the point where one no longer says "I", but the point where it is no longer of any importance whether one says "I". It follows that **a book has neither object nor subject**; it is made of variously formed matters, of very different dates and speeds. To attribute the book to a subject is to overlook this working of matters and the exteriority of their relations, like fabricating a beneficent God to explain geological movements. In a book there are lines of articulation or segmentarity, strata and territories, but also `lines of flight`, movements of deterritorialization and destratification; all these lines and measurable speeds constitute an `assemblage`. One side of an assemblage faces the strata, which make it a kind of organism, a signifying totality, a determination attributable to a subject; the other side faces a `body without organs`, which is continually dismantling the organism, letting asignifying particles or pure intensities pass and circulate. The question is thereby changed: **"We will never ask what a book means … We will ask what it functions with, in connection with what other things it does or does not transmit intensities."** A book exists only through the outside and on the outside; it is a little machine, and the only question is which other machine the literary machine can, and must, be plugged into in order to work: Kleist and a mad war machine, Kafka and a most extraordinary bureaucratic machine. They even declare: "Literature is an assemblage. It has nothing to do with ideology. There is no ideology and never has been." Writing has nothing to do with signifying, but with surveying and mapping, even realms that are yet to come. *This is a more radical version of Barthes's "death of the author" in P7: Barthes made the author give way to the reader and the text's play of meaning, while Deleuze and Guattari replace even the question of "meaning" with questions of function and connection. The sentence "there is no ideology and never has been" collides head-on with the whole tradition of P9.*

**Distinction: three kinds of book.** The first is the "root-book". The tree is already the image of the world, or the root is the image of the world-tree. This is the classical book, as noble, signifying and subjective organic interiority: the book imitates the world, as art imitates nature. The law of the book is the law of reflection, "the One becomes two". Whenever we encounter this formula, even stated strategically by Mao or understood in the most "dialectical" way possible, we are faced with the most classical, the oldest and the most weary kind of thought; nature does not work that way. The second is the "radicle-system" or fascicular root, "the figure of the book to which our modernity pays willing allegiance": the principal root has aborted or its tip has been destroyed, and an immediate, indefinite multiplicity of secondary roots is grafted on and flourishes. But the unity of the root subsists, as past or yet to come, as possible: Burroughs's cut-up method folds one text onto another, yet implies a supplementary dimension in which unity continues its spiritual labour; Joyce's words, accurately described as having "multiple roots", shatter the linear unity of the word, even of language, only to posit a cyclic unity of the sentence, text or knowledge; Nietzsche's aphorisms shatter the linear unity of knowledge only to invoke the cyclic unity of the eternal return. **"A strange mystification: a book all the more total for being fragmented."** The world has become chaos, but the book remains the image of the world: "radicle-chaosmos" rather than "root-cosmos". Only the third is the rhizome: it is not enough to shout "Long live the multiple"; no typographical, lexical or even syntactical cleverness is enough to make it heard. The multiple must be *made*. Bulbs and tubers are rhizomes; rats are rhizomes; burrows are too, in all their functions of shelter, supply, movement, evasion and breakout. The rhizome includes the best and the worst: potato and couchgrass, or the weed.

**Reading: the radicle-book and modernist nostalgia.** This threefold division can be set beside the distinction of moods between modernism and postmodernism. Barry says the modernist laments fragmentation and longs for an age when faith was full and authority intact; Deleuze and Guattari give a structural analysis of this nostalgia: the fragmented modernist work thwarts unity in the object, but lets a new unity triumph in the subject, so that the most resolutely fragmented work can also be presented as the "total work" or *magnum opus*. *The Waste Land*'s "These fragments I have shored against my ruins", Pound calling *The Cantos* a "rag-bag": these are radicle-books. **Fragments in themselves are neither modern nor postmodern; the difference lies in whether unity is preserved in another dimension.** *This also explains why the New Criticism (P2) was so at home with modernist poetry: "organic unity" is precisely that supplementary dimension.*

**Mechanism: the principles of the rhizome and the plateau.** Deleuze and Guattari enumerate several approximate characteristics of the rhizome, and the classification itself is significant:

- **Principles of connection and heterogeneity.** Any point of a rhizome can be connected to any other, and must be; this is very different from the tree, which plots a point and fixes an order. Chomsky's linguistic tree still begins at a point S and proceeds by dichotomy. Chomsky's "grammaticality", the categorial symbol S that dominates every sentence, **is more fundamentally a marker of power than a syntactic marker**: you will construct grammatically correct sentences, you will divide each statement into a noun phrase and a verb phrase (the first dichotomy …). They criticise these linguistic models not for being too abstract but for not being abstract enough, for not reaching the "abstract machine" that connects language to the semantic and pragmatic contents of statements, to collective assemblages of enunciation, to a whole micropolitics of the social field. There is no language in itself, nor are there any linguistic universals, only a throng of dialects, patois, slangs and specialised languages; there is no ideal speaker-listener, nor any homogeneous linguistic community. **There is no mother tongue, only a power takeover by a dominant language within a political multiplicity.** Language stabilises around a parish, a bishopric, a capital, forming a bulb. *This is a direct rebuttal of Saussure's concept of langue in P3: the unity of the system is not a linguistic fact but a political event. The point will return in P15's discussion of colonial and national languages.*
- **Principle of multiplicity.** It is only when the multiple is effectively treated as a substantive, "multiplicity", that it ceases to have any relation to the One as subject or object. A multiplicity has neither subject nor object, only determinations, magnitudes and dimensions, which cannot increase in number without the multiplicity changing in nature. The strings of a puppet are tied not to the supposed will of an artist or puppeteer but to a multiplicity of nerve fibres; when Glenn Gould speeds up the performance of a piece, he is not just displaying virtuosity but transforming the musical points into lines. There are no points or positions in a rhizome such as those found in a structure, tree or root; there are only lines. The notion of unity appears only when there is a power takeover in the multiplicity by the signifier; unity always operates in an empty dimension supplementary to the system (`overcoding`). All multiplicities are flat, in the sense that they fill or occupy all of their dimensions, so one can speak of a `plane of consistency` of multiplicities. The ideal for a book would be to lay everything out on such a plane of exteriority: lived events, historical determinations, concepts, individuals, groups, social formations. Kleist invented this kind of writing: a broken chain of affects and variable speeds, always in relation with the outside, the opposite at every point of the classical or romantic book constituted by the interiority of a substance or subject.
- **Principle of asignifying rupture.** A rhizome may be broken, shattered at a given spot, but it will start up again on one of its old lines, or on new lines; you can never get rid of ants, because they form an animal rhizome. Every rhizome contains lines of segmentarity according to which it is stratified, territorialized, organised, signified, attributed, as well as lines of deterritorialization down which it constantly flees. Because these lines always tie back to one another, **one can never posit a dualism or a dichotomy, even in the rudimentary form of the good and the bad**. You may make a rupture, draw a line of flight, yet there is still a danger that you will re-encounter organisations that restratify everything, formations that restore power to a signifier, attributions that reconstitute a subject: anything you like, from Oedipal resurgences to fascist concretions. "Groups and individuals contain microfascisms just waiting to crystallize." Good and bad are only the products of an active and temporary selection, which must be renewed. The orchid and the wasp illustrate the entanglement of deterritorialization and reterritorialization: the orchid deterritorializes by forming an image of a wasp; the wasp reterritorializes on that image, yet deterritorializes by becoming a piece in the orchid's reproductive apparatus, and reterritorializes the orchid by transporting its pollen. One could say that the orchid imitates the wasp, but this holds only at the level of the strata; at the same time something else entirely is going on: not imitation but a capture of code, a `becoming`-wasp of the orchid and a becoming-orchid of the wasp. "Mimicry" is therefore a very bad concept, since it relies on binary logic to describe phenomena of an entirely different nature: the crocodile does not reproduce a tree trunk, any more than the chameleon reproduces the colours of its surroundings; the Pink Panther imitates nothing, it paints the world its own colour, pink on pink. **The book is not an image of the world; it forms a rhizome with the world.**
- **Plateaus.** A plateau is always in the middle, not at the beginning or the end; a rhizome is made of plateaus. Deleuze and Guattari borrow the word from Gregory Bateson: a plateau is a continuous, self-vibrating region of intensities whose development avoids any orientation towards a culmination point or external end. Bateson takes the example of Balinese culture, in which "some sort of continuing plateau of intensity is substituted for \[sexual\] climax", war or a culmination point, and "it is a regrettable characteristic of the Western mind to relate expressions and actions to exterior or transcendent ends". A book composed of chapters has culmination and termination points; *A Thousand Plateaus* claims to be composed of plateaus, each of which can be read starting anywhere and related to any other. The tree imposes the verb "to be", but the fabric of the rhizome is the conjunction "and … and … and …", which carries enough force to shake and uproot the verb "to be". Where are you going? Where are you coming from? What are you heading for? These are totally useless questions. *Compare the narratology of P4: the Aristotelian plot moves through reversal and recognition towards an ending, and the plateau decentres precisely the "ending" that is the centre of narrative. It is also the formal counterpart of Lyotard's "the narrative function losing its great goal".*

**Implication: nomadology and the State.** They extend this opposition from the book to history itself: history is always written from the sedentary point of view and in the name of a unitary State apparatus, even when the topic is nomads; what is lacking is a "nomadology", the opposite of a history. Nomads invented a war machine in opposition to the State apparatus. The State as the model for the book and for thought has a long history: logos, the philosopher-king, the transcendence of the Idea, the interiority of the concept, the republic of minds, the court of reason, the functionaries of thought, man as legislator and subject. The war machine's relation to an outside is not another "model" but an assemblage that makes thought itself nomadic (Kleist and Kafka against Goethe). American literature, and already English literature, manifest this rhizomatic direction to an even greater extent: they know how to move between things, establish a logic of the AND, overthrow ontology, do away with foundations, nullify endings and beginnings. *Setting the "State" of philosophy beside the "court of reason" will be developed more systematically in Foucault's analysis of power and discourse in P10.*

**Conclusion:** Deleuze and Guattari supply a socio-biological image of decentring: the tree is filiation, the rhizome is alliance, uniquely alliance. It has the same enemies as Lyotard's little narratives (unity, hierarchy, dichotomy unfolding from a central point), but it further materialises Lyotard's language games: not just the heterogeneity of languages but heterogeneous connections among semiotic chains, organisations of power, the arts, the sciences and social struggles. **Its key step is to replace "what does it mean?" with "what does it connect with, and how does it work?": it is a theory that refuses hermeneutics.** Its limitation lies in its own warning: if no dichotomy of good and bad can be posited, and one can only keep renewing a temporary selection, where do the criteria for selection come from? This is the question Baudrillard will push to its limit.

### The Four Phases of the Simulacrum and Hyperreality

**Background: from the semiotics of advertising to "the loss of the real".** The second major theorist of postmodernism is **Jean Baudrillard**. The anthology's editors explain that he began his cultural work by studying the semiotics of advertising and consumption, noticing that reality was increasingly being replaced by sign systems that recode and supplant it: under the regime of controlled consumption shaped by marketing and advertising, we consume not real cars or refrigerators but signs of status or self-identity. In *Symbolic Exchange and Death* (1976) he reconceived the cultural history of the West since the Renaissance as a series of successive regimes of simulacra, ways of replacing the world with ever more powerful regimes of signification; finally, in the contemporary era, the referent disappears altogether and people live in pure simulation, copies of reality that resemble it in every respect except that they are representation through and through. Barry, for his part, takes *Simulacra and Simulation* (1981; English translation of the key essays 1983) as the mark of his entry into this field, and associates him with what is usually called `the loss of the real`: the pervasive influence of images from film, television and advertising has led to a loss of the distinction between the real and the imaginary, reality and illusion, surface and depth, the result being a culture of `hyperreality`.

**Definition: the map precedes the territory.** Baudrillard starts from a fable of Borges: the cartographers of an Empire draw up a map so detailed that it ends up covering the territory exactly; as the Empire declines, the map frays and is finally ruined, a few shreds still discernible in the deserts. Today this fable has come full circle. Today's abstraction is no longer that of the map, the double, the mirror or the concept; simulation is no longer that of a territory, a referential being or a substance, but **the generation by models of a real without origin or reality: a hyperreal**. The territory no longer precedes the map, nor does it survive it; henceforth it is the map that precedes the territory (`precession of simulacra`), the map that engenders the territory. If we were to revive the fable today, it would be the territory whose shreds slowly rot across the extent of the map; it is the real, and not the map, whose vestiges persist here and there, in the deserts that are no longer those of the Empire but our own: "*the desert of the real itself*". What really disappears is the sovereign difference between map and territory, which made up the poetry of the map and the charm of the territory, the magic of the concept and the charm of the real. With it disappears the whole of metaphysics: no more mirror of being and appearances, of the real and its concept. The real is produced from miniaturised cells, matrices, memory banks and models of command, and can be reproduced an indefinite number of times; it no longer needs to be rational, since it no longer measures itself against some ideal or negative instance; it is merely operational. The age of simulation begins with a liquidation of all referentials, and, worse, with their artificial resurrection in systems of signs. It is no longer a question of imitation, duplication or parody, but of substituting the signs of the real for the real itself. *The epigraph to Simulacra and Simulation, "The simulacrum is never what hides the truth; it is truth that hides the fact that there is none. The simulacrum is true", is signed "Ecclesiastes", but no such words appear in Ecclesiastes; a fictitious source is itself a small simulacrum.*

**Distinction: dissimulation and simulation.** To `dissimulate` is to feign not to have what one has; to `simulate` is to feign to have what one does not have. The one implies a presence, the other an absence. But the matter is more complicated, since simulation is not merely feigning. Baudrillard quotes Littré: someone who feigns an illness can simply go to bed and pretend to be ill, whereas someone who simulates an illness produces in himself some of its symptoms. Feigning or dissimulating leaves the reality principle intact: the difference is always clear, only masked; simulation, however, threatens the difference between "true" and "false", "real" and "imaginary". Since the simulator produces "true" symptoms, is he ill or not? Medicine knows only how to treat "true" illnesses by their objective causes; if any symptom can be "produced", medicine loses its meaning. Psychoanalysis transfers the symptom from the organic order to the order of the unconscious and takes the latter to be more real; but why should simulation stop at the portals of the unconscious? Why couldn't the "work" of the unconscious be "produced" in the same way as any other symptom? Dreams already are. The army traditionally unmasked malingerers by the principle of direct identification and punished them; today it may treat an excellent simulator as "truly" ill or mad: "since he is so good at mimicking madness, he must be mad." *Note the challenge to psychoanalysis here: in P6 Freud read the symptom as evidence of the unconscious; Baudrillard says in a note that when patients tell "Oedipal" stories and have "analytic" dreams to satisfy the analyst, psychoanalysis is itself producing the unconscious, and analysis becomes interminable; to Lacan's real, symbolic and imaginary "one must add the hyperreal".*

**Mechanism: iconoclasm and the wager on representation.** Beyond medicine and the army, the question of simulation goes back to religion and the simulacrum of divinity. When the deity is manifested in icons and multiplied in simulacra, does it remain the supreme authority, or does it volatilise into simulacra that display only their own pomp and power of fascination? Baudrillard thinks the rage of the iconoclasts came precisely from their sensing the omnipotence of simulacra: their capacity to efface God from the consciousness of men, and the overwhelming, destructive truth they suggest, that ultimately there has never been any God, that only the simulacrum exists, and that God himself has only ever been his own simulacrum. Had they believed that images merely obscured or masked the Platonic Idea of God, there would have been no reason to destroy them: one can live with the idea of a distorted truth. Their metaphysical despair came from the idea that the images concealed nothing at all. **The whole of Western faith and good faith was engaged in this wager on representation: that a sign could refer to the depth of meaning, that a sign could be *exchanged* for meaning, and that something could guarantee this exchange: God, of course.** But if God himself can be simulated, that is, reduced to the signs that attest his existence, the whole system becomes weightless; it is no longer anything but a gigantic simulacrum: not unreal, but a simulacrum, never again exchanged for the real, but exchanged for itself, in an uninterrupted circuit without reference or circumference. Representation starts from the principle of the equivalence of the sign and the real (even if this equivalence is utopian); simulation starts from the radical negation of the sign as value. Representation tries to absorb simulation by interpreting it as false representation; simulation envelops the whole edifice of representation itself as a simulacrum. *This is another version of the critique of the "transcendental signified" in P7: Derrida says there is no centre outside the play of signs to guarantee meaning, and Baudrillard writes this absence as an economic history, signs that have lost the "gold standard" for which they could be redeemed.*

**Definition: the four successive phases of the image.** Baudrillard gives four phases through which the sign has reached its present empty state:

| Phase | Relation of image to reality | Baudrillard's name for the order | Barry's analogy from painting |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| One | It reflects a profound reality | A "good" appearance, the order of the sacrament | L. S. Lowry's paintings of industrial Salford: drab repetition, grey air, stick-like figures, seemingly representing the basic reality of the place |
| Two | It masks and denatures a profound reality | An "evil" appearance, the order of maleficence | The Victorian painter Atkinson Grimshaw's night scenes of Liverpool and Hull: wet pavements reflecting the lights of dockside shops, the moon emerging from behind clouds; life was presumably just as hard, but the picture is romantic and prettified |
| Three | It masks the *absence* of a profound reality | It plays at being an appearance, the order of sorcery | Magritte's picture within a picture: a canvas on an easel before a window shows the view outside, but what the window shows is only another depiction, with no more authority or reality than the picture within the picture |
| Four | It has no relation to any reality whatsoever; it is its own pure simulacrum | No longer of the order of appearance at all, but of simulation | Wholly abstract painting that represents nothing, such as Mark Rothko's purple canvases of mood |

The definitions and names of the orders in this table come from Baudrillard's text, the analogies from Barry. Barry himself stresses that he is not saying these four painters are examples of the four phases of the sign, only that the four phases can be imagined as analogous to the different ways in which these four kinds of painting signify or represent things. The first two phases are fairly clear, the last two perhaps less so. Baudrillard says that **the transition from signs that dissimulate something to signs that dissimulate that there is nothing marks the decisive turning point**: the former imply a theology of truth and secrecy (to which the notion of "ideology" still belongs), the latter inaugurate the age of simulacra and simulation, in which there is no longer a God to recognise his own, nor a Last Judgement to separate the false from the true. When the real is no longer what it was, nostalgia assumes its full meaning: there is a proliferation of myths of origin and signs of reality, of second-hand truth, objectivity and authenticity, and a panic-stricken production of the real and the referential. *The proliferation of authenticity is a symptom that authenticity has been lost: this is the same reversal as "the authentic is itself an artefact" in P7, and the form the third mechanism, "essence ↔ construction", takes in consumer culture.*

*Note that Baudrillard has two numberings: the table above gives the "four phases of the image"; he also has a numbering of "orders of simulacra", the successive regimes of simulacra since the Renaissance mentioned by the editors. In the main text Borges's fable of the map retains only "the discreet charm of second-order simulacra", the law is "a second-order simulacrum", and simulation is "third-order", beyond true and false and beyond equivalences. The "third-order simulation" of Disneyland below uses the latter numbering, while its content corresponds to the third phase in the table; this is exactly how Barry matches them.*

**Example: Disneyland.** Baudrillard's own example of the third phase (the sign masking an absence) is Disneyland, which he calls "a perfect model of all the entangled orders of simulacra". It is first of all a play of illusions and phantasms: pirates, the frontier, the future world. But what draws the crowds is undoubtedly much more the social microcosm, the miniaturised and *religious* enjoyment of real America: you park outside, queue up inside, and are totally abandoned at the exit. The objective profile of America can be traced throughout Disneyland, where all its values are exalted in miniature and comic-strip form, "embalmed and pacified"; hence an ideological analysis of Disneyland is possible: a digest of the American way of life, a panegyric of American values, an idealised transposition of a contradictory reality. This is the second kind of sign, a mythologising distortion of America. But this "ideological" blanket serves precisely to cover a "third-order simulation": **Disneyland exists in order to hide that it is the "real" country, all of "real" America, that is Disneyland** (just as prisons are there to hide that it is the social in its entirety, in its banal omnipresence, that is carceral). Disneyland is presented as imaginary in order to make us believe that the rest is real, when in fact all of Los Angeles and the America that surrounds it are no longer real, but belong to the order of the hyperreal and of simulation. It is no longer a question of a false representation of reality (ideology) but of concealing the fact that the real is no longer real, and thus of *saving the reality principle*. The imaginary of Disneyland is neither true nor false; it is a deterrence machine set up to rejuvenate, in reverse, the fiction of the real: it must be the world of childishness so that we believe the adults are elsewhere, in the "real" world, and to conceal the fact that real childishness is everywhere. Los Angeles is encircled by such "imaginary stations", which feed reality, "reality-energy", to a city that is itself only an endless network of unreal circulation.

**Example: Watergate and the simulated hold-up.** The same scenario applies to politics. Watergate is a scandal-effect that conceals that there is no difference between the facts and their denunciation (the CIA and the *Washington Post* journalists used identical methods). The denunciation of scandal always pays homage to the law; it injects political morality back into the world in large doses. Formerly the task was to conceal scandal; today it is to conceal that there is none. Baudrillard criticises Bourdieu on this basis: when Bourdieu says that "the specific character of every relation of force is to dissimulate itself as such", he takes the relation of force as the *truth* of capitalist domination and denounces it as scandal, thereby occupying the same deterministic and moralistic position as the *Washington Post* journalists. *(Bourdieu has already appeared in P5; this clash anticipates the conflict between simulacrum theory and every "exposure"-type critique.)* More in the nature of a thought experiment is the simulated hold-up: would the repressive apparatus react more violently to a simulated hold-up than to a real one? A real hold-up only disturbs the order of things, the right of property; a simulated one interferes with the reality principle itself, suggesting that law and order themselves might be nothing more than a simulation. But you will not succeed: the web of artificial signs will be inextricably mixed with real elements (a police officer will really shoot, a bank customer will really faint and die of a heart attack), and you will unwittingly find yourself at once in the real, one of whose functions is precisely to devour every attempt at simulation. So order always opts for the real. *This example is telling: even in Baudrillard's own text the real returns, in the form of death and bullets. The ethical question of postmodernism begins here.*

**Reading: how to grasp the third phase.** In one of his "Stop and think" sections Barry points out that the crucial phase in the four-phase model is the third: the sign masks an absence, masks the fact that the so-called "reality" it represents is no longer there, that there is nothing beyond the play of surfaces. The concept is not easy to grasp precisely, and one can try to think of examples other than Disneyland, such as idealised images of masculinity or femininity in advertising: they are copies or representations without an original, no real person is wholly like them, yet people may strive to become like them; **the image thus tends to become the reality, and the two tend to become indistinguishable.** *This example connects simulacrum theory to P12 and P13: if gendered identity is a copy without an original, it is only a step from Butler's claim that gender is an imitation without an original.*

**Conclusion:** Baudrillard turns Derrida's philosophical critique of the transcendental signified into a historical diagnosis of media society: signs were once exchanged for meaning with God as guarantor, and now circulate only within themselves; the map precedes the territory, the model precedes the fact. His key concept is not "falsity" but "masking an absence": **the simulacrum is not a distortion of the real but a device for producing the effect that "everything else is real".** From this comes its burden: if everything is already simulacrum, where can criticism stand?

### Can "the Real" Be Given Up? The Ethical Cost of Postmodernism

**Problem: what can criticism do once depth is lost?** Baudrillard's rhetoric is grandiose and seductive. Barry sees it as a kind of latter-day Platonism: the initiate enjoys the mystic insight that the world usually taken for solid reality is really a tissue of dream images. But he at once points out the consequences of this position for literary theory itself: if this "loss of the real" is accepted as fact, it is difficult to see where literary theory can stand, since all methods of literary interpretation (Marxist, feminist, structuralist and so on) depend on distinguishing between surface and depth, between what is *visible* in a text and some *latent* meaning. **Once we accept that "what you see is what you get", there is little left for the literary critic or theorist to claim to be doing.** *This is exactly the crisis that the second mechanism running throughout, "manifest/latent double reading", meets here: Freud (P6), deconstruction (P7) and the Marxism still to come (P9) all presuppose a level that can be dug out from beneath the surface; Baudrillard, by contrast, says that the wish to restore the truth beneath the simulacrum is always a false problem.*

**Limitation: the ethical cost.** More generally, postmodernism is always attended by certain nagging questions and reservations. In this extreme Baudrillardian form, "the loss of the real" can *seem* to justify a callous indifference to suffering. Baudrillard made a now notorious claim that the Gulf War of 1990–1991 never took place, that what "really" happened was a televised virtual reality. Likewise, if we accept the loss of the real, the collapse of reality and simulation into a virtual reality, what about the Holocaust? Is it, too, part of a reality "lost" in a network of images? Barry's conclusion: **if we do not believe in certain concepts that postmodernism undermines, such as history, reality and truth, we may find ourselves in rather unsavoury company.** In a "Stop and think" section he turns the problem into a choice: if we agree that the real really has been lost, we must decide how to respond; and if we are to revel in the resulting borderless zone, we must be sure that "the real" is a concept we can do without. Recent events may suggest otherwise. Television coverage of the first Gulf War showed computer images of high-tech "smart" weapons homing in on Iraqi targets, with commentary about "surgical strikes" that could "take out" key enemy installations, and pilots talked about their own actions in the same "unreal" terms, the terms of electronic combat games, for instance; this may be a symptom of what can happen when the category of "the real" is eroded. Without the category of "the real", could we still condemn the Holocaust? Could we still campaign against racial discrimination or environmental pollution? *The last questions anticipate P14 and P16: race criticism and ecocriticism must both keep a place for some kind of "real", ecocriticism above all in its counter-attack on "everything is constructed".*

**Background: three articles and a caricature.** Yet in the ninth of his "ten events" in the history of theory, Barry reaches an almost opposite judgement on the same matter. Baudrillard (1929–2007) became, in the public imagination, the notorious French postmodern philosopher who claimed to believe the Gulf War never happened because of three articles of early 1991. Written before the war began, while it was going on, and just after it ended, they were published in the French newspaper *Libération* in January, February and March 1991, and later collected as *The Gulf War Did Not Take Place*. Baudrillard was strongly opposed to Western foreign policy in the Gulf, and expressed his views in a powerful and extreme rhetoric: savage and offensive in tone, like the rhetoric of Swift's eighteenth-century attacks on political corruption and social self-deception. In his view, what took place was not a war: of the half-million Western troops involved, more would have died in traffic accidents had they stayed at home than were killed or wounded, while the estimated hundred thousand casualties were all on one side; it was "a totally asymmetrical operation", and what was notable was the obscene, aphrodisiac function performed by the decoy of the event, the decoy of war. The sexual imagery accumulates: the war, he wrote, unfolded like a long striptease; it was promoted as a "surgical war", its typical images those relayed by cameras in the warheads of "smart weapons". This media event showed no actual human casualties; but the climax of the striptease was the television footage, at the end of the war, of the terrible and pitiless bombing of the retreating Iraqi army on the Basra road, and ironically the most enduring image of the event may be Ken Jarecke's widely published photograph of an Iraqi soldier burned to death in his incinerated vehicle.

**Mechanism: swallowed by the condition it diagnosed.** Barry thinks that, from the point of view of literary theory, the great irony of these articles is that they became victims of the very condition they diagnosed. Just as, in Baudrillard's charge, images or "simulacra" of the war were mistaken for the war itself, so the popular view of what Baudrillard wrote replaced what he actually wrote. He thus became the scapegoat of the anti-theorists, the target for condemnations of postmodernism from the moral high ground; and by the 1990s postmodernism was seen as standing for literary theory as a whole (following linguistics in the 1960s, structuralism in the 1970s and deconstruction in the 1980s). In the caricature or "simulacrum version" of what he said, this too-clever postmodernist quibbles over the concept of reality, indifferent to suffering and death that had undoubtedly taken place; if we begin by doubting the reality of the Gulf War, people said, won't we end by doubting the reality of the Holocaust? *This is exactly the question Barry himself raised in discussing postmodernism.*

**Objection: Norris and the double standard.** In the de Man affair the real damage to theory came from his defenders; in the Baudrillard affair it came partly from his attackers. **Christopher Norris**, who had defended de Man over the wartime articles, took a quite different line this time, for he had by then turned decisively against "rhetorical formalism" in general and postmodernism in particular, seeing many aspects of theory as abandoning the principles of rational objectivity and truth for relativism, consensus and pragmatism. The result was his angry and acerbic *Uncritical Theory: Postmodernism, Intellectuals and the Gulf War* (1992). Writing in the heat of events, Norris was responding to an edited version of the first article published in the *Guardian* in January 1991. He took Baudrillard's words literally (the Gulf War will not happen), and said that this proposition had been empirically refuted by the start of the bombing, though he himself conceded that to point out how wrong Baudrillard's prediction was might be to miss the point. Baudrillard was then placed among Norris's targets of the time: Rorty, Fish, Foucault and all the "anti-cognitivists" who hold that "truth" in any situation can only be a matter of the values and beliefs that happen to prevail among members of some existing "interpretive community" (P5); seeing "reality" as a "purely discursive phenomenon" belongs to the same category, as does "a popular misreading of Derrida" that takes him to be claiming, solipsistically, that "there is nothing outside the text". Barry points out the puzzle: the misreading of Derrida Norris describes seems exactly the same as his own misreading of Baudrillard, whom he reads as claiming literally that there is nothing beyond the media misrepresentation of the Gulf War. **Why must Baudrillard be read only literally, and Derrida only figuratively?** *This question stands in contrast to the two interpretations of "nothing outside the text" in P7: the same critic can read a friendly text figuratively and a hostile text literally.* Barry's conclusion is that, for all the ferocity of the attack, Norris and Baudrillard essentially agree: both denounce the unprincipled brutality of Western policy in the Gulf. What Baudrillard shows is how events were being reshaped even as they happened, an alternative reality of "smart" weapons and surgical strikes being fed to the public; whereas in fact (and this is his point) the great majority of weapons used in the war were anything but "smart", and their consequences are still being experienced. The overall result of theory's involvement with the Gulf War was to discredit it further, since it was seen (quite wrongly, in Barry's view) as endorsing an absolute principle that erodes truth and value, and as supporting the trick of blurring the boundaries between word and world, concept and perception, reality and illusion. **The theory "community" wrongly defended de Man, and wrongly attacked Baudrillard.**

**Another judgement:** The anthology's editors' summary of Baudrillard comes closer to the literal reading than Barry's defence in his history of theory: in these events reality is so shaped by the media, so replaced by representation, that the events "might as well never have happened", since everything people "know" and "experience" of them comes from carefully controlled images. For Lyotard too the editors record a similar charge: postmodernism was accused of not taking a stand on questions of value, which critics think must finally be decided; Lyotard's reply was that such decisions are indeed being made, but are usually assertions of non-rhetorical power by those who are materially dominant, and always close off debate and exclude further narrative and rhetorical competition. *The two defences are structured differently: Barry defends Baudrillard by saying that he is really still on the side of "the real", only with an extreme rhetoric; Lyotard defends himself by saying that "decision" itself is often a disguise of power. The first saves the real; the second saves dissent.*

**Implication: from the Gulf to Sokal.** Five years later, in 1996, the physicist Alan Sokal submitted to the postmodern cultural studies journal *Social Text* a hoax article cobbled together from postmodern clichés, and it was published; this "humiliation" was widely seen as a general defeat for theory, since by then postmodernism stood for theory in general. The first theorist the article quoted was Derrida, and the quotation came from the very improvised answer to Hyppolite in 1966 discussed in P7. *This event and its nationalist overtones will be developed in the timeline of the history of theory in P17.*

**Conclusion:** Barry gives two judgements on Baudrillard: in one place he worries that "the loss of the real" could justify indifference to suffering, in another he holds that Baudrillard's Gulf War articles were precisely an exposure of suffering hidden by images. The two judgements do not contradict each other; they distinguish two things: **simulacrum theory as critique (showing how images replace and obscure reality) itself needs an obscured reality; simulacrum theory as ontology (asserting that reality no longer exists) removes the ground on which critique itself stands.** The photograph on the Basra road has its force precisely because it refuses to be taken as yet another simulacrum.

**Conclusion: P8's answer.** What remains after grand narratives and the real? The answer has three layers. First, a difference of mood remains: with the same fragments, the modernist mourns and the postmodernist celebrates. Second, local, provisional legitimations remain: Lyotard's little narratives and language games, Deleuze and Guattari's rhizome. Decentring has expanded from the text to knowledge, society and history, but all of them retain an enemy: power that ends debate in the name of efficiency, and arborescent thought modelled on the State. Third, at Baudrillard's limit, perhaps only simulacra remain, and it is precisely here that theory meets its ethical floor. **The core conclusion is that decentring can be a liberation, but only if it preserves the capacity to distinguish oppression from resistance, image from suffering.**

This hands the question on to P9. Describing the two narratives of legitimation, Lyotard noted in passing that Marxism wavers between them: it can become a speculative metanarrative that puts the party in place of the university and the proletariat in place of the people (with Stalinism as a possible result), or develop into a critical knowledge declaring that science's only legitimacy lies in freeing the proletariat from alienation and repression (the position of the Frankfurt School). Baudrillard, for his part, says that the notion of "ideology" still belongs to a theology of truth and secrecy, and that ideological analysis always seeks to restore the objective process. This tradition (one of the grand narratives Lyotard named, and the critique of ideology Baudrillard declared obsolete) must therefore be examined head on. While others argue over whether "the real" can be given up, the Marxist answer has always been that the real is material, economic and class-based, and that literature, including its forms and its silences, takes part in the reproduction of this real.

## P9 How Does Literature Take Part in the Reproduction of Class Society? Marxism

P8 ended on an opposition: Lyotard listed Marxism among the grand narratives that had lost credibility, and Baudrillard declared the critique of ideology to belong to an outdated "theology of truth"; yet when it became a question whether "the real" could be given up, Marxism always gave the same answer: the real is material, economic, class-based. The question is: if society is a structure divided by class, what role does literature play in maintaining and reproducing it? In the six-layer framework this is the first part of Layer 4, text and power, whose chain runs: base/superstructure → Althusser (imaginary relation, material existence, interpellation) + Gramsci's hegemony → Macherey's silences; it will extend in P10 to Foucault and the two historicisms, and in P11 to cultural studies. The anthology's editors call this layer "political criticism" in their introduction, and point out that the debate over "bringing" politics into literary study presupposes that politics was not already in literature; yet for a novel such as Conrad's *Heart of Darkness*, about the atrocities of economic colonialism, or for Shakespeare's *Henry* plays, which depict a monarch who invades another country without good cause and causes thousands of deaths, a purely "literary" examination asks the reader to ignore too many obvious political questions.

It inherits four things from what came before. First, the New Criticism of P2: the editors say that the return of politics to literary discussion in the 1970s was less an "entry" than a "re-entry". During the Cold War between the United States and the Soviet Union, "the West" defined itself by defending capitalism against the egalitarian aspirations of Marxist socialism, and it was difficult for literary critics to frame literature politically, especially in Marxist concepts and vocabulary; the end of colonialism in the 1960s and 1970s stirred new interest in Marxism and left politics in the United States and Britain, and this generation of scholars (Richard Ohmann, Martha Vicinus, Paul Lauter, Terry Eagleton, Fredric Jameson and others) argued that the New Criticism's exclusive concern with form was itself political: one could study Donne's poems purely in terms of their structures of paradox, but that would mean ignoring the din of the English Civil War slowly unfolding in the background. Second, Bourdieu in P5: the class distribution of reading competence had already brought social structure into literary reception. Third, the psychoanalysis of P6: "overdetermination", the "unconscious", "repression", the "mirror" and "misrecognition" will be transplanted one by one into social theory. Fourth, the decentring of P7–P8: Althusser's structuralist Marxism dismantled the "centre" at the same time and in the same place as Derrida.

The mechanisms that run throughout each take a new form here. The first, the `logic of relation and difference`, appears in the form "only in certain relations": whether a machine is capital depends on its place in the relations of production. The second, `manifest/latent double reading`, is the most basic operation of Marxist criticism, and in Macherey becomes "the unconscious of the work". The third, `essence ↔ construction`, shows itself as historical social forms appearing natural and particular interests taking universal form. The fourth, `domination ↔ resistance`, appears for the first time in Gramsci's hegemony. The fifth, the `shifting boundary between text and context`, takes an unexpected turn: Marxism at first treats history as the text's external context, but ends by placing it within the silences and forms inside the text. The theory unfolds in clear layers: the foundation is the method of Hegel and Marx, commodity fetishism, and the two traditions, vulgar and Engelsian; the core of the theory of ideology is hegemony and dialogism, ideological state apparatuses and interpellation, overdetermination and relative autonomy; and finally the turn to the text: silences and form, fantasy in a cynical age, and the five operations of criticism.

### Dialectics, Base and Superstructure

**Background: the origins and aims of Marxism.** **Karl Marx** (1818–1883) and **Friedrich Engels** (1820–1895) were the joint founders of this school of thought. Marx, the son of a lawyer, was expelled from Germany after the "year of revolutions" of 1848 and spent most of his life as a political exile in England, living in extreme poverty; Engels left Germany in 1842 to work in Manchester for his father's textile firm. They themselves called their economic theory "communism", and announced its coming in *The Communist Manifesto*, written together in 1848. The anthology's editors stress the historical context of Marx's main works, *The German Ideology* (1846), *The Communist Manifesto* (1848) and *Capital* (1867): harsh industrialisation created a new class of industrial workers, which he called the "proletariat"; in 1848 monarchies across Europe were overthrown by democratic uprisings; in 1870–1871 workers seized power in Paris, and the Commune briefly established an egalitarian alternative to capitalism. That Marx was deeply shaped by his historical context is itself a lesson in Marxist method. Barry's summary is that the aim of Marxism is to bring about a classless society, based on the common ownership of the means of production, distribution and exchange. It is a `materialist` philosophy, which tries to explain things without assuming the existence of a world or forces beyond the natural world around us and the society we live in; but whereas other philosophies seek only to understand the world, Marxism (as Marx's famous dictum puts it) seeks to change it. It sees history as a struggle between classes rather than as a succession of dynasties or the gradual realisation of national identity and sovereignty, "driven" by competition for economic, social and political advantage.

**Definition: Hegel's dialectic.** One of the philosophical sources of Marxism is Hegel's `dialectic`, in which opposing forces or ideas give rise to a new situation or idea. The editors say that Hegel's method (here selected from the *Science of Logic* of 1816) is not merely a way of thinking about knowledge but also a theory of politics, law, art and history, in all of which it sees the same process: a growth from the particular to the universal, the universal finally containing within itself all concrete particulars. In Hegel's formulation, each form of consciousness, in realising itself, also sublates itself, has its own negation as its result, and so passes over into a higher form; the new concept is higher and richer than the preceding one, because it is enriched by the negation or opposite of the preceding one, containing it but also more than it, the unity of itself and its opposite. Speculative thinking consists precisely in "grasping the positive in its negative", the unity of opposites. All the oppositions assumed to be fixed, such as finite and infinite, individual and universal, are not in contradiction through some external connection; they are in and for themselves transitions. The first immediate term is lost in its other, but the other is not empty negation, not nothing, but "the other of the first", so that the first is preserved in it; this negation of the negation, the second negation, is the sublation of contradiction, at once the abolition and the preservation of mediation, a self-mediating movement rather than a static third. Hegel points out in particular that **formal thinking takes identity as its law and declares contradiction unthinkable, whereas thinking contradiction is in fact the essential moment of the concept**; formal thinking does think contradiction, but immediately looks away from it. *This forms an important contrast with Nietzsche's "there are no opposites" and Derrida's deconstruction of binary hierarchies in P7: all three refuse to treat opposed terms as fixed and external, but Hegel leads contradiction towards a higher unity ("absolute knowledge"), while Derrida refuses any final synthesis. This is exactly the dividing line between deconstruction and dialectics. When Negri says below that Spinoza has "no dialectic", that is the other side of the same line.*

**Mechanism: rising from the abstract to the concrete.** In the notebooks of 1858 known as the *Grundrisse*, Marx applied Hegel's method to economics. When we consider a country from the standpoint of political economy, it seems correct to begin with the population, since it is the foundation and subject of the entire act of production; but on closer examination this proves false. The population is an abstraction if one leaves out the classes of which it is composed; the classes in turn are an empty phrase if one does not know the elements on which they rest (wage labour, capital and so on). To begin with the population is to begin with a chaotic conception of the whole, to move analytically towards ever simpler concepts, and then to return from there to the population, which is now no longer a chaotic conception but a rich totality of many determinations and relations. **"The concrete is concrete because it is the concentration of many determinations, hence unity of the diverse."** In thought it appears as a process of concentration, as a result rather than a point of departure, even though it is the real point of departure. Hegel's error was to conceive the real as the product of thought concentrating itself, probing its own depths and unfolding itself out of itself, whereas the method of rising from the abstract to the concrete is only the way in which thought appropriates the concrete and reproduces it as the concrete in the mind, and by no means the process by which the concrete itself comes into being; the real subject retains its independent existence outside the head even after it has been grasped. *This is the crucial inversion of Hegel: the dialectic is kept as a method of knowing but is no longer the producer of being. For literary criticism it means that a text too should be understood as a "concentration of many determinations", a formula that anticipates Althusser's later "overdetermination".*

**Mechanism: life determines consciousness.** In *The German Ideology* of 1846, Marx retold human history from the standpoint of "who owns and who works", against a group of German thinkers who saw the world as the embodiment of spiritual ideas. Men can be distinguished from animals by consciousness, by religion or by anything else you like, but they begin to distinguish themselves from animals as soon as they begin to produce their means of subsistence; the way in which men produce their means of subsistence is a definite *mode of life* on their part, and as individuals express their life, so they are. The various stages of development of the division of labour are just so many different forms of ownership: tribal ownership, the communal and state ownership of antiquity, feudal or estate ownership. The production of ideas, of conceptions, of consciousness is at first directly interwoven with the material activity and material intercourse of men, the language of real life. Consciousness can never be anything other than conscious existence; and if in all ideology men and their circumstances appear upside down as in a `camera obscura`, this phenomenon arises just as much from their historical life-process as the inversion of objects on the retina does from their physical life-process. In direct contrast to German philosophy, which descends from heaven to earth, here we ascend from earth to heaven: we set out from real, active men, and on the basis of their real life-process demonstrate the development of the ideological reflexes and echoes of this life-process. Morality, religion, metaphysics and all the rest of ideology thus no longer retain the semblance of independence; they have no history, no development. **"Life is not determined by consciousness, but consciousness by life."**

**Mechanism: the ideas of the ruling class and the form of universality.** From this follows a proposition with far-reaching influence on cultural criticism: **"The ideas of the ruling class are in every epoch the ruling ideas"**; the class which is the ruling material force of society is at the same time its ruling intellectual force; the class which has the means of material production at its disposal has control at the same time over the means of mental production. The ruling ideas are nothing more than the ideal expression of the dominant material relationships. In an age and country where royal power, aristocracy and bourgeoisie are contending for mastery, and where mastery is therefore shared, the doctrine of the separation of powers proves to be the dominant idea and is expressed as an "eternal law". More important still, each new class that puts itself in the place of the one ruling before it is compelled, merely in order to carry through its aim, to represent its interest as the common interest of all the members of society, that is, **to give its ideas the form of universality, and represent them as the only rational, universally valid ones**; during the dominance of the aristocracy the concepts of honour, loyalty and so on were dominant, during the dominance of the bourgeoisie the concepts of freedom, equality and so on. Giving one's interest the form of universality is not at first pure falsehood: the interest of the revolutionary class really is more connected with the common interest of all other non-ruling classes. *This proposition is the starting point in Marxism of the third mechanism, "essence ↔ construction": a particular class interest is constructed as universal human nature and reason. It also strikes directly at liberal humanism's belief in "universal human nature" and "timeless values" in P1; Žižek's "symptom" below is its Lacanian rewriting.*

**Definition: base and superstructure.** Barry compresses these ideas into the simplest Marxist model of society: society consists of a `base` (the material means of production, distribution and exchange) and a `superstructure` (the "cultural" world of ideas, art, religion, law and so on). The central Marxist view is that the latter is not "innocent" but is "determined" (or shaped) by the nature of the economic base. This belief about culture is called `economic determinism`, and is a central part of traditional Marxist thinking. The editors state its consequences from the side of literature: unlike formalism, which isolates literary works from their historical context, Marxism starts from the assumption that literature can be understood only if its full context (historical, economic, social, cultural) is taken into account. Literature is neither, as the New Critics held, the expression of universal or timeless ideas, nor, as the Russian Formalists held, an autonomous realm of aesthetic or formal devices operating independently of its material circumstances; it is first of all a social phenomenon. And literature is an active agent in its social and cultural world: it can expose social injustice, or cover over disturbing fissures and make a class-divided society seem unified and content. **One major Marxist assumption is that culture, including literature, works to reproduce the class structure of society by representing class differences in ways that make them seem legitimate and natural.** But many writers have also used the pen as a weapon in the "class struggle": Upton Sinclair's *The Jungle*, a realist depiction of the crimes of the great American meat-packing companies, hoped to change the world by influencing public opinion, and it succeeded.
