Lacan's reading is the opposite: what the father encountered in the dream (his fundamental guilt implied by the child's reproach, the `Real` of his desire) was more terrifying than so-called external reality, so he woke up to escape into "reality", in order to go on "sleeping". "Reality is for those who cannot support the dream." So too with ideology: **it is not a dreamlike illusion we build to escape an unbearable reality, but a fantasy-construction that serves as the support of "reality" itself, offering us social reality itself as an escape from some traumatic real kernel**; this kernel is conceptualised by Laclau and Mouffe as "antagonism", a traumatic social division that cannot be symbolised. Anti-Semitism is Žižek's demonstration. It is not enough to say "we must free ourselves of anti-Semitic prejudice and learn to see Jews as they really are"; in that way we remain victims of the prejudice. Even if an "objective" examination confirmed some of the charges of anti-Semitic propaganda, this would have nothing to do with the real roots of anti-Semitism; as Lacan says of the pathologically jealous husband, even if all the facts he cites are true, his jealousy is still a paranoid construction. The right answer is not "Jews are not really like that" but "the anti-Semitic idea of the Jew has nothing to do with Jews; the ideological figure of the Jew is a way of stitching up the inconsistency of our own ideological system". By the same token, everyday experience cannot resist ideology. A German in the late 1930s, bombarded with anti-Semitic propaganda, comes home and meets his neighbour Herr Stern, a good man to chat with in the evenings, whose children play with his own. This experience does not amount to resistance: a good anti-Semite turns the gap itself into an argument ("you see how dangerous they are, it is hard to recognise their real nature"). **An ideology really succeeds when even facts that at first sight contradict it begin to function as arguments in its favour.**

**Distinction: Žižek and Baudrillard.** Žižek takes care to distinguish his position from the science-fiction theme that "reality is just a universal dream": such a generalised illusion is impossible, like Escher's drawing of two hands drawing each other; Lacan's thesis is precisely that there is always a hard kernel, a leftover that cannot be reduced to the mirror play of illusion. *This forms an exact contrast with Baudrillard in P8. Baudrillard says that ideological analysis still belongs to "a theology of truth and secrecy", and that restoring the truth beneath the simulacrum is a false problem; Žižek likewise rejects the simple metaphor of "tearing away the veil to see naked reality" (the emperor is naked only beneath his clothes), but his conclusion is the opposite: the only place where we approach the Real is precisely the dream, and the only way to break the dream of ideology is to confront the Real of desire that announces itself in the dream. For Baudrillard there is nothing beneath the surface; for Žižek there is no "content" beneath the surface either, but there is an antagonism.*

**Another way out: Negri's constitutive thought.** The last Marxist text in the anthology comes from the Italian political philosopher **Antonio Negri**'s book on Spinoza, *The Savage Anomaly* (1981). It offers not another critique of ideology but a reflection on critique itself. Negri distinguishes `negative thought` from `constitutive thought`: negative thought often halts at the limit of theoretical crisis, taking the conditions of existence of the system it criticises as the absolute conditions of doing philosophy, and ends in a cynical view of being and a pure pragmatism indifferent to all ontological content ("after Wittgenstein, Heidegger"); Spinoza, by contrast, treats the crisis itself as a reality to be mastered, grafting negation onto construction. In Spinoza there is no dialectic, because the constitutive process knows neither negation nor void; it accumulates being in quality and quantity; science can be understood not as `potestas` (power as domination) but as `potentia` (power as production), not as individual but as collective appropriation. He calls this `disutopia`: liberation is not an imagining of the future but the permeation and activation of the productive forces of the present. *Placing Negri after Žižek is suggestive: if Žižek shows that ideology lies in "doing" rather than "knowing", Negri's response is that resistance too must lie in "doing", in collective constitutive practice. This thread is continuous with Deleuze's "micropolitics" in P8 and the discussion of oppositional consumption in P11.*

**Conclusion:** Žižek moves the ideological illusion from "knowing" to "doing", and so explains why people in a cynical age no longer believe yet still obey. **The object of the critique of ideology is no longer a mistaken belief that can be corrected, but a fantasy structure that organises practice; it cannot be undone by "exposing the truth", because the truth is already common knowledge.** This is the last rewriting of the thread that began with the "camera obscura" of *The German Ideology*: ideology was first an inverted image, then an imaginary relation to reality and a material practice, then the silence of the text, and finally the fantasy that supports reality itself.

### Five Operations of Marxist Criticism

**Problem: how does theory become reading?** The basic tenet of Marxist criticism, that the nature of literature is influenced by the social and political circumstances in which it is produced, might be accepted at once as a self-evident truth. The difficulty and controversy lie entirely in deciding how close the influence is: whether to take a "determinist" position, seeing literature as the passive product of socio-economic forces, or a more "liberal" line, seeing the influence as remote and subtle. A greater difficulty is that, whichever model is adopted, "strong" or "weak", one must show how these economic forces operate in specific works: what exactly do socio-economic forces, operating directly or indirectly, look like in a work of literature? Do they appear in the content of the plot, in characterisation, or in literary form itself?

**Operations: five practices.** What Marxist critics actually do can be grouped into five practices, corresponding to different theoretical levels of Marxism. The first is to distinguish between the "overt" (manifest or surface) content of a work and its "covert" (latent or hidden) content, very much as psychoanalytic critics do, and then to relate the covert themes to basic Marxist topics such as class struggle or the progress of society through historical stages (the transition from feudalism to industrial capitalism, for instance). Thus the conflict in *King Lear* can be read as "really" a conflict of class interests between a rising class (the bourgeoisie) and a declining one (the feudal lords). *This is the most direct form in Marxism of the second mechanism running throughout, "manifest/latent double reading".* The second is to relate the content of a work to the social class position of its author, assuming (again as in psychoanalysis) that the author is not fully aware of what he or she says or reveals in the text. The third is to explain the nature of a literary genre in terms of the social period that "produced" it: **Ian Watt**'s *The Rise of the Novel* links the growth of the eighteenth-century novel to the expansion of the middle class in that period; the novel "speaks for" this class, just as tragedy speaks for monarchs and aristocrats, and the ballad for the rural and semi-urban "working class". *Marx's Robinson in Capital above, a "true-born Briton" who seizes the ledger to keep accounts, can be seen as an epitome of this reading.* The fourth is to relate a work to the social assumptions of the time in which it is "consumed", a strategy used especially by the variant later called cultural materialism (P10). *This is also the question raised by the happy-ending version of King Lear in P5: the same play is consumed in different shapes under different regimes of reception.* The fifth is the "politicisation of literary form", the claim that literary forms themselves are determined by political circumstances: some critics hold that literary realism carries an implicit endorsement of conservative social structures, others that the formal and metrical intricacy of the sonnet and the iambic pentameter is the counterpart of social stability, decorum and order.

**Reading: class in *Twelfth Night*.** Barry's example is the chapter on *Twelfth Night* in Elliot Krieger's *A Marxist Study of Shakespeare's Comedies* (1979), which mainly demonstrates the first practice. The dominant critical view of the play is that it presents various extremes of self-indulgence (Orsino wallowing in fantasies of romantic love, Sir Toby Belch indulging his appetites), set against Malvolio's extreme Puritanical abstinence, and recommends a balance and decorum that avoids both extremes and allows human nature its proper fulfilment. Krieger points out that this ignores the question of class: when "order" is restored at the end, the aristocratic characters suffer no special harm, whereas Malvolio's fate is much harsher; yet Malvolio's self-interest differs from Orsino's and Olivia's evident self-love and Sir Toby's egotistical revelry *only* in that decorum forbids someone of his rank to "glut" himself. Hence, **only the privileged class can afford the morality of indulgence**. Each member of the aristocracy has a private "second world": the uninhibited world Sir Toby reaches in drunkenness protects him from concern for others; Olivia withdraws into the private world of bereavement; Orsino withdraws into a wholly subjective world of amorous obsession, in which everything becomes an appendage and accompaniment of the duke's state of mind; in these privatised worlds each becomes a king alone. Viola is an aristocrat, but her disguise makes her choose a temporarily non-aristocratic identity, so that she becomes an object to be used and manipulated within the second worlds of Orsino, Olivia and Sir Toby. The world of the servants is full of struggles to "rise": Maria ends by marrying Sir Toby at the cost of humiliating Malvolio. Krieger thinks Maria is not a proto-bourgeois, and her ambition confirms rather than challenges aristocratic privilege; but her ability to separate self from occupation and to win promotion in rank through action makes her the only character in the play who suggests the bourgeois and Puritan emphasis on independence, competition and merit; Malvolio, by contrast, deeply reveres all the trappings of aristocracy, and attributes his imagined promotion to "fortune" and "the stars". "Fortune" in the play, like "nature", is a force that justifies or rationalises hereditary aristocratic privilege. *This connects directly with The German Ideology's claim that ruling ideas take the form of universality, and with the third mechanism running throughout, "essence ↔ construction": social rank is described as "nature" and "fortune".*

**Limitation: vulgar determinism and generalised history.** Barry's assessment is that the Marxist character of this essay lies in its introduction of the concept of social class into the interpretation of the play, its particular "intervention" in a large body of criticism that never mentions the topic; but it says almost nothing about the specific historical moment at which the play was written, weaving instead an ingenious and original reading around general notions of class conflict, class privilege and upward mobility. This points to a general limitation: contrary to popular belief, traditional Marxist criticism deals with history in a rather generalised way, talking of conflicts between social classes and clashes of vast historical forces, but rarely discussing the details of a specific historical situation and relating it closely to the interpretation of a particular text. At the other extreme is the "vulgar Marxism" of the 1930s, which reduces every verbal habit directly to the author's class evasiveness. **On one side, history that is too general; on the other, determination that is too direct. The history of Marxist criticism is largely the history of a search for an intermediate level between these two failures.** Overdetermination, relative autonomy, the silences of the text and the ideology of form are all concepts of this intermediate level.

**Conclusion: P9's answer.** How does literature take part in the reproduction of class society? The answer is a series of progressively refined models. In the simplest model, literature belongs to the superstructure, reflecting and serving the base; commodity fetishism shows that social relations appear in the form of relations between things, and historical forms appear natural and eternal; vulgar Marxism turns this model into mechanical causation, while the Engelsian tradition preserves the freedom of art. Gramsci divides domination into coercion and consent, and Bakhtin makes language an arena of struggle among social voices; Althusser defines ideology as an imaginary relation to real conditions, locates it in the material apparatuses that interpellate subjects, and releases literature "on bail" through overdetermination and relative autonomy; Macherey places history in what the text cannot say, Eagleton and Belsey place it in form; and Žižek finally moves it from "knowing" to "doing". **The way literature takes part in reproduction changes from "reflection" to "constitution": it does not merely represent class relations but helps shape the subjects, consent and fantasies that make those relations seem natural, while also exposing them in its own fissures, silences and heteroglossia.** This is where the fourth mechanism running throughout, `domination ↔ resistance`, begins: literature is both an instrument of hegemony and a site of dissent from it.

But the limitation Barry points out, that traditional Marxist criticism treats history too generally, is precisely the starting point of historicism. The editors' introduction already anticipates the next step: cultural materialists such as Alan Sinfield no longer hold that literature simply reflects and promotes the interests of the ruling class, but that all power structures are contingent and must rely on cultural narratives to secure their legitimacy, and that these narratives, in order to suppress rivals, must first evoke them. **Edmund** in *King Lear* is evoked in this way: he enters as a usurper of power, representing a dissident presence in the society of the time (a new class of merchants, small proprietors and entrepreneurs contending for power with the ruling aristocracy), and is finally killed by a "true" aristocrat. "Virtue" (the ideological term by which the aristocracy authorised its own rule) wins in the end, but it can win only by evoking evil and giving evil stage time; and by making Edmund's defeat depend entirely on an act of violence (Edgar, the true aristocrat, defeats him in a duel), the play also draws attention to the fragility of the aristocracy's claim to legitimacy. *Compared with the class reading of King Lear in Barry's first practice above, a crucial change has taken place here: class conflict is no longer just what the play is "really" saying, but a discord within the play's discourse, a fragility that power must expose in order to confirm itself.* This is the question P10 will develop: when history re-enters literary study with more specific documents and a more detailed analysis of power, is the dissidence in a text a subversion "contained" in advance by power, or a genuine "fault-line"?

## P10 How Does History Re-enter Literary Study? New Historicism and Cultural Materialism

P9 ended with a question: when history re-enters literary study with more specific documents and a more detailed analysis of power, is the dissidence in a text something contained in advance by power, or a genuine fault-line in the social order? The two historicisms give different answers. In the six-layer framework this is the second part of Layer 4, text and power, whose chain runs: Foucault's discourse and discipline → New Historicism (containment) ↔ cultural materialism (fault-lines). It inherits three things. First, Foucault in P3: there, discourse and episteme determined what could be said and known; here, discourse joins with power, the body and institutions to become "discipline". Second, the theory of ideology in P9: Gramsci's hegemony, Althusser's interpellation and Foucault's discursive practice all concern how power is internalised by those it disempowers; Macherey's "silences" will become "fault-lines" in cultural materialism, another variant of `manifest/latent double reading`. Third, the New Criticism of P2: it banished history from literary study and treated the work as a self-sufficient artefact; both historicisms begin by refusing this banishment, yet their methods keep a surprising continuity with the New Criticism in close reading.

Two of the mechanisms running throughout reach unprecedented intensity here. `Domination ↔ resistance` (the fourth mechanism, first named with Gramsci in P9) becomes the focus of the dispute between the two historicisms: Greenblatt's "subversion and containment" and Sinfield's "fault-lines and dissidence" are two answers to the same question. The `shifting boundary between text and context` (the fifth mechanism) moves to a new position: history is no longer the "background" of literature; non-literary documents are called `co-texts` and are read as closely as literary texts; cultural materialism also draws into its analysis the institutions that retell the classics today: theatre companies, curricula, publishing. The argument begins with the model of the old historicism and how it was displaced, moves to Foucault's model of power and the New Historicist view of the text, then uses "Shakespeare and the Exorcists" to show the New Historicist paradox of power; it then turns to the other British tradition (Williams and Thompson) and Sinfield's reading of *Othello*, and finally compares the disagreements between the two historicisms and the price each pays.

### Foreground and Background in the Old Historicism

**Background:** When the New Criticism called itself "new", one of the kinds of traditional criticism it set out to displace was historical. Such historical study might or might not be governed by a particular theory of history (Marxism, for instance), but it always treated history as the *context* for studying literary works. "Historical background", "historical context": the language of traditional historicism puts the literary work in the foreground and history in the background, and the critic's task is to connect the two. The literary work might represent or refer to its historical context, and the critic understands the work by studying the history it refers to: without such background knowledge, how could one understand anything from the wars in Shakespeare's plays to the property laws that govern the plots of Austen's novels? One notable consequence was that literary critics had to read widely in non-literary writings, and critical work led to the historical archive. The New Critics banished this work precisely in order to distinguish and clarify what was unique to literature, sending the historians, sociologists and biographers in literary study back to their own fields (P2). But history returned to literary study; in the anthology editors' words, "like anything repressed", its return was vengeful (P6); literary study today is pervaded by history.

**Example: Tillyard's "Elizabethan world picture".** New Historicism often defines itself against **E. M. W. Tillyard**'s *The Elizabethan World Picture* (1943) and *Shakespeare's History Plays* (1944). These books describe a set of conservative attitudes (to society, to God, to the created universe) that Tillyard took to represent Elizabethan thinking and to be reflected in Shakespeare's plays. Until the 1970s, "traditional" Shakespeare studies were characterised by the combination of this historical framework with "close reading" and the analysis of image patterns. In such work there was a hierarchical separation between the literary text and its historical "background": the former was the object of value, like a jewel, the latter merely the setting that held it, by definition of lesser value. Montrose (discussed below) characterised three older practices in Renaissance studies more sharply: combining formalist rhetorical close reading with a relatively autonomous "history of ideas" or history of literary genres and motifs, histories abstracted from their social matrix; commentary on political commonplaces, mistaking the dominant ideology of Tudor–Stuart society (that unreliable apparatus of socio-political legitimation) for a stable, coherent, collective Elizabethan world picture, and finding it clearly reproduced in canonical literary works; and erudite and sometimes eccentric scholarly detective work, treating texts as ingenious codes and trying to pin the meaning of fictional characters and plots to particular historical persons and events. **What is new in the new historical criticism is its refusal to make unquestioned distinctions between "literature" and "history", "text" and "context", and its refusal to posit and privilege a unified and autonomous individual (whether author or work) set against a social or literary background.** Greenblatt's critique of source study below is aimed at exactly this foreground/background model.

**Definition: New Historicism.** The term `New Historicism` was coined by the American critic Stephen Greenblatt in the early 1980s; his *Renaissance Self-Fashioning: From More to Shakespeare* (1980) is usually regarded as its beginning. Greenblatt later questioned the name and renamed his practice "cultural poetics", but the name had already caught on. The editors think it still useful precisely because it both acknowledges an earlier historicism and announces something new. Similar tendencies had precedents in the 1970s, such as J. W. Lever's *The Tragedy of State: A Study of Jacobean Drama* (1971; reissued in 1987 with an introduction by Dollimore), a short, epoch-making book that challenged conservative critical views of Jacobean drama by connecting the plays closely to the political events of their time. Put simply, New Historicism is a method based on the *parallel* reading of literary and non-literary texts, usually of the same historical period; it refuses (at least nominally) to privilege the literary text, and instead of a literary "foreground" and a historical "background" it gives the two kinds of text equal weight, letting them constantly inform or interrogate each other. **Giving "equal weighting" to literary and non-literary material is the first and main difference between the new and the old historicism.** Since historical documents are no longer subordinated to the work as context but analysed in their own right, they should be called `co-texts` rather than contexts; text and co-text are seen as expressions of the same historical "moment" and interpreted accordingly.

**Operations: the anecdote and the archival continuum.** The typical New Historicist essay places a literary text in the "frame" of a non-literary text. Greenblatt's chief innovation from the standpoint of literary studies, in Hugh Grady's words, was to juxtapose Renaissance drama with "the appalling colonialist policies pursued by all the major European powers of the era", attending to "the marginalization and dehumanization of suppressed Others"; he typically begins an essay by analysing a contemporary historical document that overlaps thematically with the play, and calls the appropriated historical document an `anecdote`. The typical New Historicist essay dispenses with the customary scholarly preliminaries about existing interpretations of the play and opens with a powerful and dramatic anecdote; such openings are often dated and located, carrying the force of documentary eyewitness testimony, vividly evoking the texture of lived experience rather than "history". Richard Wilson and Richard Dutton's introduction to *New Historicism and Renaissance Drama* describes this process: earlier criticism had mystified Shakespeare as the embodiment of the spoken English language, whereas New Historicism found the plays embedded in other written texts (penal, medical, colonial documents); read in this `archival continuum`, what they represent is not harmony but the violent Puritan attack on carnival, the imposition of slavery, the rise of patriarchy, the hunting down of deviants, and the slamming of prison doors at what Foucault called the dawn of the age of confinement and the carceral society. In Greenblatt's own words, this is "an intensified willingness to read all of the textual traces of the past with the attention traditionally conferred only on literary texts". New Historicism thus contains a paradox (a scandal, in some people's view): **it is a method of literary study that does not privilege literature.** *This statement needs qualifying: as we shall see below, its close reading of non-literary texts in fact extends the method of literary criticism to the whole archive.*

### Discipline and the Panopticon: Foucault's Model of Power

**Background:** P3 has already introduced **Michel Foucault**'s `discourse` and `episteme`: the conditions of possibility of knowledge are determined by the discursive rules of an age. *Discipline and Punish* (1975) carries this analysis over to power, and it is the most direct theoretical source of New Historicism. In New Historicism's reception, `discourse` is not just a way of speaking or writing but the whole "mental set" and ideology that encloses the thinking of all members of a society; discourse is never monolithic but always plural, so that the workings of power structures matter as much in the family as at the level of government, and the struggle against them may mean changing sexual politics as much as party politics. **Distinction:** Foucault distinguishes less strictly than Althusser between "repressive structures" and "ideological structures", but there is an evident kinship between Gramsci's `hegemony`, Althusser's `interpellation` and Foucault's `discursive practice`: all three concern how power is internalised by those it disempowers, so that it need not be continually imposed from outside (P9).

**Mechanism: the political technology of the body.** Foucault's starting point is the body. Historians had long since begun to write the history of the body (demography, pathology, needs and appetites, metabolic processes, germs and viruses), but the body is also directly involved in a political field: power relations have an immediate hold on it; they invest it, mark it, train it, torture it, force it to carry out tasks, to perform ceremonies, to emit signs. This political investment of the body is bound up with its economic use: the body is invested with relations of power and domination largely as a force of production; conversely, its constitution as labour power is possible only if it is caught up in a system of subjection. **The body becomes a useful force only if it is both a productive body and a subjected body.** This subjection is not obtained only by violence or ideology; it can be direct, physical, pitting force against force, and yet involve no violence; it can be calculated, organised, technically thought out, subtle, making use neither of weapons nor of terror, and yet remain of a physical order. So there may be a "knowledge" of the body that is not exactly the science of its functioning, and a mastery of its forces that is more than the ability to conquer them: together these constitute `the political technology of the body`. This technology is diffuse, rarely formulated in continuous, systematic discourse, and cannot be localised in a particular institution or state apparatus; apparatuses and institutions operate a `micro-physics of power`, whose field of validity lies between the great functionings and the bodies themselves.

The study of this micro-physics presupposes several shifts. The power exercised on the body is conceived not as a *property* but as a *strategy*: its effects of domination are attributed not to "appropriation" but to dispositions, manoeuvres, tactics, techniques and functionings; one should decipher in it a network of relations, constantly in tension, in activity, rather than a privilege that one might possess; its model should be the perpetual battle rather than the contract regulating a transaction or the conquest of a territory. **Power is exercised rather than possessed**: it is not the "privilege", acquired or preserved, of the dominant class, but the overall effect of its strategic positions, an effect manifested and sometimes extended by the position of those who are dominated. This power is not simply imposed as an obligation or prohibition on those who "do not have it"; it invests them, is transmitted by them and through them, just as they themselves, in their struggle against it, resist the grip it has on them; these relations go right down into the depths of society and are not localised in the relations between the state and its citizens or on the frontier between classes. Nor are they univocal; they define innumerable points of confrontation, focuses of instability, each of which has its risks of conflict, of struggles, and of an at least temporary inversion of the power relations; the overthrow of these "micro-powers" does not obey the law of all or nothing, and is not acquired once and for all by a new control of the apparatuses or by the destruction of institutions. Correspondingly, we should abandon the tradition that imagines knowledge can exist only where power relations are suspended, that power makes mad and that the renunciation of power is one of the conditions of knowledge. **Power produces knowledge; power and knowledge directly imply one another**: there is no power relation without the correlative constitution of a field of knowledge, nor any knowledge that does not presuppose and constitute at the same time power relations. The subject who knows, the objects to be known and the modalities of knowledge must be regarded as so many effects of the fundamental implication of `power-knowledge` and its historical transformations.

**Mechanism: from leprosy to plague.** The chapter "Panopticism" opens with an order of the late seventeenth century on the measures to be taken when plague appeared in a town: the town is closed off and divided into quarters, each governed by an intendant, each street watched by a syndic; on the appointed day everyone is ordered to stay indoors, on pain of death; the syndic locks the door of each house from the outside and hands the key to the intendant; bread and wine are passed in through small wooden channels, meat, fish and vegetables hoisted in by pulleys; only the intendants, syndics and guards move through the streets, and the "crows" who carry the corpses between the infected houses. Inspection never stops: each day the syndic stops before each house, calls every inhabitant to the window, calls the roll and asks about each person's state ("the inhabitants must speak the truth, under pain of death"); if someone does not appear at the window, the syndic must ask why. This surveillance rests on a system of permanent registration: each person's name, age and sex "irrespective of condition" are recorded, and every observed death, illness, complaint and irregularity is noted and reported; each individual's relation to his illness and his death passes through the representatives of power, their registers and their decisions. This enclosed, segmented space, observed at every point, in which individuals are inserted in fixed places, the slightest movements supervised, all events recorded, an uninterrupted work of writing linking centre and periphery, and power exercised without division according to a continuous hierarchical figure: **this constitutes a compact model of the disciplinary mechanism.** The plague is mixture, and discipline meets it with its power of *analysis*. A whole literary fiction grew up around the plague: laws suspended, prohibitions lifted, bodies mingling without respect, individuals unmasked, abandoning their statutory identity. *(This is exactly Bakhtin's `carnival` in P9.)* But there was also a political dream of the plague, which was exactly its reverse: not the collective festival but strict divisions; not laws transgressed but regulation penetrating even the smallest details of everyday life; not masks put on and taken off but the assignment to each individual of his "true" name, his "true" place, his "true" body, his "true" disease.

Foucault thus distinguishes two dreams of power. If the leper gave rise to rituals of exclusion, which to a certain extent provided the model for "the great confinement", the plague gave rise to disciplinary projects: the first a massive binary division between one set of people and another, the second multiple separations, individualising distributions, a deep organisation of surveillance and control; the leper was marked, the plague victim analysed and distributed; the first the dream of a pure community, the second the dream of a disciplined society. The two projects are different but not incompatible: the nineteenth century was characterised by applying the techniques of disciplinary partitioning to the space of exclusion, treating "lepers" (beggars, vagabonds, madmen and the disorderly formed their real population) as "plague victims", individualising the excluded and using procedures of individualisation to mark exclusion; this is what was regularly at work from the early nineteenth century in the psychiatric asylum, the penitentiary, the reformatory, the approved school and, to some extent, the hospital. All the authorities exercising individual control function in a double mode: binary division and branding (mad/sane, dangerous/harmless, `normal/abnormal`), and coercive assignment and differential distribution (who he is, where he must be, how he is to be characterised, how he is to be recognised, how a constant surveillance is to be exercised over him individually). All the mechanisms of power deployed today around the "abnormal individual" are composed of these two forms. *(This is what the phrase "the age of confinement" refers to.)*

**Mechanism: the Panopticon.** Bentham's `Panopticon` is the architectural figure of this combination: at the periphery an annular building, at the centre a tower pierced with wide windows that open onto the inner side of the ring; the peripheral building is divided into cells, each extending the whole width of the building, with two windows, one on the inside facing the windows of the tower, the other on the outside allowing the light to cross the cell from one end to the other. All that is needed is to place a supervisor in the central tower and to shut up in each cell a madman, a patient, a condemned man, a worker or a schoolboy. By the effect of backlighting, one can observe from the tower the small captive shadows in the cells of the periphery, standing out precisely against the light: so many cages, so many small theatres, in which each actor is alone, perfectly individualised and constantly visible. It reverses the principle of the dungeon, or rather of its three functions (to enclose, to deprive of light, to hide) it preserves only the first and eliminates the other two: full lighting and the eye of a supervisor capture better than darkness, which ultimately protected. **"Visibility is a trap."**

Each individual is securely confined to a cell, seen from the front by the supervisor, while the side walls prevent him from coming into contact with his companions: **"He is seen, but he does not see; he is the object of information, never a subject in communication."** The arrangement facing the central tower imposes on him an axial visibility, while the divisions of the ring imply a lateral invisibility, which is a guarantee of order: if the inmates are convicts, there is no danger of a plot or collective escape; if patients, no danger of contagion; if schoolchildren, no copying, no noise, no chatter; if workers, no disorders, no theft, no coalitions. The crowd, a compact mass, a locus of multiple exchanges, a collective effect, is abolished and replaced by a collection of separated individualities. Hence the major effect of the Panopticon: **"to induce in the inmate a state of conscious and permanent visibility that assures the automatic functioning of power."** The surveillance is permanent in its effects even if discontinuous in its action; that the prisoner should be constantly observed is both too much and too little: too little, for what matters is that he knows himself to be observed; too much, because he has no need in fact of being so. Bentham therefore laid down the principle that power should be *visible* and *unverifiable*: visible, because the inmate will constantly have before his eyes the tall outline of the central tower; unverifiable, because he must never know whether he is being looked at at any one moment, but must be sure that he may always be so. The Panopticon is a machine for dissociating the see/being seen dyad: in the peripheric ring one is totally seen without ever seeing; in the central tower one sees everything without ever being seen. It automatises and disindividualises power: the principle of power lies not in a person but in a certain concerted distribution of bodies, surfaces, lights and gazes; the ceremonies and marks by which the sovereign's surplus power was manifested become useless; almost anyone can operate the machine, and his motive does not matter. **"A real subjection is born mechanically from a fictitious relation."** So it is not necessary to use force to constrain the convict to good behaviour, the madman to calm, the worker to work, the schoolboy to application; Bentham was surprised that panoptic institutions could be so light: no more bars, chains and heavy locks, only clear separations and well-arranged openings. He who is subjected to a field of visibility, and who knows it, assumes responsibility for the constraints of power and makes them play spontaneously upon himself; **he inscribes in himself the power relation in which he simultaneously plays both roles; he becomes the principle of his own subjection.**

**Mechanism: the disciplinary society.** The plague-stricken town provided an exceptional disciplinary model: perfect, but absolutely violent. The Panopticon, by contrast, has a role of amplification: it arranges power so as to make it more economic and effective, but with the aim of strengthening the social forces: increasing production, developing the economy, spreading education, raising the level of public morality. There are thus two images of discipline: at one extreme the "discipline-blockade", the enclosed institution established on the edges of society, turned towards negative functions (arresting evil, breaking communications, suspending time); at the other the panoptic "discipline-mechanism", a functional mechanism that makes the exercise of power lighter, more rapid and more effective. The movement from the one to the other rests on a historical transformation: the gradual extension of the mechanisms of discipline throughout the whole social body in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, forming what may be called in general `the disciplinary society`. This process involves three deeper changes: the functional inversion of the disciplines, from neutralising dangers to increasing the utility of individuals (as in the army, the workshop and the school); the swarming of disciplinary mechanisms, which become "de-institutionalised" and circulate in a "free" state (Christian schools, for example, were meant not only to train docile children but also to supervise the parents' way of life and morals through them, and members of parish charitable societies inquired into the sleeping arrangements in poor households and whether couples were married); and the state-control of the mechanisms of discipline (in France the most important part of them was taken over very early by the police apparatus, which was to reach "the things of every moment" in society, by means of a hierarchical network of thousands of eyes and an immense mass of police documents recording behaviour, attitudes, possibilities and suspicions). But Foucault says explicitly that it would be wrong to think that the disciplinary functions were confiscated and absorbed once and for all by a state apparatus: **"'Discipline' may be identified neither with an institution nor with an apparatus; it is a type of power, a modality for its exercise", a technology**, which may be taken over by specialised institutions, by institutions that use it as an instrument (schools, hospitals), by pre-existing authorities that use it to reorganise their internal mechanisms of power (the family), and by apparatuses whose main function is to ensure that discipline reigns over society as a whole (the police).

A few years after Bentham, Julius issued this society's birth certificate: antiquity was a civilisation of *spectacle*, making a multitude of men see a small number of objects, a problem to which the architecture of temples, theatres and circuses responded; the modern age poses the opposite problem, making a small number, or even a single individual, see a great multitude instantaneously. Foucault concludes: **"Our society is one not of spectacle, but of surveillance"**; under the surface of images, bodies are invested in depth; behind the great abstraction of exchange, the meticulous, concrete training of useful forces goes on; the problem is not that the fine totality of the individual is amputated, repressed or altered by the social order, but that the individual is carefully *fabricated* in it, according to a whole technique of forces and bodies. "We are much less Greeks than we believe." We are neither in the amphitheatre nor on the stage, but in the panoptic machine, invested by its effects of power, which we bring to ourselves since we are part of its mechanism. The formation of discipline is also bound up with broader historical processes: the demographic explosion of the eighteenth century and the increase in the floating population (one of the primary aims of discipline is to fix; it is an anti-nomadic technique), and the growth of an ever larger and more costly productive apparatus that had to be made more profitable; discipline replaced the old principle of "levying-violence" with the principle of "mildness-production-profit"; the accumulation of men and the accumulation of capital cannot be separated (Foucault explicitly cites Marx's *Capital* here). Finally, at the juridico-political level, the process by which the bourgeoisie became the politically dominant class in the eighteenth century was masked by an explicit, codified and formally egalitarian juridical framework, and the development and generalisation of disciplinary mechanisms constituted the other, dark side of this process: the formally egalitarian system of rights was supported by essentially non-egalitarian and asymmetrical micro-powers. **"The 'Enlightenment', which discovered the liberties, also invented the disciplines."** *This sentence can be set against Lyotard's incredulity towards the grand narrative of the Enlightenment and Habermas's defence of the Enlightenment in P8: Foucault does not declare that the Enlightenment narrative has lost its credibility; he reveals its material underside.*

**Objection: the tension between two readings.** Barry's summary of Foucault is New Historicism's Foucault: New Historicism is always anti-establishment, on the side of the liberal ideal of individual freedom, celebrating every difference and "transgression", yet seemingly in despair about their survival before the repressive state. This image of an all-powerful, all-seeing state comes from Foucault's "panoptic" surveillance, maintained not by physical force but by discursive practices that circulate its ideology through the body politic; the result is that "transgressive" thoughts may become literally "unthinkable" (or *only* thinkable), the state is seen as a monolithic structure, and change becomes almost impossible. He also notes a doubleness: since power exists in private spheres such as the family, the personal sphere becomes a possible field of political action, a politically optimistic reason that may interest feminists; but since political power permeates so many spheres, fundamental change may seem very remote. *Set against Foucault's own text in the anthology, there is a clear tension between Barry's summary and what Foucault says: the text repeatedly stresses that power is not "possessed" by the state or the ruling class, that discipline cannot be identified with any state apparatus, and that micro-powers define "innumerable points of confrontation" and the risk of temporary inversions of power relations. Sinfield will also point out below that Foucault, though often treated as the theorist of containment, explicitly denies in The History of Sexuality that resistance is doomed to be a passive rebound. New Historicism's "pessimism" is thus more a way in which Foucault was received than the conclusion of Foucault's own texts.*

**Objection: Armstrong's feminist revision.** **Nancy Armstrong**, in "Some Call It Fiction: On the Politics of Domesticity" (1990), pushed Foucault's model forward from within. She opposes historical models that confine political practice to activities directly related to the marketplace, the official institutions of the state or resistance to them, and argues that any model placing personal life in a separate sphere and assigning literature a secondary, passive role in political history is unconsciously sexist. Williams and Said took down the barrier between culture and the state, but could succeed only partly so long as they ignored the `sexual division of labour` that supports and naturalises the difference between culture and politics; Ian Watt could explain Defoe, Richardson and Fielding by the socio-economic features of a new readership, but could attribute Austen's popularity only to genius (P9). Armstrong argues that *Discipline and Punish* overlooks the fact that the modern family was the founding prototype of modern institutions. She rereads Foucault's plague town: the population is divided into ever smaller units whose basic module is the household, followed by the ritual purification of each house; this produces a new family, free of unregulated intercourse with the world, its membrane open only to certain kinds of information; by contrast, Boccaccio imagines a small aristocratic group withdrawing to the country, while those left in the city resemble the grotesque, permeable body Bakhtin celebrates. Foucault extended the "political" beyond official institutions, but only to those institutions dominated by men in the course of becoming institutions; a household run by women and practised by various subgroups aspiring to "respectability" in fact took shape at least fifty years before other social institutions and entered common sense through writing, providing a rationale for distributing national wealth through wages paid to men. Her conclusion: domestic fiction separated the language of sexual relations from the language of political economy, opposing to power based on title, wealth and violence a power based on the control of literacy; people raised in institutional culture carry in their heads a voice much like a novel's narrator, sensitive to the slightest signs of disorder (a dirty word, an unbuttoned garment, food slipping from a fork), and **it keeps us in line more than fear of the police or the army does**; we watch ourselves in mirrors, clocks, bathroom scales and medical examinations. *This revision moves the Panopticon from the prison into the family and the novel, and anticipates feminism's theorisation of the political nature of the private sphere in P12.*

### The Textuality of History and the Historicity of Texts

**Definition:** The best-known definition of New Historicism comes from **Louis Montrose**: the poststructuralist reorientation towards history can be characterised, chiastically, as a reciprocal concern with `the historicity of texts` and `the textuality of history`. The historicity of texts means the cultural specificity and social embedding of all modes of writing: not only the texts critics study but also the texts in which they study them. The textuality of history has two senses: first, we can have no access to a full and authentic past, a lived material existence, unmediated by the surviving textual traces of the society in question, and the survival of those traces cannot be assumed to be merely contingent; it must be presumed to be at least partly the result of complex and subtle social processes of preservation and effacement; second, those textual traces are themselves subject to subsequent textual mediations when they are construed as the "documents" on which historians ground their own texts, called "histories"; as **Hayden White** reminds us, such textualised histories necessarily but always incompletely constitute, in their narrative and rhetorical forms, the "History" to which they offer access.

**Background:** Montrose's essay (1989) responds to **J. Hillis Miller**'s presidential address to the Modern Language Association in 1986 (*this address is one of the "ten events" in the history of theory; see P17*). Miller said, with some dismay, that literary study in the previous few years had undergone a sudden, almost universal turn away from theory oriented towards language as such, towards history, culture, society, politics, institutions, class and gender conditions, the social context, the material base. Montrose thinks this polarises language and society, whereas the general tendency of cultural studies is precisely to emphasise their reciprocal constitution: society is understood to be discursively constructed, and language use is understood to be always dialogical, socially and materially determined and constrained (Bakhtin in P9). The propositions and operations of deconstruction can be powerful tools of ideological analysis; Derrida himself says that deconstructive practice is "first and foremost political and institutional practice"; "there is nothing outside the text" (P7) can be invoked to escape the determinate necessities of history and indulge in the indeterminate pleasures of the text, but it can also be understood as an insistence on the ideological power of discourse, especially of those discourses that denigrate the work of discourse as a mere reflection of some ontologically prior reality. "Theory" does not serenely occupy a place above "ideology" but is deeply implicated in it: written representations of the world help construct the world, shape the modalities of social reality, and accommodate writers, performers and readers to the multiple and shifting subject positions within the world they constitute and inhabit. **To speak of the social production of "literature", then, is to say that it is not only socially produced but also socially *productive*: it is the product of work, and it does work when it is written, performed or read.** Montrose grants that the reference of signifiers cannot be fixed and the meaning of texts cannot be stabilised, while insisting that writing and reading are always historically and socially determinate events, performed in the world and upon the world by gendered individual and collective human agents; the task of the new socio-historical criticism is to analyse the interplay of culturally specific discursive practices, while aware that it is itself such a practice and takes part in the interplay it tries to analyse.

**Distinction: historicist ≠ historical.** The word "archive" in "archival continuum" marks the second important difference between the new and the old historicism: New Historicism is a `historicist` rather than a `historical` movement. Its concern is with history as represented and recorded in written documents, history as text; historical events themselves are regarded as irretrievably lost. This emphasis carries the influence of a view familiar in literary study: the real thoughts, feelings or intentions of a writer can never be recovered or reconstructed, and the real living person has been wholly replaced by the literary text that comes down to us; **the word of the past replaces the world of the past**. The influence of poststructuralism is absorbed too: New Historicism accepts Derrida's view that there is "nothing outside the text", in the special sense that everything about the past is available to us only in textualised form. It has been "triple-processed": first through the ideology, ideas or discursive practices of its own time, then through those of ours, and finally through the distorting web of language itself; everything represented in a text is thereby reshaped, and the New Historicist essay is itself a further reshaping of the past. The anthology's editors agree: what distinguishes New Historicism from its predecessors is mainly that the concept of history it presupposes has passed through the poststructuralist critique; history is accessible only as a collection of discourses. Since literature and history are both `representations` (a word so important to New Historicists that it became the name of their journal), neither is closer than the other to the "truth" of history; history is not some unmediated reality that the literary text reflects or refers to, not a context, but, like the literary text itself, a discourse, only of a different genre. *This distinction is the one most easily misunderstood: historicism does not deny that events happened in the past; it denies the possibility of reaching those events without the mediation of texts.*

**Operations: the synchronic cultural text.** Greenblatt later abandoned "New Historicism" for "Cultural Poetics". Montrose thinks the latter perhaps more accurate: the project reorients the axis of intertextuality, substituting for the *diachronic* text of an autonomous literary history the *synchronic* text of a cultural system; its interests and analytical techniques are at once historicist and formalist, implying a conviction that formal and historical concerns are inseparable. The editors stress instead the `circulation` of discourses: every text has its own mode of circulation and a place in the economic system, but it also circulates certain discourses; to see the discourses circulating in a period one must look at their presence not only in literature but in other kinds of cultural representation. New Historicists are selective about the archive: the historical text that illuminates a pattern might be a manifesto, a conduct manual, a broadsheet or a periodical; all texts can be called *interventions* in these patterns, since they not only reflect but act upon the cultural situations they represent; New Historicist essays often apply the same reading practice to every text they study, reading non-literary texts as closely as literary ones.

This reveals an often overlooked feature of New Historicism: although it foregrounds the word "historicism", it is in fact a major expansion of the empire of literary studies, since it demands intensive "close reading" of non-literary texts in the manner of literary criticism. Documents are rarely presented whole; a passage is extracted and intensively scrutinised, usually with little contextualisation (partly a writing strategy to heighten impact); previous studies of the same text are rarely noticed, as if the arrival of New Historicism had wiped out the accumulated scholarship. **This is a genuine "words on the page" method: context is omitted, and the material is studied like the decontextualised, isolated poems I. A. Richards gave his students for practical criticism in the 1920s (P2).** So a single historical text sometimes becomes the sole witness to, say, a change in attitudes to sexuality, bearing an enormous interpretive weight; historians should not be expected to value or admire this method, which is a way of "doing" history with a strong appeal to non-historians. Its appeal has three sources too: though built on poststructuralist thought, it is written far more readably, setting out its material and drawing conclusions, even if its interpretations of the material are open to challenge, partly because (as with Freud's theories) the empirical basis of the interpretation is openly exposed to scrutiny; its material is often fascinating and unique in literary study, and the economy that comes from not citing previous discussion makes it seem vivid and dramatic; and its political edge is sharp, yet it avoids the usual problems of "pure" Marxist criticism, seeming less polemical and more willing to let the historical evidence speak for itself.

**Reading: Montrose on *A Midsummer Night's Dream*.** Montrose's "'Shaping Fantasies': Figurations of Gender and Power in Elizabethan Culture", first published in *Representations*, the "house journal" of New Historicism, can be seen as embodying this definition. It opens with an anecdote: an Elizabethan dream, not Shakespeare's *A Midsummer Night's Dream* but one dreamed on 23 January 1597 by the astrologer-physician **Simon Forman**. In the dream Forman has an erotic encounter with the queen, by then elderly, turning on a pun between "waiting upon" the queen and "weight upon her": the queen's train is trailing in the dirt, and he offers to lift her belly up to solve the problem ("I mean to wait upon you, and not under you"); Forman has just rescued the queen from the attentions of "a weaver, a tall man with a reddish beard", which Montrose reads as an Oedipal triangle (P6). He connects it with the queen's projection of herself as mother of the nation and at the same time as a virgin given to open flirtatious provocation (a French ambassador described her very revealing dress), and further with the tensions produced by a peculiar situation: a highly patriarchal society, in which all power belonged to men, ruled by a woman with power of life and death over all her subjects, male and female, who could make or break the careers of male courtiers. The play repeatedly presents queens who are "tamed" and thereby feminised: Hippolyta, queen of the Amazons, defeated by Theseus and now obliged to submit and marry him; Titania, queen of the fairies, who defies her husband out of attachment to a changeling boy and is drugged by Puck into falling in love with the first creature she sees on waking; the play is full of the rights of fathers over daughters and husbands over wives, and male desire presupposes female submission. The "happy" ending depends on a reinforcement of patriarchy: the female pride and power of the warlike man-hater, the possessive mother, the unruly wife and the wilful daughter are all brought under the control of husbands and lords. The play can thus be seen as potentially subversive: when a virgin ruler is ostensibly the virgin mother of her subjects, themes of male fertility, self-generation and mastery of women acquire a *seditious resonance*; in royal pageantry the queen was always the focus of all eyes and her chastity the source of magical power, but in *A Midsummer Night's Dream* this power is conferred on a king; **Shakespeare's comedy symbolically neutralises the royal power to which it ostensibly pays homage.** In practice, patriarchy was maintained by constantly stressing Elizabeth's *difference* from other women: pageant and panegyric proclaimed her at once "maid, matron and mother", and so not a real woman but a religious mystery. Barry gives a modern analogy: having a woman leader did not make the Conservative Party revise its ideas about women's social role; on the contrary, reactionary ideas were reinforced under the "Iron Lady". Montrose's overall thesis is that the play, while a creation of Elizabethan culture, also creates the culture by which it is created, "shaping the fantasies by which it is shaped": the cult of the Virgin Queen was fostered by Spenser's *The Faerie Queene* and by court masques and pageants, and at the same time generated such literature. **History is textualised; texts are historicised.** The essay also represents the eclecticism of New Historicism: it borrows from psychoanalysis (especially dream interpretation) and from feminism.

**Example: *The Official Story* and "when the lions write history".** The editors point out that historicism today is both diachronic and synchronic: many historicist critics borrow the synchronic analysis of Saussure and his structuralist heirs to show that "reality" is constituted by sign systems, discursive fields that construct a version of the real (P3); understanding "history" as discursively produced makes it possible to examine the sources of a discourse (its `genealogy`, to use Foucault's important term) and the perspectives it may serve. In the film *The Official Story*, an Argentine secondary-school history teacher is forced to confront the gap between the history she teaches (the history, with its many occlusions, the government wants her to teach) and the history she has lived; she reads between the lines of the "official story" another discourse produced by the mothers of the "disappeared" (victims of Argentina's right-wing military dictatorship), a discourse that, however much the official story denies it, inhabits her own family. Another example is the fable of "the man and the lion" told by Wendell Phillips in his preface to Frederick Douglass's *Narrative*: the lion complains that it will not be so misrepresented "when the lions write history"; Douglass, a fugitive slave forbidden by law even to learn to read, is Phillips's lion, and he is writing history. The disappeared cannot tell their stories, nor can the lion; but the metaphor of their missing stories marks the place of alternative discourses, alternative histories, of all the historical work still to be done in the ever-expanding process of writing the past. *These two examples turn "the textuality of history" from an epistemological proposition into a political one: if history is accessible only in the form of discourse, then who holds the power to write becomes a question of whose past gets to exist.*

**Implication:** The practice of New Historicism typified by Greenblatt has now given way to broader historicist work. The analytical categories of feminism and gender studies, of postcolonial and ethnic studies, are themselves historical, and in the present anti-essentialist climate few would use a vocabulary without historicising it: who could utter the terms of gender or race without acknowledging that they are historically constituted? In this sense the wider success of historicism lies in its entry into almost every other critical method: from C. L. R. James's *The Black Jacobins*, on the Haitian Revolution, and Gerald Vizenor's work on nostalgic images of the "vanishing" Native American, to Paul Gilroy's *The Black Atlantic*, on the circum-Atlantic diaspora of African cultures (P12–P15).

### Subversion and Containment: The New Historicist Paradox of Power

**Problem:** If power permeates everything, as Foucault describes it, how should resistance in literary texts be understood? Under the double influence of Foucault and Marxist theories of history, New Historicists are concerned with questions of power, and especially with how power is maintained by unofficial means, such as the *theatricality* of royal display at court. The editors say that this position was stated most clearly in response to the criticism of cultural materialism: cultural materialists hold that all power is fragile, easily undermined by dissident elements within society, and that literature inadvertently reveals the cracks in power, the subversive moments where the instability of power is most palpable; Greenblatt's reply is that subversion is itself a ruse of power. At some point `subversion` and `containment` almost became the slogans of New Historicism.

**Example: "Invisible Bullets".** The editors summarise this essay as follows: the title refers to a strategy of English colonists, who explained the diseases ravaging native populations as God's punishment for disobeying their colonial masters; in Greenblatt's argument, the containment of subversion is like the "invisible bullets" of germ warfare used to contain native resistance. A playwright like Shakespeare can evoke the undermining of royal power in the *Henry* plays, but that undermining ultimately serves only to strengthen royal power more effectively. *A note: "Invisible Bullets" was first published in 1981, earlier than Political Shakespeare (1985), in which it was reprinted, so the "response" the editors speak of should be understood as logically rather than strictly chronologically prior; Greenblatt's main material is Thomas Harriot's report on the Virginia colony, and "invisible bullets" was originally one explanation the local natives gave of the deadly diseases the English brought.* Sinfield, for his part, notes that Greenblatt later denied claiming that resistance is always co-opted, and that "Invisible Bullets" is often misread.

**Mechanism: the containment model.** Sinfield calls this line of thought the `entrapment model` of ideology and power: even, or especially, the moves that seem designed to challenge the system help to maintain it. Don E. Wayne says that New Historicism often shows how different kinds of discourse intersect, contradict, destabilise, cancel or modify one another, trying to demonstrate that the dominant ideology allows alternative discourses a certain space, ultimately appropriating their vitality and containing their oppositional force. The ambiguous title of *Renaissance Self-Fashioning* already carries the problem: Greenblatt's central figures long to fashion themselves, but he finds that their selves are fashioned for them; Wyatt cannot fashion himself in opposition to power and the conventions it deploys, since it is precisely these conventions that constitute his self-fashioning. Hence Carolyn Porter's complaint that in New Historicism the subordinate seem to be merely a discursive effect of the dominant. Peter Nicholls points to a deeper theoretical consequence: New Historicism discarded the Marxist base/superstructure model (as was necessary), but in doing so tended "to replace a model of mechanical causality with one of structural homology"; homology finds synchronic structural correspondences without relations of determination, sometimes without pressure and tension, so that "the question of ideology becomes a purely superstructural one", and production and the concept of class, which might generate the theme of historical change, are displaced; the agents who sink from view are not individuals but classes, class fractions and groups.

**Reading: "Shakespeare and the Exorcists".** The best example of how subtle the New Historicist paradox of power actually is comes from this essay in **Stephen Greenblatt**'s *Shakespearean Negotiations* (1988). Its starting point is a fact long known yet always "inert". Between the spring of 1585 and the summer of 1586, a group of English Catholic priests led by the Jesuit William Weston (alias Father Edmunds) conducted a series of spectacular exorcisms, mainly in the house of a recusant gentleman at Denham in Buckinghamshire. Under a statute of 1585, the mere presence in England of a Jesuit or seminary priest constituted high treason, and harbouring one was a felony; yet these clandestine exorcisms drew hundreds of spectators. In 1603 Samuel Harsnett, then chaplain to the Bishop of London, drew on the sworn testimony of four of the possessed and one priest to write *A Declaration of Egregious Popish Impostures*. It has been known since the eighteenth century that Shakespeare read this book when writing *King Lear*: the names of the devils that Edgar, disguised as the mad beggar "Poor Tom", claims possess him, part of the language of madness, and several features of hell come from Harsnett. But once these borrowings had been carefully catalogued, the question of their significance was not only left unanswered but, until recently, not even asked. Greenblatt thinks what blocked the question was a model of source study "divided between the old historicism and the New Criticism": *King Lear*, as an autonomous, self-sufficient, disinterested work of art created by a solitary genius, has only a contingent relation to its sources; sources merely supply "raw material", and the phrase "historical background" demotes history to decorative scenery or a convenient, well-lit pigeonhole. **Once the distinctions on which this model rests begin to break down, source study must change its nature: history can no longer be set against the literary text as a stable antithesis or a stable background, and the protective isolation of texts gives way to their interaction with other texts and the permeability of their boundaries.** Montaigne said: when I play with my cat, who knows whether I am not a pastime to her more than she is to me? So when Shakespeare borrows from Harsnett, who knows whether Harsnett had not already, in a deep sense, borrowed from Shakespeare's theatre what Shakespeare borrows back? Whose interests are served by the borrowing? Does the exchange produce a larger cultural text? Greenblatt says explicitly that for him these questions lead not to exclamations of "radical indeterminacy" but to an inquiry into the `institutional strategies` in which *King Lear* and the *Declaration* are both embedded; he calls this relationship `the negotiation and exchange of social energy`.

**Mechanism: Harsnett's strategy, driving exorcism into the theatre.** These strategies were part of a fierce struggle in late sixteenth- and early seventeenth-century England to redefine the central values of society, and at the heart of the struggle was the definition of the sacred: the legitimacy of the state depended explicitly on its claim to a measure of sacredness, so who defined the sacred and who policed its boundaries was at once a religious and a secular question. Harsnett's book was a weapon of the established church for eliminating rival religious authority, its aim being to root out an opposing `charisma`, in Edward Shils's phrase "awe-inspiring centeredness". Exorcism was one of the highest manifestations of such charisma in Latin Christianity, and it depended on an audience: the great exorcisms of the late Middle Ages took place in urban centres, in churches packed with spectators. In Protestant England at the end of the sixteenth century, both Catholic exorcists and nonconforming Puritan exorcists threatened the religious authorities, since the power of fasting and prayer they extolled did not depend on the state-supported church hierarchy. Harsnett attacked first the Puritan exorcist John Darrel and then the Jesuits, his aim being not to secure a monopoly of exorcism for the established church but to expose exorcism itself as fraud, so that spiritual power would henceforth be distributed in more modest and controlled ways throughout the established hierarchy, at whose summit stood the sole legitimate holder of absolute charismatic authority, the monarch. His argument looks rational, but it is not an Enlightenment prelude to the construction of rational belief: Harsnett denies that there are devils in the possessed but finds a devil in the exorcist himself; Edmunds's dialogue with the devil is really a dialogue between "devil Edmunds and Edmunds devil", since he plays both parts.

This exposure meets a logical difficulty. The authorities forced the Puritan demoniac, William Sommers, a twenty-one-year-old apprentice, to confess and to imitate his fits in public to prove that possession was a performance; but Darrel replied that Satan, in order to make onlookers believe the possession was counterfeit, could deliberately perform some trivial counterfeit tricks. **If Satan can counterfeit counterfeiting, there can be no decisive confession, only an infinite regress of exposure and uncertainty.** What Harsnett needed was not more evidence of fraud in individual cases but a counter-strategy that could expose fraud *at any time and in any place*: one that would explain both why exorcism was empty and why it was so effective, why a few pitiful tricks could convince onlookers that they had witnessed the ultimate struggle between good and evil. He found this explanatory model in the *theatre*: exorcism is a stage play, usually a tragicomedy, that cleverly conceals its own theatricality; the theatre audience knows its misrecognition of reality to be temporary, deliberate and playful, whereas the exorcists strive to make the misrecognition permanent and invisible. The priests first talked of successful exorcisms abroad and described the symptoms of possession in detail, then waited for an opportunity to improvise: a hungry servant who had spent a night or two in the fields and been terrified by thunder, a dissolute young gentleman with an attack of "hysteria", all became signs of possession, and the naive "scholars" "played the devil" as the priests wished. Canon 72 of the new church canons of 1604 laid down that no minister might attempt to cast out devils by fasting and prayer without the bishop's licence, on pain of being accounted an impostor and deposed; since licences were almost never granted, exorcism was in effect officially halted. Parallel to this was a concrete exchange: during the Reformation, Catholic vestments were sold to actors, so that an actor playing an English bishop in a history play might wear the real vestments of the man he represented. The signs of the sacred were emptied out and made tradeable, passing from one institution to another; for the polemicists of the established church, selling Catholic vestments to players was a symbolic attack, Catholicism being "the Pope's theatre". Harsnett wanted to drive exorcism into the theatre, and in London that meant, literally, to the margins, where increasingly strict civic regulation had already driven the public playhouses.

**Reading: emptying out in *King Lear*.** As early as *The Comedy of Errors* (1590) Shakespeare had treated exorcism as comic misunderstanding; in *Twelfth Night* he made it a prank played on Malvolio (Feste, disguised as a priest, "exorcises" him, very probably alluding to the recently condemned Darrel); by *All's Well That Ends Well*, "exorcist" could be used casually as a synonym for "conjurer". When Harsnett drove exorcism towards the theatre, Shakespeare was already standing at the door of the Globe to receive it. This is not surprising: what Harsnett attacked was a theatre that pretended not to be entertainment but serious reality, and his argument depended precisely on an officially designated commercial theatre distinguished from all other public rituals by its open acknowledgement of its own fictionality; without pretending to be real there is no *fraud*. The real threat to the theatre came from the Puritans, who saw the devil in it (Gosson: "the efficient cause of plays" is the devil). This is also the logic of Sidney's defence of poetry: "the poet, he nothing affirms, and therefore never lieth." So *King Lear* stages not only exorcism but *Harsnett on exorcism*: in the five fiends Edgar lists, an audience familiar with Harsnett would recognise the maidservants of Father Edmunds's "devil theatre". Edgar makes the blind Gloucester believe he stands on Dover cliff, and after he has fallen forward switches to another role, saying he saw a fiend with a thousand noses depart from the old man: "Thy life's a miracle." This scene is a disenchanted analysis of religious and theatrical illusion: on the flat stage Edgar does to Gloucester what the theatre usually does to its audience; but the audience never accepts such fictions absolutely: **the theatre elicits from us not belief but complicity.** The play has no ghosts like those of *Richard III* or *Hamlet*, no witches like those of *Macbeth*; Lear's madness, as in Harsnett, is attributed to "hysteria" (the mother), to wind and rain and to extreme suffering, and what cures it is the doctor's prescription of sleep, not exorcism, fasting or prayer. The relation of *King Lear* to Harsnett is therefore first of all one of *reiteration*, marking a deeper, unspoken institutional exchange: the official church dismantled the powerful mechanisms of an unwelcome and dangerous charisma and ceded them to the players; the players in turn confirmed that these mechanisms were theatrical and therefore illusory.

Yet once Harsnett's arguments appear on Shakespeare's stage, they become estranged from themselves: **the closer Shakespeare seems to approach a source, the more faithfully he reproduces it, the more devastating and decisive his transformation of it.** Mocking the exorcists' preference for young women, Harsnett had used a rare adjective, "corky" (withered): it would pose all the cunning exorcists to teach an old corky woman to writhe and tumble; Shakespeare uses it in the almost unbearable scene of torture in which Cornwall orders "Bind fast his corky arms": the bullying humour is still there, but it belongs to the torturer. The argument of the *Declaration* is faithfully reiterated, but in split form: the sceptical voices are given to Cornwall, Goneril and above all Edmund, whose "naturalism" is revealed as the argument of a bastard younger son plotting to supplant his legitimate elder brother and ultimately destroying his father; fraudulent possession and exorcism are given to the legitimate Edgar, who is driven to this by nightmarish persecution, and who plays Poor Tom out of a laudable desire to survive. This bears a strange and disquieting resemblance to the situation of the English Jesuits. Greenblatt cites evidence that this possibility was not merely a product of our historical distance: in 1610 a touring company in Yorkshire performed a repertoire including *King Lear* at the manor of a recusant Catholic couple, and was informed on by Puritan neighbours. **In Shakespeare, the recognition that possession is theatrical fraud leads not to the sober satisfaction of those who are not deceived but to a deeper uncertainty and loss of bearings in the face of evil.** All the characters' attempts to invoke transcendent powers to explain or relieve suffering fail: Lear calls repeatedly on the gods, and the thunder refuses to speak; Lear asks, "Is there any cause in nature that makes these hard hearts?" and we know there is no cause *outside nature*: the evil was released by Lear himself from the structures of family and state. At the end Lear asks for a looking-glass and a feather, hoping Cordelia is still alive; this calls on the conventions of tragicomedy, in which audiences must often will a miraculous turn against the evidence of their senses; but *King Lear* reverses it: the breath of the actor playing Cordelia must surely mist the glass, the feather must surely stir, and yet we are certain that she is "dead as earth".
