The means by which the theatre could produce "counterfeit miracles" are abandoned here; the hope of redemption is emptied of institutional and doctrinal meaning, yet, like the dream of exorcism, it cannot be uprooted. *(This ending is exactly what the happy-ending adaptation discussed in P5 set out to "repair".)*

Greenblatt calls this process `emptying out`: the official position is faithfully confirmed and at the same time emptied out. It resembles Brecht's `alienation effect`, and more closely the "internal distance" spoken of by Althusser and Macherey (P9); but he thinks the most apt term comes from the very theology Harsnett professed: Hooker on the "evacuation" of the Mosaic law after the coming of Christ, where the words altar, priest and sacrifice remain but pass from literal to metaphorical use. Exorcism and Harsnett's attack on exorcism both undergo such evacuation and transformed reiteration in *King Lear*: **what was literal is now literary.** Shakespeare's theatre is a fraudulent institution that never pretends to be otherwise; it calls forth what is not, signifies absence, turns the literal into the metaphorical, empties out everything it represents, and thereby carves out for itself the hollow round space in which it survives. Its complex, limited institutional independence, its marginal and impure autonomy, comes not from some intrinsic formal reflexivity but from the ideological matrix in which it is created and re-created. There remains a final question: why does our culture embrace *King Lear*'s massive display of simulated suffering and fraudulent exorcism? Because we no longer believe in those magical rituals yet still need them, and the play performs them as clearly marked frauds for our continued consumption; and because the Harsnetts wanted to free us from the oppression of false belief only in order to bind us more firmly to the official established church, and this "solution" is hateful; so we embrace a substitute that seems to confirm the official line, thereby taking a place in the central value system, while at the same time unsettling every official line.

**Conclusion: the paradox of power.** This is the New Historicist paradox of power: Greenblatt's analysis is a model of containment (the subversive, persecuted Catholicism and the charisma of exorcism, is absorbed by the theatre, marked as fiction and offered for consumption), yet in the same essay it shows how the theatre "unsettles every official line". **Subversion and containment are not two alternative outcomes here but two faces of one and the same circuit.** *One might say that the problem is not that New Historicism cannot see subversion, but that it places the force of subversion within a dependence on power: the theatre's autonomy is "marginal and impure", and its critical force is inseparable from its dependence on institutional exchange.* Compared with Edmund at the end of P9 the difference is particularly clear: in the cultural materialist reading summarised by the editors, Edmund represents a rising class contending with the aristocracy for power, and his defeat exposes the fragility of aristocratic legitimacy; in Greenblatt, Edmund is the spokesman of Harsnett-style scepticism, and the real "crack" occurs in the institutional exchange between theatre and church rather than between classes.

### Structures of Feeling: Williams and the Other British Tradition

Most of the views of cultural materialism (and its name) come from the British left-wing critic **Raymond Williams**. In place of Foucault's "discourse", Williams coined the term `structures of feeling`, concerned with "meanings and values as they are actively lived and felt". Structures of feeling are often at odds with explicit systems of values and beliefs and with the dominant ideology of a society; they are typically found in literature and opposed to the status quo: the values in the work of Dickens, the Brontës and others represent structures of feeling of humanity at odds with the commercial and materialist values of the Victorian age. **As a result, cultural materialism is much more optimistic about the possibility of change, and is sometimes willing to see literature as a source of oppositional values.** It also lays particular stress on "reading" the present through the past, revealing the politics of our own society through what we choose to emphasise or suppress in the past.

**Background:** Williams was the most important British cultural historian from the 1950s to the 1980s, and his work is the foundation of the contemporary school of cultural materialism. *The Country and the City* (1973) examines the changing meanings of the country and the city as places in English literature from the Renaissance to the twentieth century. *Its method is quite unlike New Historicism's "anecdote": instead of juxtaposing a curious document with a classic, it first establishes a long-term economic and social structure and then asks what literature saw within it and what it could not see.*

**Mechanism: agrarian capitalism and the morality of "improvement".** By the eighteenth century nearly half the cultivated land of England belonged to some five thousand families; as the central form of this dominance, four hundred families, in a population of seven or eight million, owned nearly a quarter of the cultivated land. Under this dominance the peasantry in the classical sense had ceased to exist, replaced by an increasingly regular structure of tenant farmers and wage labourers. This is `agrarian capitalism`, and its moral vocabulary was "improvement". Literature absorbed the process in various ways. The plot of Fielding's *Tom Jones* is built on the wish to unite, through marriage, the two largest estates in Somerset; Richardson's *Clarissa* is its reverse: Clarissa is wholly exposed to a world of cold calculation, an exposure no marriage contract can sanction, and even rape cannot destroy her chastity; this is not consolidation, not the necessary bargain struck between interest and value, but a passionate guarding of the integrity of the person: first the refusal to compromise, then the acceptance of destruction. Defoe knew what was happening in the fields and the markets, yet he did not examine its underlying social reality in his novels; instead he projected an abstracted spirit of improvement and simple economic interest into other stories, most notably *Robinson Crusoe*, creating a fictional world of isolated individuals to whom other people are only temporary and functional (*Robinson Crusoe*, *Moll Flanders*). From Defoe through Arthur Young's *Annals of Agriculture* to Cobbett runs a tradition of "rural surveys", the real line of development of practical agriculture; but with few exceptions it was itself an abstraction from social relations.

**Definition: an instance of a structure of feeling.** The most influential argument of *The Country and the City* is aimed at a myth: that the transition from a rural to an industrial society was a fall, the real source of the pains and disorders of our society. Williams says the importance of this myth in modern social thought can hardly be overestimated: it is the main source of the structure of feeling he calls "the perpetual retrospect to an 'organic' or 'natural' society", and the last protecting illusion in the crisis of our own time, the belief that what injures us is not capitalism. *This use of "structure of feeling" makes Barry's definition concrete: it is not a set of explicit tenets but a generally felt direction of nostalgia; but the example also shows that structures of feeling are not always oppositional: this one works precisely to shield capitalism.* To dismantle the myth, Williams asks whether the pre-enclosure village was really a "community". The answer is hard to give: the facts vary greatly, more local studies are needed, and at such a distance estimates of "community" are always subjective. The manorial courts often cited as "community" were in steady decline before enclosure; the system of roundsmen, recurrent outbreaks of smallpox and the resulting peaks in poor relief all show that such villages were deeply involved in and exposed to the crises of an overall system, and that neighbourliness was at best relative; it was under this pressure that the earlier friendly, informal relief turned into a cold and harsh treatment of a separate class of "the poor". Williams does not deny the existence of another kind of figure: in the relative independence of country people, those with the time and spirit to observe, think and read flourished (the commoners Bewick describes, field labourers like Stephen Duck, the Sussex shepherd diarists, the amateur geologists and botanists of the Lancashire mill towns); they belong to the whole history of the labourers everywhere, with its glories and its tragedies. But local antagonism had finally to be replaced by the organisation of class against class in trade unionism and related political movements; the structure of feeling of direct moral appeal in the poems of Goldsmith or Crabbe necessarily changed into another order of thought and feeling.

**Reading: seeing only one class.** This analysis reaches its most refined point with Austen. On the border of Hampshire and Surrey, Selborne, Chawton and Farnham lie no more than a dozen miles apart: in 1793 Gilbert White died at Selborne; in 1777 the fourteen-year-old Cobbett ran away from his father's small farm at Farnham, and later, in the 1820s, rode through these villages again and again; Austen lived at Chawton. What Cobbett named as he rode past was *class*; Austen, seeing from *inside* the houses, could never see this, for all the intricacy of her social description. All her discriminations are necessarily internal and exclusive: she is concerned with the *conduct* of people who, in the complicated processes of improvement, were repeatedly trying to make themselves into a class. **"Where only one class is seen, no classes are seen."** Her characters are selected and typical individuals living well or badly in a narrow social dimension; Cobbett never looked so closely or so finely, but he saw what they had in common. Yet landed and colonial capital is already embedded directly, as a matter of course, in her novels: one could contrast Sir Thomas Bertram's estate in *Mansfield Park* with the "London" manners of the Crawfords (a common reading), were he not explicitly shown as what Goldsmith called a "great West Indian", a colonial proprietor of sugar plantations on Antigua; and the Crawfords' income in fact comes from a Norfolk estate, and they were brought up by an uncle who is an admiral. The process Cobbett observed, the arrival of "nabobs, negro-drivers, admirals, generals", is thus inserted into the long and complicated interaction of landed and trading capital, and even taken for granted. *This Antigua detail will become the centre of Said's reading of Mansfield Park in P15; Williams has already pointed to it here, but his concern is the class structure within England, whereas Said will ask about the silence of empire itself in the text.*

**Reading: E. P. Thompson reads Blake's "London".** Alongside Williams stands another British Marxist historian, **E. P. Thompson**, whose *The Making of the English Working Class* (1963) is known for its attention to the culture that shapes people's social and political action. In *Witness Against the Beast* (1993) he read Blake's "London" with a comprehensive knowledge of the social movements of seventeenth- and eighteenth-century England. The poem is one of the most lucid of the *Songs of Experience*, one that least needs an interpreter; Thompson agrees that any reader can see London at once as Blake's city, as an image of the state of English society and as an image of the human condition, and that close reading can perhaps confirm but hardly add anything. But drafts of the poem survive in Blake's notebook, which allows the rare opportunity of examining its *process of composition*.

The key revision in the first stanza changes "dirty street" and "dirty Thames" to "charter'd". Another fragment in the notebook associates "charter'd" with "cheating" and with "the little blasts of fear / That the hireling blows into my ear", referring to the government proclamations, the burnings of Paine in effigy and the political repression of the Reeves associations in the very year these poems were written. "Charter'd" of course suggests commerce: chartered companies increasingly losing their function and becoming bastions of urban privilege, and the East India Company, which in 1793 applied to have its charter extended for twenty years. But for Blake the word stood at an intellectual and political crossroads. On the one hand it was the stale liberal rhetoric of polite culture: "chartered rights", "chartered liberties" and "Magna Charta" were central to Whig ideology, and Blake's own early *King Edward the Third* had used it in this way; on the other hand chartered liberty is at the same time the denial of others' liberty: a charter is granted by some authority to some group, not claimed as a right, and it is by its nature exclusive. This was precisely the focus of the dispute between Burke and Paine: in *Reflections on the Revolution in France* Burke defined the liberties of Englishmen as "an entailed inheritance" derived from their forefathers, against "the rights of man"; Paine replied that it is a perversion of terms to say that a charter gives rights, since it operates by a contrary effect, that of taking rights away, leaving rights in the hands of a few by exclusion, and he likened the custom in chartered towns of "giving, selling and buying freedom" to the power of a garrison rather than civil government. Blake chose this word during the greatest political controversy to shake England, in 1791–93, and ironically inverted Burke's rhetoric. The second revision changes "see every face" to "mark", making "mark" fall three times on the beat; for Blake's contemporaries, especially a radical audience, it would first of all summon "the mark of the Beast" in Revelation, without which no man might buy or sell, and radical Dissenters had for generations identified the worshippers of the Beast with usurers, the rich and those successful in buying and selling. On this basis Thompson rejects another claim, that there is an allusion here to the passage in Ezekiel where a mark is set on the foreheads of those who mourn to save them from slaughter: Blake's speaker is not setting marks but observing them, and *every* person is marked; blending the two allusions into some deeper "ambiguity" would introduce a direct contradiction of intention and feeling at the centre of the poem: **ambiguity on this scale is not a fruitful multiplication of meaning.** In the second stanza "German forg'd links" (referring to the Hanoverian dynasty and the Hanoverian troops that might be used against English reformers) became "mind-forg'd manacles": they are manacles of deceit, self-interest, lack of love, law, repression and hypocrisy, stronger and harder to break than those of the German king and his mercenaries, because they bind the minds of the oppressed as well as of the oppressors, and are self-forged. The revision in the third stanza makes "Every black'ning Church appalls" an *indictment* of the church ("appals" being transitive in Blake's day, meaning to put to shame, to strike with dread), not, as some critics have inverted it, a statement that the church, under the influence of the evangelical revival, was "appalled" by the plight of the chimney-sweeping children. The last stanza was not there originally; Blake came back and tried three versions. Bateson said that to read those diseases as venereal is to read Blake too literally; Thompson replies that the soldier's blood is real, and so is the venereal disease that blinds the new-born infant and blights with plagues the "Marriage hearse"; Blake, he observes, was often a very literal man.

Thompson's conclusion is that the poem is not a list of unrelated sufferings but is organised on two levels. Literally, it is organised around the street cries of London, moving from "seeing" in the first stanza to "hearing" in the last three and then to "feeling", immersing the observer ever more deeply in the situation he walks through. Symbolically, the tone of compassion falls on the sufferers and the tone of indignation on the institutions of repression (mind-forg'd manacles, black'ning church, palace, marriage hearse), and the symbolic organisation lies within the clear and developing logic of *market relations*: from "charter'd" onwards Blake never lets go of the imagery of buying and selling, though the two words themselves never appear; what is bought and sold is in turn goods (the street cries), childhood (the chimney sweeps), human life (the soldier), and finally youth, beauty and love, the very source of life, bought and sold in the diseased harlot, who is only the obverse of the "marriage hearse". The harlot is also the Great Whore of Babylon, who for eighteenth-century radical Dissenters was not only the "scarlet woman" of Rome but the symbol of every compromise of church and state, the Church of England above all; she thus ties the imagery of market relations and the imagery of ideological domination by the state church into a single knot. **"The human condition", without further qualification, is only a metaphysical full stop; the poem is about a *particular* human condition, and offers a unified analysis of its nature.** Thompson also points out that Blake accepted part of the Paineite argument but turned it in a new direction: a Jacobin Londoner could respond to and accept the poem but could hardly have written it; the ordinary supporter of the London Corresponding Society would not have written "mind-forg'd", since he would have seen the manacles as wholly external, imposed by oppressive priestcraft and kingcraft, and his indignation might well have swamped his compassion. Blake always held aloof from the mechanical materialist epistemology deriving from Newton and Locke, so that humanity's redemption from this condition could not come from the political reorganisation of the institutions of state and church alone, but required some utopian leap, from "Mystery" to a renewed life of the imagination.

**Distinction:** *Setting Thompson beside New Historicism shows the differences within "historicism". Thompson too places a canonical poem back among the discourses contemporary with it (Burke and Paine, the radical Dissenters' exegesis of Revelation), but he uses these contexts to establish Blake's intention and the poem's unified meaning, and explicitly refuses to pile up contradictory allusions in the name of "ambiguity"; his history is the history of social movements and class experience, not a circulation of discourses as representations. Williams and Thompson represent the tradition of British Marxist cultural history, and it is from here rather than from Foucault that cultural materialism starts; this is one reason it is more willing than New Historicism to look for oppositional values in literature.*

### Fault-lines and Dissidence: How Cultural Materialism Reads *Othello*

Cultural materialism's fullest response to the containment model is **Alan Sinfield**'s reading of *Othello* in *Faultlines* (1992). Its starting point is an apparently trivial detail. When Cassio, after his drunken brawl, laments "Reputation, reputation, I have lost my reputation!", Iago replies that you have lost nothing unless you repute yourself such a loser. The reply is seductive but absurd, for reputation is by definition a social construct, depending wholly on one's standing in the eyes of others; and reputation is only a particularly obvious example: language and reality always interact and depend on social recognition; meaning works because it is shared; if you invent your own language, no one will understand you, and if you persist you will be thought mad. Iago's advice that Cassio ignore the social basis of language and make his own meanings for words is especially perverse, because Iago himself is precisely the chief manipulator of the stories current in this society.

**Mechanism: conditions of plausibility.** The whole play is a contest of stories. At the start Iago and Roderigo concoct a sexist and racist story, Desdemona fallen "to the gross clasps of a lascivious Moor"; Brabantio believes it and repeats it to the Senate; Othello replies with his "round unvarnish'd tale", whose content is precisely how he tells stories: Brabantio repeatedly questioned him about his life, and Desdemona was drawn by the story. Since the plot advances through competing stories, the `conditions of plausibility` that decide which story is believed become crucial. Brabantio's argument is that for Desdemona to love Othello is an error against nature unless witchcraft is involved; the argument depends on the plausibility, for the Senate, of the view that black people are inferior outsiders, and this is evidently a good move. Even those who want to support Othello accept that he is apparently unsuitable as Desdemona's husband: Desdemona says "I saw Othello's visage in his mind", meaning that he looks black but is really very nice; the Duke tells Brabantio "Your son-in-law is far more fair than black", meaning that he lacks the unpleasant characteristics "we all know" belong to black people and is really much like a white man. Facing such unfavourable conditions of plausibility, Othello has two strategies and uses both: one is to appear composed and responsible, as the Venetians imagine themselves to be; the other is shrewdly to exploit the exotic image racism assigns him: hairbreadth escapes, redemption from slavery, mountains whose heads touch heaven, cannibals, men whose heads grow beneath their shoulders. These adventures would not be plausible, but from an exotic person they are; when he performs his strangeness the Venetians tolerate him, because he endorses, in a milder form, part of Brabantio's argument.

Later Iago repeats his racist and sexist story to Othello and persuades him. Othello comes to believe in his own inferiority and Desdemona's infidelity and acts accordingly ("Haply, for I am black"), beginning to play the "extravagant and wheeling stranger" he has been designated. **Ania Loomba** describes the trajectory: Othello moves from being a colonised subject existing on the terms of white Venetian society and trying to internalise its ideology, to being marginalised, exiled and totally alienated, until he occupies his "true" place as this society's "other". When everyone insists on a story about you, it is hard not to be affected by it. At the end Othello tries to reaffirm himself, yet "recognises" himself as what Venetian culture had always believed him to be: an ignorant, savage outsider, like the "base Indian" who threw a pearl away. Sinfield says this is very close to what Althusser calls `interpellation`: Venice hails Othello as a barbarian, and he acknowledges that they mean him (P9). Iago himself says that the idea that Desdemona loves Cassio is "apt and of great credit". **Peter Stallybrass** points out that Iago is convincing not because he is superhumanly ingenious, but precisely because his voice is the voice of "common sense", the ceaseless repetition of what is "always already known", what is culturally "given". **The racism and sexism in the play should therefore be traced not only to Iago's character or his arbitrary devilry, but to the Venetian culture that sets the conditions of plausibility.**

**Background: the production of ideology.** Sinfield speaks of "stories" in order to connect theory, with an inclusive word, to the discourse of everyday life; in fact he is discussing the production of `ideology`. He follows the argument at the beginning of Althusser's essay: if a society is to continue, it must produce not only materially but also ideologically, needing both the various kinds of knowledge that sustain material production and an intuitive and explicit understanding of the system of social relationships, so that the whole process can proceed more or less smoothly. What ideology produces, and makes plausible, are concepts and systems that explain who we are, who others are, how the world works. Its power lies in becoming common sense, "obvious": it is already at work when we come into the world, and we acquire consciousness in its terms; certain interpretations of experience are plausible because they fit with existing experience and are confirmed by those around us; **Colin Sumner** calls this "the circle of social reality": understanding produces its own social reality, and social reality produces its own understanding. Most societies maintain the status quo not mainly because dissidents are punished or co-opted (though they are), but because many people believe that things have to be more or less as they are and that improvement is not feasible; it is because of such powerful (plausible) discourses that people acquiesce in the injustice and humiliation they experience. Recognising ideological construction does not deny individual agency (though it makes it less interesting): **Anthony Giddens**'s analogy is the uttering of a grammatical sentence, which is constrained by the vocabulary and syntactic rules of the language yet is still individual, and may, in being uttered, both confirm and slightly modify the language.

Ideology is produced everywhere, but certain institutions, by definition those that generally confirm the prevailing arrangements of power, are far more powerful than others. In Shakespeare's plays the most effective stories are given scope and direction by powerful men: they "authorise the scripts", which other characters find hard to resist; often this needs no special intervention, appearing simply as "the restoration of order", since the preferences of the ruling elite are already in tune with the running system. Conversely, scriptwriters from below immediately appear subversive: Shylock, Malvolio, Don John, Iago, Edmund, Macbeth, Caliban. Women in the early comedies may write scripts, sometimes even against their parents' wishes, but their scripts finally lead to surrendering power in the larger story of marriage; elsewhere, women who write scripts for men are bad (Goneril and Regan, Lady Macbeth), while men writing scripts for women are usually presented as doing them good. The state is the most powerful scriptwriter: the Duke offers Brabantio "the bloody book of law"; at the end Othello tries to control the story he leaves behind ("Speak of me as I am"), but the last lines belong to Lodovico, the representative of the Senate, who will "to the state / This heavy act with heavy heart relate". The state will tell Othello's story in the way it chooses; as for Iago, it will torture him until he says what it wants to hear. **When the state's command of the conditions of plausibility falters, it falls back on direct coercion.**

**Reading: the murdered Turk.** The relation between state violence and ideological power can be seen in Othello's final self-justification. Defending himself as a good Venetian, he boasts of a killing: not of Desdemona (he now agrees that was bad) but of "a malignant and a turban'd Turk" who beat a Venetian and traduced the state; he "took by th' throat the circumcised dog, / And smote him—thus", and as he says it he stabs himself. Countless critics have discussed Othello's suicide, but Sinfield has not noticed anyone concerned about the murdered Turk: since he is malignant, circumcised and turbaned, he seems not to require the sensitive attention of Anglo-American literary critics. Character criticism might take this narrative as a final revelation of Othello's long-standing proneness to violence; but the violence here does not belong to Othello alone, any more than Venetian racism and sexism belong to individuals: killing the state's enemies is just what the Venetian state likes, which is why Cassio exclaims that "he was great of heart". The state can almost be defined as what holds the monopoly of legitimate violence, and that violence is justified by stories of the barbarity of its demonised others; for Venetians and Elizabethans alike, Turks belonged among the barbarians. In reality civilisation and barbarism differ little, which is why maintaining the distinction is a continual ideological task. Othello accepts within himself the state's distinction between civilisation and barbarism, and so becomes a good subject again; this "explains" how he murdered Desdemona: it was the barbarian under, or rather in, the skin; and his suicide is better still, since it removes the intolerable confusion of finding citizen and alien in the same body. **Othello's particular situation lets those who want to see it see the violence on which the state and its civilisation depend.**

**Problem: where does dissidence come from?** At this point the argument meets its crucial problem. Marx and Engels say in *The German Ideology* that the ruling material force is at the same time the ruling intellectual force (P9); in work deriving from Althusser and Foucault, not only ideas but subjectivity itself are ideological constructs. If we acquire consciousness in a language continuous with the power structures that maintain the social order, how can we conceive, let alone organise, resistance? The feminist critics **Lynda Boose** and **Carol Thomas Neely** put this sharply: they accuse both New Historicism and cultural materialism of theorising power as an impregnable system of containment, so that subordinate groups appear merely as effects of the dominant, and female identity as something patriarchy imposes on women; if black or gay people are persuaded by the conditions of plausibility to adopt subjectivities suited to maintaining the social order, where does radical black or gay consciousness come from? **Kathleen McLuskie** argues that *Measure for Measure* and *King Lear* are organised from a male point of view, and that feminist criticism "can only expose its own exclusion from the text"; by contrast, *The Woman's Part*, edited by Lenz, Greene and Neely, represents a humanist or essentialist feminism, holding that Shakespeare's female characters are not male constructs but, like the male characters, complex and flawed, capable of passion and pain, growth and decay. Sinfield sides with McLuskie: traditional critics who saw Shakespeare's female characters in stereotypical terms were often roughly right, because they recognised the ideological structures the culture had always been producing; the disagreement is that they celebrated these patterns and collaborated in making them plausible instead of criticising them. There are really two questions here: whether there are complete persons, or whether subjectivity is an effect of cultural production; and Shakespeare's authority, whether he anticipated a progressive politics of modernity (McLuskie notes that the entertainment industry he worked in had, so far as is known, no female shareholders, actors, writers or stagehands). The two finally converge: to believe that Shakespeare's texts give access to an essential human nature transcending cultural production, and to believe this of individual characters, are the same idea. Boose complains that accepting McLuskie means giving up altogether the pleasure we get from Shakespeare; Sinfield replies that perhaps it does, but pleasure in Shakespeare is a complex phenomenon, not necessarily wholly incompatible with a critical attitude towards the ideology of the plays. *The feminist side of this dispute will be developed in the "essentialism versus constructionism" debate in P12.*

Sinfield's answer is that **dissident identity and action are unlikely to derive from individual subjectivity and agency, and more likely to derive from participation in a `subculture`.** The essentialist-humanist view of literature believes the individual to be the necessary source of truth and meaning; but thinking of oneself as essentially an individual tends to efface the processes of cultural production and to make us think ourselves autonomous and self-determining; it is not individuals but power structures that produce the systems in which we live and think, and focusing on the individual makes it hard to recognise these structures, and even when they are recognised, hard to do anything about them, since that requires collective action. (Richard Ohmann's example: each of us buys a car because we need transport, and each individual does little damage to the environment and to others; but from this standpoint it is hard to raise the question whether we should live in a car culture at all.) Gramsci says that in acquiring one's conception of the world one always belongs to a group sharing the same ways of thinking and acting; it is in such sharing that one can learn to inhabit plausible oppositional concerns and forms, and so develop a plausible oppositional selfhood; this is how successful movements work. **Judith Butler** opposes a universalist concept of "woman", because it necessarily excludes those who do not conform to its unstated normative requirements; she points out that agency does not require a prior "doer", who is constituted in the deed: "construction is not opposed to agency; it is the necessary scene of agency" (P13). If these arguments hold, there is no need, as Neely does, to imagine some "female" realm not wholly inscribed by patriarchal ideology; "women's discourse" would be a discourse women formulate together at a historical juncture, made plausible by social interaction, especially interaction among women. Desdemona comes closest to seeing the truth when she talks with Emilia (what she needs is a refuge for battered wives); Othello goes wrong because he has no reliable friend with whom to check his perceptions. Subcultures constitute consciousness in the same way as the dominant ideology, but in partly dissident forms: in the little patch of the world where a subculture runs, one can confidently say "black is beautiful" or "gay is good".

**Definition: fault-lines.** Sinfield then dismantles the containment model directly. He grants that not all work called New Historicist takes this position (Montrose does not), and that the problem of containment is widespread in functionalism, structuralism and Althusserian Marxism; but New Historicism's handling of it is especially subtle and powerful, and the idea that dissidence is usually contained has indeed captured the imagination of the whole profession. The first example that strikes at the heart of the containment model is that legitimate rulers may be unable to control the military apparatus. Valuable New Historicist analysis examines the interaction of monarch and court, and often finds "power" moving in an apparently unbreakable circle, from the monarch and back to the monarch; absolutist ideology represents the monarch as the necessary and sufficient source of national unity, but the early modern state, like any other, ultimately depended on military force. The Essex rising of 1601 is proof: the queen was old, Essex had the military glory of the capture of Cadiz, and the charismatic earl could easily think he should not remain subordinate. Ideological power and military power are in danger of splitting apart: **this is a `fault-line` in the political structure** (P7 has already introduced this geological metaphor). Soldiers overthrowing legitimate but militarily dependent political leaders still happens often; during the Korean War General MacArthur thought he could override the authority of President Truman. In *Macbeth* Duncan has legitimacy and Macbeth is the best fighter; Duncan cannot avoid delegating power to subordinates who may turn it against him; the original rebel is precisely the Thane of Cawdor, in whom he built "an absolute trust"; if the thought of rebellion could enter Cawdor's mind it will enter Macbeth's and others', and its roots are not merely individual ambition. Absolutist ideology must deny that the state has this structural flaw, and so projects the whole problem onto a supernatural background of good and evil, implying that disruption must come from outside, or at least be crucially reinforced from outside (the witches and the demonic Lady Macbeth). *Henry V* offers a magical resolution of this fault-line by making the legitimate monarch also the triumphant war leader; the Chorus to Act 5 likens Henry's return to Caesar's triumphal entry into Rome, and then to Essex's expected return from Ireland (the most specific contemporary reference in Shakespeare's plays); but the comparisons refuse to settle: Caesar threatened the government precisely after his triumphal entry; Elizabeth could become "empress" (of Ireland) only through Essex's military victory, which would in turn increase his potential for rebellion. **Fault-lines by definition resist the fantasies that try to efface them.** The Epilogue to *Henry V* has to record that the absolutist pyramid collapsed on the accession of Henry VI, who was not the strongest military leader; and Essex failed to mobilise enough support to get Elizabeth into his power.

From this follows the central proposition of cultural materialism: **the potential for dissidence derives ultimately not from the essential qualities of individuals but from the conflicts and contradictions that the social order inevitably produces within itself in the process of maintaining itself.** Williams says that ideology must always be *produced*: social order and cultural order must be seen as actively and continuously made, or they could quickly collapse. Conflict and contradiction arise from the very strategies ideology uses to contain the expectations it must evoke; it is here that failures or refusals to identify one's interests with those of the dominant may occur, and dissidence arises. Dominant and subordinate are structurally linked, but not in the way Carolyn Porter criticises: it was the social structure of Elizabethan England that produced unemployed labourers and military leaders, but it could not prevent them from conceiving and carrying out dissident practices, especially when they could constitute milieux in which dissidence became plausible.

**Reading: Desdemona's disobedience.** The second point that strikes at the containment model is women's space. When Desdemona first appears and her father asks whom among this noble company she most owes obedience, she answers that she perceives "a divided duty": she is her father's daughter, but here is her husband, and just as her mother preferred her father before her grandfather, so she claims she may profess the same duty to the Moor. This is exemplary, because when Desdemona uses "divided duty" to justify eloping with an unsuitable man, she discovers no unique and radical insight (nor does Cordelia when she uses it); she simply expounds the official doctrine plainly: a woman should obey the male head of her household, her father before marriage and her husband after. Ideally the passage from daughter to wife should be completed smoothly with the consent of all parties; but this is precisely the moment when patriarchy is insecure, and the danger comes from a basic complication in the ideology of gender relations: marriage was an institution for arranging property and securing inheritance, and also supposed to be a fulfilling personal relationship; people who married were supposed to obey their parents, and also to love each other. "Divided duty" is therefore not Desdemona's peculiar problem but the way the world is set up for her. The Reformation sharpened this contradiction: the Catholic Church listed procreation as the first reason for marriage, while Protestants stressed "mutual society, help and comfort", often putting it first, defining marriage as a reciprocal, fulfilling relationship; but they were unwilling to give up patriarchal authority, which was too important to the system. Sidney's description of an ideal couple in the *Arcadia* ends: "he ruling, because she would obey, or rather because she would obey, she therein ruling"; Burton's *Anatomy of Melancholy* says that the husband as head rules the wife, but the wife commands the husband's heart; the alternation of head and heart sounds reciprocal but is not, for we know that the head should rule the heart. In fact Protestantism strengthened patriarchal authority: with the mediating priest removed, the head of household became responsible for the spiritual life of the whole family, forming a double chain of authority from God to husband and from God to monarch; Henry Smith said that the master of a household has all the offices of Christ within the household. At one end, Smith argued that parents must control the choice of marriage partner (since they held the property); at the other, only radicals like the Digger Winstanley argued that everyone should be free to marry whom they loved; most commentators in between equivocated. The boundaries were evidently unclear, so conflict was likely, whence the clumsy bullying and cajoling in the marital disputes of Portia and Bassanio, Othello and Desdemona, Macbeth and Lady Macbeth and others. Lawrence Stone says that dutiful children experienced "an impossible conflict of role models". **On this point the dominant ideology had not yet got its act together.**

The ambiguity of official doctrine thus provided a definite point at which a woman like Desdemona could create a crisis in the story of patriarchy. Dympna Callaghan points out that despite the economic and social mechanisms reinforcing parental authority, parents were most often defied over marriage; such defiance often incurred physical and mental violence, and at least felt very unpleasant; that is what disturbing the system is like, and the tendency of ideology is precisely to produce good subjects who feel uncomfortable when they transgress. Desdemona was already exploiting this gap before she met Othello, rejecting "the wealthy curled darlings of our nation"; and her more extreme action, marrying without parental consent, outside the ruling oligarchy, outside her race, was so disruptive that the highest (male) council of state postponed its business, and this when the men were busy with a war. Of course, all Desdemona asks for is what Montrose calls "the limited privilege of giving herself", and once the men have accepted her marriage her moment of power is over; but opportunities for dissidence are always limited, otherwise we would not be living the way we do. Sinfield quotes **Stuart Hall** and others at the Birmingham Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies: the dominant culture of a complex society is never a homogeneous structure; it is layered, reflecting different interests within the dominant class (aristocratic and bourgeois outlooks, for instance), containing traces of the past (religious ideas within a largely secular culture, for instance) as well as emergent elements in the present; subordinate cultures are not always in open conflict with it; they may coexist with it for long periods, negotiating the spaces and gaps within it, eroding it from within. This account does not decide in advance whether dissidence will be contained; dissidence may not even be realised, only latent, becoming disruptive only at certain junctures. Emilia takes a notable step towards a dissident perception: she thinks wives' falls are their husbands' fault: they slack their duties, pour our treasures into foreign laps, break out in peevish jealousies, restrain us, even strike us. She has heard the doctrine of marriage as mutual fulfilment, and from the gap between doctrine and experience she is able to criticise the double standard. **At the fault-lines, dissident perspectives can be discovered and articulated.**

The crisis of marriage choice also shows how stories work in a culture. It recurs again and again: *A Midsummer Night's Dream*, *The Merchant of Venice*, *The Taming of the Shrew*, *Romeo and Juliet*, *Measure for Measure*, *King Lear*, *The Winter's Tale*, *The Tempest*; broadly speaking, in comedy the parents are finally reconciled to the children's wishes, while in tragedy hasty action without parental authorisation leads to disaster. The conflict between arranged marriage and love marriage remained a literary theme until the late nineteenth century, by which time, for most English people, the question had been settled in favour of the children's preference and so became uninteresting (though not for British families recently arrived from Asia). The other major point at which a woman might disturb the system is loving a man other than her husband, which is why adultery is so prominent in literature: it disrupts the husband's honour, his manhood and (through illegitimate children) his property; even the rumour of Desdemona's adultery is enough to plunge the powerful men of the state into another anxiety. **Fault-line stories are the ones that require the most assiduous and continuous reworking, because they address the awkward, unresolved issues where the conditions of plausibility are in dispute; the task of political criticism is to observe how stories negotiate the fault-lines that distress the prevailing conditions of plausibility.**

**Operations: reading dissidence.** Textual analysis finds it so easy to demonstrate that dissidence has been co-opted because dissidence necessarily operates with reference to dominant structures: it must invoke them in order to oppose them, and so can always be found to be reinscribing what it set out to criticise. Giddens says that power relations are always two-way: however subordinate an actor may be, the very fact of involvement in the relationship gives him some power over the other. The mutual involvement of resistance and control is systematic, arising from the way language and culture are organised: any discourse is defined by the other discourses that language makes possible, as in the duck-rabbit figure: when one sees the duck, the rabbit lurks at its edges, constituting an alternative that may suddenly leap into view. **All stories comprise within themselves the ghosts of the alternative stories they are trying to exclude.** But it does not follow that the outcome of mutual involvement is necessarily the co-optation of the subordinate. Foucault, though often treated as the theorist of containment, says in the first volume of *The History of Sexuality* that there is no single locus of great Refusal, but a plurality of resistances distributed with varying density in time and space, and denies that they are doomed to be only a passive rebound, a reaction destined to perpetual defeat. A dissident text may in fact derive leverage from its partial implication with the dominant: the legal, medical and sexological discourses on homosexuality in the nineteenth century made possible new forms of control, but also what Foucault calls a `reverse discourse`: homosexuality began to speak on its own behalf, often in the same vocabulary and categories by which it was medically disqualified, to demand recognition of its legitimacy or "naturality" (P13). The dominant discourse cannot prevent the "misuse" of its resources: even a text that tries to contain a subordinate perspective must first make it visible; even to distort it, it must first represent it. Readers need not respect the ending: they need not accept that the independent female characters of Shakespeare's comedies find their proper destiny in the marriage settlements at the end, but may insist that the expectations aroused in the middle of the play exceed the ending. Conversely, a text committed to dissidence cannot control meaning either; it cannot stop readers who want to draw reactionary inferences from doing so. When containment or resistance is more successful in a given case, this is not the nature of things but the relative strength of the two sides in that situation; so one cannot, like Jonathan Goldberg, turn the containment model upside down and say that dominant discourse allows itself to be subverted because hegemonic control is an impossible, self-deluding dream. The Essex rising failed because on that day he could not muster enough support; as Williams says, there is no way of teaching a man to read the Bible that does not also enable him to read the radical press. **Everything is still to play for.**

Sinfield therefore chooses `dissidence` rather than `subversion`: the latter seems to imply that something *has been* subverted, and since governments mostly have not fallen and patriarchy has not collapsed, it would follow that containment must have occurred; "dissidence" implies only a refusal of some aspect of the dominant, without prejudging the outcome. This looks like a weaker claim but is actually a stronger one, since it posits a necessarily continuing field of contest, in which at some junctures the dominant will lose ground and at others the subordinate will barely hold its position. As Dollimore says, the fact that dissidence may provoke brutal repression shows not that everything is a ruse by which power consolidates itself, but that the challenge *was* disturbing. Dollimore also says that nothing can be guaranteed to be subversive in advance of the event, independent of its articulation, context and reception; likewise, out of context, nothing can be said to be safely contained. **This prospect appals literary criticism, because it means that meaning cannot be adequately derived from the text on the page: the text is always a site of cultural contest, but never a self-sufficient site.** The containment model is "suspiciously convenient" for literary criticism, since it implies that little is to be gained by examining the specific historical effectivity of texts; Don Wayne shrewdly suggests that the success of prominent New Historicists may derive largely from their close-reading skills, though applied to a much wider range of texts, skills that fully satisfy the traditional performance criteria of academic criticism.

**Conclusion: the politics of plausibility.** Sinfield finally turns against criticism itself. Williams says that the real achievement of most serious novels and plays is the detailed and substantial *performance* of a "known pattern", "people like that, relationships like that"; *Othello* invites the audience to *recognise* that this is how people are, how the world is, so the criteria of plausibility are political, and literary quality does not cancel this effect: the more persuasively written, the greater the potential for political intervention. The essential activity of traditional criticism is interpretation, that is, helping the text to coherence: speculating about characters' motives, image patterns, thematic integration and structure, while finding coherence is taken to demonstrate quality (P2). But this practice can lead to reactionary politics: in Britain the easiest way to make *Othello* seem plausible is to rely on the racism, sexism and superstition latent in British culture. Why does the experienced Othello fall so easily for Iago's story? One can say black people are naturally simple. Why does Desdemona become so submissive after her elopement? One can appeal to the supposed fundamental foolishness and passivity of women. Unable to find a motive for Iago's malice, one resorts to the devil, to scepticism about traditional morality, or to homosexuality. These explanations may "work", but only because they activate regressive aspects of our cultural formation. **Coherence is an illusion: no story can contain all the possibilities it raises; coherence is always selection.** Literary criticism is itself a subculture, asserting its own distinctive criteria of plausibility; education takes as its mission the socialisation of students into these criteria, while disguising the project as the fair and true reading of fair and true texts by gifted individuals (P5's `interpretive community` acquires a political meaning here). Cultural materialist practice must therefore scrutinise the institutions that retell Shakespeare's stories, and remain self-aware about its own position within those institutions: **not only producing different readings, but changing the criteria of plausibility.**

*Compare the reading in "Shakespeare and the Exorcists" above: both start from how the theatre or the story is authorised by power, but Greenblatt sees in the theatre's "marginal and impure autonomy" a circuit of power and its critique, while Sinfield sees in the contradictions the social order cannot help producing a field of contest whose outcome is undecided; in Sinfield's framework Edmund belongs among the "scriptwriters from below", while in Greenblatt he is the spokesman of official scepticism.*

### A Family Quarrel: Three Disagreements Between the Two Historicisms

The name `cultural materialism` gained currency through the subtitle of *Political Shakespeare: New Essays in Cultural Materialism*, the 1985 collection edited by **Jonathan Dollimore** and **Alan Sinfield**. Graham Holderness calls it "a politicised form of historiography": the study of historical material (including literary texts) within a politicised framework, a framework that includes the present which those literary texts have in some way helped to shape. In their foreword the two editors say that the method combines four features: historical context, theoretical method, political commitment and textual analysis. The emphasis on historical context is meant to undermine the "transcendent" (roughly, "timeless") significance traditionally accorded to the literary text; the obvious objection is that since Shakespeare is still read today, his plays are indeed, in a simple sense, not confined by the circumstances of their production; but this is a matter of degree, and the aim is to allow the literary text to "recover its histories", such as enclosure and the oppression of the rural poor, state power and resistance to it, witchcraft, the challenge and containment of carnival. The emphasis on theoretical method means a break with liberal humanism and the absorption of structuralism, poststructuralism and other methods developed since the 1970s; the emphasis on political commitment means the influence of Marxism and feminism, and a break with the conservative-Christian framework that had previously dominated Shakespeare criticism; the emphasis on textual analysis places the critique of traditional approaches where it cannot be ignored, not merely building theory in the abstract but practising it on (mainly) canonical texts, since these remain the focus of vast scholarly and professional attention and are prominent national and cultural icons.

The two words of the name are each defined too. "Culture" includes all forms of culture (television, popular music, popular fiction) and is not confined to "high" forms such as Shakespeare's plays; "materialism" is the opposite of "idealism": idealism believes high culture to be the free and independent play of gifted individual minds, whereas materialism believes that culture cannot transcend the material forces and relations of production; culture is not merely a reflection of the economic and political system, but neither can it be independent of it (P9's `relative autonomy`). **Distinction:** These statements represent the standard beliefs of Marxist criticism, and Barry therefore points out that they may pinpoint exactly the difficulty of making a useful distinction between "pure" Marxist criticism and cultural materialism. The difference lies in an addition: the relevant history is not only that of four hundred years ago but that of every age in which Shakespeare has been produced and reproduced, including our own. Cultural materialism therefore pays special attention to the institutions that bring Shakespeare to us today: the Royal Shakespeare Company, the film industry, the publishers of school texts, and the National Curriculum, which requires all pupils to study particular Shakespeare plays. Much British work of this kind sets out to undermine Shakespeare's fetishised role as a conservative icon in British culture; in 1988 a correspondence in the *London Review of Books*, started by a review, ran for more than a year under the heading "Bardolatry".

**Distinction: three disagreements.** The two historicisms belong to the same family, but there is a continuing quarrel within it; *Political Shakespeare* itself includes New Historicist essays, and its introduction explains the differences between the two. First, Dollimore and Sinfield quote Marx: men make their own history, but not in conditions of their own choosing (P9). Cultural materialists tend to concentrate on the interventions by which people make their own history, while New Historicists tend to concentrate on the unpropitious conditions in which they do so, that is, on the power of the social and ideological structures that restrain them: **the result is a contrast between political optimism and political pessimism.** Second, cultural materialists think that New Historicists have accepted some version of poststructuralism and its radical scepticism about the possibility of reliable knowledge, and so cut themselves off from an effective political position. New Historicism's defence is that awareness of the uncertainty inherent in all knowledge does not mean giving up establishing truth, only doing so with awareness of the dangers and limits, which in fact gives its inquiries a special authority, like sailing into waters known to be dangerous having taken every sensible precaution, rather than sailing in unaware with all lights blazing. So when New Historicists claim (in Peter Widdowson's words) that Foucault gave them a "non-truth-oriented" historicist study of texts, this does not mean that they do not believe what they say to be true, but that they know the risks involved in claiming to establish truth. Third, New Historicism's co-texts are documents contemporary with Shakespeare; cultural materialism's co-texts might be the programme for a current Royal Shakespeare Company production, a pilot's quotation from Shakespeare during the Gulf War (1990–91) (P8), or a government minister's speech on education. In other words, **New Historicism places the literary text in the political situation of its own time, cultural materialism in the political situation of ours**; this is really a restatement of the difference in political emphasis between the two, and the common denominator of all three disagreements is this political difference.

The differences come partly from different intellectual frameworks. New Historicism is deeply influenced by Foucault, who held that discursive practices often reinforce the dominant ideology; cultural materialism is deeply influenced by Williams, who held that structures of feeling contain the seeds of resistance to the dominant ideology. Someone sceptical of both said that New Historicists would have difficulty explaining how the English Civil War ever started (since they seem to imagine a pervasive state power that makes resistance almost impossible), and cultural materialists would have difficulty explaining how it ever ended (since their structures of feeling keep producing new ideas and seem to make stasis impossible). **Objection:** Barry does not wholly accept this sharp dichotomy: in practice the much-mentioned political differences are far less neat and predictable than such oppositions suggest. Are the two merely two national variants of the same thing, or are there deep differences (as British cultural materialists in particular insist)? Barry thinks the question can be answered only by reading and comparing essays of both kinds; in his summary, the differences lie mainly in two respects: political stance, and the degree of emphasis on the poststructuralist perspective. *The anthology's editors' account stresses instead the polemical relation between the two: in their telling, cultural materialism's "fragility of power" thesis is a criticism of New Historicism, and "Invisible Bullets" is Greenblatt's response to that criticism. One account stresses differences of degree within one family, the other the clash of two positions; the two accounts stand side by side.*

**Example: Hawkes's "Telmah".** An informal variant of cultural materialism can be illustrated by **Terence Hawkes**'s "Telmah" (in *That Shakespeherian Rag*, whose title alludes to Eliot's *The Waste Land*). Each essay in the collection centres on an important Shakespeare critic of the early twentieth century, the overall strategy being to examine how Shakespeare is mediated and processed before being handed to us; this essay's subject is **John Dover Wilson**, famous for *What Happens in "Hamlet"* in the 1930s. The essay begins by discussing elements of circularity and symmetry in *Hamlet*: the beginning echoes the end, the same situation recurs several times (several fathers, for instance). *The title "Telmah" is "Hamlet" spelled backwards.* The second section is called "To the Sunderland Station", alluding to a famous history of the Russian Revolution, *To the Finland Station*: in 1917 Dover Wilson, sent by the government to sort out labour problems at a munitions factory, read on the train to Sunderland an article on *Hamlet* by W. W. Greg, who argued that the King's failure to react openly to the dumb show shows him to be a complex character rather than a storybook villain. If so, the King begins to attract our attention, drawing us away from the traditional response (at least since the Romantics) of concentrating on Hamlet himself. Hawkes connects Wilson's indignation at this idea with the passionate longing for order shown in his writing on Russia: he saw Russia as a picturesque "organic" feudal state, apparently a replica of the England his class longed for and feared to lose; his eagerness, in his reply to Greg and his later book, to defend the threatened cultural icon Hamlet is a symptom of the same thing. Soon after the First World War, Wilson became a member of the Newbolt Committee, whose report on the teaching of English saw English as a form of social cohesion that might save the country from Russia's fate (P1). Hawkes also quotes a letter from **Neville Chamberlain** praising *What Happens in "Hamlet"*, thereby building a pattern of appeasement and the containment of difference. A way of interpreting the play is thus placed among several co-texts of twentieth-century life, and the play itself is culturally transformed along with it. Hawkes's final reading of the end of the play is to insert an extra stage direction, and the model he chooses for this kind of criticism is the jazz musician, who does not transmit a received text but *trans*forms it in *per*forming it. Writing of this kind is vivid, personal and committed, dispensing with most of the formal conventions of academic writing: a dramatic opening, abrupt transitions, key details withheld until the moment of greatest impact, a structure of seemingly unrelated incidents that finally interlock tightly; these are features of the novel, clearly rejecting any absolute distinction between literature and criticism. As in New Historicism, literature and history are interwoven here, but the perspective and the manner of historicising belong far more to our own time.

**Operations:** The work of cultural materialist critics can be summed up as follows. They read the literary text (often a Renaissance play) so that it can "recover its histories", that is, the context of exploitation from which it emerged; at the same time they foreground those elements in the work's present-day transmission and contextualisation that caused those histories to be lost in the first place, such as the "heritage" industry's packaging of Shakespeare as pageant-like history, national poet and cultural icon. To accomplish the first task, and to break the dominance of conservative social, political and religious assumptions in Shakespeare criticism, they combine Marxist and feminist approaches; they use close-reading techniques, but often borrow those of structuralism and poststructuralism to mark a break with the tradition of close reading conducted within a framework of conservative cultural and social assumptions; and they work mainly within the traditional idea of the canon, on the grounds that studying more obscure texts rarely constitutes an effective political intervention (in debates about the school curriculum or national identity, for instance).

**Limitation:** The price each historicism pays is now visible. New Historicism's price is political pessimism (the containment model makes subversion seem merely a ruse of power) and selectivity with non-literary texts: a single document often becomes the sole witness to a change of attitude, bearing too much interpretive weight, and contextualisation is deliberately compressed, which makes its method little valued by historians; Sinfield and Don Wayne go further and point out that the containment model is "suspiciously convenient" for literary criticism, its success owing much to close-reading skills that satisfy traditional academic performance criteria. Cultural materialism's price is that it demands knowledge literary criticism scarcely possesses or even knows how to acquire (the knowledge of history and the other social sciences), together with historiographical and epistemological questions more complex than the neat poststructuralist formula "everything is, after all, text (or everything is theatre)"; Sinfield thinks the value of this prospect is in direct proportion to its difficulty, since, as Foucault says, disciplinary boundaries themselves police discourse. Add what Barry describes as the difficulty of distinguishing it from "pure" Marxist criticism, and this is its theoretical price.

**Conclusion:** **History has re-entered literary study in two ways: New Historicism reads history as a network of discourses of the same nature as literature, finding in it the circuit by which power completes itself through representation, theatre and discipline; cultural materialism reads history as a continuing contest, looking within texts for the fault-lines the social order cannot help producing, and bringing into its analysis the institutions that retell Shakespeare today.** Both share the dissolution of the text/context boundary brought by Foucault and poststructuralism (the fifth mechanism), while their disagreement centres on the fourth mechanism, "domination ↔ resistance": is dissidence contained in advance, or is everything still to play for?

This dispute is not confined to Renaissance drama. Dollimore and Sinfield had already extended "culture" to television, popular music and popular fiction; and in illustrating the layered character of the dominant culture, Sinfield quotes precisely Stuart Hall and others at the Birmingham Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies. When the object of analysis shifts from Shakespeare to punk, television and everyday consumption, the same question returns in sharper form: **is mass culture an instrument of domination or a site of resistance?** This is the theme of P11.

## P11 Is Mass Culture an Instrument of Domination or a Site of Resistance? Cultural Studies

P10 ended with an extension: when the object of analysis shifts from Shakespeare to punk, television and everyday consumption, what becomes of the question whether dissidence is contained? Cultural studies answers it. In the six-layer framework this is the third and last part of Layer 4, text and power, whose chain runs: culture industry ↔ resistance. It inherits four things. First, the Marxism of P9: commodity fetishism and reification become the "culture industry" in the Frankfurt School, and Gramsci's hegemony and Althusser's interpellation are applied by Fiske to television news. Second, the British tradition of P10: the editors regard Williams and Thompson as founders of cultural studies, the Stuart Hall whom Sinfield quotes is the leader of the Birmingham School, and Foucault's Panopticon will be placed by de Certeau on the side of "strategy". Third, the semiotics of P3: Saussure's signifier and signified, Lévi-Strauss's bricolage and homology and Barthes's analysis of myth are the tools with which Hebdige reads punk and Fiske reads television codes. Fourth, the readers of P5: Austin's speech acts, Fish's interpretive communities and Bourdieu's distinction become here the study of audiences and users.

The fifth mechanism, the `shifting boundary between text and context`, reaches its limit here: "culture" no longer means art, literature and classical music but forms of life in the anthropological sense, and the object of literary study expands to film, television, advertising, clothing, dance and shopping. The fourth mechanism, `domination ↔ resistance`, appears in its most direct form: the editors state at the outset that since the advent of Marxism culture has been seen as political, *both* a means of domination, securing the rule of one class or group over another, *and* a means of resisting that domination, expressing views opposed to those of the dominant. The argument begins with the two poles within the Frankfurt School, Benjamin's mechanical reproduction and Horkheimer and Adorno's culture industry; moves to the Birmingham School's semiotic reading of punk style, de Certeau's tactical analysis of everyday use and Fiske's double study of television codes and their reading; and ends with the "two incommensurable perspectives" proposed by the editors.

### The Withering of the Aura and Mechanical Reproduction

**Background: the new sense of "culture" and the Frankfurt School.** The word "culture" acquired a new meaning in the 1960s and 1970s. Before then culture was associated with art, literature and classical music, and to be "cultured" was to have a certain taste for particular kinds of artistic endeavour; anthropologists, however, had always used the word in a much broader sense, for forms of life and social expression: the ways people eat, talk, form sexual partnerships, interact at work, attend family gatherings and other ritualised social behaviour. This broad definition includes language and the arts, but also the regularities, procedures and rituals of human life in a community. The Frankfurt School was one of the earliest attempts to politicise culture: founded in 1923 as an Institute for Social Research attached to the University of Frankfurt, it practised a criticism that tried to combine Freud and Marx and drew on certain aspects of Formalism; its best-known figures are **Walter Benjamin**, who committed suicide in 1940 while fleeing the Nazis, Herbert Marcuse, a major source of 1960s radical thought, and Adorno (Brecht in P9 belongs to the same lineage of exiles).

**Definition: aura.** Benjamin's "The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction" (1935) argues for a connection between changes in cultural technology (the development of film and photography) and changes in consciousness. The work of art has in principle always been reproducible; woodcut, etching and lithography appeared in turn, lithography foreshadowing the illustrated newspaper and photography the sound film; by around 1900 technical reproduction could not only reproduce all transmitted works of art, profoundly changing their impact on the public, but had won a place of its own among artistic processes. Yet even the most perfect reproduction lacks one element: **its presence in time and space, its unique existence at the place where it happens to be.** This unique existence determines the history to which the work has been subject: changes in its physical condition and in its ownership. The presence of the original is the prerequisite of the concept of `authenticity`; confronted with manual reproduction (usually branded as forgery), the original preserves all its authority, but not so with technical reproduction. There are two reasons: technical reproduction is more independent of the original than manual reproduction (the lens can bring out aspects inaccessible to the naked eye, enlargement and slow motion can capture images that escape natural vision); and technical reproduction can put the copy of the original into situations out of reach of the original itself (the cathedral leaves its site to be received in the studio of a lover of art, the choral work is heard in a drawing room). The authenticity of a work is the essence of all that is transmissible from its beginning, from its substantive duration to its testimony to the history it has experienced; when substantive duration ceases to matter, historical testimony is jeopardised too, and what is really jeopardised is the *authority* of the object. Benjamin calls the eliminated element the `aura`: **"that which withers in the age of mechanical reproduction is the aura of the work of art."** In a note he defines the aura as "the unique phenomenon of a distance, however close it may be", which is nothing but a formulation of the work's `cult value` in terms of the categories of spatial and temporal perception: the essentially distant object is unapproachable, and unapproachability is the chief quality of the cult image.

**Mechanism: from ritual to politics.** The technique of reproduction detaches the reproduced object from the domain of tradition: by making many reproductions it substitutes a plurality of copies for a unique existence, and by permitting the reproduction to meet the beholder or listener in his own particular situation it reactivates the object reproduced. These two processes lead to a tremendous shattering of tradition and are intimately connected with contemporary mass movements; their most powerful agent is film, whose social significance is inconceivable without its destructive, cathartic aspect: the liquidation of the traditional value of the cultural heritage. The uniqueness of a work of art is inseparable from its being embedded in tradition: an ancient statue of Venus stood in one traditional context with the Greeks, who made it an object of veneration, and in another with the clerics of the Middle Ages, who saw it as an ominous idol; but both were equally confronted with its uniqueness, that is, its aura. The earliest works of art originated in ritual, first magical, then religious; the auratic mode of existence of the work is never entirely separated from its ritual function, which remains recognisable even in the secular cult of beauty since the Renaissance. With the advent of the first truly revolutionary means of reproduction, photography, simultaneously with the rise of socialism, art sensed the approaching crisis and reacted with the doctrine of *l'art pour l'art*, a theology of art, which gave rise to the negative theology of "pure" art, denying not only any social function of art but also any categorising by subject matter (in poetry Mallarmé was the first to take this position). *(This is a historicist explanation of the idea of "artistic autonomy" in the liberal humanism and formalism described in P1 and P2.)* **"For the first time in world history, mechanical reproduction emancipates the work of art from its parasitical dependence on ritual."** The work of art reproduced becomes more and more the work of art designed for reproducibility: from a photographic negative any number of prints can be made, and to ask for the "authentic" print makes no sense; and once the criterion of authenticity ceases to apply to artistic production, the whole function of art is reversed: instead of being based on ritual, it begins to be based on another practice, *politics*. Cult value and `exhibition value` are the two poles of the work: a bust is easier to exhibit than the statue of a divinity fixed inside a temple, a panel painting easier than a mosaic or fresco; with the various methods of technical reproduction, the quantitative shift in exhibitability turns into a qualitative change in its nature: just as prehistoric art, through the absolute emphasis on its cult value, was first of all an instrument of magic and only later recognised as art, so today the work of art, through the absolute emphasis on its exhibition value, becomes a creation with entirely new functions, among which the one we are conscious of, the artistic function, may later be recognised as incidental.

**Reading: film and the masses.** Mechanical reproduction changes the reaction of the masses to art: the reactionary attitude towards a Picasso painting changes into a progressive reaction towards a Chaplin film. The progressive reaction is characterised by the direct, intimate fusion of visual and emotional enjoyment with the orientation of the expert; before the screen, the critical and the receptive attitudes of the public coincide, because individual reactions are predetermined by the mass audience response they are about to produce. Painting cannot present an object for simultaneous collective experience, as architecture, the epic and today the film can; so the same public that reacts progressively to a grotesque film reacts reactionarily to surrealism. Film also enriches our field of perception with methods that can be illustrated by Freudian theory: *The Psychopathology of Everyday Life* made slips of the tongue analysable (P6), and film, with its close-ups, its focus on hidden details of familiar objects, its exploration of commonplace milieux under the guidance of the camera, has brought about a similar deepening of perception across the whole visual and acoustic world. Our taverns and metropolitan streets, our offices and furnished rooms, our railway stations and factories appeared to have locked us up hopelessly; **then came the film and burst this prison-world asunder by the dynamite of the tenth of a second**, so that now, in the midst of its far-flung ruins and debris, we calmly and adventurously go travelling. The close-up expands space, slow motion extends movement; a different nature opens itself to the camera than opens to the naked eye: a space informed by the unconscious takes the place of a space consciously explored by man. **"The camera introduces us to unconscious optics as does psychoanalysis to unconscious impulses."**

**Conclusion: the aestheticisation of politics and the politicisation of art.** The growing proletarianisation of modern man and the increasing formation of masses are two aspects of the same process. Fascism attempts to organise the newly created proletarian masses without affecting the property structure the masses strive to eliminate: it gives the masses not their right but a chance to express themselves. The logical result of Fascism is the introduction of aesthetics into political life, and all efforts to render politics aesthetic culminate in one thing: war; only war can set a goal for mass movements on the largest scale while respecting the traditional property system, and only war makes it possible to mobilise all of today's technical resources while maintaining the property system. The Futurist Marinetti, in his manifesto on the Ethiopian colonial war, declared war beautiful because it enriches a flowering meadow with the fiery orchids of machine guns, and combines gunfire, cannonades, ceasefires, scents and the stench of putrefaction into a symphony.
