Benjamin's analysis is that if the property system hinders the natural utilisation of productive forces, the increase in technical means, in tempo and in sources of energy will press for an unnatural utilisation, and this is found in war; imperialist war is a rebellion of technology: instead of draining rivers, society directs a human stream into the bed of trenches; instead of dropping seeds from aeroplanes, it drops incendiary bombs over cities; and through gas warfare the aura is abolished in a new way. Fascism says *Fiat ars—pereat mundus*, "let art be created, though the world perish", which is evidently the consummation of *l'art pour l'art*. Mankind, which in Homer's time was an object of contemplation for the Olympian gods, now is one for itself; **"Its self-alienation has reached such a degree that it can experience its own destruction as an aesthetic pleasure of the first order. This is the situation of politics which Fascism is rendering aesthetic. Communism responds by politicizing art."** *(This ending makes Benjamin's opposition clear: the withering of the aura is both an opportunity for liberation and a site where Fascism manufactures "ritual value" anew; the same technology points towards two opposite politics. Compared with P8, what Baudrillard saw in the reporting of the Gulf War is another consummated form of what Benjamin feared.)*

### The Culture Industry as Mass Deception

**Background:** The wartime exile of European intellectuals brought **Max Horkheimer** and **Theodor Adorno**, who had worked together at the Institute for Social Research in Frankfurt before the war, to Los Angeles. In *Dialectic of Enlightenment* (1944) they examined American popular culture and reached highly pessimistic conclusions: it consists of routinised forms, diminishes the complexity of human experience and serves the interests of powerful corporations. The editors' summary: mass culture (the culture of television, radio, film and cheap paperbacks) is an instrument of domination, the way capitalism offers brief satisfactions to people condemned to a lifetime of toil.

**Mechanism: sameness.** One sociological theory holds that the loss of the support of objectively established religion, the dissolution of the last remnants of pre-capitalism, and technological and social differentiation and specialisation have led to cultural chaos; this theory is disproved every day, **for culture now impresses the same stamp on everything**. Film, radio and magazines make up a system that is uniform as a whole and in every part; under monopoly capitalism all mass culture is identical. Those interested explain the `culture industry` in technological terms: since millions participate in it, certain reproduction processes are necessary, and these inevitably require identical needs in innumerable places to be satisfied with identical goods; the technical contrast between few production centres and widely dispersed consumption points demands organisation and planning by management; standards were based in the first place on consumers' needs, which is why they met with so little resistance. The result is a circle of manipulation and retroactive need in which the unity of the system grows ever stronger. But no mention is made of the fact that the basis on which technology acquires power over society is the power of those whose economic hold over society is greatest. **"A technological rationale is the rationale of domination itself."** Any trace of spontaneity in the public is controlled and absorbed by talent scouts, studio competitions and official programmes of every kind; the public does seem to prefer the culture industry's system, but this attitude is part of the system, not an excuse for it. When a movement from a Beethoven symphony is crudely "adapted" for a film soundtrack, or a Tolstoy novel garbled in a film script, to say this is done to satisfy the public's spontaneous wishes is empty talk. The culture monopolies are weak and dependent in comparison with the most powerful sectors of industry, steel, petroleum, electricity and chemicals: the most powerful broadcasting company depends on the electrical industry, the film industry on the banks. Marked differentiations, such as those of A and B films or of stories in magazines at different prices, depend not so much on subject matter as on classifying, organising and labelling consumers: **"Something is provided for all so that none may escape."** Everybody must behave (as if spontaneously) in accordance with his previously determined and indexed level, and choose the category of mass product turned out for his type; consumers appear on the charts of research organisations as statistics, divided by income groups into red, green and blue areas. The differences between Chrysler and General Motors products are basically illusory, and so are those between Warner Brothers and Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer productions.

Hit songs, stars and soap operas are cyclically recurrent and rigidly invariable types; the specific content of the entertainment is derived from them and only appears to change; the details are interchangeable, ready-made clichés to be slotted in anywhere. **"As soon as the film begins, it is quite clear how it will end, and who will be rewarded, punished, or forgotten."** The development of the culture industry has led to the predominance of the effect, the obvious touch and the technical detail over the work itself. The detail had once won its freedom, becoming, from Romanticism to Expressionism, a vehicle of protest against organisation: in music the single harmonic effect obliterated the awareness of form as a whole, in painting the individual colour was stressed at the expense of composition, in the novel psychology became more important than structure; the totality of the culture industry put an end to this, crushing the insubordination of the detail and subordinating it to the *formula* that has replaced the work. Whole and parts alike suffer this fate: there is no antithesis and no connection; their prearranged harmony is a mockery of what the great bourgeois work of art strove for. The stunting of the mass-media consumer's powers of imagination and spontaneity need not be traced back to any psychological mechanism; it must be ascribed to the objective nature of the products themselves, especially the most characteristic, the sound film: understanding them requires quickness, observation and experience, yet sustained thought is out of the question if the spectator is not to miss the relentless rush of facts; all the entertainment products the spectators have seen have taught them what to expect, and they react automatically. **"The might of industrial society is lodged in men's minds."** Leisure resembles work; every sound film and every broadcast is a model of the huge economic machinery that sustains the masses, and the culture industry moulds people into the type unfailingly reproduced in every product. *(Compared with P8: Baudrillard's theory of simulacra can be seen as the version of the culture-industry thesis that comes after the complete semiotisation of the commodity, but it gives up the critical standpoint Adorno still insisted on.)*

**Mechanism: the secret of style.** Horkheimer and Adorno do not, for all this, mourn the "authentic style" of the past. In the culture industry one can see that the idea of a genuine style is the aesthetic equivalent of domination: the stylistic unity of the Middle Ages and the Renaissance expressed the different structures of social power, not the obscure experience of the oppressed. The great artists were never those who embodied a wholly flawless and perfect style, but those who used style as a way of hardening themselves against the chaotic expression of suffering, as a *negative truth*; up to Schoenberg and Picasso, the great artists retained a mistrust of style. Style in every work of art represents a promise: what is expressed is subsumed through style into the dominant forms of generality (the language of music, painting or words) in the hope of reconciliation with the idea of true generality. This promise is both necessary and hypocritical: it implies that fulfilment lies in the aesthetic derivative, and so posits the existing forms of life unconditionally; **in this sense the claim of art is always ideology too.** Yet only in confrontation with tradition, of which style is the record, can art express suffering. That factor in a work of art which enables it to transcend reality lies not in achieved harmony, in the doubtful unity of form and content, individual and society, but in those features in which discrepancy appears: **"in the necessary failure of the passionate striving for identity."** The style of the great work achieves self-negation in this failure, while the inferior work relies on its similarity with others, on a surrogate identity. In the culture industry this imitation becomes absolute; having ceased to be anything but style, it reveals style's secret: **obedience to the social hierarchy.** "To speak of culture was always contrary to culture": culture as a common denominator already contains in embryo that schematisation, cataloguing and classification which bring culture within the sphere of administration; industrialised subsumption subordinates every branch of intellectual creation in the same way and for the same end, occupying people's senses from the time they leave the factory in the evening to the time they clock in again the next morning with matter bearing the impress of the labour process they themselves have to sustain throughout the day.

**Distinction: Benjamin and Adorno.** Though both belong to the Frankfurt School, their judgements of the same technical change are almost opposite. Benjamin sees in mechanical reproduction the disintegration of the aura and the liberation of art from ritual, in the masses' progressive reaction to Chaplin a fusion of criticism and enjoyment, in the close-ups and slow motion of film a deepening of perception; Horkheimer and Adorno see in the same technology standardisation and mass production, the stunting of imagination and automatic reaction, the sound film being exactly their most typical example. *Benjamin was not blind to the danger: his analysis of Fascism's "aestheticisation of politics" is precisely a warning about the same technology being used for mass mobilisation. Their disagreement therefore lies not in whether they see domination, but in whether they believe that the relation between this technology and the masses is still a site of contest; this is the earliest form of what the editors call the "two incommensurable perspectives".* The relation to P9 is also clear: the culture-industry thesis is the extension of `commodity fetishism` into the cultural realm, the most pessimistic form of the concepts of "reification" and "ideology".

**Limitation:** *The culture-industry thesis is often charged with looking down on mass culture from the standard of high modernist art (Schoenberg, Picasso). The Birmingham School, de Certeau and Fiske, who follow, all in fact answer it from the opposite direction: they do not deny that the culture industry exists, but refuse to see consumers as passive "types" wholly moulded by it.*

### The Birmingham School: Style, Bricolage and Homology

**Background: Britain's other concept of culture.** In the 1960s a concept of culture quite different from the Frankfurt School's emerged in Britain, and it later became the basis of the new discipline called "cultural studies". Richard Hoggart, Williams and Thompson (P10) saw culture as a means of resisting capitalism: if illiteracy kept the poor and the labouring from the intellectual tools that might prompt them to rebel, then literacy, in the form of clandestine pamphlets and underground newspapers, was a way of sustaining alternative perspectives outside the progress of industrial capitalism and its demand that the population be absorbed into factory labour. In the United States cultural studies was carried on mainly in departments of anthropology and communications and took rather empiricist forms such as audience surveys; in Britain, in the late 1960s and the 1970s, a distinctive convergence of disciplines and intellectual currents occurred at the University of Birmingham's `Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies`. Under the leadership of **Stuart Hall**, researchers at the Centre wove together sociology, Marxist political theory and structuralist semiotics to analyse how the media portray the world in ways favourable to those in power, thereby "policing" economic crisis, or how working-class youth resist their assigned social roles through rituals of clothing, dance and music that provide a counterpoint to the work routines of modern economic life. *(Hall has already appeared in P10 as Sinfield's authority: the dominant culture is layered, and subordinate cultures can coexist with it for long periods, negotiating its gaps and eroding it from within.)* One of the Centre's best-known products is **Dick Hebdige**'s *Subculture: The Meaning of Style* (1979), which examines the resistance in punk's styles of clothing and music, seeing punk as a resistant making of meaning, an anti-bourgeois style resembling in some respects the earlier literary avant-garde.

**Definition: style as refusal.** Hebdige opens with Genet's *The Thief's Journal*: in a search, the Spanish police confiscated a tube of vaseline from Genet, and this "dirty, wretched object" proclaimed his homosexuality to the world, provoking laughter and hostile insinuations at the police station; but later, in his cell, Genet was sure that this paltry object would stand up to them, its mere existence enough to exasperate all the police in the world; he would rather have shed blood than repudiate that silly object. Genet explored the subversive implications of style in life and art more deeply than anyone: the status and meaning of revolt, style as a form of `Refusal`, the elevation of crime into art (in subcultures "crime" is only a broken code). The study of subcultures is concerned with the expressive forms and rituals of subordinate groups (Teddy boys, mods and rockers, skinheads and punks), who are alternately dismissed as a threat to public order and treated as harmless buffoons; with how the most mundane objects (a safety pin, a pointed shoe, a motorcycle), like the tube of vaseline, take on a symbolic dimension, becoming a form of stigmata, tokens of self-imposed exile. These styles have a double meaning: on the one hand they warn the "straight" world in advance of a sinister presence, the presence of *difference*, drawing vague suspicion and uneasy laughter; on the other, for those who erect them into icons and use them as words or curses, they become signs of forbidden identity, sources of value. **The meaning of subculture is thus always in dispute, and style is the area in which opposing definitions clash with the most dramatic force.** The process begins with a small "crime" against the natural order (growing a quiff, buying a scooter or a record or a certain kind of suit) and ends in the construction of a style, a gesture of defiance, a smile or a sneer. Hebdige hopes that the refusal is worth making, that these gestures have subversive value, even if in the end they are no more than the darker side of sets of regulations, graffiti on a prison wall; and graffiti express both impotence and a kind of power: the power to disfigure.

**Example: punk style.** Punk style is sometimes directly offensive (T-shirts covered in swear words), sometimes threatening (terrorist/guerrilla outfits), but it is above all defined by the violence of its "cut ups". Like Duchamp's "ready-mades", manufactured objects that qualified as art because he chose to call them such, the most unremarkable and inappropriate items (a pin, a plastic clothes peg, a television component, a razor blade, a tampon) could be brought within the province of punk (anti-)fashion; anything could become part of what Vivienne Westwood called "confrontation dressing", so long as the rupture between "natural" and constructed context was clearly visible. Lavatory chains were draped in graceful arcs across chests encased in plastic bin-liners; safety pins were taken out of their domestic "utility" context and worn as gruesome ornaments through the cheek, ear or lip; "cheap" trashy fabrics (PVC, plastic, lurex, imitation leopard skin) long since consigned to the dustbin by the high end of the fashion industry were salvaged by punks and turned into garments offering self-conscious commentaries on notions of modernity and taste. Conventional ideas of prettiness were jettisoned along with the traditional feminine lore of cosmetics: contrary to the advice of every women's magazine, make-up for boys and girls alike was worn to be seen; faces became abstract portraits, studies in alienation; hair was obviously dyed, and T-shirts and trousers told the story of their own construction with visible zips and seams; fragments of school uniform were symbolically defiled (shirts covered in graffiti or fake blood, ties left undone). Perversion and abnormality were valued intrinsically, and the illicit iconography of sexual fetishism (rubberwear, leather bodices, fishnet stockings, the straps and chains of bondage) was exhumed from the boudoir, the wardrobe and the pornographic film and placed on the street, where it retained its forbidden connotations; some young punks even wore the dirty raincoat, the most prosaic symbol of sexual "kinkiness", expressing deviance in suitably proletarian terms. *(The rupture between "natural" and constructed context is exactly a subcultural version of the defamiliarisation of Russian Formalism in P2.)*

Punk did more than upset the wardrobe; it undermined every relevant discourse. Dancing, usually an involved and expressive medium in British rock and mainstream pop culture, was turned into a blank, robotic mime: overt heterosexual interest was generally scorned, and the traditional courtship patterns had no place in the pogo, the pose and the robot; the pogo was a caricature, a reductio ad absurdum of all the solo dance styles associated with rock music, repeating the same abbreviated movements in time to the strictly mechanical rhythms of the music, so that improvisation became redundant. The music likewise differed from mainstream rock and pop: whether deliberately or through lack of skill, it was uniformly basic and direct (Johnny Rotten declared that they meant to be amateurs; "we're into chaos, not music"). The names of the bands (the Unwanted, the Rejects, the Sex Pistols, the Clash, the Worst) and the titles of songs reflected the deliberate profanity and voluntary assumption of outcast status characteristic of the whole punk movement. In performance, punk bands tried to come closer to their audiences physically, lyrically and in lifestyle; the line between artist and audience has often been a metaphor in revolutionary aesthetics (Brecht, the Surrealists, Dada, Marcuse) for the wider barrier that under capitalism separates art and dream from real life, and examples of ordinary fans stepping from the dance floor onto the stage abounded. Above all, this was the first predominantly working-class youth culture to try to provide, within the subculture, an alternative critical space to counter the hostile, or at least ideologically inflected, coverage punk received in the media: fanzines such as *Sniffin' Glue* were printed, stapled and distributed as cheaply as possible, full of swear words, with typing errors, grammatical mistakes and jumbled pagination left uncorrected, giving an urgency like that of a memo from the front line; one of the most inspired pieces of propaganda was a diagram of three finger positions on a guitar fretboard, captioned to the effect that here is one chord, here are two more, now form your own band: the definitive statement of punk's "do-it-yourself" philosophy. The typography of record sleeves and fanzines was homologous with punk's underground anarchic style: either the graffiti-like scrawl of the spray can or the ransom note made of single letters cut out of various newspapers and magazines; the sleeve of the Sex Pistols' "God Save the Queen" used both, roughly assembled lettering stuck over the queen's eyes and mouth. Finally, this ironic self-abasement extended even to the name "punk" itself, with its pejorative connotations of "petty vice", "rotten" and "worthless", which hard-core members preferred to the neutral "new wave".

**Mechanism: homology.** The punk subculture signified chaos at every level, but this was possible only because the style itself was so thoroughly ordered: the chaos cohered as a meaningful whole. Hebdige resolves the paradox with another concept from Lévi-Strauss: `homology`. Paul Willis first applied the term to subcultures in his studies of hippies and motor-bike boys, using it to describe the symbolic fit between the values and lifestyle of a group, its subjective experience and the musical forms it uses to express or reinforce its focal concerns: contrary to the popular myth that presents subcultures as lawless, the internal structure of any subculture is characterised by extreme orderliness, each part organically related to the others, and it is through the fit between them that members make sense of the world; the homology between an alternative value system ("tune in, turn on, drop out"), hallucinogenic drugs and acid rock made hippie culture cohere for the individual hippie as a "whole way of life". *Resistance Through Rituals*, by Hall and others, crossed homology with `bricolage` (Lévi-Strauss's term in P3) to answer the question of what a subcultural style means to the members of the subculture themselves: the objects appropriated and reassembled in distinctive subcultural combinations were used to "reflect, express and resonate … aspects of group life", homologous with the subculture's focal concerns, activities, group structure and collective self-image. The skinheads are an example: boots, braces and cropped hair were considered appropriate, and therefore meaningful, because they communicated the desired qualities of "hardness, masculinity and working-classness".

Punk seems to bear out this thesis entirely: there is a homological relation between the trashy cut-up clothes and spiky hair, the pogo and amphetamines, the spitting, the vomiting, the format of the fanzines, the insurrectionary poses and the "soulless", frantic music; punk clothes were the sartorial equivalent of swear words, and punks swore as they dressed, with calculated effect; they made "noise" in the calmly orchestrated "crisis" of everyday life in the late 1970s, a noise that made (non)sense in exactly the same way and to exactly the same extent as a piece of avant-garde music. Poly Styrene's famous "Oh Bondage, Up Yours!" could serve as punk's epitaph: the forbidden was permitted, but by the same token nothing, not even these forbidden signifiers (bondage, safety pins, chains, hair dye), was sacred and fixed. **This absence of a permanently sacred signifier poses a problem for the semiotician: how can one discern any positive values in objects chosen only to be discarded?** One could say that early punk outfits pointed to signifieds such as "modernity" and "working-classness": safety pins and bin-liners signified a relative material poverty, standing in turn for the spiritual paucity of everyday life, what Paul Piccone calls the shift from "empty stomachs" to "empty spirits"; even if the poverty was parodied, the unacceptable, disfigured face of capitalism lurked beneath the clown make-up. But to go further, and call punk music "the sound of the Westway" or the pogo "the high-rise leap", or to say that bondage reflected the narrow options of working-class youth, would be both too literal and too speculative: these are extrapolations from the subculture's own copious rhetoric, and rhetoric is not self-explanatory; it may say what it means, but it does not necessarily "mean" what it "says".

**Reading: the emptiness of the swastika.** The swastika shows the difficulty most clearly. The symbol reached the punks through the "Berlin" phase of Bowie and Lou Reed, reflecting their interest in a decadent, evil, "no future" Germany; conventionally, for the British, the swastika signified "the enemy". Yet punks in general did not sympathise with parties of the far right; their clashes with revived Teddy boys and their widespread support for anti-fascist movements such as Rock Against Racism show that the punk subculture grew up partly as an antithesis to the resurgence of racism in the mid-1970s. So one must resort to the most obvious explanation: the swastika was worn because it was guaranteed to shock (asked why she wore one, a punk replied, "Punks just like to be hated"). This is not merely a simple inversion of an object's usual meaning: **the signifier (the swastika) is deliberately detached from the concept (Nazism) it conventionally signifies**; though it is repositioned in another subcultural context (as "Berlin"), its primary value and appeal derive precisely from its lack of meaning, from its potential for deceit; it is exploited as an empty effect; the central value "held and reflected" in the swastika is the communication of the absence of any identifiable values, and the symbol is ultimately as "dumb" as the rage it provokes. *(This is a radicalisation, within subculture, of Saussure's signifier/signified relation in P3, and it connects with Baudrillard's "sign without a referent" in P8.)* Punk style therefore coheres not through a set of identifiable central values but *elliptically*, through a chain of conspicuous absences, characterised by its unlocatedness and its blankness. In this it contrasts with the skinheads: the skinheads theorised and fetishised their class position in order to effect a "magical" return to an imagined past; the punks dislocated themselves from the parent culture, stood outside it, and "appeared" in the world as aliens, as the incomprehensible, from a science-fiction future; their rituals, accents and objects were deliberately used to signify working-classness, but the exact origins of individuals were disguised or symbolically disfigured by make-up, masks and aliases, a stratagem, as in Breton's art, for "escaping the principle of identity".

**Conclusion: expression through rupture.** This working-classness therefore retained, even in practice, even in its concretised forms, an ideal dimension: it was abstract, disembodied, decontextualised, lacking the necessary details (a name, a home, a history), refusing to be "read back" to its origins; and it was juxtaposed with another important punk signifier, sexual "kinkiness", so that the two forms of deviance, social and sexual, together gave an impression of multiple distortion sufficient to disturb the most liberal observer. Punk referred again and again to the realities of school, work, family and class, but these references made sense only at one remove: they were passed through the fractured circuitry of punk style and re-presented as "noise", disturbance, entropy. **Punk dress did not "magically" resolve experienced contradictions; it *represented* the experience of contradiction itself in visual puns (bondage, the ripped T-shirt); the unity it formed with the group's relations, situation and experience was at once "ruptural" and "expressive", or more precisely, it expressed itself through rupture.** Hebdige also cautions that not all punks were equally aware of the disjunction between experience and signification on which the whole style was based: the difference between the first wave of self-conscious innovators and those who joined after the subculture surfaced and was publicised is always important (the distinction between "plastic punks", "safety-pin people" and "the real thing"; the mods' contempt of the "faces" and "stylists" for the mundane "kids" and "scooter boys"); a subculture can be, for different people, an axis around which to build a secret and pure identity, or merely a moment's diversion from the dreary yet crucial realities of school, home and work; in most cases, as Phil Cohen says, it is used "magically" for both purposes at once. But if a style is to catch on, it must say the right things in the right way at the right time, embodying a sensibility; the sensibility punk style embodied was essentially dislocated, ironic and self-aware. *(The editors say punk style resembled the earlier literary avant-garde in some respects, and Duchamp, Dada, the Surrealists and Brecht all appear in Hebdige's account; this shows a hidden thread linking the Birmingham School's analysis of "style" with the defamiliarisation of Russian Formalism in P2 and the modernist collage of P8: the same formal devices are called avant-garde in high art and deviance in working-class youth.)*

### Strategies and Tactics: The User in Everyday Life

**Problem: what do consumers do with products?** Hebdige studied spectacular subcultures; **Michel de Certeau**'s *The Practice of Everyday Life* (1984) pushes the same question into the most inconspicuous places: ordinary people's dwelling, walking, speaking, reading, shopping and cooking. His starting point is `la perruque` (literally "the wig"), the worker's own work done on the employer's time. Despite all the measures taken to repress or conceal it, the practice infiltrates everywhere; it is only one of many practices that introduce *artistic* tricks and competitions of *accomplices* into a system that reproduces and partitions through work or leisure. From this angle the dividing line no longer falls between work and leisure (*exactly the opposite of Adorno's judgement that "leisure resembles work": Adorno says the imprint of work invades leisure, de Certeau says the tricks of leisure invade work*) but between *modalities* of action, *forms* of practice: *la perruque* is grafted onto the industrial assembly line, a variant, within the factory, of the activity that takes the form of `bricolage` outside it. **Background:** The anthology's editors describe de Certeau as the "other side" of Bourdieu's highly deterministic model of the cultural universe: social and cultural life is not wholly accounted for by models of total determination, and human agency has some room to "wander" off the lines laid down by the overall structure of society (P5).

A North African living in Paris or Roubaix inserts into the system imposed on him by the construction of a low-income housing development, or by the French language, the ways of "dwelling" (in a house or in a language) peculiar to his native Kabylia; without leaving the place where he has no choice but to live and which lays down its law for him, he establishes within it a degree of plurality and creativity, drawing unexpected results from his situation by an art of being "in between". De Certeau says that after the existing analyses of "cultural products", their system of production and the geography of their distribution, these products can be treated no longer merely as statistical data but as a repertory with which users carry out operations of their own: having analysed the images broadcast by television and the time spent watching it, one should still ask what the consumer *makes* of these images during these hours. This is the riddle of the consumer-sphinx: a child can still scrawl in his schoolbook, and even if punished for it he has made a space for himself and signed his existence as an author; the television viewer, however, cannot write anything on the screen; he is expelled from the product, deprived of authorship, and seems to become a pure receiver. **But in reality a rationalised, expansionist, centralised, spectacular and clamorous production is confronted by an entirely different kind of production, called "consumption", characterised by its ruses, its fragmentation, its poaching, its clandestine nature, its tireless but quiet activity, in short by its quasi-invisibility, since it shows itself not in its own products (where would it place them?) but in an art of using those imposed on it.**

**Example: Spanish colonisation and the Indians.** The discreet yet fundamental inversions brought about by consumption have long been studied in other societies. The spectacular victory of Spanish colonisation over the indigenous Indian cultures was diverted from its intended aims by the use made of it: even when subjected, even when consenting to their subjection, the Indians often used the laws, practices and representations imposed on them by force or by fascination to ends other than those of their conquerors; they subverted them from within, not by rejecting or transforming them, but by many different ways of using them in the service of rules, customs and convictions foreign to the colonisation. **They metaphorised the dominant order: they made it function in another register.** They remained other within the system that assimilated them and that they assimilated, diverting it without leaving it. To a lesser degree the same is true of the use made in "popular" milieux of the cultures diffused by the "elites" who produce language: the so-called "popularisation" or "degradation" of a culture is, from this angle, a partial and caricatural aspect of the revenge that the tactics of use take on the power that dominates production. The consumer cannot be identified or qualified by the newspapers or commodities he assimilates: between the person who uses them and these products (indices of the "order" imposed on him) there is a gap of varying proportions opened up by his use of them. *(This example has an evident kinship with Bhabha's theory of mimicry in P15.)*

**Mechanism: use as speech.** The model for analysing use comes from language. Gilbert Ryle, borrowing Saussure's distinction between `langue and parole` (P3), likened the former to a *capital* and the latter to the *operations* it makes possible; in consumption one could almost say that production furnishes the capital, and users, like renters, acquire the right to operate on and with this fund without owning it. The branch of linguistics that studies use, `pragmatics`, and especially the study of indexicals (words and sentences whose reference cannot be fixed without knowing the context of use), rests on a problematic of `enunciation`. Enunciation presupposes four things: a *realisation* of part of the potential of the linguistic system through a speech act (language is real only in the act of speaking); an *appropriation* of the language by the speaker; the positing of an interlocutor (real or fictive), and thus the constitution of a relational *contract*; and the establishment of a *present* through the act of the "I" who speaks, which organises temporality. The speech act is thus at once a *use* of language and an operation performed *on* it. De Certeau's hypothesis is that this model can be extended to non-linguistic operations such as walking and dwelling. *(This is an extension into cultural studies of Austin's speech-act theory in P5: meaning lies not in the system but in situated use.)* But these operations must also be seen from another angle: not their relation to a system, but how *relations of power* define the networks in which they are inscribed and delimit the circumstances they can exploit; one must move from a linguistic frame of reference to a *polemological* one, attending to the battles and games between the strong and the weak, and to the "actions" that remain possible for the weak.

**Definition: strategies and tactics.** Statistics can grasp only the *material* used by consumer practices, not the *form* proper to these practices: what is counted is *what* is used, not the *ways* of using. Consumers are unrecognised producers, poets of their own affairs, trailblazers in the jungles of functionalist rationality, tracing "indeterminate trajectories" that seem meaningless; even though they use the *vocabulary* of established languages (television, newspapers, the supermarket or city planning) and remain within prescribed *syntaxes*, these "traverses" remain heterogeneous to the systems they infiltrate. To account for them de Certeau proposes a distinction. A `strategy` is the calculus of force relationships that becomes possible when a subject of will and power (a business, an army, a city, a scientific institution) can be isolated; it postulates a `proper` place, a place that can be delimited as its *own* and serve as the base from which relations with an exterior composed of targets or threats can be managed: a Cartesian attitude, and the typical attitude of modern science, politics and military strategy. This has three effects: the "proper" is *a triumph of place over time*, allowing one to capitalise acquired advantages and prepare future expansions; it is also a mastery of places through sight, the division of space making possible a *panoptic practice* that transforms foreign forces into objects that can be observed and measured (Foucault in P10); and **a certain power is the precondition of this knowledge, and not merely its effect or attribute**: military and scientific strategies have always been inaugurated through the constitution of their "own" areas (autonomous cities, "neutral" institutions, laboratories pursuing "disinterested" research).

A `tactic`, by contrast, is a calculated action determined by *the absence of a proper locus*. The space of a tactic is the space of the other; it must play on and with a terrain imposed on it and organised by the law of a foreign power; in von Bülow's phrase, it is a manoeuvre "within the enemy's field of vision". It cannot plan a general strategy or view the adversary as a whole; it operates move by move, taking advantage of and depending on "opportunities", without a base where it could stockpile its winnings: **what it wins, it cannot keep.** It must vigilantly make use of the cracks that particular conjunctions open in the surveillance of the proprietary powers, poaching in them, creating surprises, turning up where it is least expected. **In short, a tactic is an art of the weak.** Clausewitz, discussing deception in *On War*, already noted that the greater a power, the less it can afford to mobilise part of its means in the service of deception: power is bound by its very visibility; trickery, by contrast, is possible for the weak, and often their only possibility. He also likened trickery to wit: just as wit is sleight of hand with ideas, trickery is sleight of hand with actions. Through the procedures Freud brought out in discussing wit, a tactic boldly juxtaposes diverse elements to produce a sudden flash that illuminates the language of a place (P6). The old art of the sophists offers another illustration: Aristotle cites Corax's formula, "making the weaker argument seem the stronger" (the rhetoric of P4).

**Conclusion: space and time.** Strategies, by establishing a place of power (the property of a proper), elaborate theoretical places (systems and totalising discourses) and then organise physical places, in which they try as far as possible to reduce temporal relations to spatial ones; tactics, by contrast, derive their efficacy from the pertinence they lend to time: the precise instant of an intervention transforms a conjuncture into a favourable situation, the rapidity of movement changes the organisation of a space. **Strategies pin their hopes on the resistance that *the establishment of a place* offers to the erosion of time; tactics on *a clever utilisation of time*.** Dwelling, moving about, speaking, reading, shopping and cooking are all clever tricks of the "weak" within the order established by the "strong". The "figures" and "tropes" analysed by rhetoric are especially illuminating: relative to the legality of syntax and the "proper" sense, the drift of metaphor, the condensation of ellipsis and the miniaturisation of metonymy are the speaker's uses of language in situations of ritual or actual linguistic combat, indices of consumption and of games of force. *("Proper place" and "proper sense" are both propre in French: de Certeau makes strategy stand to space as grammar stands to proper meaning, and tactic stand to strategy as figure stands to grammar. This also echoes Derrida's deconstruction of the proper/metaphor hierarchy in P7.)*

**Implication: the night-side of society.** On the scale of contemporary history, the generalisation of technocratic rationality has detached these practices from the stable local units that once regulated them, and they have begun to drift everywhere in a space both more homogeneous and more extensive: **consumers are transformed into immigrants.** The system in which they move is too vast to fix them in one place, but too constraining for them ever to be able to escape from it and go into exile elsewhere; there is no longer an elsewhere; and the strategic model too has been defeated by its own success, since the "proper" has become the whole. *(This picture agrees with postmodernism's diagnosis of "no outside" in P8.)* De Certeau also turns against criticism itself: it is not surprising that the field of research prefers the problematic of "repression", since scientific institutions belong to the system they study; ideological critique does not alter its functioning, but only creates for the scientists within the institution an appearance of distance; the elucidation of the apparatus itself has a drawback: it **does not see** the practices heterogeneous to it, which it represses or thinks it represses. Looking closely at this fleeting and permanent reality, one has the impression of exploring the *night-side of societies*, a night longer than their day, a dark sea from which successive institutions emerge, and on which social, economic and political structures are only ephemeral islands. *This is an implicit revision of the Foucauldian analysis of discipline in P10: the Panopticon belongs on the side of "strategy", and strategy's field of vision by definition cannot see tactics.* But de Certeau also concedes that this is the "imaginary landscape" of an inquiry, not without value but not without rigour: the evidence it offers can only be fictional rather than scientific; of all the things people do, how much is ever written down?

### The Codes of Television and Resistant Decoding

**Definition: culture is political.** **John Fiske** states the premises of the Birmingham tradition most clearly. The "culture" in "cultural studies" is neither aesthetic nor humanist but political: it is not the ideals of form and beauty in great art, nor the voice of "the human spirit" transcending time and nation and speaking to a hypothetical universal "man" (the gender is deliberate: women had little place in this notion); not a bulwark against the tide of industrial materialism and vulgarity (the Arnold tradition of P1), but a way of living within an industrial society that encompasses all the meanings of that social experience. Cultural studies is concerned with the generation and circulation of meanings in industrial societies, and its basic assumptions are these: meanings and their making (which together constitute culture) are inseparable from the social structure and can be explained only in terms of that structure and its history; conversely, the social structure is held in place by the meanings culture produces (Stuart Hall says that a set of social relations obviously requires meanings and frameworks that underpin it and hold it in place); these meanings are not only meanings of social experience but also meanings of the self, that is, constructions of social identity. Capitalist societies are divided societies: the main axis of division was originally thought to be class, but gender and race are now equally important, together with nation, age, religion, occupation, education, political allegiance and so on; society is not an organic whole but a network of groups with different interests, related to one another by their relations of power with the dominant classes. In the cultural domain, social struggle takes the form of *a struggle for meaning*: the dominant classes try to "naturalise" the meanings that serve their interests as the "common sense" of society as a whole, while subordinate classes resist this process in various ways and to varying degrees, trying to make meanings that serve their own interests; Angela McRobbie and Lisa Lewis have both shown how girls contest the patriarchal ideology in films such as *Flashdance* or in pop stars such as Madonna and Cyndi Lauper, producing feminine readings. The dominant classes' naturalisation of their meanings rarely comes from the conscious intention of individual members (whereas resistance often is conscious); it is the work of an ideology inscribed in the cultural and social practices of a class.

**Background: from "false consciousness" to interpellation.** The cultural studies tradition does not understand ideology in the vulgar Marxist sense of "false consciousness" (P9), since that presupposes that a true consciousness is not only possible but will be realised with the arrival of a proletarian society; what the late twentieth century seemed to demonstrate was not capitalism's inevitable self-destruction but its capacity to reproduce itself and to incorporate forces of resistance and opposition (something Marx did not foresee). Structuralism also denies the possibility of a true consciousness, since reality can be understood only through language or other cultural systems of meaning (P3); truth must be understood in terms of how, for whom and when it is made "true". Althusser and Gramsci provided ways of bringing structuralism (and Freudianism) and the history of twentieth-century capitalism into Marxism. Fiske's restatement of Althusser is a clear review (P9): ideology is a dynamic process constantly reproduced in practice; `overdetermination` replaces the base/superstructure model; the `ideological state apparatuses` (family, education, language, media, the political system) are each "relatively autonomous", with no overt connection among them, yet do similar ideological work: they are all patriarchal, all concerned with acquiring and keeping wealth, all endorse individualism and competition between individuals; and their most important common feature is that they all present themselves as socially neutral institutions that treat everyone equally, concealing that the norms defining "equality" and "fairness" derive from white, male, middle-class interests. At the micro level, "the subject" should replace "the individual": **the individual is produced by nature, the subject by culture.** The subject is a social rather than a natural construction, so that a biological female may have a masculine subjectivity (understanding the world and herself through patriarchal ideology), a black person a white subjectivity, a member of the working class a middle-class subjectivity. *This connects with Lacan in P6 and with feminism's theorisation of the gendered subject in P12: Fiske himself points out that the ideological and psychoanalytic theories of the subject differ only in emphasis, the former stressing social and historical conditions, the latter rooted more in psychic processes.*

**Mechanism: hailing and interpellation.** Fiske distinguishes `hailing` from interpellation. The first thing we do when we communicate with someone is to "hail" them, as we hail a taxi; to respond, they must recognise that we are speaking to *them*, and this recognition comes from the signs carried in our language of who we think they are: we hail a child differently from an adult, a man differently from a woman, someone of lower status differently from someone of higher status. In responding, addressees recognise the social position our language has constructed for them, and if their response is cooperative, they adopt this position. **Hailing is the process by which language identifies and constructs a social position for the addressee; interpellation is the larger process by which language constructs social relations for both parties in an act of communication, and so locates them in the wider map of social relations.**

**Reading: the rail strike news.** Fiske analyses an American network news report of April 1991 on a national rail strike. The anchor's opening says that there is growing concern about the possible economic impact of a national rail strike set for midnight, with "the unions and the railroads" still deadlocked; the reporter says that by morning 230,000 rail workers could be off the job, a strike that "threatens millions of Americans". The word "strike" hails us as anti-union, since a "strike" is constructed as a negative action by which unions threaten the nation; attributing responsibility to the unions conceals management's role in the dispute. The report sets the unions against not "management" but "the railroads", thereby excluding the unions from the railroads and making the unnamed management synonymous with them; it then constructs the railroads as a national resource rather than an industry, using them as a metonym for "the nation" and ultimately for "us" (Jakobson in P3). In recognising ourselves as the national "we" interpellated here, we take part in the work of ideology, adopting the anti-union subject position offered to us. Passengers' complaints and the reporter's remarks about freight construct the national "we" as hard-working producers; the recurring "heart" metaphor ("at the heart of this recession threatens the heart of American industry") turns "America" into a living body, and the unions into a potentially fatal disease. The causes of the dispute are mentioned only in abstract terms ("wages, health care, the number of workers per train"), in contrast with the concrete figures of 230,000 workers off the job and millions of Americans threatened; the unions are not allowed to speak for themselves "live", their case is placed in the reporter's words and classified as mere "complaints", while management's case is given the stronger status of "charges".

**Distinction: interpellation vs hegemony.** Fiske points out that this view of ideology as a process constantly at work finds strong support in Gramsci's theory of `hegemony`: the dominant classes win the willing consent of the subordinate classes to the system that ensures their subordination, and this consent must be won again and again, since people's material social experience constantly reminds them of the disadvantages of subordination. But there is an important difference between the two: Althusser's theory sometimes implies that the power of ideology and the ideological state apparatuses to form subjects is almost irresistible; hegemony theory, by contrast, posits a constant contradiction between ideology and the social experience of the subordinate, making this interface an inevitable site of ideological struggle: **the big guns are on the side of the powerful, but victory does not necessarily go to the big guns, or at least not total victory.** Ideology must not only extend its power but also hold on to the territory it has already colonised. *This is the counterpart in cultural studies of Sinfield's critique of the containment model in P10: Althusser ≈ containment, Gramsci ≈ fault-lines.*

**Mechanism: the three levels of television codes.** In *Television Culture* (1987) Fiske first gives a traditional semiotic account: television broadcasts programmes full of potential meanings, but tries to control and focus this richness of meaning into a more singular `preferred meaning` that does the work of the dominant ideology. A `code` is a rule-governed system of signs whose rules and conventions are shared by members of a culture and used to generate and circulate meanings in that culture; codes are the links between producers, texts and audiences, the agents of intertextuality. He divides television codes into three levels:

1. **Level one, "reality"**: an event to be televised is already encoded by `social codes`: appearance, dress, make-up, environment, behaviour, speech, gesture, expression, sound and so on.
2. **Level two, representation**: these are encoded electronically by `technical codes` (camera, lighting, editing, music, sound), which transmit `conventional representational codes` shaping the representation of narrative, conflict, character, dialogue, setting, casting and so on.
3. **Level three, ideology**: these are organised into coherent, socially acceptable wholes by `ideological codes` such as individualism, patriarchy, race, class, materialism and capitalism.

Fiske himself cautions that these categories are arbitrary and slippery: he classes speech as a social code and dialogue as a technical code, but conversation in "real life" is often scripted by the culture's conventions of interaction; the difference between casting and appearance is only one of intentionality and explicitness, the casting director simply using these codes more consciously and conventionally, that is, more stereotypically. **The point is that "reality" is already encoded: there may be an objective, empirical reality, but there is no universal, objective way of perceiving and making sense of it; what passes for reality in a culture is the product of that culture's codes, and "reality" is never "raw".** Even a tree reflected in a lake is fully encoded before it is filmed and made into the setting of a romantic narrative. The production of meaning is a process of constant movement up and down between the three levels, and meaning is produced only when "reality", representation and ideology merge into a coherent, seemingly natural unity; semiotic or cultural criticism deconstructs this unity, exposing its "naturalness" as a highly ideological construction. *(This is a television version of Barthes's analysis of "myth" in P3, and an application of the second mechanism, "manifest/latent": the manifest level is plot and image, the latent level the ideological codes.)*

**Reading: two scenes from *Hart to Hart*.** Fiske takes as his example two scenes from the long-running prime-time series *Hart to Hart*: a wealthy husband-and-wife detective team pose as passengers on a cruise ship to investigate a jewel theft; in the first scene they prepare for a dance and discuss how the theft might have been carried out, while the second introduces the villain and villainess, who have already noticed the jewellery Jennifer Hart is flaunting. At the level of technical codes: the camera, through angle and deep focus, gives the viewer a perfect view, and much of the pleasure of television realism comes from this sense of omniscience; television's normal shot distance is mid-shot to close-up, but the villains are also shown in extreme close-up: only three scenes in the whole episode use extreme close-ups, and of the twenty-one extreme close-ups, eighteen are of the villains and only three of the heroes, so that the extreme close-up becomes a coded way of presenting villainy. The convention is not confined to fiction: in General Westmoreland's libel suit against CBS in 1985, techniques such as placing interviewees in half-shadow and using extreme close-ups when putting the most pointed questions were challenged, since viewers may associate a tense appearance with lying or guilt. The code of shot distance has two sources: the social code of interpersonal distance (in Western culture the space within about 60 centimetres of the body is coded as private, and entry into it is hostile if unwelcome and intimate if invited), and the technical code that "seeing close is seeing clearly", so that viewers can see *into* the villain, *through* his words, gaining the power and pleasure of "dominant spectatorship". In editing, the heroes get more time (72 seconds) and more shots (10) than the villains (49 seconds, 7 shots); the music linking the two scenes moves from a major to a minor key.

At the level of social and ideological codes, casting is crucial. Television characters are not merely representations of individuals but "embodiments of ideological values". Gerbner's research found that heroes and villains are equally likely to use and initiate violence, but heroes' violence succeeds while villains' violence finally fails; the "killer-to-killed ratio" calculated by age, gender, class and race shows that characters who are white, male, middle-class (or classless) and in the prime of life are almost certain to survive to the end, while characters who deviate from these norms are killed in proportion to their deviation. One can infer that heroes are socially central figures who embody the dominant ideology, while villains and victims are members of deviant or subordinate subcultures who embody it less fully; the opposition of hero and villain and their violence become metaphors for social relations of power. The male villain of this episode carries un-American overtones (his accent was classed by some viewers as British, his looks seen by others as Hispanic), while the villainess is blonde, white, pretty and younger; by Gerbner's findings one would predict that he will die and she will survive, and the prediction is right: she finally changes sides and helps the heroes, and he is killed; her condemnation of the male villain's greed has already placed her nearer the centre of economic discourse. In setting and costume, the heroes' cabin is larger, with drapes and flowers, while the villains' cabin is all sharp angles and harsh lines; the male villain wears a uniform marking him as a servant or employee. The codes of hero, villain and attractiveness work fairly openly, while the codes of class, race and morality beneath them are less open and more questionable: **their ideological work is to naturalise the association between the lower classes, the non-American, and what is less attractive, less moral and therefore villainous.** The displacement of morality onto class is a common feature of popular culture: Dorfman and Mattelart point out that Disney cartoons consistently represent evil through working-class looks and manners. Even lipstick is at work: the villainess has several signs that contradict her villainy, foreshadowing her eventual change of sides, but she cannot yet look too much like the heroine, so her lips are drawn thinner than the heroine's; **ideology works most effectively precisely in the sum of these apparently trivial codings.** In both cabins it is the woman who dresses and the man who plans, and the mirror makes her see herself as "the bearer of her own image"; because this is the same for heroes and villains, it is placed outside the narrative conflict, in the everyday common sense on which the narrative is built; so too is the acquisition and keeping of wealth as a motive for action.

**Reading: three narrative devices.** If viewers decode with the same ideological practices with which the programme was encoded, they are drawn into the position of a white, male, middle-class American (or Westerner) of conventional morality: a `reading position`. To understand the programme in this way is to maintain and legitimate the dominant ideology, the reward being the easy pleasure of recognising the familiar and its adequacy; we have become the "reading subject" constructed by the text. This practice works hardest in three narrative devices. The first is the "window / porthole / laundry" joke: Freud says jokes serve to relieve anxiety caused by repressed, unwelcome meanings (P6); this joke turns on the "feminine" inability to use technical language and the understanding of everything in domestic discourse: "porthole" is technical, masculine discourse, "window" and "laundry" domestic, nurturing, feminine discourse; the anxiety it relieves is that the heroine, as a detective, takes part in the technical world that belongs to men in patriarchy, and the joke recuperates the contradictory signs into the dominant system. The second is the "honey and bees" metaphor: it naturalises women's sexual attraction for men, and extends this naturalness to explain the attraction of other people's jewellery for lower-class, non-American villains, naturalising at once the cultural constructions of gender, class and race. The third is the jewellery itself, where three codes (economic, gender and class) intersect: the villains stress the jewellery's investment/exchange function ("worth at least fifty thousand wholesale", "a retirement plan"), a function left unspoken for the heroes and their class, for whom jewellery is a sign of class, wealth and aesthetic taste; the heroine deliberately wears too much, so as to look vulgar and lure the lower-class villains, and the villain betrays his own inferior taste by likening it to "icing on a cupcake". As Bourdieu has shown, the function of the aesthetic in our society is to make class-based differences of taste appear universal and natural, the metaphor of "taste" displacing class difference onto a bodily and therefore natural sense (P5). In the gender code, jewellery is the money with which woman, as a patriarchal commodity, is bought; wearing it signifies both that she is possessed by a man and his economic and social status; and here there is no class difference between heroes and villains: the economics of patriarchy is the same for all classes, which makes "a man provides for his woman" appear universal and natural. *(This analysis anticipates Rubin's "traffic in women" in P12.)*

**Turn: from textual strategies to viewers' social experience.** This analysis shows the complexity of the meanings encoded in what is taken to be superficial, and implies that this complexity and subtlety have powerful effects on viewers: the various codes cohere into a unified set of meanings that maintain, legitimate and naturalise the dominant ideology of patriarchal capitalism. But Fiske then turns: **analysis must attend less to the text's preferred and closed strategies and more to the gaps and spaces that open television to non-preferred meanings, meanings that come from the reader's social experience.** Reading is not gathering meaning from the text but a dialogue between the text and the socially situated reader. David Morley says that the meaning of a text must be thought of in terms of which discourses it encounters in a particular situation, an encounter that may restructure both the meaning of the text and the discourses it meets; the key is the range of discourses available to the audience. Texts and subjectivities are both discursive constructions, both containing competing or contradictory discourses, and the `polysemy` of the text and the diversity of readings arise from this. *(This is a sociological version of the reader theory of P5: Fish's "interpretive community" becomes here a subculture in the sense of class, age and race.)*

**Example: *Prisoner* and *Diff'rent Strokes*.** Hodge and Tripp found that one of the favourite programmes of Australian junior high school students was *Prisoner*, a soap opera set in a women's prison, an apparently surprising choice. At various levels of consciousness the children found and articulated useful similarities between prison and school: students are shut in, separated from their friends, would not be there unless forced, do their work only because they will be punished if they do not, are powerless against unfair teachers; some teachers bully the students; among the students there are gangs and leaders, and stupid rules that everyone tries to break. Both institutions have recognisable character types (the hard-bitten old warder/teacher, the soft new one, those who can be exploited and those who cannot); among the prisoners there are those who resist the system in every way, the goody-goodies who comply, and those who seem to comply while secretly opposing it; and there are shared strategies of resistance (secret languages, winks, double meanings); the oppositional subculture of the prison laundry corresponds to the oppositional subcultures of school toilets and changing rooms, areas the official culture constantly tries to colonise and control. *(This is a counter-example to Foucault's Panopticon: even in disciplinary institutions there are all sorts of tactics for "using" the system; P10.)* Turnbull found that young female fans found in it meanings they could use to produce subcultural identity and self-esteem: images of tough, active women struggling against the system and winning small victories (though finally submitting) gave them the pleasure of resistance and a discourse in which to articulate it. Hodge and Tripp's study of Australian Aboriginal children is more striking still: the children constructed a cultural category that included American blacks, American Indians and themselves, a tool for thinking with, conceptualising the political and narrative powerlessness of non-whites in white society; their favourite *Diff'rent Strokes* had as its hero a black American child adopted by a white family, whom they saw as Aboriginal; in westerns they sided with the Indians against the white cowboys, knowing that this side was bound to lose and knowing too that reading westerns this way was "perverse". **Reading television in this way gave them a means of articulating their own experience of powerlessness in a white-dominated society, and being able to articulate one's experience is a necessary precondition for developing the will to change it.** Mattelart's study of Third World reception of Hollywood television reached a similar conclusion: the messages of mass culture can be neutralised by the dominated classes, who can produce their own antidotes, creating the seeds of a new, sometimes contradictory, culture.

### Two Incommensurable Perspectives in Cultural Studies

**Conclusion: two perspectives.** The editors sum up the field with a sharp contrast: cultural studies can be approached from two rather *incommensurable* perspectives. One sees the media, television, film and so on as instruments of economic, ethnic and gender domination: owned by large corporations and run mainly by men, they allow only certain kinds of images and ideas to reach the masses, and so cannot help assisting the reproduction of the social system; produced by those at the top of the social hierarchy, they necessarily promote attitudes and perceptions that ensure the continuation of that hierarchy. The other looks at culture from below, attending more to how musical forms, from African American spirituals to the blues to rock and roll, express energies and attitudes fundamentally at odds with the attitudes and presuppositions of the capitalist social order (deferring gratification in order to work better, for example): **culture comes from below; it can be harnessed in profitable and ultimately socially conservative ways, but it also represents the permanent possibility of eruption, of discord, of an alternative imagination of reality.** The material above can be arranged along this opposition: Horkheimer and Adorno's culture industry and Fiske's first-stage analysis of ideological codes belong to the former; Hebdige's punk, de Certeau's tactics and Fiske's second-stage readings from below belong to the latter; Benjamin straddles both, seeing in mechanical reproduction both the shattering of tradition and the liberation of the masses, and Fascism's aestheticising use of the same technology.

**Background: Bourdieu and the reproduction of hierarchy.** The editors also place **Pierre Bourdieu** from P5 in this picture. Culture, like capitalist society itself, is hierarchical, and Bourdieu sees culture as a way of distinguishing positions in the social hierarchy: those born into the upper classes acquire dispositions that enable them to appreciate certain cultural forms (high art, for example), and this ability helps them secure high positions in the class hierarchy; the working class acquires from its home environment and the schools it attends cultural dispositions that prepare it for life at the bottom; **the social system thus reproduces itself through culture and schooling** (for the mechanisms of `habitus` and `distinction` see P5; the thread of "English" as an institution joins P1 here). Fiske already used this insight in analysing the jewellery in *Hart to Hart*: the function of the aesthetic is to make class-based, culturally specific differences of taste appear universal and natural. The editors' introduction to de Certeau sets the two explicitly against each other: in Bourdieu's highly deterministic model, structure supersedes and shapes all the individual decisions social actors might make, while de Certeau describes its "other side": agency still has room to "wander" off the lines laid down by social structure. **The same opposition is thus repeated at three levels: Adorno ↔ Hebdige concerns cultural products; Bourdieu ↔ de Certeau concerns social structure and action; Fiske's ideological codes ↔ readings from below concerns texts and viewers.**

In the United States the Marxist critic Fredric Jameson developed a more sophisticated version of the Frankfurt School's model of domination, yet argued that a perceptible *utopian impulse* exists in mass culture; along these lines, Janice Radway studied despised popular forms such as the romance novel and interpreted them as a way in which women resist the patriarchal structures imposed on their lives. *This is a middle position between the two perspectives: the framework of domination is kept, but within the products of domination are found the desires they cannot help evoking, a structure identical to Sinfield's argument in P10 that ideology must first evoke expectations in order to contain them.*

**Reading: Krims and a third position.** Adam Krims's *Rap Music and the Poetics of Identity* (2000) offers a third position. He studies how Ice Cube's "The Nigga Ya Love to Hate" projects and helps form a certain kind of community and identity, but declares at the outset that "identity" here is not necessarily "resistant identity"; the only premise is that these identities are formed *in some way* in the symbolic, not that they necessarily overturn the discursive structures they oppose; what Jody Berland calls "the optimism of cultural studies" is replaced by a description closer to the "semiotic", and further judgements about political function require closer examination of how discursive acts circulate and of their sometimes surprising futures in capital and its remote social effects. He takes his concept of culture from James Clifford: contemporary cultural identity is not an archaic survival but a politically contested, historically unfinished process, a form of individual and collective self-fashioning; if authenticity is relational, there are no essences, only essences as political and cultural inventions, "a local tactic". Martin Stokes, for his part, points out that music does not merely provide a marker in a prestructured social space but is a means of transforming that space; subcultures borrow, inflect and invert the signs of the dominant culture, producing a bricolage in which the signs of the dominant culture are "present" and just recognisable, yet form an entirely different, subversive whole; this comes close to what Gates calls the core of black cultural production, `Signifyin(g)` (P14).

Krims's analysis goes down to the level of individual bars and tracks. A major authenticating strategy of early "gangsta rap" was the symbolic superimposition of the MC on the artist: the MC himself *is* that persona, a voice from "the street" speaking from authentic experience; Ice Cube's whole early public image depended on this superimposition, whose force can be gauged from later fans' accusations that he had "sold out". The song comes from his first solo album after leaving NWA, produced by Public Enemy's production team, The Bomb Squad, and so borrows a new sound closely bound up with Black Nationalist politics. Krims argues that the song shapes not a black identity in general but a political position *within* the ethnic group, a "black revolutionary identity", opposed not only to hegemonic culture but also to other black people whom it sees as helping to perpetuate injustice. The lyrics reject the dancing black image of *Soul Train*, marking the pleasures of rhythm and dance with a negative value; but musically a series of added tracks gradually turns the ever-present synthesiser from pitched material into unpitched percussive material, so that rhythm returns just after it has been explicitly opposed to black revolutionary identity: **this is the appropriation and transformation of a cultural seme.** The song's violent imagery (drive-by shootings aimed at the police and the media, lynching) is therefore a revision of the black identity constructed by these institutions. Krims does not evade the song's misogyny: Ice Cube introduces a female questioner who challenges his calling women "bitch", and tries to restrict the word to women who "sell out" black identity, but his own discourse reinscribes the misogyny; if the song's project is to create a black revolutionary identity, it remains unfinished so long as it excludes or marginalises half (or more) of the black population. **The revision of "blackness" may be an open, unfinished process rather than a triumphant "sublation".** Krims's methodological conclusion is that "close reading" of musical processes does not necessarily reinscribe the ideology of the artwork, but may instead lead to a larger "extramusical" social reality. *This is another return of the close reading of P2 in cultural studies: as in the New Historicism of P10, formal analysis is not replaced by political analysis but becomes its tool.*

**Limitation:** The price of each perspective has been pointed out by the theorists themselves. The price of the domination thesis is totalisation: if the culture industry moulds people into the type unfailingly reproduced in every product, it cannot explain why Australian Aboriginal children side with the Indians when watching westerns, or how punks could produce meaning from rubbish. The price of the resistance thesis is to take symbolic refusal for political change: Hebdige himself concedes that punk's gestures may in the end be no more than the darker side of sets of regulations, "graffiti on a prison wall"; Fiske's conclusion is only that finding a discourse in which to understand one's powerlessness in a positive way is the "first step" towards changing it; de Certeau concedes that his picture of tactics is an "imaginary landscape", whose evidence can only be fictional rather than scientific; and Krims simply rejects "the optimism of cultural studies". *Moreover, the viewers' readings Fiske cites come from reports by other researchers (Hodge and Tripp, Turnbull), which suggests that the evidence for "resistant reading" is itself collected and selected, the same kind of problem as New Historicism's selectivity with documents in P10.*

**Implication: the trajectory of the fourth mechanism.** `Domination ↔ resistance`, first named with Gramsci in P9, became in P10 the dispute between Greenblatt and Sinfield over whether dissidence is contained, and here becomes the dispute between Adorno on the one hand and Hebdige, de Certeau and Fiske on the other over the nature of mass culture. All three have the same structure: the dominant side occupies production, institutions and the "proper place", while the subordinate side can act only with the dominant's materials and on its ground; the disagreement is whether this action is contained in advance, or can make the dominant order "function in another register". *De Certeau's Indians, who "metaphorised" the conquerors' laws and representations, will reappear in another form in P15: Bhabha's `mimicry` and `hybridity`, the internal splitting of colonial authority when it is repeated.*

One thread remains to be drawn together. Every important analysis in cultural studies ran into gender: Fiske read the codes of patriarchy in *Hart to Hart* (the woman asks and the man answers, the woman dresses and the man plans, the jewellery is the money with which woman as a patriarchal commodity is bought); McRobbie and Lewis recorded how girls produced feminine readings from *Flashdance* and Madonna; Radway read the romance novel as women's resistance; Hebdige's punks threw out the traditional feminine lore of make-up along with heterosexual courtship rituals; and Krims found misogyny within black revolutionary identity. Armstrong's revision of Foucault and the Sinfield–McLuskie–Neely dispute in P10 already pointed in the same direction. **If the meanings of culture are always produced in contest, then gender is not one of the things contested but one of the structures that decide who contests and in what capacity.** P12 thus enters the first part of Layer 5, "whose universal?": how gender is written, and how women write.

## P12 How Is Gender Written, and How Do Women Write? Feminism

When a work is declared to express "universal human nature", has that "human" already been given a gender? P12 answers exactly this question: whose universal is the universal in literature? It opens the first part of Layer 5 of the six-layer framework, "whose universal? identity and difference". Layer 5 applies the tools built in the first four layers to gender, sexuality, race and empire, and broadly follows a three-step pattern: "expose stereotype and silence → reconstruct a tradition → question the categories of identity themselves"; feminist criticism went through precisely these three steps, in order, in its own history.

P12 inherits a great deal. The liberal humanism of P1 believed in an unchanging human nature, and feminism first reveals the male face of this "human nature"; Lévi-Strauss's theory of the exchange of women in P3 will be critically reread here by Rubin and Irigaray; the Oedipal model of P6, Lacan's Symbolic and Chodorow's theory of mothering make up the history of feminism and psychoanalysis from rejection to rereading; Derrida's deconstruction of binary hierarchies in P7, and Johnson and Jardine's pointers to phallocentrism, become in Cixous and Irigaray a theory and a writing of sexual difference; Marx's analysis of the commodity and Althusser's interpellation in P9 are put to new use by Rubin, Irigaray and Spivak; P10 and P11 kept running into gender: Armstrong's revision of Foucault, the Sinfield–McLuskie–Neely dispute, the patriarchal codes Fiske read in television. Of the five mechanisms running throughout, **the third, "essence ↔ construction", is fully developed here for the first time**; the first, "relation and difference", reappears in Cixous's table of binary oppositions; the second, "manifest/latent double reading", is turned by Kahn against Freud's own text; the fourth, "domination ↔ resistance", takes on the dimensions of race and nation in Lorde and Heng; and the fifth, the "shifting boundary between text and context", is pushed by Spivak all the way to the colonial legal archive.

### Where Feminist Criticism Came From: From the Women's Movement to Literary Criticism
