The oppressed are also expected to bear the responsibility of educating the oppressor (Black people educating white people about their humanity, women educating men, lesbians and gay men educating the heterosexual world), while the oppressors thereby keep their position and evade responsibility. **Conclusion:** It is not difference itself that separates people, but the refusal to recognise difference, and the distortions that result from misnaming it.

**Definition:** At the edge of consciousness there is what Lorde calls a `mythical norm`: in America it is usually defined as white, thin, male, young, heterosexual, Christian and financially secure, and it is with this norm that the trappings of power reside. Those outside power often identify one way in which they are different, take it to be the primary cause of all oppression, and forget other distortions around difference, some of which they may themselves be practising. In the women's movement today, white women focus on their oppression as women and ignore differences of race, sexual preference, class and age; the word "sisterhood" conceals a homogeneity of experience that does not exist.

**Example:** Class difference even determines the forms creativity takes. A group of editors of a women's magazine decided that one issue would print only prose, on the grounds that poetry is a less "rigorous" art form; yet poetry is the most economical of the arts, requiring the least physical labour and material, and can be written between shifts, in the hospital pantry, on the subway, on scraps of surplus paper. **"A room of one's own may be a necessity for writing prose, but so are reams of paper, a typewriter, and plenty of time."** *This sentence directly rewrites Woolf's A Room of One's Own.* The consequences of racial difference are graver: white women, ignoring their built-in privilege of whiteness and defining "woman" by their own experience alone, make women of colour "other". The literature of women of colour seldom enters women's literature courses, often on the grounds that it is "too different" and hard to "get into", while those who give this reason have no difficulty teaching Shakespeare, Molière, Dostoevsky and Aristophanes. Black women and white women also face different traps: Black women are easily used by the power structure against Black men, not because they are men but because they are Black; white women face the danger of being seduced into joining the oppressor in the name of sharing power. "You fear your children will grow up to join the patriarchy and testify against you; we fear our children will be dragged from a car and shot down in the street, and you will turn your backs upon the reasons they are dying." The threat of difference blinds people of colour too: within Black communities the need for unity is often misnamed as a need for homogeneity, Black feminism is treated as a betrayal of common interests, and anti-sexism is misnamed as anti-Black; and Lorde refuses to be encouraged to "pluck out some one aspect of myself and present this as the meaningful whole".

**Conclusion:** Lorde's most famous sentence appears here: **"The master's tools will never dismantle the master's house."** The tools it refers to are the old patterns of relating to difference based on dominance and subordination; drawing on Freire's *Pedagogy of the Oppressed*, she points out that the true focus of revolutionary change is never merely the oppressive situations we seek to escape, but that piece of the oppressor planted deep within each of us, which knows only the oppressors' tactics and relationships. *By contrast, Irigaray, discussed above, argues precisely for deliberately repeating the master's discourse and disabling it through "mimicry"; the two strategies make opposite estimates of whether "the master's tools" can be turned against him. Later Kimberlé Crenshaw (1989) named this inseparable multiplicity of oppressions `intersectionality`; Lorde's essay can be seen as its precursor.*

Lorde's critique takes place within the United States; **Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak**'s "Three Women's Texts and a Critique of Imperialism" (1986) places the same question on the scale of empire. **Background:** It should not be possible to read nineteenth-century British literature without remembering that imperialism, understood as England's "social mission", was a crucial part of the cultural representation of England to the English, nor without remembering the role of literature in the production of cultural representation. That these two "obvious facts" continue to be disregarded itself testifies to the continuing success of the imperialist project in more modern forms. If the "Third World" is treated as distant cultures, exploited but with rich intact literary heritages waiting to be recovered and translated into the curriculum, one forgets how it was `worlded`. This is particularly unfortunate when the emergent perspective of feminist criticism reproduces the axioms of imperialism: an isolationist admiration for the literature of the female subject in Europe and Anglo-America establishes the norms of "high feminism", while Third World literature is approached with an information-retrieval method that is self-consciously and justifiably "non-theoretical".

**Mechanism: childbearing and soul making.** Spivak first makes a qualification: her object is printed books, not "authors". A deconstructive reading would loosen the boundary between book and biography, but that would be too risky here, so she takes shelter "strategically" in an essentialism, continuing to respect the suspect binary oppositions of book and author, individual and history, so as not to lose the important advantages already won by mainstream American feminism; her reading does not belittle Brontë as an individual artist, but hopes to provoke anger at the imperialist narrativisation of history that gave her so abject a script. Her premise is that in the age of imperialism the stakes of female individualism were precisely "the making of human beings", the subject being `interpellated` (P9) not only as an individual but as an "individualist". These stakes were represented on two levels: childbearing (domestic society through sexual reproduction, cathected as "companionate love") and soul making (civil society through social mission, that is, the imperial project). As the female individualist, not quite/not male, articulates herself in shifting relation to these stakes, the "native female" as signifier is excluded from any share in this emerging norm. Read only from the isolationist perspective of the metropolis, all one sees is the psychobiography of a militant female subject.

**Reading: *Jane Eyre*.** The opening is a scene of marginalisation and privatisation: "There was no possibility of taking a walk that day … I was glad of it." Jane does not enter the drawing-room where the family is, but slips into the breakfast-room "adjoining" it, where there is only a bookcase; she draws the red moreen curtain and is "shrined in double retirement". She reads not the text but the pictures, a peculiar hermeneutics that turns the outside into the inside: the creative imagination of the marginal individualist. The course of the novel can be laid out as a series of family/counter-family pairs: the Reeds and Jane; the Brocklehursts and the female community of Jane, Miss Temple and Helen Burns; Rochester and the madwoman Mrs Rochester, the legal family, with Jane and Rochester as the illicit counter-family; then Jane restores full family status to the Riverses; and at the end the "community of families" centred on Jane, Rochester and their children. What moves Jane from the counter-family to the legal family? **The active ideology of imperialism provides the discursive field.** The white Jamaican Creole Bertha Mason is a product of the axioms of imperialism: "In the deep shade, at the farther end of the room, a figure ran backwards and forwards. What it was, whether beast or human being, one could not, at first sight, tell." She blurs the boundary between human and animal, thereby weakening her entitlement in spirit if not in the letter of the law; Rochester describes "a fiery West Indian night" as hell, until "a wind fresh from Europe" blows and Hope says to him: "Go, and live again in Europe."

**Distinction: three readings.** A Marxist critic such as Terry Eagleton sees this movement only in terms of the governess's ambiguous *class* position; Gilbert and Gubar see Bertha only psychologically, as Jane's dark double, and call the novel "Plain Jane's progress", that is, a female protagonist substituted for the male one, without noticing the distance between sexual reproduction and soul making. The formula of soul making comes from a travesty of Kant's `categorical imperative`: every rational being is an end in itself; therefore *make the heathen into a human* so that he can be treated as an end in himself. In the novel this project appears as a tangent, the story of St John Rivers: he is granted the task of ending the *text*, placed within the allegory of *The Pilgrim's Progress*, his life in Calcutta equivalent to an unhesitating choice of death.

**Reading: *Wide Sargasso Sea* as rewriting.** Jean Rhys, born on the Caribbean island of Dominica, was moved by Bertha Mason when she read *Jane Eyre* as a young woman: "I thought I'd try to write her a life." *Wide Sargasso Sea*, published in 1966, is that life. Rhys keeps Bertha's humanity, even her lucidity as a critic of imperialism. In *Jane Eyre*, when Bertha attacks her visiting brother Richard Mason, there is "a snarling, snatching sound, almost like a dog quarrelling"; when Rhys rewrites the scene, Grace Poole tells her that he said he could not interfere "legally" between her and her husband, and "it was when he said 'legally' that you flew at him". What drives the violence is not innate bestiality but the pretence Bertha sees through in the word "legally". Antoinette (whom Rochester forcibly renames Bertha), a white Creole child at the time of emancipation, is caught between English imperialists and black natives. Rhys rewrites in her the theme of Narcissus: the black girl Tia had been her close companion ("I will live with Tia and I will be like her"); but Tia throws a stone at her, and "we stared at each other, blood on my face, tears on hers. It was as if I saw myself. Like in a looking-glass." In Ovid, the madness of Narcissus lies in recognising the other as self; Rhys makes Antoinette recognise the self as other: in a gilt-framed mirror in the corridors of Thornfield she sees "the ghost. The woman with streaming hair." The dream ends there; she leaps, calling to Tia, and on waking says: "Now at last I know why I was brought here and what I have to do." This cardboard house where she walks at night is not England, she says: it is a book between cardboard covers. She must play out her role in this fictive England, setting fire to the house and killing herself, **so that Jane Eyre can become the feminist individualist heroine of British fiction**. Spivak reads this as an allegory of the general `epistemic violence` of imperialism: the construction of a self-immolating colonial subject for the glorification of the coloniser's social mission. At least Rhys does not allow the woman from the colonies to be sacrificed as an insane animal for her "sister's" consolidation.

**Objection: Rhys's limit.** *Wide Sargasso Sea* marks with uncanny clarity the limits of its own discourse, and the limit is Christophine, Antoinette's black nurse. She comes from Martinique and, in the novel's taxonomy of characters, is a "good servant" rather than a "pure native", yet she is the first interpreter in the text, the first named speaking subject; she is a commodified person ("She was your father's wedding present to me"), yet the only one allowed to deliver a hard-hitting analysis to Rochester's face, reminding him that it was he who travelled all the way to her house, he who begged her to marry him, and asking what he has done with her money. She declares, "This is free country and I am free woman", yet after the man threatens her with law and order she is driven out of the story without any narrative or characterological explanation: "Read and write I don't know. Other things I know." Spivak says that in the five times she taught the book, students easily stepped over Christophine's Creole dialect at the opening, and no one asked what it might mean. This illustrates a principle: **no perspective critical of imperialism can turn the other into a self**, because the project of imperialism has always already historically refracted what might have been the absolutely other into a domesticated other that consolidates the imperialist self. Christophine is to *Wide Sargasso Sea* what St John Rivers is to *Jane Eyre*: an unfinished tangent.

**Example: *Frankenstein*.** Mary Shelley's novel, by contrast, does not use the axioms of imperialism to organise its narrative. Victor's laboratory is an artificial womb, in which the projects of childbearing and subject making are carried on at once, and his real rival is woman as the maker of children; he refuses to make a female creature because she might become "ten thousand times more malignant than her mate", and her children would propagate a race of devils on the earth. The monster's education in humanity comes from overhearing the instruction of Safie, an "Arabian" woman converted to Christianity, from Volney's *Ruins of Empires*; Safie flees from him when she sees him. In the novel's frame there is a woman who is neither tangential nor encircled: Margaret Saville, the addressee of the letters. She is the irreducible "addressee function", neither responding nor closing the text, so that the frame is at the same time not a frame, and the monster can step out of the text, "lost in darkness and distance". **Conclusion:** Literary criticism cannot reopen the epistemic fracture of imperialism merely by rearranging the curriculum within existing norms; the critic must turn to the archives of imperial governance. Spivak is extending Rhys's most powerful suggestion: that *Jane Eyre* can be read as staging Bertha's self-immolation as the suttee of the "good wife", a suggestion whose force depends on knowledge of the history of how the British government in India legally manipulated widow sacrifice. *The fifth mechanism, the "shifting boundary between text and context", reaches one of its extremes here: the context is no longer literary history but the colonial legal archive; P15 will take up this thread.*

**Geraldine Heng** (1997) pushes the question from racial difference within America to the state structures of the Third World. **Definition:** Third World feminism is a many-headed, unpredictable presence: in some countries it is a national movement with networks and regional branches; in others it is only a kind of "hit-and-run guerrilla feminism", arising spontaneously around particular issues, forming temporary neighbourhood groups, even refusing the name "feminism", or lodging within non-governmental organisations. A feminist theory that wants global application must be prepared to be surprised by these strategies and forms.

**Mechanism: three conditions.** First, historical origins: almost without exception, Third World feminism grew up at the same time and in the same soil as nationalist movements (anticolonial struggles, movements of national modernisation and reform, revivals of religious or cultural nationalism), and between the two there has been sympathy and support, mutual exploitation and unacknowledged contest. Nationalism needs women's issues, not only to mobilise as many groups as possible, but because it needs a vocabulary of self-articulation: "motherland", "mother tongue", "mother culture", "father of the nation", binding land, language, history and people into the emotional core of nationalist ideology; women's emancipation symbolises at once the break with the past, the present in action and the imagined future. Second, the state: early feminism and nationalism used each other, but contemporary feminism must enter a more dangerous oppositional relation with the nation-state, which at its most benign is a fiscal beneficiary of the exploitation of women and at its least benign an active organiser of it. The gross national product of Thailand and the Philippines depends on the sex industry; the Philippines exports sixty thousand female domestic workers to Hong Kong alone, receiving about a billion Hong Kong dollars a year in remittances; the "maid levy" Singapore charges employers is often higher than the maid's own wage. Third, an ambivalence towards modernity: nationalism accepts the technological and economic machinery of modernisation but resists its social and cultural consequences, often equating the "modern" with the "Western"; so merely claiming that a social movement originates in the West is enough to delegitimise it.

**Example: Singapore.** In 1959 the People's Action Party, not yet in power, announced in its election platform, through a speech by the women's leader Chan Choy Siong, a feminist-socialist utopia: equal rights to work for men and women, maternity leave, crèches, reform of the marriage laws that permitted polygamy; the party's history records the contribution of its women's league in the plain language of "use": canvassing door to door, cooking for party members, distributing leaflets. Once in power, Chan Choy Siong was marginalised and never entered the cabinet. The Women's Charter of 1961 was at once a moment of empowerment and of dispossession: it gave women rights that were genuinely crucial at the time, while legally defining a female identity coded around marriage, divorce and relations with children, with no corresponding law defining male identity; thereafter it was widely felt that women "had no more problems", and women's groups long existed only as recreational, charitable and professional associations. In 1983 Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew linked the survival of the nation with the unwillingness of well-educated women to marry and have children. The national airline sold a sexualised Asian femininity as a commodity: the "Singapore Girl" (always a "girl", not a "woman", let alone merely a "flight attendant") was judged by Madame Tussaud's to be the most recognisable airline image in the world; faced with feminist criticism, the airline and its advertising agency instinctively put on nationalist costume, while editors of the mainstream press implied that human rights and women's rights were a Western fashion that weakened Third World competitiveness. In 1987 the government arrested twenty-two people under the Internal Security Act in the name of a "Marxist conspiracy", two of them founding members of the feminist organisation AWARE; AWARE kept silent and thereafter turned to services, counselling and research, its constitution's Article 23(e) forbidding any "political activity", with what counts as political decided by the state at any moment.

**Reading:** This outcome is exactly the mirror image of Lorde. The single-axis feminism Lorde criticises is white women's blindness to race and class, born of privilege; in Singapore, feminism was forced to set aside race, class, ethnicity and sexual orientation and to refrain from analysing state power and transnational collusion: **single-axis here is not a blind spot of privilege but the result of state coercion.** On the other hand, faced with the charge that feminism is a Western import, Third World feminism's strategy is often to put on nationalist dress itself: invoking contemporary Islamic exegetes' rereadings of the Qur'an on the equality of the sexes, or finding an indigenous genealogy for feminism: the priestesses of the pre-Spanish Philippines, the Trưng sisters and Lady Triệu of Vietnam, the founding matriarchs of Singapore, and the "traditionally high status" of women in the region before colonisation. Seen through the spectacles of First World feminism, these strategies may look naive, nativist, even essentialist; but for them an unimpeachable indigenous genealogy must have decisive priority. **Conclusion:** Heng distinguishes two things. Rights *granted* to women by patriarchal authority to achieve nationalist goals, even if of real benefit to women, are not necessarily feminist acts; rights *seized* and practices initiated by women for what they imagine to be their collective good, even if they fit the received descriptions of feminism poorly, are indisputably feminist practices.

The end of the anthology's introduction pushes this question to the borders of feminism itself. If feminism's inspiration comes from the painful particularity of each person's experience, from their right to be heard after centuries of deafness and systematic silencing, how can it name the divided and diverse lives of women around the world, even within a single community, as one undifferentiated identity, in phrases like "a better world for women"? Should women not know better than anyone what it is like to need to speak and be denied a language? Yet to speak for "other" women, those outside the lamplight of the tent of a highly literate literary culture, even to take the platform of history on behalf of their cause, is that not to do what men have always done for women? On 30 March 1997 a woman was stoned to death for being in the company of someone who was not her "relative". If silence is complicity, what form should speech take: the language of rights created by men, or a less abstract construction of the problem, enraged by painful experience and therefore more "feminist"? The introduction's answer is that at its outer edge feminist literary criticism discovers in language and literacy the conditions and limits of its own possibility; beyond that limit it meets its own origin: the pain of being denied speech, and the presumption of being assigned to speak. *"Can the Subaltern Speak?" (1988), to which Spivak points in a note, is the most famous statement of this predicament; P15 will develop it within the postcolonial framework.*

**Limitation:** Returning to feminist criticism as a whole, four limits must be borne in mind. First, Cixous's écriture féminine, in describing the body as a source unsoaked by social codes, slides into the essentialism it opposes; her defenders can cite the distinction between "two bisexualities" and her attribution of écriture féminine to Genet and Joyce as well. Second, the "Anglo-American/French" classification conceals the existence of British socialist feminism, and also conceals a distribution running against the classification: French and British feminists were friendlier to psychoanalysis, American feminists more suspicious. Third, anti-essentialism makes it hard to generalise about "women" at all, and so may make it hard to politicise women as a group. Fourth, the more dimensions identity has, the harder it is for a reading to attend to all of them at once. Gilbert and Gubar's reading of *Wuthering Heights* does not comment on Heathcliff's being described as a racial other ("gypsy", "a little Lascar, or an American or Spanish castaway"), but reads his darkness as Catherine's alter ego or id, set against the Thrushcross Grange presided over by the fair-haired Edgar, which is presented (however ironically) as "heaven", "society" and "reason". **This amounts to conflating racial otherness with the irrational forces of the unconscious**, which might be thought insensitive. This raises a question: is there a `super-reader` equally sensitive to gender, class, race and sexual orientation? In practice, for most readers one issue tends to eclipse all the others; and striving to be a super-reader may produce only blandness and superficiality.

**Conclusion:** P12 has gone through the three steps of Layer 5 internally. First, exposing stereotype and silence: images-of-women criticism showed how images of women in male texts provide role models for socialisation, and how the double image of angel and monster pre-empts the self-definition of women writers. Then reconstructing a tradition: gynocritics rewrote literary history, and écriture féminine attempted another language. Finally, questioning the categories of identity themselves: "woman" was first revealed by Rubin and Irigaray as a product of systems of exchange, then became the focus of contest in the dispute between essentialism and constructionism, and finally was opened up by Lorde, Spivak and Heng as a site where race, class, empire and nation intersect. The third mechanism, "essence ↔ construction", is fully developed here for the first time, and its lesson is not that one side wins. **The choice between essentialism and constructionism is often not a once-and-for-all theoretical verdict but a strategy that changes with the political situation.** Spivak says she "strategically" takes shelter in an essentialism; the indigenous-genealogy strategies Heng describes look essentialist through First World spectacles; and the thoroughgoing constructionist must answer whether "woman", once dismantled, can still act as a political subject.

P13 continues from here. Rubin has already pointed out that the suppression of the homosexual component of human sexuality, and the oppression of homosexuals, come from the same rules and relations as the oppression of women; Cixous's "other bisexuality", Butler's `performativity` mentioned in the editors' introduction, and Lorde's self-description as a Black lesbian all push the question from "woman" towards gender and sexuality themselves. If gender is produced, heterosexuality is produced too. The question thus becomes: how are sex and gender regulated, and how are they disrupted?

## P13 How Are Sex and Gender Regulated, and How Are They Disrupted? Gender Studies and Queer Theory

When one kind of sexuality is called "normal" and another "perverse", is the distinction given by nature, or is it produced, enforced, and in need of constant repetition to be maintained? P13 is the second part of Layer 5, "whose universal? identity and difference". P12 asked whether universal human nature already had a gender; P13 asks whether it was already heterosexual. Following the three steps of Layer 5, this part moves from exposing the history of oppression and the homophobia of mainstream literature, through reconstructing a counter-tradition of gay and lesbian writing, to questioning the stability of all gender and sexual identities, including "normal" heterosexuality.

P13 takes up its thread directly from P12: Rubin had pointed out that the repression of homosexuality and the oppression of women come from the same sex/gender system, Irigaray had described patriarchal society as "hom(m)o-sexuality" among men, Cixous had distinguished two bisexualities, and Lorde had refused, as a Black lesbian, to be taken apart. It also mobilises earlier tools: Saussure's logic of difference in P3 lets heterosexual/homosexual be seen as a pair of differences with no positive terms; Austin's performative utterance in P5 is the prehistory of Butler's `performativity`; of Freud's repression and the uncanny in P6, the one is challenged here and the other reused; the deconstruction of binary hierarchies and the transcendental signified in P7 is applied directly to sexuality; and Foucault's disciplinary power in P10 unfolds in *The History of Sexuality* into the production of sexuality. The third mechanism, "essence ↔ construction", is advanced here from "what is woman?" to performativity; the first, "relation and difference", explains how the term "normal" depends on the marked term; the second, "manifest/latent double reading", reads in Sedgwick and Moon the same-sex desire disavowed within heterosexuality; and the fourth, "domination ↔ resistance", is rewritten by Foucault's productive power.

**Definition: what queer criticism is.** A comparison with feminist criticism helps define the field: just as not all criticism written by women is feminist, books about gay writers or written by gay critics do not necessarily belong to lesbian and gay studies, and books in the field are not written only for gay readers or concerned only with homosexuality. *The Lesbian and Gay Studies Reader* (1993) says that "lesbian/gay studies does for sex and sexuality approximately what women's studies does for gender": it establishes sexual orientation as "a fundamental category of historical analysis and understanding". Like feminist criticism it has social and political aims, above all an "oppositional design": resistance to `homophobia` and `heterosexism`, to the ideological and institutional practices of heterosexual privilege. **Background:** The field became prominent as a distinct field only in the 1990s: Eagleton's *Literary Theory: An Introduction* (1983) and the first edition of Selden's *A Reader's Guide to Contemporary Literary Theory* (1985) say nothing about it. The University of California at Los Angeles already offered a course in lesbian and gay literature in 1976; the British pioneer was the Centre for the Study of Sexual Dissidence, founded in 1990 by Alan Sinfield and Jonathan Dollimore in the English department of the University of Sussex (*Sinfield from P10 appears here in another capacity*); in the same year Sedgwick published *Epistemology of the Closet* and Butler *Gender Trouble*. **1990 was not the beginning of the field, but the beginning of its present disciplinary prominence.** Its terms of reference are fluid, driven by the wish to be as inclusive as possible; the commonest at present is LGBT or LGBTQ (Q for "queer" or "questioning").

### "The Homosexual" as an Invented Species

**Background: Stonewall.** The anthology's introduction opens with a "revolution": a group of gay men, lesbians and drag queens refused to accept the harassment and arrests the New York police had long taken as routine, sparking the Stonewall riots of June 1969. It seemed at the time a small, chance act of defiance, yet it was the first major crack in the crystal palace of a certain social order. That order is what Adrienne Rich calls `compulsory heterosexuality`: if women are compelled to become the reproductive wives of the dominant heterosexual male group, their friendships will be suspect and lesbianism forbidden; if men must act according to the dictates of compulsory heterosexuality, their friendships are equally suspect and male homosexuality forbidden too; those who dare to challenge the system (Oscar Wilde is one example) meet with slander and even violence; and all this is called "normal", while "that" is stigmatised as "perverse", science and medicine being complicit. The gay and lesbian liberation movement intersected in the late 1960s and early 1970s with feminists concerned with sexual and gender identity: for a while the two seemed to share common ground, women and homosexuals alike being objects of oppression by the dominant heterosexual male group; but in other respects they had reasons to diverge. In the 1980s it was discovered that the universality of the category "woman" might conceal differences among women in sexual object choice, sexual practice and psychological identity (some of which might be "masculine"): a masculine woman, for 1970s feminists "male-identified", might be for the gender studies that emerged in the 1980s just one of many possible gender and sexual positions. The work of Rubin, of the historian Alan Bray and of Foucault showed that sexual practices are coded differently in different societies and histories: certain sexual acts between men were common in Greek society of the fifth century BC, and were not "discovered" as the mark of an identifiable "perversion" until the late nineteenth century (according to Foucault); Christianity, lying between the two, probably had much to do with why non-procreative sexual practices were gradually stigmatised.

**Problem: repression or proliferation?** The first volume of **Michel Foucault**'s *The History of Sexuality* (1976; English translation 1978) begins with a possible objection: was not the great proliferation of discourses on sex in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries meant to drive out of reality the forms of sexuality not amenable to the strict economy of reproduction, to ensure population, reproduce labour capacity, perpetuate the form of social relations, in short to constitute a sexuality that was economically useful and politically conservative? His answer: whatever the ultimate aim, the means employed were not reduction but proliferation: a dispersion of sexualities, a strengthening of their disparate forms, a multiple implantation of "perversions". Until the end of the eighteenth century the three great explicit codes governing sexual practices (canon law, the Christian pastoral and civil law) all centred on matrimonial relations: the sex of husband and wife was beset with rules and recommendations, while everything else remained much more confused; "sodomy" had an uncertain status, and children's sexuality was of no concern; breaking the rules of marriage and seeking strange pleasures were equally condemned; acts "against nature" were merely an extreme form of acts "against the law", and the "nature" on which they were based was still a kind of law. The explosion of discourse brought two changes to this system: heterosexual monogamy was spoken of less and less, functioning as a stricter but quieter norm; what came under scrutiny was the sexuality of children, madmen and criminals, the sensuality of those who did not like the opposite sex, who were called upon to come forward and make the difficult confession of what they were. The "unnatural" thus became a specific dimension in the field of sexuality: beneath the figure of Don Juan, the great violator of the rules of marriage, one glimpses an individual driven by the sombre madness of sex: "underneath the libertine, the pervert".

**Mechanism: four operations of power.** When these clusters of disparate sexualities were labelled one by one, was the aim to exclude them from reality? Foucault's answer is that the function of the power exercised here is not prohibition but four operations quite different from simple interdiction. First, `lines of penetration`: the old prohibition of consanguine marriages tried to achieve its end through an asymptotic decrease of what it condemned, whereas the control of children's sexuality since the nineteenth century achieved its end through the simultaneous propagation of its own power and of the object on which it bore: educators and doctors combated children's onanism like an epidemic, constituting these tiny pleasures as secrets so as to discover them, installing devices of surveillance wherever they might appear, making parents and teachers suspect all children of guilt; the child's "vice" was less an enemy than a support, through which power advanced and multiplied its relays. Second, `the incorporation of perversions` and `the specification of individuals`: **in the old civil or canonical codes, sodomy was a category of forbidden acts, their perpetrator nothing more than their juridical subject; the nineteenth-century homosexual became "a personage, a past, a case history, and a childhood, in addition to being a type of life, a life form, and a morphology". "The sodomite had been a temporary aberration; the homosexual was now a species."** Foucault dates the birth of the psychological, psychiatric and medical category of homosexuality to Westphal's famous article of 1870 on "contrary sexual sensations": homosexuality was characterised as a kind of sexual sensibility, a certain way of inverting the masculine and the feminine in oneself, transposed from the practice of sodomy onto a kind of interior androgyny, a "hermaphrodism of the soul". At the same time nineteenth-century psychiatrists gave the various minor perversions strange names in the manner of entomology. The machinery of power aimed not to suppress these aberrations but to give them an analytical, visible and permanent reality: implanting them in bodies, slipping them in beneath modes of conduct, making them a principle of classification and intelligibility. Third, `perpetual spirals of power and pleasure`: medical examinations, psychiatric investigations, pedagogical reports and family controls functioned as mechanisms with a double impetus: the pleasure that comes of exercising a power that questions, monitors, watches, spies, searches out, palpates and brings to light, and the pleasure kindled by having to evade this power, fool it or travesty it. Fourth, `devices of sexual saturation`: the nineteenth-century family was not so much a monogamous conjugal cell as a network of pleasures and powers linked together at multiple points: the separation of parents' and children's bedrooms, the relative segregation of boys and girls, strict instructions about nursing, attention to the dangers of masturbation, the presence of servants both valued and watched; schools and psychiatric institutions too marked out zones of extreme sexual saturation. **Conclusion:** "Modern society is perverse, not in spite of its puritanism or as if from a backlash provoked by its hypocrisy; it is in actual fact, and directly, perverse." One must therefore abandon the hypothesis that modern industrial societies ushered in an age of increased sexual repression. *This is a head-on challenge to the Freudian `repression` model of P6, and a continuation of the disciplinary power of P10: power does not hold down a pre-existing sexuality but produces, classifies and fixes sexualities. The fourth mechanism, "domination ↔ resistance", thereby becomes complicated: if the identity "homosexual" is itself a product of power, resistance in the name of that identity cannot simply be understood as recovering a repressed authenticity.*

**Distinction: the birth of the name.** Barry gives another date: "homosexual" is a medico-legal term first used in Germany in 1869, eleven years before the corresponding word "heterosexual"; **in this sense heterosexuality came into existence as a consequence of the crystallisation of the idea of homosexuality.** *The two dates point to the same moment: Barry records the coinage of the word, Foucault the formation of the medical category. Together they show that in the structuralist logic of difference (the first mechanism, P3) the marked term of an opposition may be named before the unmarked, "normal" term.*

**Example: from the earl to San Francisco.** Gayle Rubin's "Thinking Sex" (1984) gives Foucault's argument social content through history and anthropology. Industrialisation and urbanisation reshaped traditional rural and peasant populations into a new urban industrial and service workforce, and also generated a new sexual system characterised by distinct types of sexual persons, populations, stratification and political conflict, an "erotic speciation". Homosexual behaviour has always existed among humans, but in different societies and periods it may be rewarded or punished, required or forbidden, a passing experience or a lifelong vocation. In some New Guinea societies homosexual activity is obligatory for all males and considered thoroughly masculine, yet these men are not "homosexuals". In 1631 the Earl of Castlehaven was tried and executed for sodomy: from a twentieth-century point of view he clearly had psychosexual problems requiring the services of an analyst; from a seventeenth-century point of view he had deliberately violated the law of God and the law of England, and required the simpler services of an executioner. He had no self-understanding as a particular kind of sexual individual; homosexual self-awareness, gay bars, a sense of group commonality, even the word "homosexual", were not part of his world. By contrast, a modern gay man might migrate from rural Colorado to San Francisco, live in a gay neighbourhood, work in a gay business, and take part in an elaborate experience that includes a self-conscious identity, group solidarity, a literature, a press and a high level of political activity. **In modern Western industrial societies, homosexuality has acquired much of the institutional structure of an ethnic group.** The migration of workers to cities made voluntary communities possible: most large cities of nineteenth-century Western Europe and North America had areas where men cruised for men; by the 1890s there were several cafés near the Place Pigalle in Paris catering to a lesbian clientele; by the late 1970s sexually motivated migration had become large enough to affect American urban politics. Prostitution underwent a similar metamorphosis, from temporary work into the long-term occupation of an outcast group. "The modernisation of sex" has thus generated a continuing system of "sexual ethnogenesis": bisexuals, sadomasochists, transsexuals and transvestites are all in various states of community formation and identity acquisition; "sexualities keep marching out of the *Diagnostic and Statistical Manual* and on to the pages of social history". *Compared with "The Traffic in Women" in P12, this is a turn by Rubin herself: from a gender-centred analysis of kinship to treating sexuality as an autonomous system of stratification; "Thinking Sex", cited by Sedgwick below, is the theoretical statement of this turn.*

### Lesbian Feminism: Woman-Identification and the Continuum

**Background:** Queer theory is not a unified system: there are differences of emphasis between lesbian and gay male theory, and within lesbian theory there are two main lines of thought. The first is `lesbian feminism`, best understood in terms of its origins within feminism: lesbian studies emerged in the 1980s as a kind of subsidiary field of feminist criticism before gaining disciplinary independence. One reading of the academic situation of the 1990s is that feminism had become so successful and so institutionalised that lesbian studies occupied the radical ground feminism had vacated. On this reading, feminism found it hard to accommodate difference and tended to universalise the experience of white, middle-class, urban heterosexual women. The critique began with African American critics, who pointed out that academic feminism, by excluding the voices and experiences of black women, reproduced within itself the unequal structures of patriarchy; bell hooks's *Ain't I a Woman?* (1982) is a famous statement of it (Lorde in P12). Lesbian critics made a similar charge: feminism assumed an essential female identity shared by all women regardless of race, class or sexual orientation. Bonnie Zimmerman, in "What Has Never Been: An Overview of Lesbian Feminist Criticism", attacked this "essentialism", arguing that a "heterosexist perceptual screen" prevented pioneering feminist writing from considering lesbian issues: a feminist critical classic such as *The Madwoman in the Attic* mentions lesbianism only once, in passing.

**Definition: the woman-identified woman and the lesbian continuum.** "Classic" feminism marginalised or ignored lesbianism; the counter-attack was to argue that lesbianism should be seen as the most complete form of feminism. The Radicalesbians group's "The Woman-Identified Woman" (collected in 1973) placed lesbianism at the centre of feminism: lesbians refuse the various forms of complicity with patriarchal exploitation, and are constituted by relations between women which are by definition a resistance to, and a radical reorganisation of, established forms of social relation. The conflict this opened between heterosexual feminists and lesbians was partly eased by **Adrienne Rich**'s "Compulsory Heterosexuality and Lesbian Existence", which introduced the concept of the `lesbian continuum`: a term that includes a range of woman-identified experience running through each woman's life and through history, not simply the fact that a woman has had or consciously desired sexual experience with another woman. It thus refers to a broad range of female behaviour, from the informal networks of mutual support women build in particular professions or institutions, through mutually supportive female friendship, to sexual relationships; Zimmerman comments that the merit of this definition is that it suggests the interconnections among the various ways women bond. **Objection:** Paulina Palmer points out that seeing lesbianism this way has an oddly desexualising effect: it becomes almost a purely political act rather than a sexual orientation, and is thereby "sanitised" and transformed into something else; the corollary of this position is also a moral condemnation of female heterosexuality, seen as a betrayal of women and their interests, attaining completeness only through lesbianism. The two ideas overlap considerably, but both introduce notions of choice and affiliation into questions of sex and gender, so that sexuality is no longer seen as simply "natural" and unchanging but as a construct that can be changed. The anthology's editors also point out that lesbian studies tends more towards separatism than gay male studies, perhaps because lesbians are doubly oppressed as women; Monique Wittig's "The Straight Mind" (1980) and Irigaray (P12) provide its theory, the latter holding that lesbians can exist as lesbians only in a world of their own, separate from patriarchal culture.

**Turn: from transcendental signified to historical construct.** As a result of these critiques the lesbian approach separated from mainstream feminism throughout the 1980s, but it was not until the 1990s that lesbian criticism also rejected the essentialism it could be said to have inherited from feminism. Ten years later, surveying the field again in "Lesbians Like This and That", Zimmerman found that her earlier essay had assumed lesbianism to be a stable category, a `transcendental signified` (P7), a transhistorical constant, whereas it was in fact a late nineteenth-century construct. **The second line of thought**, which Palmer calls `libertarian lesbianism`, broke with feminism and allied itself instead with gay men, seeing itself as part of "queer theory", although the word "queer" in this context had homophobic, abusive origins; these terms (at least as institutionally accepted) date from the "Queer Theory" conference at the University of California, Santa Cruz, in 1990. The key question in choosing between these two alliances is: **in personal identity, which is more fundamental, gender or sexuality?** To choose the latter is to stress lesbianism as a sexuality rather than a form of female bonding or patriarchal resistance; it tends to endorse "experimental" forms of lesbian sexuality, such as sadomasochism and butch-femme role-play. Some, however, argue that one consequence of accepting the umbrella term "queer theory" has been, in the end, to perpetuate the patriarchal pattern of subordinating women's interests to men's. *This question is the practical form of Sedgwick's axiom "sexuality ≠ gender" below.*

**Background: AIDS and the reappropriation of "queer".** In the mid to late 1980s AIDS took many lives in the gay community. The queer theory that emerged around this time was in some respects a response to the epidemic: providing gay men and lesbians with a common term under which to unite, and drawing attention in a more radical way to the issues it raised. **Queer theory took a stigmatising word ("queer" was a term of abuse for homosexuals) and turned it into a badge of pride, turning it back against those who stigmatised.** The change of name also marked a change of analytical strategy: gay theorists began to explore the "queerness" of supposedly "normal" sexual culture itself. *Reappropriating an insulting name as a self-designation corresponds structurally to Butler's "subversive repetition": another repetition of the same word.*

### Performativity: Imitation Without an Original

**Background:** **Judith Butler**'s *Gender Trouble* (1990) argued powerfully against confining lesbian studies within feminism: it deconstructed the very idea of "woman" as an identity, arguing that all gender identity is a performance, a surface substance produced by prior acts of imitation. The anthology's editors, in their headnote, sum up her starting point as an argument with Freud: in Freudian theory lesbianism has no secure ontological status, being only a neurotic imitation, a woman's desire to be a man; Butler uses Freud's own account of how identities are formed to argue that **all gender can be understood as an imitation of an ideal or norm, so that original and imitation cannot be distinguished.** Barry cites her argument in *Inside/Out*: identity categories such as "homosexual" and "heterosexual" tend to be instruments of regulatory regimes, whether as the normalising categories of oppressive structures or as rallying points for a liberatory contestation of that oppression; in this sense the very concept of homosexuality can be said to be part of homophobic discourse. Hence "identity can become a site of contest and revision", and all identity, including gender identity, is "a kind of impersonation and approximation … a kind of imitation for which there is no original". The distinction between the normalised heterosexual "self" and the repudiated homosexual "other" is thereby shaken too: the "other" is both outside us and inside us; self and other are always *implicated* in each other, in the root sense of the word, intertwined and folded together; as elementary psychology shows, what is identified as the external "other" is often a repudiated, and therefore outwardly projected, part of the self.

**Mechanism: stylised repetition.** The essay "Performative Acts and Gender Constitution" (1988), included in the anthology, gives the philosophical genealogy of this view. Philosophers rarely think about "acts" in the theatrical sense, yet they have a discourse of "acts" semantically related to theories of performance: Searle's "speech acts" (*Austin's* `performative utterance` *in P5 is its forerunner*), the "action theory" of moral philosophy, and the phenomenological theory of "constituting" acts in Husserl, Merleau-Ponty and Mead, which has a more radical use, treating the social agent as an *object* rather than the subject of constitutive acts. Beauvoir's "one is not born, but rather *becomes*, a woman" is precisely an appropriation and reinterpretation of this doctrine of constitution. Accordingly, **"gender is in no way a stable identity or locus of agency from which various acts proceed; rather, it is an identity tenuously constituted in time—an identity instituted through a stylized repetition of acts."** Gender is instituted through the stylisation of the body, and must be understood as the mundane way in which bodily gestures, movements and enactments of various kinds constitute the illusion of an abiding gendered self. If gender is instituted through acts that are internally discontinuous, then the "appearance of substance" is precisely that, a constructed identity, a performative accomplishment which the mundane social audience, including the actors themselves, come to believe and to perform in the mode of belief; and the possibility of gender transformation lies in the arbitrary relation between these acts, in the possibility of a different sort of repeating, in the breaking or subversive repetition of that style.

**Mechanism: the body as historical situation.** Merleau-Ponty says the body is "a historical idea" rather than "a natural species", a set of possibilities continually realised; Butler infers that one is not simply a body but, in some very key sense, one *does* one's body, and does it differently from one's contemporaries, predecessors and successors. The word "performative" thus has a double meaning: "dramatic" and "non-referential". But "project" suggests the originating force of a radical will, whereas gender is a project whose end is cultural survival, so "strategy" better suggests that gender performance always takes place under duress: **"as a strategy of survival, gender is a performance with clearly punitive consequences"**; those who fail to "do" their gender right are regularly punished. Precisely because there is neither an "essence" that gender expresses or externalises nor an objective ideal to which gender aspires, the various acts of gender create the idea of gender, and without those acts there would be no gender at all; gender is a construction that regularly conceals its genesis, and its authors are mesmerised by their own fictions.

**Mechanism: binary gender and the heterosexual contract.** To guarantee the reproduction of a culture, the various requirements established in the anthropological literature of kinship place sexual reproduction within a marriage system based on heterosexuality. As Foucault and others have pointed out, linking a natural sex to a discrete gender, and then to an ostensibly natural "attraction" to the opposite sex, is an unnatural conjunction of cultural constructs in the service of reproductive interests. Lévi-Strauss showed how the incest taboo channels sexuality into various modes of heterosexual marriage, and Rubin argued convincingly that the incest taboo produces certain discrete gender identities and sexualities (P12); Butler adds that one way in which this system of compulsory heterosexuality is reproduced and concealed is through the cultivation of bodies into discrete sexes with "natural" appearances and "natural" heterosexual dispositions. **Contemporary gender identities are so many marks or "traces" of residual kinship.**

**Example: the transvestite on the stage and on the bus.** The relation between theatrical and social roles is complex, but one thing is clear: gender performance in non-theatrical contexts is governed by more clearly punitive and regulatory social conventions. The transvestite on stage can win pleasure and applause, while the same transvestite on the seat next to us on the bus can provoke fear, rage, even violence. In the theatre one can say "this is just an act", de-realising the act and maintaining one's sense of reality in the face of a temporary challenge to existing ontological assumptions about gender; on the street or the bus the act becomes dangerous precisely because there are no theatrical conventions to delimit its purely imaginary character. From the standpoint of established categories, one says: but this is *really* a woman (or a man), and the appearance contradicts the reality of gender. **The transvestite not only expresses the distinction between sex and gender but implicitly challenges the distinction between appearance and reality on which much popular thinking about gender depends: if the "reality" of gender is constituted by the performance itself, the transvestite's gender is as fully real as that of anyone who conforms to social expectations.**

**Distinction: expression and performance.** Popular theories of action see acts and gestures as *expressive* of gender, assuming gender to be a substantial core preceding the various acts, the spiritual or psychological correlate of biological sex. If gender attributes are not expressive but performative, these attributes effectively constitute the identity they are said to express or reveal; there is then no pre-existing identity by which an act might be measured, no true or false, real or distorted acts of gender, and **"the postulation of a true gender identity would be revealed as a regulatory fiction."** Gender therefore cannot be understood as a *role* that expresses or disguises an interior "self": against Erving Goffman's view, which posits a self that assumes and exchanges roles in the "play" of modern life, this self is irretrievably "outside", constituted in social discourse, and the ascription of interiority is itself a publicly regulated and sanctioned form of "essence fabrication". Yet people are compelled to live in a world in which genders constitute univocal signifiers: performing one's gender wrongly initiates a set of punishments both obvious and indirect, while performing it well provides the reassurance that there is an essentialism of gender identity after all; and that this reassurance is so easily displaced by anxiety, that culture so readily punishes or marginalises those who fail to perform the illusion of gender essentialism, is itself a sign that on some level there is social knowledge that the truth or falsity of gender is only socially compelled and in no sense ontologically necessitated.

**Objection: performance ≠ free choice.** In summarising Butler, Barry says this opens the way to a "postmodernist" view of identity: identity as a series of roles and positions continually switched among an inexhaustible database of potentialities. Butler's own formulation is more restrained: as public action and performative act, gender is neither a radical choice or project reflecting a merely individual choice, nor imposed or inscribed on the individual, as some poststructuralist displacements of the subject would have it; the body is not a lifeless recipient passively inscribed with cultural codes, but neither does the embodied self pre-exist the cultural conventions that signify bodies. **"The actor is always already on the stage, within the terms of the performance."** Just as a script may be enacted in various ways, the gendered body acts its part in a culturally restricted corporeal space and enacts interpretations within the confines of already existing directives. *The difference between the two formulations is not small: Barry's version stresses fluidity and choice, Butler's stresses compulsion, punishment, and deviation possible only within repetition. Misreading performativity as "gender can be put on at will" is the commonest misunderstanding of the theory.*

**Conclusion: the politics of performativity.** Butler grants that her view can serve a variety of political strategies. She mentions Spivak's argument that feminists need to rely on an "operational essentialism", a false ontology of women as a universal, in order to advance a feminist political programme (*this is another statement of Spivak's "strategically taking shelter in an essentialism" in P12*); Kristeva too suggests using "women" as a political tool without attributing ontological integrity to the term; and Mary Anne Warren's *Gendercide* warns that, in an age when some population policies aim to eliminate the existence of women, declaring that "women do not exist" may be politically risky. Butler's distinction: it is one thing to use the term while knowing its ontological insufficiency, and another to articulate for feminist theory a normative vision that celebrates or emancipates an essence, a nature or a shared cultural reality that cannot be found. As Foucault said of humanist efforts to liberate the criminalised subject, the liberated subject is even more deeply shackled than originally thought. **"There is nothing about femaleness that is waiting to be expressed; there is, on the other hand, a good deal about the diverse experiences of women that is being expressed and still needs to be expressed."** The norm she proposes is not utopian: to acknowledge the existing complexity of gender that our vocabulary invariably disguises, and to let it into dramatic cultural interplay without punitive consequences. Gender is what is put on, invariably, under constraint, daily and incessantly, with anxiety and pleasure; if this continuous act is mistaken for a natural or linguistic given, one relinquishes the power to expand the cultural field bodily through subversive performances of various kinds.

### The Closet and the Homosocial: "Panic" in Heterosexuality

**Mechanism: deconstructing the hetero/homo binary.** Queer theory differs theoretically from lesbian feminism in its heavy reliance on the poststructuralism of the 1980s. One of the main points of poststructuralism is the "deconstruction" of binary oppositions (P7): showing first that the distinction between paired opposites is not absolute, since each term can be understood and defined only through the other, and then that the hierarchy within these pairs can be reversed. In gay and lesbian studies the pair heterosexual/homosexual is deconstructed in exactly this way; Diana Fuss says in her introduction to *Inside/Out* that much current work aims "to question the stability and ineradicability of the hetero/homo hierarchy". **Example: Rock Hudson.** Richard Meyer writes about the film star Rock Hudson, once the epitome of attractive heterosexual masculinity on screen but in fact gay. More disruptive of categories than this fact is that the very qualities that made his image attractive to women were associated with his homosexuality: on Meyer's account, Hudson offered heterosexual women a sexually safe position, one that would accept domesticity without insisting on male dominance; heterosexual male viewers were relieved too, having found a model who could "measure up" without the onerous labour of manliness. Deconstructing the hetero/homo dichotomy in this way has radical implications, since all such distinctions are constructed in the same way, and to challenge one is to challenge the rest.

**Definition: the homosocial.** **Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick**, in *Between Men* (1985), noted that male heterosexual desire is always modelled on another man's desire, always tinged with the `homosocial`; the male bonding that stitches patriarchy together is necessarily homophilic, forming a continuum with homosexuality. The editors draw from this a general finding of gender studies: heterosexuality can be understood as forming a continuum with homosexuality, since ideals such as heterosexual masculinity seem inseparable from an element of "panic", an apotropaic gesture, a turning away from a certain homosexuality that in fact helps construct heterosexuality. *This concept shares its origin with Irigaray's "hom(m)o-sexuality" and Rubin's "traffic in women" in P12: women circulate among men, and the bonds between men are the real structure of patriarchy. Sedgwick's contribution is to bring into the analysis both the suppressed same-sex desire in this structure and the panic about it.*

**Mechanism: the closet.** *Epistemology of the Closet* examines why "coming out", publicly declaring one's homosexual orientation, is not a single, absolute act: one may be out to family and friends, less fully to employers and colleagues, and not at all to one's bank or insurance company. Being "in the closet" or "out" is therefore neither a simple dichotomy nor a once-and-for-all event; different degrees of concealment and disclosure coexist in the same person's life. Nor does sexual orientation itself often make someone a complete outsider, untainted by any patriarchal or exploitative stain: a gay man may be a comfortable tenured academic, in the eyes of a small-town factory worker (gay or not) precisely a privileged insider. **The identity of the subject is necessarily a complex mixture of chosen affiliations, social positions and professional roles, not a fixed inner essence.** *This is Barry's popularised summary of Sedgwick; the introduction to Epistemology of the Closet included in the anthology places its emphasis on the structures of knowledge and binary opposition.*

**Problem: a puzzle.** *Epistemology of the Closet* (1990) begins with a puzzle. One person's sexual activity can be distinguished from another's along very many dimensions (preference for certain acts, zones or sensations, physical types, frequency, symbolic investments, relations of age or power, species, number of participants), yet from the turn of the century on, precisely one dimension, *the gender of object choice*, emerged and has remained the dimension denoted by the now ubiquitous category of "sexual orientation". The hysterical woman, the masturbating child and the various "entomological" sexological classifications Foucault mentions were all new "specifications of individuals"; but why has the category "the masturbator" now entirely lost its power to designate a kind of person, an identity, while "the homosexual became a species" has become ever more real? So the heterosexual became a species too, and humanity has come to be ever more divided between these two species. Sedgwick does not explain the causes of this sudden, radical condensation, but examines its unpredictable consequences.

**Distinction: minoritising and universalising.** While this speciation went on, less stable and less identity-bound understandings of sexual choice also persisted and developed, often in the same people and woven into the same systems of thought. Sedgwick calls the two `minoritizing` and `universalizing` definitions of sexuality: the first sees homosexuality as an issue for a distinct minority population, the second as an issue running through the sexuality of everyone. She thinks there is at present no standpoint from which to adjudicate the "truth" of either; her subject is the performative effects of the self-contradictory discursive field of force created by their overlap, a field never formed in emotional and analytical impartiality, but under the urgent homophobic pressure to devalue one of the two nominally symmetrical options.

**Mechanism: the three steps of deconstruction.** One main line of Sedgwick's argument is deconstructive: categories a culture presents as symmetrical binary oppositions (here heterosexual/homosexual) in fact subsist in a more unsettled and dynamic tacit relation: first, B is not symmetrical with A but subordinated to it; second, the ontologically valorised A depends for its meaning on the simultaneous subsumption and exclusion of B; hence, third, the question of priority between the supposed central and marginal categories of each pair is irresolvably unstable, since B is constituted as at once internal and external to A. *This is exactly Derrida's logic of the `supplement` in P7 applied to sexuality.* **Objection: unstable ≠ ineffective.** But Sedgwick at once warns that understanding these conceptual relations as irresolvably unstable does not mean they are ineffective or innocuous. Barthes predicted that "once the paradigm is blurred, utopia begins", meaning and sexuality being freed from binary prisons; this is at the very least premature. On the contrary, **a deconstructive understanding of these binarisms makes it possible to identify them as peculiarly densely charged sites of potential manipulation**, precisely through their self-contradictory definitions, through double binds. An understanding of their instability has always been available, and has always lent discursive authority to anti-gay as well as gay cultural forces; the oppressive sexual system of the past hundred years was perhaps born and grew precisely amid the most notorious decentrings and exposures. The contest for discursive power can thus be specified as a contest for the material or rhetorical leverage required to set the terms of, and to profit from the operations of, such definitional incoherence. *This is an important correction to a certain deconstructive optimism in P7: exposing the instability of a binary does not automatically bring liberation.*

**Definition: the master term.** Sedgwick argues that the homo/heterosexual definition has been a master term of the past century, as important to the whole of modern Western identity and social organisation (not merely to gay identity and culture) as the more traditionally visible categories of gender, class and race; the chronic crisis of this definition has left an indelible mark on a whole series of binary oppositions: secrecy/disclosure, knowledge/ignorance, private/public, masculine/feminine, majority/minority, innocence/initiation, natural/artificial, health/illness, same/different, active/passive, in/out, sincerity/sentimentality … She concedes that the hypothesis cannot be "tested": gathering examples that common sense would see as unrelated to sexual definition is no good refutation, since the skills needed for the most forceful interpretation are precisely those not valued by the "common sense" of this "epistemologically split culture"; these homologies can only be used, not proved or disproved by a few examples. *This is an open weakness: a hypothesis that cannot be tested by counter-examples has an explanatory power that is equally hard to assess; this is the same type of problem as the question of evidence in Freudian interpretation in P6.*

**Axiom: sexuality ≠ gender.** Sedgwick's second axiom is: **"The study of sexuality is not coextensive with the study of gender; correspondingly, antihomophobic inquiry is not coextensive with feminist inquiry. But we can't know in advance how they will be different."** Opening a space between "sex" (chromosomal sex) and "gender" has been one of feminism's most successful projects (Rubin's `sex/gender system`, P12); but the whole realm modern culture calls "sexuality" (acts, expectations, narratives, pleasures, identity formations and knowledges) can hardly be located on this map. Insofar as it is tied to procreation, it seems as biological and given as chromosomal sex; but as Freud argued and Foucault assumed, the distinctive nature of human sexuality lies precisely in what exceeds procreation, and in this respect "sexuality" may lie even closer than "gender" to the relational, socio-symbolic, constructed pole. Sedgwick quotes Rubin's "Thinking Sex": feminism is the theory of gender oppression, and should not be the privileged site of a theory of sexuality. The two analytical axes are distinguishable, though only minimally, as gender and class, or class and race, are. More sharply, the very concept of gender may contain a heterosocial or heterosexual bias: any analysis of gender must ultimately appeal to the boundary of difference between the genders, which gives relations between the sexes a conceptual privilege.

**Implication: what to learn from feminism.** Antihomophobic inquiry can still benefit from the questions feminism has learned to ask, so long as it does not demand the same answers. First, how oppressions are systematically intertwined, and especially how the same person may, by virtue of the same position, be disempowered in one set of oppressions and empowered in another: a woman who uses her husband's surname marks at once her subordination as a woman and her privilege as a presumed heterosexual. Sedgwick credits socialist feminism and the thought of women of colour (Lorde in P12) with the recognition that oppressions are not all congruent but differently structured, and so must intersect in complex embodiments. Second, raising questions of gender in texts whose subjects are not explicitly gendered: dichotomies such as culture/nature, public/private, mind/body, active/passive may be implicit allegories of relations between men and women (Cixous in P12). **The homo/heterosexual dichotomy fits the template of deconstruction even more neatly than male/female itself**: almost everyone is publicly and irreversibly assigned to one gender from birth, whereas sexual orientation has a much greater potential for rearrangement, ambiguity and representational doubleness, and essentialism of object choice is far harder to maintain than any essentialism of gender.

### Female Masculinity and the Contingency of the "Normal"

**Problem:** What is "masculinity"? If masculinity is not the social, cultural and even political expression of male identity, what is it? **Judith Halberstam**, in *Female Masculinity* (1998), suggests that although we seem to have great difficulty defining masculinity, we have little trouble recognising it, and spend much time and money ratifying and supporting the versions of masculinity we enjoy and trust; and many of these "heroic masculinities" depend absolutely on the subordination of other forms of masculinity. **Far from being an imitation of male identity, female masculinity actually affords a glimpse of how masculinity is constructed *as* masculinity**: female masculinities are framed as the rejected scraps of dominant masculinity, so that male masculinity may appear to be the real thing. **Mechanism:** If "dominant masculinity" appears as a naturalised relation between male identity and power, there is little point in looking to men for the contours of its social construction; masculinity becomes legible precisely where it leaves the white middle-class male body. Arguments about "excessive" masculinity tend to focus on black bodies (male and female), Latino or working-class bodies, while "insufficient" masculinity is often projected onto Asian or upper-class bodies; these stereotypical and mutable constructions of masculinity mark out the process by which masculinity becomes dominant masculinity in the sphere of the white middle-class male. So she looks for Elvis in the female impersonator Elvis Herselvis, for the political contours of male privilege in the lives of cross-dressing European aristocratic women of the 1920s, and describes differences of masculinity by comparing butch lesbians with female-to-male transsexuals.

**Example: Bond and M.** In *GoldenEye* (1995) James Bond performs as usual his suave action-adventure hero, relying as usual on a pile of gadgets (a retractable belt, a bomb disguised as a pen, a laser watch), but the film is curiously lacking in believable masculine power: his boss M is a distinctly butch older woman who calls him a dinosaur and rebukes him as misogynist and sexist; Moneypenny accuses him of sexual harassment; his male partner betrays him. Masculinity here is mainly *prosthetic*, having little to do with biological maleness and functioning more as a technical special effect; it is M who performs masculinity most convincingly, and she does so by exposing the falseness of Bond's performance. And the slightly effeminate gadget scientist who gleefully demonstrates the new equipment to Bond is called Q, the agent of *queer*. **M's female masculinity and Q's gay masculinity display the utter dependence of dominant masculinity on minority masculinities.** Take away his toys, and Bond's masculine performance has little to support it.

**Example: the tomboy and "I don't care".** Tomboyism usually refers to an extended childhood period of female masculinity, and is generally thought to be more tolerated than the corresponding cross-identification in boys; but Halberstam points out that this tolerance lasts only until puberty. With the onset of adolescence the full force of gender discipline comes down on girls: if adolescence is for boys a rite of passage (lavishly celebrated in Western literature as the `Bildungsroman`, P12) leading to some social power, for girls it is a lesson in restraint, punishment and repression, in which the tomboy instincts of millions of girls are remodelled into docile femininity. In Carson McCullers's *The Member of the Wedding*, twelve-year-old Frankie Addams is "an unjoined person who hung around in doorways, and she was afraid"; she tries to change her name to "F. Jasmine Addams" and asks why changing one's name is against the law; Berenice answers, "Because things accumulate around your name", and concedes that "we all of us somehow caught". McCullers's pessimism lies in the fact that language, the most basic "order of things", forces non-members into memberships they cannot fulfil. Halberstam refuses this futility: Frankie's rebellion is not opposition to the law but indifference to it; she simply does not care. **Power may inhere in different forms of refusal**, without taking the futile path of what Foucault calls "saying no to power"; she also borrows what Sedgwick calls `nonce taxonomies` (the classifications we use every day to make sense of the world, so useful that we fail to notice them), arguing for the production of new taxonomies that intervene in the dominant processes of naming and definition.

**Example: the bathroom problem.** If thirty years of feminist theory have thoroughly unsettled the notions that anatomy is destiny, that gender is natural and that male and female are the only options, why do we still live in a world that assumes "either male or female"? Halberstam goes into the women's restroom at Chicago's O'Hare airport, and no sooner is she in the stall than someone knocks: "Open the door, security!" Once again she has been taken for a man or a boy; as soon as she speaks, the guard mumbles an apology and leaves; on the return journey, at Denver airport, the same thing happens again. Jess in Leslie Feinberg's *Stone Butch Blues* and Remedios, the Filipino bus conductor in Nice Rodriguez's story, face the same situation: Remedios would rather hold it in for half a day; she was once thrown out of a women's restroom and beaten by a bodyguard; her father told her to be careful, and she understood that "careful" meant swinging her hips and sticking out her chest when entering the women's room. The accusation "you are in the wrong bathroom" says two things: your gender does not match your sex; and single-sex bathrooms are only for those who clearly belong to one category. In the women's room it is mainly codes of gender that operate, in the men's room codes of sexuality. Halberstam also criticises Marjorie Garber's conception of the transvestite as a "third space" that breaks the binary: **every attempt to break a binary with a third term ultimately tends to stabilise the other two.** A deeper paradox is that precisely because almost no one fully fits the definitions of male and female, the two categories derive their power from their very impossibility; the elasticity of "man" and "woman" guarantees their longevity. She therefore proposes replacing the compulsory gender binary with "gender preference": people could come out as a gender just as they come out as a sexual orientation.

**Objection: texts or "real" queer lives?** The sociologists Arlene Stein and Ken Plummer criticise queer theorists for rarely venturing beyond texts, playing with free-floating signifiers in texts while ignoring the "real" queer lives materially lived around the world. Halberstam replies that social-science methods such as questionnaires often merely prove, in matters of sexuality, what their designers already believe, and that there is no research on sex that is not text-based: ethnographers of sex study texts too, and social historians collect textual evidence; text-based methods tend towards abstraction, sociological research towards over-rationalising sexual behaviour. She argues for a "scavenger" `queer methodology` that combines methods often seen as conflicting and refuses the compulsion of disciplinary coherence. *This dispute echoes, in the study of sexuality, the dispute between the two perspectives of cultural studies in P11.*

**Michael Moon** pushes the contingency of the "normal" into desire itself. **Mechanism: disorientation through mimesis.** Since René Girard's critique of the "object theory" of desire, a view has developed that what is primary in the formation of desire is not the supposed object of desire but mimesis; Mikkel Borch-Jacobsen says that desire "is mimetic before it is anything else", that desire "is not oriented by pleasure but (dis)oriented by mimesis". Moon accordingly proposes `sexual disorientation`: sexuality is less *oriented* by the gender, age, race, class, body type or dress of the object than *disoriented* by mimesis. **Example: the Mapplethorpe controversy.** The controversy over the Corcoran Gallery's cancellation of a Robert Mapplethorpe photography exhibition showed that far more people react strongly to images of male-male sadomasochism than identify themselves as gay male sadomasochists.
