**Reading: formal revision and literary history.** *Their Eyes Were Watching God* is itself a signifying structure, a structure of intertextual revision, because it revises key tropes and rhetorical strategies of precursor texts by Du Bois and Toomer, among others. From this Gates derives a proposition about literary history: **African American literary history is characterised by a threefold formal revision**: Hurston (1937) revises Du Bois (1911); Morrison revises Ellison and Hurston; Ellison revises Wright, and Ishmael Reed revises both; black writers read and critique other black texts as an act of rhetorical self-definition: **"Our literary tradition exists because of these precisely chartable formal literary relationships."** There are several modes of formal parody. One fills a fairly exact repetition of a given narrative or rhetorical structure with incongruous or absurd content, as T. Thomas Fortune's "The Black Man's Burden" signifies upon Kipling's "The White Man's Burden": "What is the Black Man's Burden, / Ye hypocrites and vile, / Ye whited sepulchres / From th' Amazon to the Nile?" Another suggests a structure by *not* coinciding with it, evoking similarity through dissimilarity: formal repetition and inversion through variation are central to jazz, as in the comparison of John Coltrane's rendition of "My Favorite Things" with Julie Andrews's "vapid" original. Ellison's account of his relation to Wright amounts to a definition of narrative signification or critical parody: he had no wish to attack the limits of Wright's vision, but he wanted to write his own books, which would themselves be implicit criticisms of Wright's, just as all the novels of a given historical moment make up an argument about the nature of reality; and replying to Irving Howe he said that protest is an element of all art, and can appear in a novel as a *technical assault* on the styles that went before. This critical parody of repetition and reversal is what Gates calls `critical signification`, and it is also his metaphor for literary history.

**Example: from *Native Son* to *Invisible Man*.** The signifying begins with the titles: Wright's *Native Son* and *Black Boy* both connote race, self and presence, and Ellison tropes them with *Invisible Man*: "invisible" is an ironic response, by absence, to the presence presupposed in "black" and "native", while "man" suggests a more mature and powerful status than "son" and "boy". Ellison signifies upon Wright's distinctive naturalism with a complex modernism; Wright's protagonist, voiceless until the very end and capable only of "reacting", is rewritten by Ellison as a nameless protagonist who has nothing but his voice, who shapes, edits and narrates his own story, uniting action with the representation of action. In Wright's novella "The Man Who Lived Underground", Fred Daniels stumbles in the darkness of the sewers upon the body of a dead baby, his fate signified by what he trips over; Ellison repeats this scene of underground discovery, but has his protagonist burn the papers through which he had let others define him. **By explicitly repeating and reversing the key images of Wright's fiction, Ellison reveals that naturalism is merely a hardened convention of representation for the "Negro problem", perhaps itself part of the problem.** Gates connects this relation with Bakhtin's `double-voiced discourse` (P9): in "hidden polemic", another's speech act remains outside the boundaries of the author's speech, yet is implied or alluded to and shapes the author's speech from within; the author's discourse, while directed at its referential object, mounts a polemical attack on another speech act on the same topic, and the two utterances clash on the very ground of the referent.

**Example: *Mumbo Jumbo*.** Reed's third novel, *Mumbo Jumbo* (1972), is a book about writing itself. Its title signifies upon the ethnocentric Western name for all black religious rites and black languages: Webster's glosses the phrase as needlessly involved and incomprehensible language, gibberish, and the *Oxford English Dictionary* says its origin is unknown; yet anyone who speaks Swahili knows that it comes from the common greeting *jambo* and its plural *mambo*, meaning roughly "What's happening?". The force at the centre of the novel, "Jes Grew", takes its name from Topsy's "I 'spect I grow'd" (which James Weldon Johnson used to describe the anonymity of the composition of black spirituals), and it is searching for its text; the principal speaking character, Papa La Bas, has a name combining two of Esu's names, meaning in French "over there", linking "there" (Africa) with "here"; he is the figure of the critic who pursues the text and reads its signs. Gates argues that Reed, through the art of pastiche, criticises an idealism in African American literature: a transcendent, whole, self-sufficient and plentiful black subject, a black signified "always already" there, which could be represented in the received forms of the West, like water drawn from a deep well, which can be poured into a glass, a cup or a jar and yet remains water. **For Reed, so-called "black experience" cannot be imagined as fluid content poured into pre-existing static containers; it is the signifier that shapes and defines each signified.** Reed's short poem "Dualism: in ralph ellison's invisible man" figures history as a caged animal: the speaker at first thinks he stands outside history and can watch it through the bars, then discovers that he is inside it, and that it is hungrier than he had imagined. The poem signifies upon the `double consciousness` of Du Bois's *The Souls of Black Folk*: "this sense of always looking at one's self through the eyes of others … One ever feels his twoness,—an American, a Negro; two souls, two thoughts, two unreconciled strivings; two warring ideals in one dark body." Ellison rewrote this trope in the epilogue of *Invisible Man* ("only in division is there true health"), and Reed's poem says: **these are only figures, rhetorical constructions, not some predetermined reality; to read them literally is to be fooled by the figure, like the signified Lion.**

**Distinction: native theory and the "Black Aesthetic".** Gates's theory of Signifyin(g) differs in direction from the "Black Aesthetic" of the Black Arts movement of the 1960s. Parker notes that Gates rejects the idea of a Black Aesthetic, proposing instead a critical theory inscribed within the black vernacular tradition that in turn shapes the African American literary tradition; Gates also warns that a tradition defined first by "ethnicity" cannot be given an artificial unity by a descriptive formalism, and that expecting authors to be responsible spokespersons for their group overburdens "ethnic" writers, leading to demands for the ideological "correctness" of works and to a prescriptive criticism that demands loyalty and conformity. Here lies the anti-essentialism of the theory of Signifyin(g): **a tradition is constituted not by a shared black essence but by chartable repetitions and differences between texts**: an application of the first mechanism, "relation and difference", to literary history, which also makes the second step of Layer 5, "reconstructing a tradition", and the third, "questioning identity", happen at once in Gates. *Gates himself says his analysis of Ifa divination is only roughly analogous to Bloom's use of the Kabbalah; compared with Bloom's theory of misreading, driven by an Oedipal "anxiety of influence", Gates stresses the pleasure Reed and Hurston take in the "play" of tradition.*

**Objection: whose theory explains the "native"?** Parker cites Sandra Adell's discussion of the efforts of Houston Baker and Gates to establish a specifically African American criticism, the gist of which is that the more the black theorist writes in the interests of blackness, the more Eurocentric he becomes. Gates's theory of Signifyin(g) does draw everywhere on the vocabulary of Western theory: Saussure's signifier and signified, Bloom's master tropes, Bakhtin's double-voiced discourse, Kristeva's "signifier itself", a Derridean refusal of the transcendental signified; and he himself says he had to step outside his culture and translate it into a new discourse before he could see its critical potential. This can be read as a weakening of nativeness, or as yet another practice of Signifyin(g) itself: appropriating the master's tropes through repetition and difference. Lewis Nkosi says that the further African artists go in exploring their own traditions, the closer they come to the European avant-garde; Parker adds that European modernist avant-garde art itself depended on African art. **Influence is never one-way; the "native" and the "Western" take shape in exchange with each other.**

### Borderlands, Mestiza Consciousness and Linguistic Terrorism

**Background:** **Gloria Anzaldúa**'s *Borderlands/La Frontera: The New Mestiza* (1987) is a multilingual work that interweaves her personal experience of growing up on the US-Mexico border with the history of that land, the forcible dispossession by European Americans of lands held by Hispanics, its topics ranging from geography to language and sexuality. She was a contributor to *This Bridge Called My Back*, and *Borderlands* became a key text of "border theory". The text itself moves between languages: Spanish passages often go untranslated, and readers must cross the border themselves.

**Mechanism: cultural tyranny and the "Shadow-Beast".** She recalls an old photograph of herself at six: standing between her parents, holding her mother's hand; to this day she is not sure where she found the strength to leave the source, the mother, the family, her land and people; she was the first in six generations to leave the Valley. There is a rebel in her she calls the `Shadow-Beast`: it refuses to take orders from outside authorities, refuses even the commands of her own conscious will. Culture forms our beliefs, and **culture is made by those in power, men: men make the rules and laws, women transmit them**. Mothers and mothers-in-law tell their sons to beat wives who disobey, who are "big-mouthed", who gad about, who expect husbands to help with the children and housework, who want to be something other than housewives; culture and the Church insist that women are subservient to men; the rebellious woman is a "bad woman", the woman who will not give herself up for men is selfish. In her culture there used to be only three directions for a woman: to the Church as a nun, to the streets as a prostitute, or to the home as a mother; today a few have a fourth choice: entering the world through education and a career and becoming autonomous persons, "a very few". Because women create flesh-and-blood bodies in the womb, bleed every month without dying, and are in tune with nature's cycles, women are feared; according to Christianity and most major religions, woman is carnal, animal, closer to the undivine, and so must be "protected", protected from herself. **Woman is the stranger, the other, the fragment of man's nightmare he has recognised, his Shadow-Beast.** Culture (read: men) claims to protect women, but in fact fixes them in rigidly defined roles.

**Example: *mita' y mita'*.** There was a girl near her home whom the townspeople called "of another kind", a woman six months of the year and a man the other six; they called her *mita' y mita'*, "half and half", neither one thing nor the other, a strange doubling, a frightening deviation of nature. Anzaldúa says that, contrary to certain psychiatric dogmas, the "half and half" does not suffer from a confusion of sexual identity or gender; **what we suffer from is an absolute despot duality that says we are able to be only one or the other**; like other queers, she is "two in one body", an internal union of opposite qualities, the "sacred marriage" (*hieros gamos*). For a lesbian of colour, the ultimate rebellion she can make against her native culture is through her sexual behaviour: she breaks two moral prohibitions at once, sexuality and homosexuality. "As a lesbian, raised Catholic, indoctrinated as straight, I made the choice to be queer (for some it is genetically inherent)." When she taught at a college in New England, the presence of a few lesbians threw the more conservative heterosexual students and faculty into a panic; in a discussion with them, a student said: "I thought homophobia meant fear of going home after a residency." How apt, she thought: **homophobia is the fear of going home**, the fear of being abandoned by the mother, the culture, *la Raza*, for being unacceptable, faulty, damaged. *This pun rewrites the homophobia of P13 from the fear felt by heterosexuals into a fear felt by homosexuals themselves: the excluded internalise the exclusion.*

**Problem: who betrayed whom?** The Mexican curse on Malinali Tenepat (Malintzin), called *la Chingada* and reviled as the whore who sold her people to the Spaniards, is in Anzaldúa's view the worst kind of betrayal: it makes us believe that the Indian woman in us is the betrayer, so that we Indian and mestiza women police, mutilate and condemn the Indian in ourselves. She says again and again: "Not me sold out my people but they me." For three hundred years dark-skinned women have been silenced, gagged, caged, bound into servitude by marriage, sterilised in the twentieth century, colonised by the Spaniards, the Anglos and their own people. She will neither glorify her native culture nor leave it: she will defend her race and culture when non-Mexicans attack them, but she knows the sicknesses of her culture; she abhors the way culture cripples women and makes caricatures of men as machos; she understands why the sisters with more Anglo blood glorify the values of the culture of colour more stubbornly, to offset the extreme devaluation of it by white culture, which is a legitimate reaction, **but she will not glorify those aspects of her culture that have injured her in the name of protecting her**. What she wants is an accounting with all three cultures, white, Mexican and Indian: if the way home is denied her, she will stand and claim her space, making a new culture, `una cultura mestiza`, with her own lumber, her own bricks and mortar, her own feminist architecture. She is a turtle: wherever she goes she carries "home" on her back.

**Example: how to tame a wild tongue.** As the dentist cleans all the metal out of her mouth, he says, "We're going to have to control your tongue", and adds that he has never seen a tongue so strong or so stubborn. She thinks: how do you tame a wild tongue, train it to be quiet, bridle and saddle it? She remembers being caught speaking Spanish at recess and getting three licks on the knuckles with a ruler; trying to tell her Anglo teacher how to pronounce her name, and being sent to the corner for "talking back": "If you want to be American, speak 'American.' If you don't like it, go back to Mexico where you belong." Her mother was ashamed of her speaking English with a Mexican accent: to get a good job, she told her, you have to speak good English. At Pan American University all Chicano students were required to take two speech classes, whose purpose was to get rid of their accents. **"Wild tongues can't be tamed, they can only be cut out."** The first time she heard a Puerto Rican woman and a Cuban woman say the feminine plural "we", *nosotras*, she was shocked: she had not known the word existed; Chicanas, men and women alike, use the masculine plural *nosotros*: "We are robbed of the female being by the masculine plural. Language is a male discourse."

**Definition: border language.** Many Latinos accuse her: "*Pocho*, cultural traitor, you're speaking the oppressor's language by speaking English, you're ruining the Spanish language." Chicano Spanish is regarded by purists as deficient, a mutilation of Spanish. But it is a border language that developed naturally: for a people who are neither Spanish nor living in a country where Spanish is the first language, a people living in a country where English is the reigning tongue but who are not Anglo, a people who cannot entirely identify with either standard (Castilian) Spanish or standard English, what recourse is left but to create their own language? A language that is neither Spanish nor English but both, a "forked tongue". She lists the eight languages she speaks: standard English, working-class and slang English, standard Spanish, standard Mexican Spanish, North Mexican Spanish dialect, Chicano Spanish (with regional variations by state), Tex-Mex, and Pachuco (*caló*); which one she speaks to whom depends on who the other person is: Chicano Texas Spanish with her mother and older relatives, Tex-Mex with her siblings and Texan peers, switching within the same sentence or even the same word; only English with most California Chicanas; Pachuco is the language of rebellion of the zoot-suiters, rebelling against both standard Spanish and standard English, a secret language that adults and outsiders cannot understand. She also describes phonetic and lexical features of Chicano Spanish: the merging of adjacent vowels, the dropping of intervocalic consonants (*lado* becomes *lao*), and the retention of "archaisms" that have disappeared from standard Spanish (*semos*, *truje*, *haiga*), because the Chicanos of the South Texas Valley were geographically isolated from other Spanish speakers, and the colonisers of the Southwest came mostly from Extremadura and Andalusia. *This list is a living illustration of Bakhtin's heteroglossia in P9: a person's "language" is layered through and through with social dialects; it also echoes the claim of Deleuze and Guattari in P8 that there is no mother tongue, only a seizure of power by a dominant language.*

**Mechanism: linguistic terrorism.** "We're your linguistic nightmare, your linguistic aberration, your linguistic mestisaje." Chicanas who grew up speaking Chicano Spanish have internalised the belief that they speak "poor Spanish": that it is illegitimate, a bastard language; and because we have internalised how the dominant culture uses our language against us, we use linguistic differences against each other. Chicana feminists often approach one another with suspicion and hesitation; she later understood why: getting close to another Chicana is like looking into a mirror, and we are afraid of what we will see there: shame, inferiority. Chicanas feel uncomfortable speaking Spanish with Latinas, fearing their censure, because the latter's language was never outlawed in their own countries; and among themselves Chicanas speak English at parties and conferences, while fearing that the other will think them "agringadas", Americanised, so that "we oppress each other trying to out-Chicano each other", vying to be the "real" Chicana. **There is no one Chicano language, just as there is no one Chicano experience.** Her conclusion: "Ethnic identity is twin skin to linguistic identity—I am my language. Until I can take pride in my language, I cannot take pride in myself"; and as long as she has to accommodate English speakers rather than having them accommodate her, her tongue will be illegitimate. The "terrorism" here is not rhetorical exaggeration: the systematic devaluation of a form of language, through schools, workplaces and the mutual surveillance of compatriots, is internalised as speakers' shame about themselves. *This thread will reappear in P15 in the debate between Ngũgĩ and Achebe over whose language to write in.*

**Distinction: names and peoplehood.** "If you asked my mother, 'What are you?' she would say, '*Soy mexicana*.'" Between them, *mexicanos* refers not to Mexican citizens, not to a national identity, but to a racial identity; being Mexican is "a state of soul". When they call themselves "Spanish", it is as a linguistic group, and also a "copping out", forgetting their predominant Indian blood; when they call themselves "Hispanic" or "Latino", they link themselves to the other Spanish-speaking peoples of the Western Hemisphere, and this too is a copping out (a note says that "Hispanic" is a term designated by the US government to make it easier to handle them on paper, and that the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo of 1848 "created the Mexican American"); "Mexican American" signifies being neither Mexican nor American; *mestizo* is used to affirm both Indian and Spanish ancestry, though, she notes, we hardly ever own our Black ancestry; "Chicano" refers to a politically aware people born or raised in the United States. She writes: **not until the mid- to late 1960s, when Cesar Chavez united the farmworkers (1965), *I Am Joaquín* was published (1967), and La Raza Unida Party was formed in Texas (1970), did Chicanos know they were a people**; with that recognition, with a name and a language reflecting that reality, the fragments began to come together. *Within five years, a strike, a poem and a party appeared one after another.* This is the most direct illustration of constructionism: a "people" exists as a people only at the moment it acquires a name and an organisation; in the opposite direction from Haney López's Mexicans turning from a nationality into a race, this time the naming is done by the named themselves.

**Limitation:** In Anzaldúa's text the vocabularies of constructionism and essentialism coexist. On the one hand, she "chose" to be queer, declares that she will carve her own face and make her own gods out of her entrails; on the other, she speaks of the Mexican in her as something in her very system, says that Chicanos are seventy to eighty per cent Indian, roots her Chicana identity in the history of resistance of the Indian woman, and appeals to Aztec goddesses and the myth of the "sacred marriage". Fishkin's note explains "mestiza consciousness" as an identity that fuses Anglo, Spanish, Mexican and Indian cultures, languages and gene pools; yet the very concept of "mixture" still presupposes "pure" components that have been mixed. This tension can be read as inconsistency, or as a strategy: for a people deprived of its history, narratives of ancestry are a political resource; but it also carries the risk Zimmerman warned of in P13, of romanticising one border identity as the symbol of every transgression. **Conclusion:** Anzaldúa's situation makes concrete the "dismantling" that Lorde refused in P12: as a woman she resists the patriarchy of Mexican culture, as a Chicana the racism of Anglo culture, as a lesbian the homophobia common to both, as the daughter of a working-class family exclusion from education, and as a speaker of a border language the purism of two "standard languages"; **these oppressions cannot be handled separately, one by one, because they act on the same tongue.**

### Heterogeneity, Hybridity, Multiplicity: Against the Essentialising of Ethnicity

**Example: breaking tradition.** **Lisa Lowe**'s "Heterogeneity, Hybridity, Multiplicity: Marking Asian American Differences" (1991, published in the first issue of the journal *Diaspora*) opens with two poems. In Janice Mirikitani's poem a second-generation Japanese American (*nisei*) mother describes the rebellion of her third-generation (*sansei*) daughter: the daughter repudiates Japanese American culture and its particular notions of femininity, reminding the mother that she too once repudiated her elders, rebelling against her more traditional first-generation (*issei*) mother. The mother in the poem wants to open the room where women dress in the dark, yet admits she does not know what is in her daughter's room. The crises that shaped the second-generation speaker (the internment camps, frightening voices of madness) are unknown and unheard to the third-generation daughter. In Lydia Lowe's poem a young Chinese American woman supervises an older Chinese woman in a garment factory: when the closing bell rings, the boss has her search everyone's bags; she has miscounted the old woman's piece tickets, shorting her six zippers; the old woman squints at the cheque in her hand as if watching a magic trick she cannot follow; the young woman cannot look up, and can only apologise in Cantonese. The structure of the factory places the English-speaking young woman above the Cantonese-speaking older woman; the economic relations of capitalist society compel the young supervisor to discipline her elder, and she is deeply ashamed that her conduct cannot express the respect traditionally owed to elders. Both poems thematise a "break in tradition", but the second shows a stratification that is not only generational but also one of class and language.

**Problem: why is the generational narrative essentialising?** In many Asian American novels, the loss or transmission of an "original" culture is often represented as a family narrative, as a generational conflict between a China-born first generation and an American-born second generation: Louis Chu's *Eat a Bowl of Tea* (1961) allegorises in a father-son relationship the difference between "native" Chinese values and a new "Westernised" Chinese American culture, while Kingston's *The Woman Warrior* and Tan's *The Joy Luck Club* (1989) can be read as versions of this generational pattern re-represented as relations between mothers and daughters. Lowe's argument is that **interpreting Asian American culture only through master narratives of generational conflict and filial relation essentialises it**: it obscures the specificity and incommensurability of class, gender and national differences among Asians, reduces ethnic cultural politics to a struggle between first and second generations, and displaces (and privatises) differences within the community into a familial opposition. To avoid this "vertical" model she introduces the "horizontal" relations represented in Diana Chang's short story "The Oriental Contingent": two young women, Connie and Lisa, both avoid talking about their Chinese backgrounds, because each is terribly afraid that the other is "more Chinese", with a more "authentic" connection to the original culture; Connie decides that Lisa's ease is "Chinese-Chinese" and feels herself "a failed Chinese"; it turns out that Lisa, born in Buffalo and adopted by non-Chinese parents, reproaches herself even more harshly than Connie for being "inauthentic": the only time she feels Chinese, she says, is when she is embarrassed at not being Chinese enough, which is itself a thoroughly Chinese reflex she would give anything to be rid of. **Both have internalised a definition of "Chineseness" as pure and fixed, so that any deviation is constructed as lesser, lower, shameful.** The narrator of *The Woman Warrior* asks: "Chinese-Americans, when you try to understand what things in you are Chinese, how do you separate what is peculiar to childhood, to poverty, insanities, one family, your mother who marked your growing with stories, from what is Chinese? What is Chinese tradition and what is the movies?"

**Background: Asian American heterogeneity.** From the perspective of the dominant culture, Asian Americans may be constructed as others different from European Americans; but from the perspective of Asian Americans, they may be even more different from one another: they differ in distance from an "original" Asian culture and in generation, and the original cultures themselves (Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Filipino, Indian, Vietnamese) differ; they are born in the United States or born in Asia, have two Asian parents or are of mixed race, are urban or rural, refugee or non-refugee, communist-identified or anti-communist, fluent in English or non-English-speaking, educated or working class. The historical contexts and compositions of successive waves of immigration differ too: the first Chinese immigrants of 1850 came from four villages in Guangdong province, with a male-to-female ratio of about ten to one, mostly of peasant origin; recent Chinese immigrants come from Hong Kong, Taiwan, the People's Republic of China or the Chinese diaspora of Southeast Asia, and are more often educated, middle-class men and women. After arriving in the United States, few Asian immigrant cultures remained enclosed communities: they intermarried with other ethnic groups, lived next to them, worked on the same production lines. From the late nineteenth to the early twentieth century, Asian immigrants were regulated by exclusion acts and quotas, measures that depended on racist conceptions of Asians as a homogeneous group (a note lists the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, the act of 1924 barring Japanese immigration, the act of 1934 limiting Filipino immigration to fifty persons a year, and the internment during the Second World War of 120,000 Japanese Americans, two-thirds of them American-born citizens); the contemporary myth of the "model minority" and informal quotas against Asians in university admissions are present-day versions of this homogenisation, a myth that constructs Asians at once as grinds "unlike us" and as good assimilators "like us".

**Mechanism: the creation of hegemony.** Lowe's argument has two purposes, both ultimately aimed at disrupting the current hegemonic relationship between "dominant" and "minority" positions. The first is to stress the heterogeneity of Asian Americans in order to destabilise the dominant discourse's construction of them as a homogeneous group; if minority immigrant cultures are constantly changing in composition, form and signifying practice, then the "majority" or dominant culture with which they stand in continuous relation is likewise unstable and unclosed. Here she invokes Gramsci (P9): hegemony refers not only to the process by which a dominant group exerts influence, but equally to the process by which minority groups organise to contest any particular hegemony; any particular hegemony, even if temporarily dominant, is never absolute or conclusive. **Hegemony is not only the political process by which one group constitutes itself as "one" or a "majority" so that "minorities" are defined as "others", but equally the process by which various other positions can ally and constitute a new majority, a "counter-hegemony".** What Gramsci calls the `subaltern classes` are by definition "not unified", their history fragmentary and episodic, recognisable only in retrospect; they transform and disrupt the apparatus of a particular hegemony in their own non-equivalent ways, together constituting a "new historical bloc". California's growing and changing ethnic minority population is such an example, where hegemony means not "the maintenance of hegemony" in the usual sense but the often neglected "creation of hegemony". Heterogeneity therefore has two political consequences: society is no longer conceived as two camps overdetermined by numbers, but as many non-equivalent groups, of which Asian Americans are only one; and Asian Americans can make explicit group demands based on their particular histories of exclusion, while this "non-closure", which reveals rather than conceals differences, opens political lines of alliance with labour unions, other racial and ethnic groups, gay and lesbian and feminist groups. *In a note Lowe lists as a view she opposes a certain New Historicist use of Foucault according to which all "subversion" is ultimately "contained" by the dominant ideology (the debate over "subversion and containment" in P10), siding instead with Williams and with Laclau and Mouffe: the social is an open and uneven field of competing articulations.*

**Objection: the risks of identity politics.** The second purpose is to open a dialogue within Asian American discourse. "Asian American identity" as an organising tool provides a concept of political unity that enables various Asian groups to understand their unequal situations and histories as related; building "Asian American culture" is also crucial. But essentialising Asian American identity and suppressing differences of national origin, generation, gender, party and class carries several dangers: it underestimates the differences and hybridities among Asians, **inadvertently supporting the racist discourse that constructs Asians as "all alike"**; it accepts the dominant logic of the binary schema that organises heterogeneous racial and ethnic diversity into "one" and "other"; it reproduces the same subordination internally: when the discourse generalises Asian American identity as male, women become invisible, and when Chinese are presumed to be the model for all Asians, other Asian groups are neglected; and it displaces differences between men and women, workers and managers within the community into a false opposition between "nationalism" and "assimilation": Asian American feminists who criticise Asian American sexism are branded "assimilationists" who betray Asian American "nationalism". **Even an identity established to refute the dominant culture's stereotypes remains bound by, and overdetermined by, the dominant culture's logic.** Binary constructions always privilege the first term and subordinate the second (P7); what Lowe proposes is a different conception of difference, one that takes seriously the conditions of heterogeneity, multiplicity and non-equivalence.

**Background: Fanon's critique of nationalism.** Lowe draws on Fanon's *The Wretched of the Earth* (1961), a book cited in the 1960s as a manifesto of nationalist identity politics, which, reread in the 1990s, became a source of serious critique of nationalism (the Fanon of P6 appears here as a political theorist). Fanon argues that the challenge facing any movement to dismantle colonialism is to establish a new order that does not reproduce the social structures of the old regime: it must avoid the simple assimilation of the emerging group into the roles and positions of the dominant culture (which would only be a caricature of the old colonialism), and must be equally wary of an uncritical nativism or racialism that appeals to essentialised notions of precolonial identity. His most striking move is to see bourgeois assimilation and bourgeois nationalism as **one and the same logic**, both reproducing the structures of cultural domination: the nationalism of a neocolonial government easily twists into racism, regionalism, separatism, or the ethnic dictatorship of one tribe or regional group over others; the national bourgeoisie replaces the colonisers while the socio-economic structure remains unchanged; and these separatisms, these "micro-nationalisms", are themselves legacies of colonialism: "By its very structure, colonialism is separatist and regionalist. Colonialism does not simply state the existence of tribes; it also reinforces them and separates them." **Nativism and assimilationism are not opposites but similar logics articulating the old order.** Lowe adds that the category of "nation" often erases differences between men and women as well, and that feminist theory has gone furthest in theorising multiple inscription and positionality: an Asian American subject is never purely and solely "ethnic"; she always has a particular class, gender and sexuality, and acknowledging these differences does not weaken the group but provides greater political opportunity for alliance with groups based on other dimensions of oppression. *The first mechanism here takes a political form: nationalism and assimilation, seemingly opposed, are in fact two positions in one structure. This thread leads directly into the postcolonial criticism of P15.*

**Reading: from opposition to heterogeneity.** The attacks on Kingston by Frank Chin, Ben Tong and others were framed as nationalist criticism of an "assimilationist" work: *The Woman Warrior* is almost the only "canonised" work of Asian American literature, appearing in the Modern Language Association's series of teaching guides alongside *Don Quixote* and the *Inferno*. Chin not only accuses Kingston of exoticising Chinese American culture, but argues that she has "feminised" Asian American literature, weakening Asian American men's ability to counter white racist stereotypes: Kingston and Tan exaggerate the patriarchal structures of Chinese history, making Chinese society appear more misogynist than European society. Lowe, like Elaine Kim, sees this debate as a symptom of the tension between nationalist and feminist concerns in Asian American discourse: **it is not a dispute between nationalism and assimilationism but one between identity and heterogeneity**: Chin and others insist on a fixed masculinist identity, which Kingston, Tan and feminist critics such as Shirley Lim and Amy Ling repeatedly question by representing differences among women and criticising sexism in Chinese culture. Just as Fanon pointed out that certain nationalisms obscure class, Asian American feminists point out that Asian American nationalism obscures gender; the very figure that opposes nativism to assimilation may itself be a colonialist image, used to displace the challenge of heterogeneity or subalternity into the charge of "assimilationism" or "anti-ethnicity". In *Eat a Bowl of Tea* this opposition is allegorised in strictly masculine terms: the father, Wah Gay, wants his son Ben Loy to submit to Chinese tradition and paternal authority; the son is forced into an arranged marriage, and, sexually active before it, finds himself impotent after it: at the nativist Chinese pole he cannot find erotic pleasure, while at the assimilationist American pole he has great sexual freedom; the novel's resolution lies in a third, "Chinese American" option: only after the couple move elsewhere, away from the father, can he enjoy erotic pleasure with his Chinese wife. Lowe sees this as an early masculinist version ending in an Oedipal resolution: **perhaps only in retrospect can one see that the opposition is itself a construction, allegorising the dialectic between the articulation of an essentialised ethnic identity and a context of heterogeneous differences.**

**Example: the beauty parlour and the Great Wall.** *The Joy Luck Club* re-represents generational conflict among women and across multiple sites, neither privileging nor centring any one resolution: Ying-ying St. Clair complains that her daughter listens only to her Sony Walkman, her cordless phone and her important husband, while the daughter, Lena, thinks her mother superstitious and domineering; after her mother's death, Jing-mei goes to China to meet the two daughters her mother had been forced to abandon, and as the Polaroid develops she sees that together the three of them look like their mother: a utopian belief in recovering the past and coinciding with the mother; and in the beauty parlour, the American-born Waverly thinks that treating her mother to a fashionable hairstyle is a generous gift, while the China-born Lindo takes it as evidence that her daughter is ashamed of her mother's looks, and smiles what she calls her American face, the face Americans think is Chinese. The scene marks not only a generational separation but differences of class and culture: for a country mother who escaped poverty only by marrying the son of a somewhat more respectable family in a neighbouring village, an expensive beauty parlour is a pointless luxury; for the mother, female identity consists in a daughter's deference to her elders, while for the daughter it consists in economic independence, economic equality with men, the ability to speak her own desires, and middle-class styles of female beauty. **The privileged mother-daughter trope makes differences such as class- and culture-specific definitions of gender invisible.** Peter Wang's film *A Great Wall* (1985), by contrast, questions the binary of native and assimilated through its very form: the camera shuttles back and forth between Beijing and Northern California, in a continuous cinematic "migration"; neither pole is a pure origin: a Chinese youth who has just sat the university entrance examination is handed a bottle of Coca-Cola by his scholar father, village children crowd around the only television to watch a Chinese opera singer imitate Pavarotti, Chinese students learning English recite the Gettysburg Address; Lili, the daughter in Beijing, learns from her American cousin that it is wrong to read other people's letters, and her mother retorts that Lili is not "other people" but her daughter, and asks what this "privacy" is supposed to be; when Lili explains that "privacy" cannot be translated into Chinese, her mother accuses her of wanting to hide things from her own mother and of using a Western word to deceive her; at the end the two families play a lively game of touch football on the ancient, immovable Great Wall. The Great Wall is itself a monument showing that even ancient China was not "pure", but coexisted with the "foreign barbarians" it was built to keep out. *The image of the Great Wall thus stands opposite Anzaldúa's "borderlands": a wall imagined as sealing off inside from outside is in fact a place where exchange happens.*

**Conclusion: migratory ethnicity and strategic essentialism.** Lowe concludes with a nomadic or migratory model of ethnic identity: the production and practice of Asian American culture are nomadic, unsettled, taking place in travel between cultural sites and in the polyphony of heterogeneous and conflicting positions. **The grouping "Asian American" is not a natural or static category but a socially constructed unity, a situationally specific position assumed for political reasons.** It is "strategic" in Spivak's sense, "a strategic use of positivist essentialism in a scrupulously visible political interest" (P12): one can use ethnic signifiers of identity such as "Asian American" to contest and disrupt the discourses that exclude Asian Americans, while revealing their internal contradictions and slippages, so as to ensure that these essentialisms will not be appropriated and proliferated by the very apparatus we seek to undermine. She does not advocate abolishing Asian American identity, and stresses that emphasising difference alone could endanger the hard-won unity of Asian American politics over the previous two decades; she even argues that **the freedom of the 1990s to explore the hybridities concealed beneath the desire for identity was made possible precisely by the context of a forcefully articulated essentialist politics**: just as the articulation of a desire for identity depends on a fundamental horizon of difference, the articulation of difference dialectically depends on a socially constructed and practised notion of identity.

**Background: two thresholds.** **Robert Dale Parker**'s *The Invention of Native American Literature* (2003) represents a group of newer scholars who rely more on contemporary critical methods than on traditionalist assumptions about Native cultures. He distinguishes two thresholds: one in the literature, where the volume of Native literature has become large enough for critics to move beyond stale generalisations about rediscovered identity, eloquent simplicity, nonlinearity, orality and the like; one in the criticism, where the field has established its own texts and increasingly takes part in the theoretical debates of the humanities. The "invention" of the title has two senses: the creation *of* Native literature, how it began historically; and the creating done by Native literature, the ideas it invents, *inventio* in the rhetorical sense of finding one's topics. He uses the word "invention" to suggest provisionality, ongoing process and construction, against the view that Native art is the natural and necessary expression of Native identity: that view assumes Native identity to be ahistorical, static and absolute, whereas in fact it has always been produced, by Native people and by others as well: **after all, without non-Indians, no one could conceive of "Indians" as a category.** He traces four topics to which Native writing keeps returning: the threatened masculinity of young men, orality, poetics, and the renegotiation of Native cultures' estrangement from "authority" as the dominant culture understands it; for example, the restless young men with "nothing to do" in two novels of the Depression era, caught in an often misogynist cultural myth: contact with European Americans stripped Native men of their traditional roles without stripping women of theirs in the same way.

**Objection: is there an "Indian aesthetic"?** Many critics argue that Native writing has an aesthetic different from that of non-Native writing: for example, that Silko's *Ceremony* (1977) is cyclical rather than linear, in keeping with a Native nonlinear view of time; Paula Gunn Allen made this argument famously in *The Sacred Hoop*, and Kimberly Blaeser, in an elegant essay, sums up Native writing in a list like a prose poem: nonlinear telling, the interweaving of this world and the other world, crossing the boundaries of genre, the circle rather than the line as aesthetic form, the refusal to give stories endings, the writing of reality rather than of literature. Parker thinks this mostly comes down to cliché. To a reader of Woolf, Faulkner, Borges or Angela Carter, or earlier of Cervantes, Swift or Sterne, Silko's commitment to nonlinear plot, however much it defines *Ceremony*, will not seem distinctive for its nonlinearity as such; the aesthetic Blaeser describes is practised by more non-Native than Native writers, and does not necessarily suit all Native writers. The deeper problem is logical: **in narrative, nonlinearity never exists independently of linearity**; even if the cyclical or nonlinear is seen as the negation of the linear, each partakes of and defines the other. The dichotomy in narrative theory between "story" and "plot" (P2, P4), which he prefers to call "what is told" and "the telling", applies equally to (and equally distorts) all narratives, Native or not. Hertha Dawn Wong points out that nonlinearity has been claimed as a feature both of Native autobiography and of feminist autobiography; it also plays an important role in Cixous's `écriture féminine` (P12), and Cixous herself acknowledges that male writers write it too.

**Mechanism: form has no cultural specificity.** Parker borrows from communication theory the "fallacy of technological determinism" (the belief that a technology, the printing press, the railway, radio, necessarily produces a particular cultural consequence, whereas in fact the consequences vary with the way the technology is used) to explain literary form: **the novel, autobiography, free indirect discourse, parallelism and repetition do not necessarily carry a predictable cultural meaning**, even though we read back onto forms the cultural contexts we have already associated with them. Navajo prayer has much to do with parallel structure ("My feet restore for me, / My limbs restore for me, / My body restore for me …"), but parallel structure does not necessarily lead to Navajo prayer; if we deny this plasticity of form, we limit our chances of reading how a particular tradition *uses* the form. Sherman Alexie's "Song of the Stick" varies the rhythms of the songs of the "stick game" popular in his region; in another context, a non-Indian or Indian writer choosing a similar form would evoke different associations; the form itself carries no cultural determinants outside the context through which we read it, even though that context makes the form of his poem very "Indian" indeed. **Parker therefore reads the "Indian" in Indian writing historically rather than formally: he offers formalist readings, but reads form historically, not treating form as a transhistorical container of essentialist identity.** He invokes Derrida's critique of Lévi-Strauss's "A Writing Lesson" (P7): Lévi-Strauss wanted to separate oral cultures sharply from literate ones, defending orality in anticolonial form as a special quality of Native peoples tragically disappearing under the colonial impact; Derrida sees this wish as **ethnocentrism disguised as anti-ethnocentrism**: the assumption that oral discourse lacks the complexity of written discourse is precisely the typical assumption of those who romanticise oral cultures. Adell's point about the Black Aesthetic has the same structure: Native identity cannot be conceived apart from contact and exchange between Native and non-Native cultures; before that there could be no concept of "Indians" at all, so the idea of an "Indian aesthetic" depends on non-Indians, just as the concept of "Western" culture gains its illusory coherence from the world it tries to expel. This does not mean that there is no Indian (or European) aesthetic, but that determining what it is runs into a recursive difficulty.

**Distinction: the inelegant exception.** The poet and anthologist Duane Niatum says he has a bone to pick on this question: there is no Native aesthetic recognisable as having principles different from the standards of Western European and American artists, and claiming that there is encourages formulaic, prescriptive responses and stifles the reader's imagination. Yet analysing a poem about a storm by the English poet Ted Hughes, he says there is "one exception": a Blackfeet, Navajo or Swinomish writer, *if* well versed in the traditions of his or her ancestors *and* caring enough about those values to fuse them into his or her art, *might* respond to the storm in a more humble and open way. Parker thinks this "inelegant" exchange ("exception", "if", "might") is exactly right, more trustworthy than any elegant formulation, any "well wrought urn" to hold an Indian aesthetic: **there is no specific Native form, but there are tendencies and topics**, at least among writers with the knowledge and the desire to weave their writing into Native traditions. *"Well wrought urn" alludes to the title of Brooks's New Critical classic* The Well Wrought Urn *(P2).* This resembles the debate in African American literature: the classic formulations of the Black Aesthetic in the 1960s were often more measured than what their critics left to cultural memory: Hoyt Fuller defined the Black Aesthetic as a system for isolating and evaluating those works of black artists that reflect the special character and imperatives of black experience, and never said that all black works of art have this function; Julian Mayfield said he could not, and would not, define his Black Aesthetic, nor let anyone else define it for him, and Don L. Lee said that to define the Black Aesthetic completely would automatically limit it; many theorists of the Black Arts movement saw the Black Aesthetic as a programme for the future rather than a description of existing black writing. Thomas King, for his part, laments that in discussing Native literature we try to imagine that city-raised full-bloods, ranch-raised mixed-bloods, reservation-raised quarter-bloods, Indians adopted by white families, Indians who speak their tribal languages and Indians who speak only English all share some racial common denominator, when of course, he says, we know there is none.

**Implication: the aesthetic and the political are inseparable.** Parker insists that his motive for studying Native literature is aesthetic and literary. New Critics and their followers often disguised political judgements as aesthetic ones, pretending to write politics out of criticism; some who study neglected writing, out of urgent social motives, have tried in turn to pry aesthetic questions out of criticism, unwittingly letting conservative readers believe that non-canonical works are not interesting as art. He holds that the politics and the aesthetics of Native writing are not the same, but not separable either: **we read for the political and the aesthetic, reading the rhythms and resonances of each as part of the rhythms and resonances of the other**; a criticism that pursues the social without regard to the aesthetic, in Spivak's phrase, degenerates into "information retrieval". The pleasures he finds are mostly the same as those found in canonical writing (McNickle's rhythmic reticence, Young Bear's lyricism, Joy Harjo's plainness and anaphora, Louise Erdrich's finely wrought metaphors, Thomas King's wistful, intimate irony), and one of his aims is to recover the extraordinary "everydayness" of Native writing: the pleasure in the habitual, in continuity and the beauty of daily life, what Young Bear and others repeatedly call "being". He also reflects on his own position: as a white scholar, he would rather people treated his work with extra scepticism; but just as his failures cannot be reduced to his whiteness, reducing the insights of Native scholars to their Native identity belittles the work it takes to reach those insights. To write *about* a people or its literature is not to write *for* them, still less to speak *on behalf of* them: Elizabeth Cook-Lynn says that the assumption that a Native poet speaks for the tribe is one of the heaviest burdens on contemporary American Indian poets, an assumption that, in her view, is not only unwise but probably impossible, and surely arrogant. *This is the form the question of Spivak's "Can the Subaltern Speak?" in P12 takes in critical practice: "representation" means both "portraying" and "speaking for", and confusing the two is exactly where the critic's risk lies. Parker's notes also mention this essay specifically.* In Robert Allen Warrior's words, Native studies is still too preoccupied with narrow questions of identity and authenticity, devoted to proving why something or someone "is Indian"; **Parker's attention is not on *whether* or *why* someone or something is Indian, but on *how* they are Indian.**

**Limitation:** Anti-essentialism still has an edge in Native studies, because the pressure to essentialise remains strong there; but it also has opponents. In a note Parker mentions Craig Womack's *Red on Red: Native American Literary Separatism* (1999), which defends essentialism and implies that non-Native critics cannot make useful contributions to the discussion of Native literature; Parker does not accept this argument, but concedes that the often ugly history of white writing about Native people gives us reason to take Womack's view seriously. This is the form taken in ethnic studies by the political cost of anti-essentialism that Barry describes in P13: when a group's land, language and culture were once taken away by outsiders' definitions, outsiders now declaring that "they never had a fixed essence anyway" can sound like the last step of dispossession. Lowe's answer is strategic essentialism; Parker's is to replace "whether" with "how"; Womack's is to refuse to change the subject.

**Conclusion:** The authors of P14 push the same proposition from different directions: **race and ethnicity are fabricated, but what is fabricated is real.** Haney López dismantles biological race in the law while insisting that social race decides fates; critical race theory shows that in a society already organised by race, "not seeing race" means letting race go on working without being named; Morrison and Fishkin turn "whiteness" from an unnamed norm into a construction requiring explanation, showing that white identity depends on the black presence it excludes; Gates reconstructs from within the vernacular tradition a tradition constituted by repetition and difference rather than a shared essence; Anzaldúa bears on one "forked tongue" the oppressions of race, gender, sexuality and language at once; Lowe and Parker refuse to treat "Asian" or "Indian" as identities with fixed content, yet each retains identity, one as political strategy, the other as historical process. The three steps of Layer 5 are here not successive stages but simultaneous tensions: exposing silence requires a silenced "we", reconstructing a tradition requires a continuous "we", and questioning identity questions precisely this "we". The third mechanism, "essence ↔ construction", which reached performativity in P13, here meets its most material form: hair, skin, blood and legal presumptions; the fourth mechanism shows that the languages of resistance (colour-blindness, nation, identity) can likewise be appropriated by the dominant, or reproduce the structures of domination in the hands of the resisters.

P15 goes beyond national borders from here. Almost every thread of P14 already points to empire: the anthology's editors say that although ethnic studies is sited in the United States, its existence is a product of the transnational processes of colonialism, slavery and immigration; Haney López's Mexicans became a race only after the annexation of 1848, and Anzaldúa says that Chicanos have undergone 250 years of Spanish/Anglo colonisation; Lipsitz lists "conquest and colonialism" among the sources of whiteness, and Morrison says that South America, England, France, Germany and Spain all took part in an "invented Africa"; Fortune's "The Black Man's Burden" signifies upon Kipling's imperial apologia "The White Man's Burden"; Lowe, through Fanon, points out that nativism and assimilation are both continuations of colonial logic. If the "whiteness" of American literature depends on a disavowed Africanist presence, does the canon of English literature (Jane Austen's estates, Yeats's Byzantium, "English" itself taught in classrooms as universal culture) also depend on a disavowed empire?

## P15 After Empire, How Is the Canon Reread? Colonial, Postcolonial and Transnational Studies

When the order of a novel's country house is sustained by a Caribbean plantation mentioned only in passing, and when a discipline taught in the name of "universal human nature" serves in every corner of an empire as the yardstick of civilisation, what is it that the canon disavows? In whose language, and in what forms, should the colonised write themselves? And does "postcolonial" really mark the end of colonialism? P15 is the fourth and last part of Layer 5, "whose universal? identity and difference". Layer 5 widens its scope in the order "gender → sexuality → race → empire": P12 asked whether universal human nature already had a gender, P13 whether it was already heterosexual, P14 whether it was already white, and P15 asks whether it was already European. The three steps appear once more. Exposure: the stereotypes of Orientalism and the silence of *Mansfield Park*. Reconstruction: Ngũgĩ's African languages, Brathwaite's "nation language", "the empire writes back". Questioning: Bhabha's hybridity, and Loomba's and McClintock's dismantling of the very word "postcolonial".

P15 inherits a great deal. Most directly from P14: the "invented Africa" in which, Morrison says, South America, England and France all took part; Lowe's point, made through Fanon, that nativism and assimilation are one and the same logic; Anzaldúa's "linguistic terrorism". In P12 Spivak had already read Bertha's self-immolation in *Jane Eyre* as the widow-sacrifice of the colonial legal archive, leaving the question of "Can the Subaltern Speak?" to be taken up here. The history of the discipline of English in P1 (English born as a substitute for religion) acquires a global dimension here, and Bourdieu's thesis in P11 that education reproduces class becomes, in the colonial school, education reproducing empire. Foucault's discourse and power in P10 is the methodological source of Said's Orientalism; the hegemony of P9 explains why empire was chiefly "cultural rather than constitutional", and Macherey's "silences of the work" is the model for Said's reading of Austen; Derrida's *différance* in P7 together with Freud's disavowal, fetish and uncanny in P6, and Lacan's "camouflage", make up Bhabha's conceptual tools. All five mechanisms reach the end point of Layer 5 here. The first, "relation and difference", appears as the Orient as the West's "underground self"; the second, the "manifest/latent double reading", completes in Said's reading of *Mansfield Park* the chain that runs from Freud (P6) through deconstruction (P7), Macherey (P9) and the fault-line (P10); the third, "essence ↔ construction", unfolds in the critique of "authentic traditional culture"; the fourth, "domination ↔ resistance", runs from Gramsci (P9), New Historicism and cultural materialism (P10) and cultural studies (P11) to Bhabha's mimicry; and the fifth, the "shifting boundary between text and context", moves a Caribbean island from the background of a novel to its centre.

**Background:** Postcolonial criticism emerged as a distinct category only in the 1990s: neither the first edition of Selden's *A Reader's Guide to Contemporary Literary Theory* (1985) nor Jeremy Hawthorn's *A Concise Glossary of Contemporary Literary Theory* (1992) mentions it; it became widespread through the influence of books such as Spivak's *In Other Worlds* (1987), Ashcroft and others' *The Empire Writes Back* (1989), Bhabha's edited *Nation and Narration* (1990) and Said's *Culture and Imperialism* (1993), while Gates's edited *"Race," Writing, and Difference* (1986), though it did not use the term, was an important related collection. Barry begins from its challenge to the liberal humanism of P1: if great literature has timeless and universal significance, cultural, social, regional and national differences are demoted or ignored; Hardy's "Wessex" is often said to be a canvas for exploring universal aspects of the human condition, and his novels are seen not as regional, historical, male, white or working-class novels, but simply as "novels". **Whenever a work is claimed to have universal significance, white, Eurocentric norms and practices are smuggled in as the universal, and everything else is relegated to a subsidiary, marginal position.** Its genealogy can be traced to Fanon's *The Wretched of the Earth* (1961): the first step for a colonised people in finding a voice and an identity is to reclaim its own past, since colonial powers had dismissed the precolonial era as a precivilised void, and both black and white children were taught to think that history, culture and progress began with the arrival of the Europeans; the second step is to erode the colonialist ideology through which that past had been devalued. On this account Said's *Orientalism* (1978) can be said to inaugurate postcolonial criticism in the strict sense. The anthology's editors come at it from the other end: not from a critical creed but from an institution, "English".

### "English" as an Imperial Institution

**Background:** The editors title their section on postcolonial studies "English Without Shadows". They begin by retelling a commonplace in a defamiliarising manner: what is called "English" is nothing more than the writing in a dialect of the south-eastern part of an island off the west coast of Europe, which in the late nineteenth century replaced the "classics" (the literature of two Mediterranean peninsulas from more than two thousand years earlier) as the texts of cultural training for young English professional men; Homer, Aeschylus and Cicero gave way to Shakespeare, Milton, Pope and Wordsworth. **Had this substitution occurred in an ordinary country, it might not have mattered much; it occurred at the centre of a global empire, and so "English" became an extremely powerful global cultural institution.** In the age of empire, English as a language provided the political and economic lingua franca for vast stretches of the world, and English as an institution provided a set of "supposedly universal" ideals of proper living; at the same time, people's lives were changed and their bodies moved: Africans enslaved and transported to the Caribbean and North America formed a "counter-reality" in the cruellest contrast with the gentle values that the English tradition cultivated. The editors choose their words carefully: English itself was not the imperial enterprise, but it was certainly used to create a more "cultured", one might also say more docile, colonised class able to help administer the empire; and it is precisely for imperial reasons that it long held a central place in literature departments in many parts of the world. They call this a cultural misrecognition, "mistaking the local for the universal": this is the global form of the "universal human nature" of liberal humanism in P1, and the imperial version of Bourdieu's point in P11 that education legitimates a particular culture as universal culture.

**Mechanism:** Empire created an "imperial frontier", the line of contact between colonisers and colonised, where mutual admiration and adoration were as plentiful as mutual fear and resentment. On one side of the frontier stand Forster's *A Passage to India* and Kipling's *Kim*; on the other, Jean Rhys's *Wide Sargasso Sea* and Jamaica Kincaid's *A Small Place*. Once English could no longer present itself as a treasury of good values and decorous style (because those values were linked to imperial violence by metonymy rather than metaphor, and that style was the result of the forcible displacement of other forms of language, whose only misfortune was that their speakers had smaller guns or none at all), scholars began to notice that many great works of English literature promoted beliefs about other regions and peoples, from Shakespeare's Caliban to Charlotte Brontë's Mrs Rochester, beliefs that created the cultural preconditions for the work of empire. Said saw this promotion as part of a larger process of discursive construction; Bhabha and *The Empire Writes Back* turned to the complex interface between colonisers and colonised, where parody and mimicry are as plentiful as domination; and Paul Gilroy's *The Black Atlantic* (1993) left behind demarcations between nations or ethnic groups to turn to transnational, transregional cultural flows: from the Caribbean to New York to London, black culture pays no heed to traditional literary boundaries.

**Objection:** The editors go on to point out that the early anti-imperialist thinking of the field has itself been rethought by scholars influenced by structuralism, feminism and poststructuralism. Pioneers such as Du Bois and Fanon often appealed to unproblematised concepts of ethnic identity, or to ideals of a traditional "people's culture". Later thinkers point out that racism and ethnic nativism share the same ideological formation; that it is a mistake to assume the existence of ethnic identities where shifting and temporary settlements of kinship are more common; and that opposing a more "authentic" traditional culture to imperial or neocolonial domination only reduces complex histories of cultural change to inaccurate folkloric myths, and mistakes certain "quaint tribal" customs for origins without history. Feminists add that there is no ethnic identity without the coercive constraint and channelling of women's reproductive capacities along the lines of blood families and clans, and that the cult of national cultural identity covers over internal fissures of gender and sexual domination: the perspective of P12 intersects here with the postcolonial question. Poststructuralists go further: all supposedly stable equations between place, ethnicity and national political institutions are imaginary constructions, which displace displacement itself, replacing a history of permanent migration and dislocation with an ontologised image of home, a "native ground" on which falsely pure ethnic groups can authenticate themselves. **This is the sharpest form of the third mechanism in Layer 5: not only "whiteness" and "Europeanness" are constructions, but so is the "nativeness" that resists them.** P16 will question this radicalisation of constructionism from another direction.

**Distinction:** Du Bois was the first to formulate `two-ness`: being at once American and black, loyal to a country and yet a victim of its prejudice against minorities. In Fanon, two-ness reappears in another guise: the traveller from the colonial periphery to the imperial centre who, out of a sense of the inferiority of native culture, takes imperial culture as his own (the theme of *Black Skin, White Masks* in P6). And for a new generation whose immigrant roots do not conflict with being "at home" in an imperial centre such as Britain, two-ness gives way to parallel cultures and multiple belonging, with no one identity more standard than another. Linguistically this means not the "Creole **or** English" Fanon saw, but "Creole **and** English".

**Conclusion:** Hence the meaning of the title. If one source of empire was the national parochialism that taught only one's own national literature, and the new ethnic, postcolonial and international criticism shows that **all national literatures cast shadows, and are therefore always shadowed by their others, from Caliban to Mrs Rochester to Beloved in *Beloved***, then "English without shadows" is an illusion. English should be reconceived as a knowledge project bounded by national and linguistic frontiers. The literature department of the future that the editors envision would be at once national, international and non-national; students would be as familiar with African literature as with English literature, and would learn neither false universal values nor accurate but narrow national traditions, but the complex realities of difference. *They themselves mock this, in parentheses, as an "imperial shadow": the new plural English is once again proposed as a "model".*

**Example: documents of the imperial idea.** The historian **C. C. Eldridge**'s *The Imperial Experience* (1996) compresses the history of this "imperial idea" into a series of quotations. His material shows that a sense of mission, a sense of duty and pride in overseas achievement ran through the whole nineteenth century. In 1828 William Huskisson told the House of Commons that England had sown the seeds of freedom, civilisation and Christianity in every corner of the globe, carrying with it its language, its free institutions and its system of laws; in 1850 the *Edinburgh Review* put it more bluntly: the nobler task was to spread over a newly created world "the laws of Alfred, the language of Shakespeare, and the Christian religion"; the literary canon stands here beside law and religion as one of the three gifts of imperial export. The Colonial Secretary Earl Grey said that by acquiring colonies Britain had taken on a responsibility it could not shed; Lord Carnarvon, Colonial Secretary in 1878, described the vast population of India as sitting, like children, in the shadow of doubt, poverty and sorrow, looking up to England for guidance. **Comparing the ruled to children: this is the same grammar by which patriarchy compares women to children in P12, and the core metaphor of colonial "paternalism".** Carlyle, for his part, set the English two tasks in world history: to conquer more than half of this planet "for the use of man", and then to share the fruits of conquest constitutionally.

**Example: poetry and the novel.** Two of Eldridge's literary observations are crucial for Said below. First, Tennyson's political poems show the evolution of the imperial idea: "Hail Briton!" of 1833 still begins by saying that England's greatness lies "not" in an imperial power that could stretch from the ruined walls of Delhi to Quebec, whereas after 1870 he repeatedly revised his earlier work to add a more explicit imperial dimension, and a manuscript of 1886 ends with a blessing on the Empress-Queen. Second, and more important: **it is often assumed that the absence of strident jingoism in the early and mid-Victorian period meant indifference to empire, but in fact empire penetrated even the serious domestic novel.** India intrudes into Austen's *Sense and Sensibility*, Charlotte Brontë's *Jane Eyre* and Gaskell's *Cranford*, to say nothing of Thackeray's *Vanity Fair*; the West Indies are present in *Mansfield Park* and *Jane Eyre*; Australasia figures prominently in Dickens's *Great Expectations* and *David Copperfield*, in the latter of which New South Wales is where the Peggottys prosper and Mr Micawber becomes a colonial magistrate. In these novels empire is sometimes mere background colour or light relief, a convenient device for getting characters on and off stage, a place of exile or rebirth, a utopia where even the unfortunate can prosper. "A convenient device for getting characters on and off stage": the point Eldridge passes over lightly, in a historian's voice, is exactly what Said will press: is a place that merely provides "convenience" really only background?

**Background: Little Englanders and the colonial remedy.** Eldridge also reminds us that the imperial idea did not always advance triumphantly. At the end of the eighteenth century Britain suffered two blows: the loss of the American colonies, and Adam Smith's attack on the old colonial system in *The Wealth of Nations* (1776). With the rise of free trade, the Manchester School saw colonies as a burden on the treasury, and Goldwin Smith, Regius Professor at Oxford, asked in *The Empire* (1863) what use there was in maintaining the connection, since the colonies did nothing for us and we did nothing for them; Trollope even hoped that Australia would one day follow the path of the United States. Yet a new justification soon replaced mercantilism: empire was used as **a remedy for the social ills of the mother country**. After Malthus's theory of population (1798), surplus population and surplus capital were seen as sources of crisis; in 1812 Southey called on Britain to become the hive of nations and send out its swarms; Wordsworth, in Book IX of *The Excursion* (1814), likened the ocean to the air through which the swarms leave the hive; Coleridge called colonisation Britain's imperative duty; Mill declared in his *Principles of Political Economy* (1848) that colonisation was "the best affair of business" in which the capital of an old and wealthy country could engage. By the 1850s Bulwer-Lytton's *The Caxtons* had turned Australia from a place of transportation into a place of redemption. **Romantic poets and liberal philosophers, the core figures of the "humane" tradition on which the discipline of English in P1 relied, all had a place in the arguments for empire.** This leads directly into Said's argument: he uses the very same book of Mill's to read *Mansfield Park*.

**Example: the Nairobi literature debate.** The cultural consequences of empire are clearest in the colonial classroom. The Kenyan writer **Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o** recalls the English education he received at Makerere University in Uganda (1959–1964): after the Second World War the University of London set up overseas colleges in Uganda, Nigeria, Ghana, Sierra Leone, Kenya and Tanzania, whose syllabuses almost copied London's, from Shakespeare, Spenser and Milton to Joyce and Eliot, and on to I. A. Richards and the "inevitable" F. R. Leavis. Arnold's pursuit of sweetness and light for a "Hellenised English middle class", Eliot's Anglo-Catholic feudal high culture, and Leavis's "great tradition" with its insistence on the moral significance of literature: these three governed the students' daily essays, in which moral significance was sought in every paragraph, every word, even Shakespeare's commas and full stops (the whole tradition of P1 and P3 reappears here in the form of colonial education). Professor Warner of Makerere gave an inaugural lecture entitled "Shakespeare in Africa", in which he noted almost ecstatically that some students could recognise characters from Jane Austen's novels in their own African villages: **English literature applied to Africa too, and the defence of "universality" was complete.** In September 1968 James Stewart, head of the English department at the University of Nairobi, put forward a development plan describing the department as studying "the historic continuity of a single culture" through the period of the emergence of the modern West. A month later three African lecturers, Owuor Anyumba, Taban Lo Liyong and Ngũgĩ himself, called for the abolition of the existing English department and posed the crucial counter-question: **"If there is need for a 'study of the historic continuity of a single culture', why can't this be African? Why can't African literature be at the centre so that we can view other cultures in relationship to it?"** All sides of the debate in fact agreed that African, European and other literatures should all be taught; the real disagreement was over what was centre and what periphery, and from where one took off. The new principle eventually established was: African oral literature (*orature*), literature from the African continent, the Caribbean and black America, the "Third World" literatures of Asia and Latin America, and the literature of the rest of the world, roughly in that order, with English as the mediating language. A conference on the teaching of literature in secondary schools in 1974 went further, its resolutions stating that the existing language and literature syllabuses were so organised that a Kenyan child came to know himself through London and New York.

**Mechanism:** Ngũgĩ divides the literature African students encountered in classrooms and libraries into three kinds, and the classification is itself an analysis of how the "universal" works. The first is the great humanist and democratic tradition of Europe: Aeschylus, Shakespeare, Balzac, Dickens, Dostoevsky, Tolstoy, Gorky, Brecht. Even at their most humane and universal, these works necessarily reflect European historical experience; and the critical tradition taught these writers, who had the sharpest observations of European bourgeois culture, as brainless geniuses concerned only with "universal themes" such as love, fear, birth and death, their greatness sometimes presented as yet another gift England had given the world besides the Bible and the needle; one teacher once said that Shakespeare and Jesus both used very simple English, until someone pointed out that Jesus spoke Hebrew. **The "great tradition of English literature" was the great tradition of "literature": this is precisely the mechanism of mistaking the local for the universal.** The second kind is the literature of liberal Europeans who took Africa as their theme: the perfect hero of Alan Paton's *Cry, the Beloved Country*, the Reverend Kumalo, who rejects violence and turns the other cheek to his enemies; the African of Joyce Cary's *Mister Johnson*, full of childlike emotional vitality, whose greatest wish after being sentenced to death is to be shot by the European district officer himself, a wish the officer grants, as one would, the logic runs, for one's horse or cat; Karen Blixen's *Out of Africa*, which writes Africans as a special race possessing either great spirituality and mystical intuition or animal instinct and vitality, precisely the qualities "we Europeans" have lost. The third kind is the openly racist literature of Rider Haggard and others: there are only good Africans and bad Africans; the good are the collaborators who help the colonisers conquer their own people, and are endowed with strength, intelligence and beauty; the bad are the resisters, written as ugly, cowardly and treacherous. Of the three, the second deserves the most attention, because it has the same formation as the "Africanism" Morrison analyses in P14: sympathy and praise do not change the fact that the imagined African exists only for European self-understanding.
