**Conclusion:** Ngũgĩ's summary is that economic and political control of a people can never be complete without cultural control; the universities set up in the colonies after the war were meant from the start to train a local elite that would later sustain the empire. The cool, clear-headed imperial servant of Kipling's poem "If—", who can keep his head in the storm of revolt and "meet with Triumph and Disaster / And treat those two impostors just the same", now put on African robes in the postwar schools and universities of an ageing imperialism. The Caribbean poet and historian **Edward Kamau Brathwaite** describes the same situation: the Caribbean education system recognised only the language of the conquerors (planters, officials, Anglican clergy); students knew far more about the kings and queens of England than about their own national heroes and slave rebels, and were more enthusiastic about Sherwood Forest and Robin Hood than about Nanny of the Maroons, whose name some of them had not even heard a few years before. They had every model for describing falling snow, but no syllables for describing the hurricanes that come every year. Children used to write, beneath pictures of snowy fields and corn-haired figures, "The snow was falling on the fields of Shropshire." And the Creole adaptation was a small child writing "The snow was falling on the canefields." She had not yet reached the obvious statement that it was not snow at all but rain; she was trying to have both cultures at once, **and that is creolisation**. This example will recur twice below: in Brathwaite's theory of "nation language", and in Bhabha's theory of hybridity, which will tell us that the spread of the English book in India had an explicit institutional aim, foreshadowed almost word for word in the Burdwan Plan of 1818, before Macaulay's notorious "Minute on Education" of 1835: to train a body of well-educated native labourers proficient in English, able to serve as teachers, translators and compilers. **In empire, "English" was never merely a series of texts but an institution for producing subjects: the function of English in P1 as a substitute for religion, used to civilise the domestic working class, is re-enacted in the colonies in a more naked form.**

### Colonialism, Empire and the "Post": Defining the Terms

**Background:** Before discussing theory, a historical map is needed. The British scholar **Dennis Walder** begins with Columbus: believing he had reached India, he called the inhabitants, in V. S. Naipaul's phrase, "Indians", and Indians they have remained. For Naipaul, grandson of Indian indentured labourers who replaced freed African slaves on the sugar plantations of Trinidad, the "impossible", "colonial" identity of an "East Indian from the West Indies" was created by Europeans like Columbus: **colonisation is first of all an act of naming, the Christian dream of Adam naming the world**. Las Casas, conquistador turned priest, recorded in his *Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies* (1552) how a mission of trade and conversion became genocide, the first attempt, as Walder puts it, to speak for those who could not speak because they had been killed, silenced or simply ignored. Todorov's *The Conquest of America* argues that the conquest of the Americas set the pattern for the subsequent history of Western colonialism, and that this pattern is closely bound up with the creation of the "other". The Enlightenment did not break with this presupposition: Hume asserted that black people were "naturally inferior to the whites", on the very grounds that they lacked "civilised" arts such as writing, the passage Gates recounts in P14. At the end of *Gulliver's Travels* Swift has Gulliver hesitate to report his discoveries to the government, because the typical process of extending the king's dominions is this: a crew of pirates is driven by a storm they know not whither, goes ashore to rob and plunder, is entertained with kindness by a harmless people, gives the country a new name, takes formal possession of it in the king's name, murders two or three dozen of the natives, and this crew of butchers is "a modern colony sent to convert and civilize an idolatrous and barbarous people". Naming and possession coincide here once again. Walder notes that it is no accident that this anticolonial passage came from an Irishman: the first English settlement of North America coincided with the far larger settlement of Ireland, both aiming to bring the native inhabitants "to civility"; the Ireland of Yeats and Joyce below has this as its background.

**Background: the shape of the British Empire.** Walder goes on to trace the slave trade (Britain abolished the slave trade in 1807 and slavery itself in 1834), the "civilising mission", and the changes after the Indian uprising of 1857: feudal princes who supported the status quo became puppet rulers of "independent" states, a pattern developed in tropical Africa into Lugard's "indirect rule", by which a handful of Britons administered millions through traditional chiefs; at its best it minimised the impact of colonial culture, but it also preserved all the injustices of an older conservative social order. The historian Seeley's famous remark was: "We seem, as it were, to have conquered and peopled half the world in a fit of absence of mind." Until the 1880s colonial expansion was carried out mainly by commercial companies rather than the state; thereafter the European powers fell into a fever of domination, and by 1914 controlled more than three-quarters of the world. The most influential account of this "new imperialism" remains the liberal Hobson's *Imperialism* (1902), which reinforced Lenin's conviction that imperialism was a product of monopoly capitalism. Race drew hierarchies within the empire: white settler colonies such as Australia and South Africa moved towards self-government, while "native lands" and crown colonies did not. One turning point was the Jallianwala Bagh massacre at Amritsar in 1919, in which some four hundred unarmed civilians were shot; then came Indian independence in 1947, the independence of forty countries within fifteen years, and the Bandung Conference of non-aligned Asian and African states in 1955. Walder's conclusion strikes an unusual balance: the constructive, or at least modernising, effects of colonial rule (railways, schools, hospitals, the rediscovery of cultures) are as evident as its violence, and its effects on Europe were equally profound and contradictory; the postcolonial era cannot expect to agree on the weight of these factors.

**Definition:** The Indian scholar **Ania Loomba**, in *Colonialism/Postcolonialism* (1998), begins with the dictionary. The *Oxford English Dictionary* traces *colony* to the Roman *colonia* (farm, settlement), defining it as a body of people who settle in a new locality, "forming a community subject to or connected with their parent state". This definition, "quite remarkably", makes no mention of anyone other than the colonisers, the people who already lived there, and so empties the word of "encounter", "conquest" and "domination". **The dictionary definition is itself a Machereyan silence** (P9). By contrast, Shakespeare's one major addition in *The Tempest* to the pamphlets about the Bermuda shipwreck was to make the island inhabited before Prospero's arrival (according to Hulme), and that addition turns an adventure story into an allegory of colonial encounter. "Forming a community" necessarily means unforming or re-forming communities that already exist. So **colonialism can be defined as the conquest and control of other people's land and goods**. In this sense it runs through human history: the Roman, Mongol, Aztec, Inca, Ottoman and Chinese empires. What distinguishes modern European colonialism, on a Marxist distinction, is that it was established alongside capitalism: it did not merely extract tribute but **restructured the economies of the conquered countries**, so that human and natural resources flowed between the two: slaves were shipped from Africa to the Americas to produce sugar for Europe on West Indian plantations; raw cotton from India was shipped to Britain to be woven into cloth and sold back to India, whose own textile industry suffered as a result. Whichever direction people and goods moved in, the profits always flowed back to the "mother country". In this sense colonialism was the "midwife" at the birth of European capitalism.

**Distinction:** How are imperialism and colonialism to be distinguished? Calling the precapitalist kind colonialism and the capitalist kind imperialism will not do, since both Tsarist Russia and the Spanish empire were precapitalist. Lenin, in *Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism*, gave the word a new meaning: surplus finance capital could not be profitably invested at home, where labour was limited, and had to be exported, subordinating non-industrialised countries to it. In this sense direct colonial rule is not necessary; economic dependence and control suffice: this is "neocolonialism". Loomba proposes a useful distinction: **distinguish the two not temporally but spatially: imperialism is the process originating in the metropolis that leads to domination and control, colonialism is what this domination produces in the colonies; imperialism can function without formal colonies (as American imperialism does today), colonialism cannot.** But ambiguity remains: if imperialism is a political system, political independence announces its end; if it is primarily the economic penetration and control of markets, political change scarcely affects it. This ambiguity is the source of all the difficulties of the word "postcolonial".

**Problem: the two senses of "post".** The prefix *post* implies two kinds of "after": the temporal "coming after", and the ideological "supplanting". It is the second that is contested: if the inequalities of colonial rule have not been erased, announcing the demise of colonialism is premature. A country can be at once postcolonial (formally independent) and neocolonial (economically or culturally dependent). Even taken only in the temporal sense, the word cannot be unified: formal decolonisation spans three centuries, from the Americas, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries to Angola and Mozambique in the 1970s; hence Ella Shohat's pointed question: "When exactly, then, does the 'post-colonial' begin?" The deeper problem is internal hierarchy. The Spanish colonies of Latin America became "mixed" societies in which locally born whites (Creoles) and mestizos dominated an indigenous labouring population; according to Klor de Alva, for those at the bottom of the hierarchy, still on the farthest economic margins of the nation-state, there is nothing "post" about their colonisation, while the elites who won the wars of independence were never colonial subjects at all; Mary Louise Pratt likewise says that the Creole elites tried to create an independent, decolonised American society while retaining European values and white supremacy. White settlers in Australia, New Zealand and Canada also want to be seen as postcolonial subjects, but historically they were agents of colonial rule, and did not suffer the genocide and political exclusion suffered by indigenous peoples. The most absurd example is South Africa: nationalist Afrikaners saw themselves as victims of British colonialism, and used this imagined victimhood to justify apartheid.

**Example: "Shishu".** Even in India, whose postcolonial status no one questions, the fissures exist. The Bengali writer Mahasweta Devi's story "Shishu" ("Children") concerns a well-meaning government official, Mr Singh, whose attitude to tribal people reproduces the coloniser's attitude to non-Westerners: mysterious, superstitious, uncivilised, backward, like children who need to be set on the right path. The rebels have been driven into the forest and starved year after year. At the story's climax these "children" appear before him: they are the last fourteen Agaria of the village of Kuva, their bodies stunted by long starvation, yet adults, adult citizens of free India, whose growth has been stunted precisely by free India. Singh realises that what they hate is his height and the normal growth of his body: his normality is a crime they cannot forgive. Yet the story at the same time draws another line: Singh too is only an ordinary Indian, without the stature of a healthy Russian, Canadian or American, unable to eat the calories the World Health Organization considers the human body's due. **The metaphor of the "child", the same metaphor Carnarvon used of Indians above, is taken up after independence by the Indian state itself and applied to tribal people.** Loomba's conclusion: anticolonial movements have rarely represented the interests of all the people of a colonised country; "colonialism" is not only something that happens from outside and operates through the collusion of internal forces; some version of it can be reproduced within. Independence did not automatically improve the position of women, workers and peasants, a point developed below in the literature of "disillusionment" discussed by Okonkwo.

**Objection: oppositional definitions and their costs.** One alternative is to understand the postcolonial not literally as "after colonialism" but as the contestation of colonial domination and its legacies. Klor de Alva argues that postcoloniality should signify a subjectivity of opposition to imperialising and colonising (that is, subordinating and subjectivising) discourses and practices, and, on the grounds of the poststructuralist deconstruction of single linear narratives of progress, frees the word from dependence on a prior colonial condition; on this view people of African, Asian and Caribbean descent in Britain can also be postcolonial subjects. But other critics accuse postcolonial theory precisely of depending too much on poststructuralism: its emphasis on multiple histories and fragmentation blurs the fact that transnational capital is linking these histories in new ways, making the world appear, in Dirlik's view, seemingly shapeless. Understanding the postcolonial as an oppositional stance means that it refers to particular groups or individuals rather than to a place or a social order; **the charge against postcolonial theory is precisely that it shifts the focus from places and institutions to individuals and their subjectivities, so that postcoloniality becomes a vague condition of anyone anywhere**. This charge will reappear with Bhabha. Loomba uses Janet Suzman's production of *Othello* at the Market Theatre in Johannesburg to show why differences cannot be flattened: casting a black actor as Othello in a South Africa that prohibited interracial marriage was radical, making people rethink the play from "his" source culture; whereas the long performance history either had white actors play Othello or ignored the play's racial politics in favour of "universal" themes such as male jealousy and ill-fated love (another example of the "universal" concealing the specific). But Shakespeare's Othello is a lone black man in a white society, whereas black South Africans are a marginalised majority, and black Americans are citizens of the most powerful country in the world: these situations cannot be merged.

**Objection: two simplifications of origins.** Colonialism itself was not monolithic either: by the 1930s it governed 84.6 per cent of the earth's land surface, and its strategies and modes of representation varied with time and place. Spivak treats nineteenth-century India, especially Bengal, as the privileged model of the colonised world; Laura Chrisman finds that the binary of "East/West" absorbs continents and colonies (such as Africa) that do not belong to this axis, ignoring the strategy by which colonial discourse exaggerated and exploited the differences between different others: a prior correction to Said's Orientalist model. At the "colonial" end there is another problem: colonisation was not written on a blank slate. Spivak warns repeatedly that "nostalgia for lost origins can be detrimental to the exploration of social realities within the critique of imperialism": the precolonial has always already been rewritten by colonial history and cannot be retrieved in any pristine form; she refuses to romanticise colonised societies as distant cultures, exploited but with rich, intact heritages waiting to be rediscovered. *This warning comes from Spivak's "Can the Subaltern Speak?" (1988), whose argument is discussed in P12 and in the section on Bhabha below.* Appiah and others likewise criticise the "nativism" that celebrates the precolonial past. But Loomba warns that this caution can lead to the opposite simplification: the "Third World" is defined entirely by its relation to colonialism, whereas in many formerly colonised places historians regard colonialism as a brief interruption in a long and complex history (Vaughan). **The essentialist "authentic tradition" and the anti-essentialist "everything shaped by colonialism" are the two extremes of the third mechanism here, and both treat colonialism as the sole coordinate of history.**

**Conclusion:** Loomba finally compares "postcolonial" with "patriarchy" in feminism: patriarchy refers to male domination of women, yet its ideologies and practices vary with history, geography and culture, and feminist theory has had to move back and forth between the universal and the particular; "postcolonial" likewise is a useful generalisation only when it refers to a **process** of disengagement from the colonial syndrome; in Hulme's words, "'post-colonial' is (or should be) a descriptive not an evaluative term", not a "merit badge" to be worn at will. Metropolis and colony were both deeply altered by the colonial process, and so both are restructured by decolonisation, but not in the same way. Once detached from specific locations, the word begins to obscure the very relations of domination it seeks to reveal. **This is the first mechanism (relation and difference) applied to theory itself: the value of a concept lies in how much difference it preserves.**

### Orientalism: The Other as "Underground Self"

**Definition:** The Palestinian American critic **Edward Said**'s *Orientalism* exposes a Eurocentric universalism that takes for granted the superiority of Europe or the West and the inferiority of the non-West. "Orientalism" is a long-standing European cultural tradition that identifies the East as an "other" inferior to the West. In the Western mind the Orient is "a sort of surrogate and even underground self". Barry's gloss: the Orient becomes a repository or projection of those aspects of themselves that Westerners do not choose to acknowledge (cruelty, sensuality, decadence, laziness, and so on); at the same time, and paradoxically, it is seen as a fascinating realm of the exotic, the mystical and the seductive. It tends to be seen as homogeneous: its people are anonymous masses rather than individuals, their actions determined by instinctive emotions (lust, terror, fury) rather than conscious choices; their reactions are always explained by race (they behave like this because they are Asians, blacks, Orientals) rather than by individual identity or circumstance (because he happens to be someone's sister, uncle, or a collector of antique pottery). After quoting a colonial official's 1907 description of life in Damascus, Said says that in such statements "'the Arab' or 'Arabs' have an aura of apartness, definiteness, and collective self-consistency such as to wipe out any traces of individual Arabs with narratable life histories".

**Mechanism:** The anthology's headnote names Said's methodological source: Foucault. Said examines how Western academic discourse described the non-Western countries being colonised, a discourse that often underwrote colonial policy and licensed further imperial enterprise. This is precisely the "knowledge/power" of P10: knowledge is not a neutral description of pre-existing objects, but a discursive practice that produces its objects and rationalises domination; novels, geographical treatises and philological studies belong to the same process of discursive construction. **Orientalism shows that the first mechanism (relation and difference) is not only linguistic but also geographical and political: the "West" acquires its identity by depending on a fabricated "East", just as whiteness in P14 depends on a fabricated Africanist presence.** And the phrase "underground self" brings the psychoanalytic projection and disavowal of P6 into political geography. Walder supplies the other side: Enlightenment scholars who called themselves "Orientalists" studied and admired Sanskrit, expounding its kinship with the classical languages of Europe, and "Brahmin" and "savage" were for a time terms of praise; but none of this admiration halted the expansion of colonialism and slavery, or shook the presupposition of "otherness". Adoration and denigration are two faces of the same binary structure.

**Example: Yeats's Byzantium.** Barry's example is Yeats's two Byzantium poems, "Sailing to Byzantium" (1927) and "Byzantium" (1932). Read with an "Orientalist" perspective, we become critically aware that the Istanbul of the poems, the former eastern capital of the Roman Empire, is equated with languor, sensuality and exotic mysticism. At such moments Yeats adopts an ethnocentric or Eurocentric perspective, seeing the East as an exotic "other" and making it a foil for the poet's own pursuits and concerns, which the poems present as the norm. *In "Sailing to Byzantium" the aged speaker leaves a country that belongs to youth and the procreation of the flesh and sails to Byzantium, praying the sages to gather him out of his decaying body and turn him into an immortal artefact wrought by goldsmiths; Byzantium is thus at once a city of spiritual transcendence and a city of gorgeous ornament: precisely the double image of the "mystical" and the "sensual" familiar to Orientalism.* Yet the same Yeats is read in a postcolonial context in another essay by Said (collected in *Culture and Imperialism*): the longing, expressed again and again in Yeats's work, to re-establish contact with an earlier, mythical, nationalist Ireland is the typical gesture of the writer in a postcolonial situation, closely related to Fanon's idea of reclaiming the past: postcolonial writers often evoke or create a precolonial version of their own nation, rejecting the modern and contemporary, tainted by colonial status. **The same poet is both Orientalist and colonised: this is not a contradiction but a discovery of the postcolonial perspective: the same subject can be central on one axis and marginal on another.** This is where the first feature of postcolonial criticism in Barry's list (awareness that non-Europeans are represented as exotic or immoral "others") leads into the third (the doubleness of identity).

### Country House and Plantation: Said Reads *Mansfield Park*

**Problem:** If empire penetrated the domestic novel, in what form does it exist there? Said's "Jane Austen and Empire", in *Culture and Imperialism*, is the exemplary answer to this question; collected in several anthologies, it has acquired a kind of "classic" status. He first rules out a misreading. He agrees with Kiernan that "empires must have a mould of ideas or conditioned reflexes to flow into"; the great humane ideas and values promoted by mainstream European culture were precisely this mould; even the liberal Mill said that the sacred duties which civilised nations owe to the independence and nationality of each other are not binding towards those "to whom nationality and independence are either a certain evil, or at best a questionable good". But he refuses to reduce the question to causality, because that produces a "rhetoric of blame": Wordsworth, Austen or Coleridge did not "cause" the formal British rule of India after 1857 merely because they wrote before 1857; nor did Carlyle directly drive Rhodes. **What he seeks is not causation but "counterpoint": a counterpoint between the overt patterns of English writing about England and the representations of the world beyond the British Isles; and the internal pattern of this counterpoint is not temporal but spatial.** What he really cares about is this: why did the great humanistic ideas, institutions and monuments of England, which we still celebrate for their power to command assent ahistorically, do so little to impede the accelerating imperial process? Why did these humanistic ideas coexist so comfortably with imperialism? This is one of the sharpest questions ever put to the liberal humanism of P1.

**Background:** Said's starting point is Raymond Williams's *The Country and the City* (P10). Williams says that Austen's novels express "an achievable quality of life", and that she watches from inside the houses; for all the subtlety of her social description, she never sees the classes Cobbett named as he rode past: "where only one class is seen, no classes are seen". Said finds this description excellent, but thinks Williams's treatment of empire less concentrated and extensive than the reality requires, and that he dates the impact of empire to after the mid-nineteenth century; if one looks for a world map of empire in English literature, it appears with astonishing insistence and frequency well before then. **This is a self-correction within Layer 4: cultural materialism has its own "single class" blind spot: it saw class, but saw only one nation.** Said also connects the formation of national identity at the end of the eighteenth century with Anglo-French rivalry: "Englishness" was always manufactured in contrast with "the French"; Thackeray's Becky Sharp is an upstart partly because she is half French; the abolitionist stance of Wilberforce and others stemmed partly from a wish to make French hegemony in the Antilles more difficult. In *Mansfield Park*, when the Crawfords propose staging a play, the faintly dubious French colouring of their background is thus significant.

**Reading: spatial clarification.** Said says that Austen's imagination works with "steely rigor" through what may be called "geographical and spatial clarification". The ignorance of the ten-year-old Fanny Price on her arrival at Mansfield is shown by her inability to put together the map of Europe; every issue in the first half of the novel has space as its common denominator: where Fanny lives, where she reads and works, where fires are lit; Sir Thomas is far away putting his estates in Antigua in order, while at home things drift with no one at the helm, until the rehearsal of Kotzebue's *Lovers' Vows* turns the living space into a theatre. Then Sir Thomas suddenly returns from "abroad" and within a day or two wipes out every trace, burning every unbound copy of the play in the house. For Said, he is not only a Robinson Crusoe setting things in order but also an early Protestant eradicating every trace of frivolous behaviour. **Nothing in the novel would contradict our assuming that Sir Thomas does exactly the same things, on a larger scale, on his Antigua "plantations": to own and rule Mansfield Park is to own and rule an imperial estate in close association with it.** When Fanny revisits her family home in Portsmouth, she finds there no regard for time and season, no regulation of subject, no propriety and attention; Said's summary: in **too small a space** you cannot see clearly, you cannot think clearly, you cannot have proper regulation and attention. Order needs space, and space needs overseas sustenance.

**Mechanism: the displaced commodity.** Fanny and her brother William must first leave home, "as a kind of indentured servant, or, to put the case in extreme terms, a kind of transported commodity", before they can earn their right to Mansfield; her small-scale movements in space correspond to Sir Thomas's larger, more public colonial movements. She is called by everyone a "comfort" and an "acquisition"; in this novel blood is not enough to guarantee continuity, hierarchy and authority at either the domestic or the international level, and must be supplemented by a tested outsider. The second part of the novel includes the failure of Edmund's courtship of Mary Crawford, the disabling of the elder son Tom, the launch of William's naval career, and a disgraceful elopement. Said's key word is *assuming*: with "a curious combination of casualness and stress", Austen reveals herself to be **assuming** the importance of empire to the situation at home, just as Fanny *assumes* in both senses: she "supposes", and she "takes on, takes over" (in the end she takes over the spiritual sovereignty of the estate). Since Austen uses Antigua in this way, readers have a corresponding responsibility to understand concretely the historical value of the reference: **Sir Thomas's Caribbean property must have been a sugar plantation maintained by slave labour (slavery was not abolished until the 1830s); this is not dead historical fact but an evident reality that Austen certainly knew.** Mill, in his *Principles of Political Economy*, says that the West Indian colonies are "hardly to be looked upon as countries", but more properly as "outlying agricultural or manufacturing estates belonging to a larger community", places where England finds it convenient to produce sugar and coffee. At the end of the novel Austen wants "to restore everybody, not greatly in fault themselves, to tolerable **comfort**", and the word comfort recurs throughout the last chapters: the outlying elements are properly installed within, becoming "native" to Mansfield. **Comfort is the moral currency into which plantation wealth is converted.**

**Example: "such a dead silence".** The moment in the novel closest to slavery comes when Fanny tells her cousin that she once asked Sir Thomas about the slave trade, and that what followed was "such a dead silence". Said says it is as if the two worlds could not be connected, because there was simply no common language between them. That is true. But what gives this striking discrepancy its life is the rise and decline of the British Empire itself, and the emergence afterwards of a postcolonial consciousness, through which, Said suggests, the day will come when slavery is no longer met with dead silence. **This is the completed form of the manifest/latent mechanism in Layer 5.** Freud (P6) located the latent layer in the subject's unconscious, deconstruction (P7) in the text's self-contradiction, Macherey (P9) in what ideology cannot say, and New Historicism (P10) in juxtaposition with contemporary non-literary texts; Said locates it in a concrete geographical and economic relation, and says that this silence can be broken by history. Historiography itself belongs to this process: Ragatz (1928), the classic student of the Caribbean planter class, could still write of the "Negro race" as given to theft, lying, laziness and superstition, and such "history" was later superseded by the revisionist work of Caribbean historians such as Eric Williams and C. L. R. James: interpretation depends on **who** interprets and **when**, and, just as importantly, from **where**.

**Conclusion:** Said's position is not to abandon Austen. "We cannot easily say that since *Mansfield Park* is a novel, its affiliations with a sordid history are irrelevant or transcended, not only because it is irresponsible to do so, but because we know too much to say so in good faith." But he equally refuses the "rhetoric of blame", in which subaltern, minority or disadvantaged voices retrospectively attack Austen for being white, privileged, insensitive, complicit. She belonged to a slave-owning society, but do we therefore throw out her novels? Said's answer is a firm no. Our interpretive vocation is to make connections, to read what is there and what is not there, **to see complementarity and interdependence instead of isolated, venerated, formalised experience**. A novel encodes experience rather than simply repeating it; the task is to lose neither a true historical sense of Antigua nor a full appreciation of Mansfield. This is the meaning of `contrapuntal reading`: two melodic lines heard at once, neither dissolving the other.

**Reading: Barry's assessment.** Barry says that Said "foregrounds the background", and that its central irony is this: the English country house that stands for the ideals of order and civilisation is sustained by another estate on the other side of the world. One consequence is that the dating of the imperial phase of English culture must be moved back from the beginning of formal empire to the eighteenth century; Austen becomes the starting point of a line of fiction leading to Conrad and Kipling. This reading "concretises" a dimension largely latent in the novel: it need not claim that all of this is "in" the novel, only that this is the right way to read it; yet Said does insist that these things are unmistakably there, in the suggestiveness of her allusive and abstract language, and appeals to close reading. Barry finds this convincing for the most part, but in the end it appeals to the conscience of (above all) white middle-class readers. In any case, after reading the essay, any "innocence" about this aspect of the novel disappears: the absent settler-planter is in one sense at the centre of everything, and in another always withdrawn and marginal. Barry places it as **a Marxist criticism influenced by poststructuralism**, locating the centre of the book in an absence, in contrast with the "more literal" Marxism of Krieger in P9; and like New Historicism (P10), it concretely names the details of a specific social/colonial situation, the absentee planter of eighteenth-century Antigua, rather than merely evoking a generalised notion of colonial exploitation.

**Limitation:** The weakness of this reading lies where its strength does. First, it oscillates between two claims: "this is how it should be read" and "this really is in the text". The former is the reader's responsibility to historicise; the latter puts the weight of the argument on what Austen herself "certainly knew", sliding towards the intentional fallacy against which the New Criticism of P2 warned; Said says both that Austen "assumes" empire and that she "knows" the facts of the plantation, and the distance between the two is not fully argued. Second, Antigua appears in the novel only a handful of times, in a discrete and reticent way; the thinness of the evidence is out of proportion to the weight of the conclusion, and contrapuntal reading here risks becoming the "levering of the whole from a marginal detail" of deconstruction in P7. Third, although Said himself refuses the rhetoric of blame, Barry points out that the essay finally appeals to conscience, and conscience is precisely the emotional resource of the rhetoric of blame. **The question is not whether Said is right, but whether "counterpoint" can be sustained without one melodic line drowning out the other.**

**Problem: is a superreader possible?** In a "stop and think" section on postcolonial criticism, Barry raises a question that the whole of Layer 5 must face. Feminism, Marxism, queer theory and postcolonial criticism each focus on gender, class, sexual orientation and cultural difference; is it possible, then, to be a "superreader" who can respond to a text equally and fully in all these ways? In practice, for most readers one of these issues tends to eclipse all the others. His example comes from P12: Gilbert and Gubar's reading of *Wuthering Heights* in *The Madwoman in the Attic* does not comment on an aspect that would interest postcolonial critics, Emily Brontë's description of Heathcliff in terms of racial "otherness": a gypsy, "a little Lascar, or an American or Spanish castaway". Gilbert and Gubar describe him as Catherine's "other self or Id", contrasting his darkness with the fair-haired Edgar who presides over Thrushcross Grange, which, however ironically, is presented as "heaven", "society" and "reason". **This conflation of racial otherness with the id, or the irrational forces of the unconscious, might be thought insensitive: it is exactly the projective structure of "the Orient as underground self" above, re-enacted unnoticed in a feminist classic.** Should we strive to become superreaders with multiple layers of sympathy and awareness, or will such efforts produce only blandness and superficiality? Barry's answer: an evenly distributed awareness of all these issues is theoretically possible, but pursuing it merely for the sake of political correctness almost inevitably leads to superficiality; real interest in any one of them can only spring from some aspect of your own situation. **These perspectives cannot be put on and taken off like suits of clothes; they must emerge and assert themselves with a certain urgency.** *Compare Crenshaw's "intersectionality", mentioned in P12 and P14: it does not require the reader to wear every perspective at once, but to recognise the invisibility produced by the very intersections of those perspectives; this is one possible correction to Barry's argument from "urgency".*

**Example: Antigua today.** The Antigua that is silent in the novel begins to speak in the work of an Antiguan writer. The Antigua-born writer **Jamaica Kincaid**'s *A Small Place* (1988) deals with what the headnote calls "secondary colonisation": the inhabitants of rich, developed Northern or Western countries turn poor, formerly colonised Southern or Eastern countries into places or objects of useful pleasure. Tourism is the most obvious example; there are more symbolic forms too, such as turning these places into opportunities for secondary colonisers to create cultural meaning or realise themselves; the headnote says that *A Passage to India* is one example. Kincaid speaks in the second person to a North American or European tourist: you land at V. C. Bird International Airport, and may wonder why a prime minister would name an airport rather than a school or hospital after himself; but you have not yet seen Antigua's schools and hospitals; you love the dry, sunny weather here, but would not think what it is like to live in constant drought, surrounded by sea yet counting every drop of fresh water. The library was damaged in the earthquake of 1974, and the sign in front, "Repairs are pending", still hangs there more than a decade later; after independence Antiguans go to church every year on the anniversary to thank God, and an English God at that. You have brought with you a new book of economic history about how the West grew rich: not through the labour, undervalued for generations, of people like her, but through the cleverness of small shopkeepers in Sheffield and Lancashire and the invention of the wristwatch. For Kincaid this is the last straw: not only must they bear the unspeakableness of slavery, but even the small satisfaction of knowing that it was they who made their masters rich is taken from them. **This is a demonstration of Said's argument from the opposite side: if a historical account deletes the plantation from the story of how the West grew rich, it repeats the silence of *Mansfield Park* at the level of scholarship.**

**Reading:** The sharpest stroke is on the sea. Looking out from your hotel window, you see water shading from deep blue to transparent silver, more beautiful than any you have ever seen; but you should not think about where what you flush away goes: Antigua has no proper sewage disposal system, and it may well be in the water you want to swim in. And the Caribbean Sea, Kincaid reminds the tourist, is very big, the Atlantic bigger still; the number of black slaves this ocean has swallowed would amaze even you. Within a single sentence, the holiday view, present pollution and the history of the Middle Passage are layered in the same water. Then comes the tourist's self-portrait: an ordinary good person, lonely in his own city, who on becoming a tourist turns into "an ugly human being", unaware that the locals laugh at him behind closed doors. Her explanation: **"every native of every place is a potential tourist, and every tourist is a native of somewhere."** Natives too want to escape banality and boredom, but most of the world's natives cannot go anywhere: they are too poor, too poor to escape, and too poor to live decently in the place where they live, which is precisely the place tourists want to go. What they envy is the tourist's ability to turn their own banality into his pleasure. **This is a reversal of the first mechanism: "native/tourist" are not two kinds of people but relational positions distributed by wealth and poverty; secondary colonisation no longer needs governors, only flights and exchange rates.** Said's contrapuntal reading is the scholar at the imperial centre pushing the margin into the foreground; Kincaid is the margin itself turning round to make the centre, the reader himself, the object watched and laughed at. This is a literal instance of what Barry calls "the empire writing back".

### Whose Language? From "a New English" to "Nation Language"

**Problem:** If English is an imperial institution, what does it mean for colonised writers to write in English? Barry lists language as the second area of concern of postcolonial criticism. He begins with Ireland: Yeats's injunction to Irish poets to "learn your trade" implies a humble stance of apprenticeship; this recalls the scene in chapter five of Joyce's *A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man* in which Stephen Dedalus is condescended to by an English priest for using a local dialect word, and Stephen says to himself: "The language in which we are speaking is his before it is mine … My soul frets in the shadow of his language." The word "shadow" answers the editors' title exactly. More recently, the Northern Irish poet Seamus Heaney, in "The Ministry of Fear" (in *North*, 1975), recalls the unease and self-consciousness he felt as a child about his English pronunciation; the poem pictures heavy country footsteps trampling the fine lawns of "elocution", and says that Ulster was British but had no right to enter English lyric verse. *The poem's title is borrowed from Graham Greene's 1943 novel of the same name.* Barry's summary: this linguistic deference amounts to feeling that the furniture of the language belongs to someone else and should not be moved without permission; some postcolonial writers concluded that **the coloniser's language is permanently contaminated, and that writing in it means acquiescing at a crucial point in the structures of colonialism.**

**Background: Makerere 1962.** Ngũgĩ traces the problem to the Berlin Conference of 1884: at the conference table the capitalist powers of Europe carved a continent of many peoples, cultures and languages into colonies, and so carved Africa into the languages of the European powers; to this day African countries define themselves as "English-speaking", "French-speaking" or "Portuguese-speaking". The historic conference at Makerere in 1962 was called the "Conference of African Writers of English Expression", a title that automatically excluded those who wrote in African languages: Ngũgĩ, as a student, qualified to attend on the strength of two short stories, whereas Shaaban Robert, then the greatest Swahili poet of East Africa, and Fagunwa, the great Nigerian writer in Yoruba, could not possibly have qualified. Yet the first item on the conference's agenda was "What is African literature?"; everything was discussed except the fact that our languages and cultures were dominated by those of imperialist Europe. English was taken as the natural medium among Africans; Mphahlele said that English and French were the common languages of the nationalist front against white oppressors; Senghor said, in effect, that the aura of words in African languages was mere sap and blood, while French words gave off a thousand rays like diamonds. Achebe's statement of 1964 is the most famous: a man abandoning his mother tongue for someone else's looks like a dreadful betrayal, "But for me there is no other choice. I have been given the language and I intend to use it"; English would be able to carry the weight of his African experience, "But it will have to be a new English, still in full communion with its ancestral home but altered to suit its new African surroundings." Gabriel Okara rendered expressions from his Ijaw almost word for word into English, arguing that just as there are American, West Indian and Australian Englishes, there should be a Nigerian or West African English. Ngũgĩ asks: why should African writers be so attached to enriching other people's languages with their mother tongues? Why not bring Balzac, Tolstoy, Brecht, Lu Xun and Neruda into African languages? Why did Okara not build literary monuments in Ijaw?

**Mechanism: the morning of the chalk and the blackboard.** Why were African writers so timid in asserting their own languages and so aggressive in asserting the colonisers'? Ngũgĩ's answer: the Berlin Conference was carried out through the sword and the bullet, but "the night of the sword and the bullet was followed by the morning of the chalk and the blackboard". Physical violence on the battlefield was followed by psychological violence in the classroom, the former visibly brutal, the latter visibly gentle. He cites the Senegalese writer Cheikh Hamidou Kane's novel *Ambiguous Adventure*: after the cannon came the new school, which had the nature of both the cannon and the magnet, and made the conquest permanent: "the cannon forces the body and the school fascinates the soul". **This is the colonial version of Gramsci's theory of hegemony (P9) and Althusser's ideological state apparatuses (P9): coercion is followed by the production of consent, and the school is its principal site.** His own schooling is a case of this mechanism. As children they spoke Gikuyu in the fields, at home, around the fire; the hero of their stories was the small but clever hare, from whom the children learned that the weak can outwit the strong; a good storyteller could tell the same story so that it was always fresh, and the children learned to understand the suggestive power and the music of words. His first four years of schooling were still in Gikuyu. After the declaration of the state of emergency in Kenya in 1952, the schools run by nationalists were taken over by the colonial regime, and English became the language of instruction, "more than a language: it was *the* language". Anyone caught speaking Gikuyu near the school was given corporal punishment or made to wear a metal plate inscribed "I AM STUPID" or "I AM A DONKEY"; the teacher would give a button to one pupil, who passed it on to the next pupil caught speaking the mother tongue, and at the end of the day the trail was followed: **children were turned into witch-hunters, and learned to betray the interests of their own community**. Conversely, any achievement in English was rewarded, and English became the measure of intelligence and ability: in 1954 a boy in his class with distinctions in every subject except English failed the whole examination because he failed English, and later became a bus conductor; Ngũgĩ, with only passes but a credit in English, went on to an elite secondary school. The books he read changed from hare, leopard and lion to abridged Dickens, Stevenson and Rider Haggard: "Language and literature were taking us further and further from ourselves to other selves."

**Definition: the dual character of language.** From this Ngũgĩ draws a theory. Every language has a dual character: it is both **a means of communication** and **a carrier of culture**. For Swedes and Danes, English is only a means of communicating with non-Scandinavians; for the English it also carries, inseparably, their culture and history. As communication, language has three aspects: what Marx called "the language of real life", the relations people enter into in the labour process; speech, which imitates the language of real life; and writing, which imitates speech. As culture, language also has three aspects: it is the product and reflection of history; it forms images of the world in the mind of the child; and it transmits these images through the sounds of a particular language: "language as culture is the collective memory bank of a people's experience in history". The colonial child met a total rupture of all six aspects: the written language of school was separated from the spoken language of home, and learning became a cerebral activity rather than an emotionally felt experience: the word "missile" always sounded distant and alien to him until he learned its Gikuyu equivalent, *ngurukuhi*; he was forced to "stand outside himself to look at himself". Ngũgĩ calls this `colonial alienation`.

**Example: internalised images.** The mother tongue became associated in the child's mind with inferiority, humiliation, corporal punishment, stupidity and barbarism, and the association was reinforced by the world he met in the works of "racist geniuses" like Rider Haggard, to say nothing of Hume, Jefferson and Hegel, the last of whom likened Africa to a land of childhood still enveloped, as regards the development of self-conscious history, in the dark mantle of night. The Kenyan scholar Micere Mugo recalls that after reading the description of the old African woman Gagool in *King Solomon's Mines*, she felt mortal terror for a long time whenever she met an old African woman; Sidney Poitier says in his autobiography that because of the literature he had read he associated Africa with snakes, and when he arrived in Africa and stayed in a modern hotel in a modern city he still could not sleep for looking for snakes under the bed. These two could still point to the source of their fears; for most people the negative images are internalised and affect their cultural and even political choices. Banda of Malawi founded Kamuzu Academy to help the brightest students master English, with Latin at the centre of the curriculum, and no Malawians allowed to teach there; Ngũgĩ asks whether there could be a better illustration of hatred of what is national and servile worship of what is foreign, even if dead. **This is the institutional form of the psychological mechanism described by Fanon in *Black Skin, White Masks* in P6.** He does not think British indirect rule essentially different from the French and Portuguese policies of assimilation: Senghor's embrace of the "universal mission" of French is no different from Achebe's gratitude in 1964 for the legacy of English. **"The final triumph of a system of domination is when the dominated start singing its virtues."**

**Conclusion:** Ngũgĩ's conclusion is radical: work by Africans in English, French or Portuguese is not "African literature" but "Afro-European literature"; African poetry is poetry written by Africans in African languages: every Somali-speaking herdsman can recite the political poems of the anti-imperialist fighter Hassan, while not a single line by the best African poets writing in foreign languages will be remembered by any African peasant. His *Decolonising the Mind* (1986) opens with a farewell: the book is his farewell to English as a vehicle for his writing; from then on he would write only in Gikuyu and Swahili. Intellectually, his position combines Marxism (language rooted in relations of production) with a theory of language and culture close to the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis (language as "mental spectacles" shaping a world view), and stands in interesting contrast with Saussure's differential linguistics in P2: Saussure held that language divides up the world, while Ngũgĩ asks **whose** language is doing the dividing. **This is also a point of tension in the third mechanism: he opposes colonial construction, yet treats the harmony of "mother tongue, culture, community" as the original state that was broken, which is precisely the image of "home" that the poststructuralists in the editors' introduction call into question.**

**Distinction: another Caribbean path.** Brathwaite's *History of the Voice* deals with a situation in which there is no "mother tongue" to return to. The languages of the Caribbean form a spectrum: the imperial language, English (and French, Dutch, Spanish); Creole English; what he calls `nation language`, the English spoken by the transported slaves and labourers; and remnants of ancestral languages: Hindi, varieties of Chinese, and African languages that have miraculously survived, while the Amerindian languages almost entirely disappeared with the destruction of the Amerindians. For the descendants of Africans there is no single mother tongue to go back to, as Ngũgĩ goes back to Gikuyu; resistance must take place within English. His key distinction is between "nation language" and "dialect": dialect carries a pejorative sense, "bad English", "inferior English", the language used to make fun of people, with a history from the plantation, where people's dignity was distorted through their language; nation language is the submerged part of dialect more closely connected with African experience; its lexicon may be English, but its syntax is not, still less its rhythm and timbre: it is like a howl, a burst of machine-gun fire, the wind, a wave, and also like the blues. **The problem is not vocabulary but syllables: the model English gave Caribbean poetry was the pentameter, "The curfew tolls the knell of parting day" (Gray's *Elegy*), but "the hurricane does not roar in pentameters".** The girl writes "The snow was falling on the canefields" because she has the syllabic intelligence to describe falling snow but not the hurricane. The Caribbean answer is an old form that has always been there: calypso (*kaiso*), which uses not the iamb but the dactyl, its intonation sinking and deepening within the line rather than moving forward on a single plane like Shakespeare's pentameter. Another feature of nation language is that it belongs to "total expression": reading is isolated and individualistic, whereas oral tradition requires an audience to complete the community; the sound the poet makes is answered and returned by the audience, and meaning lives in this continuum: a kind of "reader" the reader-response theory of P5 never imagined. He also places his demand within Europe's own history: Dante, in *De vulgari eloquentia* (1304), argued for the Tuscan vernacular to replace Latin as a "nation language", and these successful European nation languages went on to suppress Basque, Gaelic and the languages of the overseas colonies. **The vernacular's revolt against an imperial language is a recurring structure, and every victorious vernacular can become a new imperial language: English itself is an example.**

**Example: from McKay to Miss Lou.** Brathwaite uses a series of recordings to show the stages of Caribbean poetry. Claude McKay, born in Jamaica and later a leading figure of the Harlem Renaissance, claimed in a recording late in life to be a "poet" rather than a "Negro poet"; for the sake of the "universal" he abandoned the nation language of his early work and turned to the sonnet: his sonnet on St Isaac's Cathedral in Petrograd could have been written by any post-Victorian European poet, and the only thing that remained distinctive was the poet's voice in performance, which now and then said *de* for *the*, elisions that subtly eroded the classical pentameter of the sonnet. Brathwaite says that what interests him is the terrible price paid for universality. George Campbell's best poem, written for Jamaica's move towards self-government in 1945, was still a Miltonic ode. Then comes the calypsonian Mighty Sparrow, who in a song of the early 1960s criticised colonial education for turning people into idiots with stories of Robin Hood, King Alfred and the cakes, King Arthur and the Knights of the Round Table: a structure of "answering". Finally there is Louise Bennett (Miss Lou), who wrote all her life in nation language and was for that reason long neglected: she performed her work in crowded village halls across the island from around 1936, but could not publish in the island's largest newspaper until 1945; by 1962 she had published nine books, yet was not among the poets of the *Independence Anthology of Jamaican Literature*, but placed at the end of the book, as an afterthought, if not an embarrassment. *Bennett's work, written in Jamaican Creole, consists largely of dramatic monologues for stage performance; she later became a household name in Jamaica through radio and television programmes: institutional recognition came much later than the recognition of her audiences.* **This sequence is itself a version, in the history of poetry, of Barry's three stages of "adopt, adapt, adept" below.**

**Distinction: double identity.** Barry introduces the third feature of postcolonial criticism here. Yeats, as a member of the Irish Protestant ruling class, had the double identity of being both coloniser and colonised, and acknowledging such double identities is one of the strengths of the postcolonial perspective. When the Nigerian novelist **Chinua Achebe** published his first novel, *Things Fall Apart*, in 1958, an early reviewer criticised him for pretending to identify with African villagers, when his university education and his broadcasting work in the capital, Lagos, ought (the implication was) to have made him identify with the "civilised" values supposedly brought to Africa by Europeans. **The reviewer's premise is that identity must be single, that one can belong to only one culture. What postcolonial criticism stresses is precisely the doubleness, hybridity and instability of identity.** On one level, Achebe's village Africa corresponds to the precolonial, mythical, heroic Ireland Yeats evokes; on another level, such double or hybrid identity is exactly what the postcolonial situation produces. *The title of* Things Fall Apart *is taken from the line "Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold" in Yeats's "The Second Coming" (1920), which adds another layer to Barry's juxtaposition of Yeats and Achebe: an anticolonial novel borrows its title from a colonial poet of double identity.* This also explains why the dispute over language above cannot be settled simply: Ngũgĩ resists English with the mother tongue, Achebe and Brathwaite resist English with a transformed English; the former presupposes a cultural whole to which one can return, the latter that hybridity is itself a form. Anzaldúa's "border language" and "linguistic terrorism" in P14 belong to the latter kind; Bakhtin's "heteroglossia" in P9 provides its general theory: every national language is already internally a dialogue of many social languages, and "pure English", like the "pure mother tongue", is a product of centralising forces. **So the question shifts from "whose language?" to "what happens to the coloniser's language when it is repeated?": precisely Bhabha's question.**

### The English Book and Mimicry: Bhabha's Hybridity

**Background:** Said, Ngũgĩ and Brathwaite deal broadly with how imperial consciousness works in literature and culture; other scholars have noticed the instability and ambivalence inherent in any attempt to impose domination on another people. The Indian-born theorist **Homi K. Bhabha**, in "Signs Taken for Wonders" (1985), introduced `ambivalence`, `mimicry` and `hybridity`. He starts from a scene that recurs in the writing of English colonial culture and that, through this repetition, "inaugurates" a literature of empire: in the wild and wordless emptiness of colonial India, Africa or the Caribbean, the sudden, fortuitous discovery of **the English book**. The first scene: in the first week of May 1817, Anund Messeh, one of the earliest Indian catechists, hurried from the mission station at Meerut to a grove of trees outside Delhi, where he found some five hundred people sitting in the shade reading and talking. They said it was "God's book", given to them by an angel at the fair at Hurdwar: an angel of God to them, in fact a learned pundit; it was the Gospel in Hindustani, some copies printed, some copied by hand from printed ones. When Anund told them it was the book of the religion of the European Sahibs, they asked in turn how it could be the Europeans' book, when they believed it was God's gift to them. They were willing to be baptised, but would never take the Sacrament, "because the Europeans eat cow's flesh"; when Anund invited them to Meerut to be baptised, they politely declined: "We must now go home to the harvest; perhaps the next year we may come to Meerut." The second scene: nearly a hundred years later, Conrad's Marlow discovers in the "night of first ages" of the Congo Towson's *An Inquiry into some Points of Seamanship*, sees in this unremarkable book a "singleness of intention", and concludes that its author must be English. The third scene: half a century after that, a young Trinidadian, Naipaul, discovers the same book in this passage of Conrad, and draws from it a view of literature and a lesson of history: being a colonial had once been a kind of security, and Conrad had already been everywhere, with his vision of the world's "half-made societies".

**Mechanism: the deferral and splitting of authority.** These texts, written in the name of the father and the author, seem to proclaim the triumph of the colonial moment: the discovery of the book establishes the sign of proper representation; the word of God, truth and art create a beginning for history and narrative. But the institution of the Word in the wilderness is also an *Entstellung*, Freud's term (P6) for displacement, distortion, dislocation, repetition: the dazzling light of literature lights up only areas of darkness. The book is wondrous precisely because it is repeated, translated, misread, displaced. **Between the edict of Englishness and the assault of the dark, unruly spaces of the earth, the colonial text emerges uncertainly through an act of repetition.** Anund Messeh disavows the natives' disturbing questions and repeats instead the now questionable "authority" of evangelical dogma; Marlow turns away from the African jungle and recognises, in retrospect, the "English" quality of the discovery; Naipaul turns his back on the hybrid, half-made colonial world and fixes his gaze on the universal domain of English literature. This is ambivalence: originary authority can be present only in repetition, and repetition necessarily brings difference. Bhabha calls this a *différance* produced in the act of enunciation: Derrida's *différance* in P7 moves here from the text into power. He says explicitly that he wishes to depart from the aims of Derrida's "The Double Session": from the vicissitudes of interpretation in a mimetic reading towards the effects of power, the strategies of individuation and domination that construct colonial space; his tools here turn from Derrida to Foucault (P10). The representative of English authority depends less on a universal symbol of English identity than on its productivity as a sign of difference: the Bible translated into Hindi and propagated by Dutch or native catechists is still the "English book"; a Polish émigré deeply influenced by Flaubert, writing about Africa, produced an English classic.

**Definition: hybridity.** Colonial power needs to produce differentiations, individuations and identity effects so that discriminatory practices can map out the governed population. The reference of discrimination produced through strategies of disavowal is always to a process of splitting: the distinction between mother culture and its bastards, self and its doubles, where the trace of what is disavowed is not repressed but repeated as **something different**: a mutation, a hybrid. Hence Bhabha's definition: **"Hybridity is the sign of the productivity of colonial power, its shifting forces and fixities; it is the name for the strategic reversal of the process of domination through disavowal (that is, the production of discriminatory identities that secure the 'pure' and original identity of authority)."** The definition has three layers. First, hybridity is not a mixing of two ready-made cultures: it is not a "problem" of genealogy or identity, to be resolved as an issue of cultural relativism, but a "problematic" of colonial representation and individuation that reverses the effects of colonialist disavowal, so that other "denied" knowledges enter the dominant discourse and estrange the basis of its authority, its "rules of recognition". Second, it is not a simple inversion either, a claim that the original is "really" only an "effect" of an *Entstellung*. Third, it has a precise psychoanalytic structure: Freud says that disavowal maintains a narcissistic demand while acknowledging difference; two contradictory knowledges split the ego, and the fetish is both a substitute for the phallus and the mark of its absence. **The difference between fetish and hybrid lies in temporal order: the fetish "fixes" authority before difference is perceived, while hybridity revalues the identity of authority after difference has been perceived.** He calls this partializing process a "metonymy of presence": some symbol of authority is retained, "less than one", and repeated, "double".

**Reading: expelling the copula.** So the natives' questions literally turn the origin of the book into an enigma. The first question: **how can the word of God come out of the flesh-eating mouths of the English?** This confronts the assumption of the unity and universality of authority with the cultural differences of the historical moment of its enunciation. The second question: **how can it be the Europeans' book, when we believe it is God's gift to us?** Anund Messeh's discourse first introduces the presence and mediation of the English, "God gave it long ago to the Sahibs, and THEY sent it to us", and then disavows this political and linguistic "imposition" by attributing it to the power of God; what he and the disguised English Bible must conceal are their specific conditions of enunciation: the Burdwan Plan's design of using "natives" to destroy native culture and religion. Taking their stand on dietary law, the natives resist the miraculous equivalence of God and the English. **They expel the copula, or middle term, "English", from the evangelical equation "power = knowledge", and so dismantle the structure of equivalence "God = the English".** The paradigmatic presence of the Bible as the word of God is carefully preserved (the natives assent unconditionally only to direct quotations from the Bible), but its syntagmatic supports, the codes, connotations and cultural associations that give it cultural and political authority, are emptied out. This is the structural-linguistic toolkit of P2, the paradigmatic and syntagmatic axes, used to analyse a colonial scene. In demanding an Indianised Gospel, they use the power of hybridity to resist baptism and put the project of conversion in an impossible position: the Bishop of Calcutta, in his Christmas sermon of 1815, said that Christianity was "a historical religion", and permitted no adaptation of it.

**Mechanism: mimicry as camouflage.** The metonymic strategy produces the signifier of colonial **mimicry**, the affective effect of hybridity, which is at once a mode of appropriation and a mode of resistance. When discrimination turns into the assertion of the hybrid, the insignia of authority becomes a mask, a mockery. After the natives' questioning, Bhabha says, it is hard to agree entirely with Fanon that the psychic choice is only to "turn white or disappear"; there is a third, more ambivalent choice: **camouflage, mimicry, black skins/white masks**. He invokes Lacan: the effect of mimicry is camouflage in the strictly technical sense: not harmonising with the background but, against a mottled background, becoming mottled, like the camouflage techniques used in human warfare. **Bhabha's mimicry takes its psychic dimension from Fanon; one can see here how it also corrects Fanon: the white mask is no longer only a symptom of alienation; it can also be a tactic.** The missionaries' own records confirm this. J. A. Dubois, who worked in Madras for twenty-five years, said in effect that native Christians were never more than phantoms, that they would never entirely give up their superstitions, and that there was not one "undisguised" Christian among them; an archdeacon complained that when you pressed them with their gross misconceptions of the nature of God, they would turn the question aside with `sly civility`, or with a popular, careless proverb. Was it this sly civility that led those native Christians to spar with Anund Messeh for so long, and to take polite leave for the harvest as soon as baptism was mentioned? Bhabha sums up this discursive disturbance with an image: the wily barber of the Bombay bazaar does not rob his customer with the Lacanian "your money or your life", but feels in his customer's pocket while loudly exclaiming how bright His Honour's complexion is. Even the fate of the Bible itself is hybrid: one missionary began to discover, to his annoyance, that everyone was glad to receive a Bible: to keep as a curiosity, to sell for a few pice, or to use as waste paper.

**Conclusion: resistance as an effect of ambivalence.** This is the end point of the fourth mechanism (domination ↔ resistance) in Layer 5. For Gramsci in P9, resistance is a counter-hegemony; for New Historicism in P10, subversion is often contained by power; for cultural studies in P11, resistance takes the form of subcultural style. Bhabha's resistance is neither an oppositional intention nor a simple negation of the "content" of another culture: **resistance is not necessarily an oppositional act of political intention, but an effect of the ambivalence within the rules of recognition of dominating discourses: authority must be repeated in order to take effect, and repetition necessarily brings difference.** When the master's discourse becomes a site of hybridity, a sign of native struggle, he says, we may not only read between the lines but even seek to change the often coercive reality they so lucidly contain. This also explains why the editors say the imperial frontier is full of mutual admiration and adoration: mimicry is what the coloniser demands (Macaulay's well-educated native labourers), and also what the coloniser fears.

**Example: settler mimicry.** Bhabha's concept is usually used to describe the pitiful or absurd performances of the colonised; the Australian scholar **Alan Lawson**, in "The Anxious Proximities of Settler (Post)colonial Relations" (2000), turns it on white settlers, whose claim to "postcolonial" identity Loomba has already questioned. He begins with a moment of anxiety: in 1997 the Australian populist politician Pauline Hanson founded the One Nation party, whose supporters published an anonymous book, *The Truth*, reviving colonial-era simplistic narratives of Aboriginal cannibalism and Aboriginal violence, and citing the discredited "waves of migration" theory to claim that the ancestors of today's Aborigines had violently displaced more "original" inhabitants. The trigger of this cultural crisis was two land cases: in the *Mabo* case of 1992 the High Court of Australia declared untenable the doctrine of *terra nullius*, by which British and Australian law had denied Aboriginal land claims for two centuries (the term is often understood as "empty land", more precisely "land belonging to no one"); in the *Wik* case of 1996 the court ruled that pastoral leases did not necessarily extinguish native title entirely, so that two laws could apply to the same land. *Mabo* still retained the idea of separation, but *Wik* required a "grammar of unequal proximity", in the phrase Bhabha adapted from Derrida, "overlapping but not equivalent". Lawson uses Freud's "uncanny" (P6) to explain the affective structure of the anxiety: its source is not the strange, but what Gelder and Jacobs call being "in place and out of place" at the same time: "ours" may also be "theirs", a place is always already another place. It is here that mimicry becomes unavoidable for the settler: the settler subject is doubly inscribed between the imperial centre (*Imperium*) and the indigene, exercising authority over the indigene and the land while converting desire for them into a desire for indigenous authenticity; he speaks at once to two "first worlds", Europe as the source of culture and the indigene in the geographical, legal and temporal sense. Settlement is always a project of **displacement and replacement**, and so settlers tell stories of the disappearance of the indigene: the "last of the tribe" of *The Last of the Mohicans*, the "dying race", and the story of "pre-original" Aborigines replaced by present Aborigines; both narratives erase indigenous claims to "full" indigeneity; whites meanwhile claim to be "native" in the figures of the pioneer, the stockman, the bushman, completing their "indigenisation". **In the founding of cultural nationalism, one axis of difference (settler–indigene) is replaced by another (settler–imperial centre), and the colonisers themselves become the new "colonised": a strategic disavowal of the colonial act.** This is Bhabha's logic of disavowal re-enacted on the colonisers' side. The figure he finds for this mediated relation is `zeugma`: one word governing two others in the same grammatical relation but with two quite different senses, as in Pope's *The Rape of the Lock*: "Or stain her honour, or her new brocade". He also borrows Jameson's `ideologeme` from *The Political Unconscious* to explain why these narratives go on sedimenting and emitting ideological signals after their content has become outdated: Hanson's narrative is legible because it is the ultimate form of the old narrative of the "dying race": discursive space, like physical space, needs to be "cleared".

**Distinction: Bhabha and Spivak.** P12 described how Spivak read Bertha's self-immolation as widow-sacrifice, leaving the question of "Can the Subaltern Speak?" to be taken up here. Bhabha, in his acknowledgements, thanks Spivak for suggesting that he develop the concept of colonial mimicry further, and Loomba cites her warning about nostalgia for origins. *Spivak's essay of 1988 takes as its example the British colonial government's prohibition of widow-sacrifice in 1829, arguing that between the colonial discourse of "white men saving brown women from brown men" and the native patriarchal discourse of "they wanted to die", the voice of the female subaltern is nowhere to be found; her conclusion is that the subaltern cannot speak, not because subalterns are silent, but because there is no discursive position from which their speech could be heard, and intellectuals' attempts to "represent" them repeat this silencing.* The contrast between the two thus becomes clear: Bhabha's natives in the grove outside Delhi put sharp questions and send the catechist on his way; their resistance, though not oppositional, is **visible**, written into the missionaries' own records. Spivak's female subaltern leaves not even such a trace. **On the manifest/latent mechanism, Bhabha believes the archive can be read "against the grain" to bring out resistance, while Spivak asks about those who have no place in the archive at all: this is the farthest point the manifest/latent chain of Layer 5 can reach: the latent layer may be unrecoverable.**

**Objection:** Barry places Bhabha in the theoretical camp influenced by Derrida and Foucault, his writing forbiddingly difficult on the surface, his route to political action necessarily indirect, roughly corresponding to the "French" feminism of Kristeva and Cixous in P12; Said, by contrast, theorises less openly, seems to accept some premises of liberal humanism, and takes a more "direct" political stance (he identified with the cause of the Palestinian Arabs), closer to "Anglo-American" feminism. The criticism Loomba reports is sharper: postcolonial theory shifts the focus from places and institutions to individuals and their subjectivities, precisely as a result of its dependence on literary criticism and poststructuralism. To use Bhabha's own example: the Bible from the Hurdwar fair was indeed estranged by the natives' questions, but the Burdwan Plan and Macaulay's Minute still transformed the education system of all India; a theory that counts only the contradictions of discourse may underestimate the institutional success of colonial power. **McClintock will pull this question back from the subject to geography and time: what exactly does the "post" of "postcolonial" refer to?**

### The Pitfalls of the "Post": Linear Time and After Independence

**Problem:** **Anne McClintock**'s "The Angel of Progress: Pitfalls of the Term 'Post-colonialism'" (1992) begins with an exhibition. The "Hybrid State" exhibition on Broadway in New York required visitors first to pass through "The Passage": a dark antechamber, where a white word, COLONIALISM, invited you forward; stooping, you passed through a low door and were shut into another black space, the curators' brief nod to Fanon's "The native is a being hemmed in"; a second white word, POST-COLONIALISM, invited you through a slightly larger door into the next stage of history, after which you walked "fully upright" into the bright, noisy "Hybrid State". The exhibition's promise of "hybrid history" (multiple times) was contradicted by the linear logic of "The Passage", which re-enacted one of colonialism's most persistent tropes: in colonial discourse **space is time**, and history is shaped into two movements: the "progress" of humanity from stooped deficiency to erect, enlightened reason, and the reverse regression from (white male) adulthood to a primitive blackness, usually embodied in women. She juxtaposes the essay's epigraph (the angel of Benjamin's "Theses on the Philosophy of History", facing the past while blown into the future by the storm called "progress") with this exhibition, and points out that the ritually ubiquitous "post-" words of contemporary culture (postcolonial, postmodern, poststructural, post-Cold War, post-Marxist, post-apartheid, post-feminist) mark a widespread, epochal crisis in the idea of linear historical "progress".

**Mechanism: the axis of time replaces the axis of power.** Her central argument is that while "postcolonial" theory seeks to challenge Western historicism and its train of binary oppositions, the **term** "post-colonialism" reorients the globe around a single binary opposition: colonial/postcolonial. It shifts theory from the binary axis of power (coloniser/colonised) to the binary axis of time, which is even less politically nuanced, since it does not distinguish between the beneficiaries and the victims of colonialism.
