The affair dragged on and began to resemble a farce, like an episode of *Porterhouse Blue*, Tom Sharpe's 1974 novel satirising the struggle between traditionalists and reformers in a fictional Cambridge college. The proceedings of the appointments committee were leaked, and the university announced that the ancient "Court of Seven Men" (*Septem Viri*) would investigate the leak; the students passed a vote of no confidence in the faculty board and demanded a public inquiry into the state of the English faculty. The inquiry was held in the Senate House, inevitably described in reports as "oak-panelled"; it ought to have been a high-level intellectual debate between structuralists, Marxists and humanists, but of course it was not: it was about procedure, administration and committees. Higher education was then expanding rapidly while its funding was being tightly cut by the Thatcher government: buildings had dry rot, there were too few cleaners, students complained of too little contact time with their supervisors, and supervisors were increasingly pressed to do research. In the end the affair petered out: the two sides compromised, MacCabe's post was extended for a year, but in July 1981 he left Cambridge to take up a chair at the go-ahead University of Strathclyde in Glasgow. **On the whole, theory benefited from this publicity: a keen young talent whose future was threatened by reactionary forces gave theory its own martyr, and a stronger sense of cohesion and self-importance.** *The affair shows a pattern that will recur in event 9: the "theory" the public sees is always one step behind the actual state of theory, and the media image of theory replaces theory itself. It also shows a paradox of the fourth mechanism: being suppressed is precisely what gives the suppressed an identity.*

**1983: the publication of Eagleton's *Literary Theory: An Introduction*.** The spread of theory since the 1970s seems, in retrospect, unstoppable, but it actually depended on finding effective ways of *teaching* it, not only ways of studying it at the level of teachers and graduate students. The MacCabe affair had already exposed some of the difficulties. The major primary texts of theory were mostly written in French, a few in German or Russian, and not all had been translated; without "mediating" introductions usable as textbooks for undergraduate and master's courses, literary theory was doomed to remain an elite minority interest. The Methuen "New Accents" series, founded in 1977, first met the need for basic exposition, providing short introductory books on structuralism, deconstruction, poststructuralism and so on (*the series' general editor was Terence Hawkes, whom we will meet again under presentism below*). The first book to meet the need for an overall survey was **Terry Eagleton**'s *Literary Theory: An Introduction* (Blackwell, 1983). It was an immediate success because it was lively and provocative, and resisted the temptation to write an elephantine tome that might impress colleagues but would not suit students seeking initial enlightenment. These qualities distinguish it from most of its successors, and from the course "readers" of theory that have appeared since the late 1980s: readers collecting key essays and chapters by the major figures can be very useful if they are selective and genuinely meet their users' needs, but such books long ago succumbed to competitive "super-sizing", publishers playing an absurd game of poker to see who could produce the biggest theory reader, seeing a rival's thirteen hundred pages and raising them another thirteen hundred. *One irony: Rivkin and Ryan's* Literary Theory: An Anthology *is just such a reader, its second edition running to about thirteen hundred pages of text and its third to more than fifteen hundred. The difference between introduction and reader is also one of form: one integrates information in narrative, the other "lets the theorists speak for themselves".*

Eagleton, by contrast, kept things simple: the introduction is titled "What is Literature?", the first chapter tells the history of the rise of English as a discipline (P1), the next four chapters discuss phenomenology, structuralism, poststructuralism and psychoanalysis in turn, and the conclusion is titled "Political Criticism". He makes no pretence of neutrality: he is a Marxist critic writing from an explicit position, not a wine-taster who swills each "ism" round the mouth and spits it out before moving on to the next. The omissions are striking: the index (this is 1983) has no entry for "feminism" or "feminist theory" (*P13 has already noted that it says nothing about queer theory either*); and in a book called *Literary Theory* it is a little odd to begin with "What is literature?" rather than "What is literary theory?". The general argument is forceful but laboured: the answer to "What is literature?" is that literature does not exist "in the sense that insects do". One might impatiently retort that literary theory certainly exists, perhaps even in the sense that insects do, since Eagleton has written a book about it. But for Eagleton the purpose of literary theory seems to be anti-literary, which distinguishes it from literary criticism, usually (one would assume) on literature's side: theory is like a super-virus attacking literature from within with the aim of bringing about its death (but if literature does not exist, how can it die?). This is just the kind of theological question raised by the famous allegorical ending:

> I shall end with an allegory. We know that the lion is stronger than the lion-tamer, and so does the lion-tamer. The problem is that the lion does not know it. It is not out of the question that the death of literature may help the lion to awaken.

As **John Bayley** put it in his review in the *Times Literary Supplement* (10 June 1983), the question is: "What is the lion?" The lion is presumably the proletariat, the lion-tamer literature, and so the task of theory is to oppose literature, stripping it of its power to subdue and tame the masses. But Barry says that Eagleton's lion seems cleverer than he allows: the lion knows that the tamer holds a whip, and it is the whip that makes the tamer stronger than the lion. The metaphor must therefore conceive of literature as the whip, part of what Althusser called the "ideological state apparatuses" that control us by ideology rather than violence (P9). *Bayley's question is itself a reading in the theoretical sense: he asks for the literal referent of a figure, while Eagleton's allegory depends precisely on the indeterminacy of its referent. It forms an interesting contrast with the lion in P14 who took the monkey's figure literally, except that this time the one demanding the literal meaning is a reader sceptical of theory.* The book's strength lies in its overall energy, wit and intellectual agility, and in its deft summaries of a great many systems of thought: the structuralism chapter is extremely concise and informative, the poststructuralism chapter raises questions others discussed only a decade or more later, the psychoanalysis chapter is more ordinary, and the last chapter lays his Marxist cards uncompromisingly on the table, though in a way that anticipates the ethical and moral questions that would concern him twenty years later: what it means to be a "better person", he says, must be concrete and practical. **Eagleton's book did much to "consolidate" literary theory, establishing it firmly in the undergraduate curriculum and convincing teachers that it could be taught systematically; in the history of ten events it marks the peak of theory's rise.**

**1986: J. Hillis Miller's presidential address to the Modern Language Association.** By the mid-1980s signs of theory's coming decline had already appeared. The Modern Language Association is the main professional body of American university teachers of English; its annual convention is a major event of the discipline, and the president's keynote address is its climax, a "state of the discipline" statement that often points to future directions. **J. Hillis Miller**, one of the "Big Five" of *Deconstruction and Criticism*, had long championed deconstruction; his address ("The Triumph of Theory, the Resistance to Reading, and the Question of the Material Base") shows that he had expected the confident momentum of the early 1980s, when deconstruction seemed to be sweeping through the English departments of America's leading universities, to continue. What actually happened was that theory's dominance was checked by a new countervailing force: the historicist approaches rising from the field of early modern studies, inaugurated in the United States by Greenblatt's *Renaissance Self-Fashioning* (1980) and in Britain by Dollimore and Sinfield's *Political Shakespeare* (1985) (P10). Miller saw that historicism was the opposite of deconstruction, which had become in the 1980s the most prominent public incarnation of theory itself, succeeding structuralism in that role from the 1970s; so he said that "the triumph of theory" had been interrupted by a regrettable outbreak of historicism: literary study had undergone a sudden, almost universal turn away from theory oriented towards language as such, towards history, culture, society, politics, institutions, class and gender conditions, the social context, the material base (P10 has quoted this passage).

Barry's reading has three layers. First, on Miller's own formulation it seems fairly obvious why many chose the side he disapproved of: "history, culture, society … the material base" sounds far more interesting than "orientation towards language as such". Deconstructive theory held that students should study "literariness" itself rather than literature, the process of conceptualisation in general rather than the specific meaning of *Middlemarch*; in practice this "literariness as such" always proved hard to turn into a workable undergraduate course, as the elephantine theory readers themselves demonstrate. Pursuing an "orientation towards language as such" is a bit like staring at the sun in literary study: you cannot do it for long, it may be harmful, and you soon want to look elsewhere. Studying historical, cultural and gender conditions is much more concrete, and not hard to turn into courses students will want to take, so it is no surprise that the tide turned from deconstruction to historicism.

Second, one must distinguish **history** from `historicism`. Historians use diligent research to recover the past, letting us walk again the streets of Shakespeare's London and go to the playhouse to see a performance of *Hamlet*: we would know what the streets looked like, smell the smells, hear the sounds, know exactly what coins to have ready to get into the theatre (*just Stephen's mental fantasy in the "Scylla and Charybdis" chapter of Joyce's* Ulysses). These are all external, material things, representing what historical research digs up; its ultimate product might be the Globe on London's Bankside, an Elizabethan theatre as authentic as possible, where one can stand in the open air to watch a play like the groundlings of the time and, if the performance uses "original pronunciation", even hear the English the Elizabethans heard (provided one can ignore the constant noise of jets heading for Heathrow). But historicists do not really care for such enterprises, because external, material things are not ultimately their goal. What interests them is the internal: not so much what Elizabethans saw in the playhouse as *what it felt like to see it*; they are interested too in "identity" ("early modern identity", "gender identity", "national identity"), something deeper that pervades or transcends the material fabric of a period. Their attitude is, as it were: who cares what kind of shirts the Elizabethans wore or how they pronounced English? I want to understand what it felt like to be an Elizabethan. So historicists are mainly concerned with "discourse", "structures of feeling" (Williams in P10), "mentalities" and "identities". In Barry's view they are generally more confident than "real" historians that these fundamental and intangible elements of the past can be recovered, and want to go straight to the level of "identity", skipping the tedious archaeological digging on which historians spend most of their time. **Historians, that is, are always materialists, and historicists always idealists.** This, says Barry, is the kind of thing Morris Zapp, the literary-theorist hero of David Lodge's novels, would say.

Third, in his address Miller ignored the distinction between historians and historicists, and saw the opposing historicist force as a Gradgrindian obsession with facts (*the headmaster in Dickens's* Hard Times *who wants nothing but "Facts"*), so naturally he could not understand how it could compete with the allure of "language as such". **In Barry's reading, this sixth event is a sign that theory's vast and rapid success had begun to breed a certain complacency: its great influence in highly privileged Anglo-American institutions led it both to underestimate the appeal of other approaches and to overestimate the shelf life of its own ideas.**

**Comparison: Montrose's reply.** The New Historicist Montrose's "Professing the Renaissance: The Poetics and Politics of Culture" is a direct reply to the same address (P10 has discussed it in detail). Putting the two responses together reveals three interpretations of the same event. Miller's scheme is "theory versus history": turning to history means turning away from theory. Montrose refuses this polarisation: society is discursively constructed, language use is socially and materially determined, the propositions of deconstruction can become tools of ideological analysis, and "theory" does not dwell serenely above "ideology" but is deeply implicated in it; so turning to history is not turning away from theory but theory continuing in history, and "the textuality of history" is itself a poststructuralist proposition. Barry's scheme is "history versus historicism": turning to historicism is not turning to the historians' history either, because historicists are idealists. **Barry and Montrose unexpectedly agree on one point: New Historicism is not the positivist return to the "material base" that Miller feared; it retains theory's textuality. Where they differ is in evaluation:** Montrose sees this as theory's maturity, a new historical criticism aware that it too is a discursive practice taking part in the interactions it analyses; Barry sees it as an unearned confidence, a belief that intangible "identities" can be recovered from textual traces. *This disagreement will receive a third formulation in presentism's critique of historicism: if identities are historically constructed, how can we step outside our own constructed identities to discern those of another age?*

**1986: the Strathclyde "Linguistics of Writing" conference.** Theory's complacency seemed to show itself again at a high-profile theory conference in Glasgow at which many of the most famous theorists were speakers. *The conference was held in July 1986; its proceedings,* The Linguistics of Writing: Arguments between Language and Literature, *were published in 1987, edited by Nigel Fabb, Derek Attridge, Alan Durant and Colin MacCabe; in the same year the television documentary* Big Words … Small Worlds, *written and presented by David Lodge, was broadcast on Channel 4. One of the editors was the very MacCabe who had left Cambridge for Strathclyde five years earlier.* In retrospect the conference was both the peak of theory's glamour and success and the beginning of another era: a certain triumphalism began to provoke dissent and resistance, and not only from diehard traditionalists. Barry likens it to the notorious "Sheffield rally" held by the British Labour Party before the 1992 general election: Labour was far ahead in the polls, but on television the rally looked like a victory party begun before the victory, the poll lead evaporated, and Labour spent another five years in opposition. The same atmosphere of triumphant celebration appeared at Strathclyde, oddly mixed with an attempt to revive the prestige of linguistics: the conference was organised by the university's "Programme in Literary Linguistics" and tried to repeat the impact of the Indiana conference of 1958, so it opened with a "closing statement" and closed with an "opening statement", as if certain it was launching a whole new era of theory. But the conference was not always brilliant: several famous linguists seemed very "monodisciplinary", in this sense a step back from Indiana's missionary interdisciplinarity. David Lodge began his lecture on Bakhtin by reminding his audience that the Indiana conference had included a paper, full of statistics and tables, on stylistic deviation in suicide notes; as the conference went on, the Glasgow conference came more and more to resemble **a long suicide note for literary theory**.

Derrida gave a lecture entitled "How to Avoid Speaking", an especially laborious and unrelenting lecture on negative theology which Barry recalls as lasting nearly two hours, its last half-hour constantly interrupted by the sound of the lecture-theatre doors opening and closing as exhausted listeners drifted away. The discussion is included in the volume: questions were written the day before and handed to the chair, who passed them to Derrida, giving him time to consider them. Most startling was his announcement that he had never said or thought that the metaphysics of presence was bad; he tended to think, on the contrary, that it was good. It took the audience a few minutes to grasp the implication: if the metaphysics of presence is good, why spend an entire academic career deconstructing it? This was exactly the question **Jonathan Culler** put on the spot. The answer was essentially theological: the desire for presence is natural, but its fulfilment would be death itself, so one is obliged to deconstruct it, showing again and again that what we take to be the full presence of something is in fact the glimmer of *différance* (P7). From this came his subsequent refrain, "deconstruction is not a method", that it does not consist of a set of methodological rules, though he also said it has certain methodological effects, without explaining how this differs from being a method. *Barry does not accept this claim at face value: the three-stage model of deconstruction in P7 is precisely a demonstration and quantification of its practice.* It was an impressive performance, but it foreshadowed the rest of Derrida's career: he was always ready to say what deconstruction (or anything else) was not, but never seemed able or willing to explain what it was; the theory world increasingly tended to claim that people had misunderstood him, or understood him too literally, too naively, and his supporters endlessly repeated this complaint: whenever someone said he was wrong, the reply was always that this was not what he had said or meant.

As the conference went on, frustration accumulated. Having the conference filmed for television seemed a masterstroke, but the lights and microphones were intrusive: even during tea breaks the film crew circled the big names with huge boom microphones, and rushed at delegates who had asked questions to get them to sign release forms. The "opening statement" on the last morning was interrupted from the floor by people who wanted to speak, above all about the deeply divisive power structure the conference had laid bare; the delegates voted to have the studio lights switched off and the film crew asked to leave, and the conference ended in disarray, the resounding "opening statement" having lost its impact. What went wrong? Too many large plenary sessions (almost all with American and British male speakers), responses dominated by the same people, and little space or time for open and democratic exchange. **However socially progressive the message of literary theory, it must also be socially progressive in its methods.** Almost imperceptibly, in just a few years, theorists had become the new establishment and new elite of academia, and seemed to take their position for granted; like the Labour shadow cabinet ministers arriving at that ill-fated Sheffield rally in a fleet of pseudo-ministerial black limousines, the big names suddenly seemed to take the triumph of theory too much as a *fait accompli*. *The fourth mechanism is here applied reflexively to theory itself for the first time: a discourse whose business is analysing power cannot see the power structure in its own conference hall. It is also an ironic variant of the containment model of P10: the rebels' victory made them the very thing that needed opposing.*

**1987–1988: the scandal of de Man's wartime writings.** The Belgian-born **Paul de Man** (1919–1983) was one of the "Big Five" of *Deconstruction and Criticism*; his three books, *Blindness and Insight* (1971), *Allegories of Reading* (1979) and *The Resistance to Theory* (1986), were enormously influential, and at his death he was revered as the austere embodiment of literary deconstruction. But on 1 December 1987 a front-page article in the *New York Times*, "Yale Scholar Wrote for Pro-Nazi Newspaper", revealed that as a young man in Nazi-occupied Belgium he had written nearly two hundred articles for *Le Soir* in the early 1940s, some with an evident antisemitic colouring; the original discoverer was Ortwin de Graef, a Belgian student researching de Man's early life and writings. **The facts were shocking, but what damaged the reputation of deconstruction, and of literary theory in general, was mainly not de Man's personal guilt but the grounds on which other theorists defended him.** In Barry's view, especially counterproductive was Derrida's long essay in *Critical Inquiry*: the original defence ran to seventy-five pages, the reply to the responses to another sixty. Derrida began by speculating on whether it is possible to respond to questions, what responding means, whether it means taking responsibility, and what responsibility is: one could see at once that a defence conducted in this way would be very long, when what was needed was exactly what Derrida never provided: clarity, concision, brevity, and the force of conviction and sympathy. The defenders' position was in any case impossible. Barry thinks the best "defence" might have been to publish all the articles, leave them on the record, and briefly state the mitigating considerations: de Man's youth; that he may not, at least at first, have known what was happening to the Jews of Europe; that there may have been threats or dangers, so that he acted out of fear rather than conviction. This may not amount to much, but it is probably all that could be done. Former friends and colleagues had no need to turn and condemn him, and should not have, but neither need they have felt obliged to defend him. Theorists may have felt intellectually that if de Man could not be defended, deconstruction and literary theory would sink with his reputation; but a defence driven by such self-interested professional motives would do great damage. Derrida as a friend did feel the need to defend de Man, yet he seemed to mobilise all the subtleties of deconstruction in that defence, so that the whole set of beliefs about the unreliability of language and the fragility of truth and the self was pressed into service, with an inevitable result: **these concepts themselves began to look morally suspect, because questioning the very concept of responsibility seemed to slide into denying that we are responsible for what we say and do.** To write in the 1940s that "a solution of the Jewish problem that would lead to the creation of a Jewish colony isolated from Europe would not entail, for the literary life of the West, deplorable consequences" was to endorse publicly (at best) deportation; given de Man's later career as a literary scholar, what is especially shocking is that he endorsed antisemitism *as a literary intellectual*. Literary theory was thus badly damaged by the de Man affair, and never fully recovered its prestige, its confidence, or its sense of moral and political legitimacy. *What is tested here is the "undecidability" of P7: a method that refuses final judgement in reading was used, in a situation demanding clear moral judgement, to evade judgement, and so the method itself was convicted by association.*

**1991: Baudrillard and "The Gulf War Did Not Take Place".** The significance in the history of events of the three articles Baudrillard published in *Libération* from January to March 1991 (P8 has discussed their contents and Norris's attack in detail) lies in a huge irony: **they became victims of the very condition they diagnosed.** Just as, in Baudrillard's charge, images or "simulacra" of the war were mistaken for the war itself, what people thought he had written replaced what he had actually written. He thus became a whipping boy for anti-theorists, a target for high-moral-ground condemnations of postmodernism, which by the 1990s was seen as standing for literary theory as a whole. In the "simulacrum" version of Baudrillard, this too-clever-by-half postmodernist quibbles about the concept of reality, indifferent to suffering and death that (people were indignantly told) had undoubtedly occurred; and, it was said, if one begins by doubting the reality of the Gulf War, might one not end by doubting the reality of the Holocaust? *The charge worked partly because the de Man affair had already linked "theory" with the shadow of antisemitism.* **In the de Man affair the real damage to theory came from his defenders; in the Baudrillard affair it came partly from his attackers: the theory "community" wrongly defended de Man and wrongly attacked Baudrillard.** *Barry's verdicts on the two events are symmetrical: in both, the very distinction theory taught people, between figurative and literal readings, was used selectively.*

**1996: the Sokal affair.** **Alan Sokal**, a professor of physics at New York University, wrote a hoax article entitled "Transgressing the Boundaries: Towards a Transformative Hermeneutics of Quantum Gravity", pieced together largely from what he considered postmodernist clichés, and submitted it to *Social Text*, a Duke University journal of postmodern cultural studies, which accepted and published it. On the day the article appeared, he revealed the hoax in another publication (*the magazine* Lingua Franca), arguing that the article's acceptance exposed the emptiness of postmodern theory and, given postmodernism's prominence at the time, implicitly of all cultural theory. The article was later included in Sokal and **Jean Bricmont**'s *Intellectual Impostures* (French 1997, English 1998). The book and the article were not a wholesale attack on postmodern theory (though they were widely understood that way), but an exposure of the misuse of ideas from physics and mathematics by famous French theorists, chiefly Lacan, Kristeva, Irigaray, Baudrillard, and Deleuze and Guattari; the ideas borrowed were broadly those that seemed to lend support to "constructionist" or "relativist" views of reality (Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, Gödel's incompleteness theorem, Einstein's theory of relativity and so on). Sokal's implication was that much postmodern "jargon" seems to have no concise or "rigorous" meaning, so that the editors of an important journal could not recognise that approved terms and formulations had been mixed and multiplied into an article with no overall coherence or logic. Had the editors simply admitted their mistake after the hoax was revealed and tightened their reviewing procedures, the affair might soon have blown over, but they did not, and the controversy quickly escalated.

Since the accuser was American and the accused almost all French, the hoax was seen as an attack on the standing of French intellectuals. Kristeva, one of those most severely criticised in the book, replied in *Le Nouvel Observateur* (25 September 1997) that after a Francophile period the pendulum had swung the other way, and that "a real Francophobia" (*une véritable francophobie*) was emerging in America. Derrida was not a sustained target of the article or the book, but he was the first theorist the article quoted, and that quotation was described as the article's first important quotation of gibberish; it came, rather oddly, from Derrida's improvised reply to Hyppolite in 1966 (P7). *The reply concerns "the Einsteinian constant".* Derrida's comment on the Sokal affair (first published in *Le Monde*), in contrast to his intervention in the de Man affair, was very brief, and is usually quoted only for the phrase "poor Sokal", referring to the plight of a physicist famous for a hoax rather than for physics. But Derrida likewise saw the affair in national terms: the "credit" he, a "foreign professor", had received in America was thought excessive, so he and other French authors were attacked for a fault (the loose use of metaphors from science and mathematics) evidently not confined to the French; he said he would like to say more about "the American context and the political context", but had no space.

Barry concludes that the Sokal affair did carry the nationalist overtones Kristeva and Derrida detected. **American intellectual life, having invited literary theory in in 1958 and 1966 and played host to it for some forty years, now seemed to be serving notice to quit: theory's "moment" had lasted long enough, and the theorists should pack their bags and go home.** Since postmodernism now stood for theory in general, the humiliation of postmodern theory by Sokal's hoax (as the event was widely seen) was taken as the total failure of "theory". There were indeed strong forces in America working to reclaim the humanities curriculum and re-Americanise it, gaining momentum through the 1990s: a general counter-revolution took place in American universities against a cluster of targets (political correctness, relativism, postmodernism, multiculturalism and so on), tendencies that hardened in the climate after 9/11. General anxiety about new terrorist attacks made international conferences harder to hold; together with growing concern about global warming and carbon footprints, and with email, videoconferencing and social networking making gatherings less necessary, intellectual life became more enclosed and more national than international, and literary theory did not escape. Barry therefore expects that in coming decades there will be greater divergence between the versions of literary theory prevailing in different parts of the world, rather than total domination by a few global brands, which he regards as an exciting new situation. *This expectation connects directly with the spread of "English" from the imperial centre to the rest of the world in P15 and with the "American–British" division of ecocriticism in P16: the future of theory may no longer be one theory but many local theories.*

**Conclusion: one arc, three kinds of damage.** The ten events can be read as a complete narrative. In the rising phase (1958–1983), theory entered the humanities on the scientific prestige of linguistics, heard poststructuralism at a structuralist conference, declared war on the status quo with the practice of deconstruction, gained a martyr at Cambridge, and gained a curriculum in Eagleton's textbook. At the peak and turning point (1986–1987), theory complained in a presidential address of an "outbreak" of historicism, and revealed its new elite status at a triumphalist conference in Glasgow. In the declining phase (1987–1996), the three events caused three kinds of damage: the damage of the de Man affair was **moral**, theories of language and the subject being suspected of evading responsibility; the damage of the Baudrillard affair was **political and epistemological**, the analysis of "the real" being suspected of indifference to suffering; the damage of the Sokal affair concerned **intellectual rigour**, the language of theory being suspected of being meaningless jargon. **Theory entered literary study in 1958 in the name of science, and was declared out in 1996 in the name of science.** Throughout the arc, the theory seen by the public was always a step behind theory itself, and a little cruder: *The Times* of 1981 took it for grammar, the critics of 1991 for a denial of war. Theory's public fate is itself a history of representation and simulacra. *Of the ten events, four are conferences, two are books, one an appointment and three scandals. Theory is not only a set of ideas but also a social institution made of conferences, book series, posts, reviews and television; its rise and fall depended on these institutions as much as on its arguments.*

### What Theory Left Behind: The Legacy and Four Turns

**Problem: is there life after theory?** That was precisely the question asked by an important British conference in 2003: "Is there life after theory?" The proceedings were titled *life.after.theory* (edited by Michael Payne and John Schad), and included interviews with leading participants such as Derrida, Kermode, Toril Moi and Norris. Interestingly, the conference's title was a question, while the book's title can be read as a declaration of faith: there is indeed life after theory. In the introduction to the first edition of *Beginning Theory* in 1995, Barry had already mentioned the widespread feeling that the real business of theory was over, citing Thomas Docherty's 1990 book *After Theory*; Eagleton used *After Theory* as a title again in 2003, implying that theory remained (so to speak) in a state of "being over"; and Eagleton's book itself came "after" Valentine Cunningham's *Reading After Theory* (2001), without mentioning it. Cunningham is on the whole glad that theory has run its course, and sees himself as one of those beginning to repair aspects of criticism damaged by theory and to restore them to their proper place in literary study, like someone starting to clear up after a flood or a hurricane. There were also more local "repair" books, such as David Scott Kastan's *Shakespeare After Theory* (1999). In this book "after theory" is understood as **not the period after theory has passed away, but the period in which theory is no longer news.** Theory is no longer newsworthy, one might say, because many of its core ideas have been generally accepted, its impact and glamour "routinised", to borrow a term from the sociologist **Max Weber** (*Weber used "the routinisation of charisma" to describe how charismatic personal authority is converted into everyday institutional authority*). It no longer needs to proclaim its distinctiveness, having flowed into the general stream of thought; this "unassertive" temper can be seen as a general feature of theory after "theory": the "evangelical" phase is over precisely because so many of its ideas have become the currency of the intellectual climate in which we live.

**Definition: four mindsets.** Which ideas that were fiercely resisted twenty-five years ago now seem ordinary and taken for granted? A rough list contains four items. First, identity is both fixed and fluid: being British, gay, a woman or a religious believer is not possessing some fixed entity or view, unchanged all along, but having identities that drift constantly with various currents, currents that act differently on different people; "after theory", our notions of "being" always contain an important element of "becoming". Second, literary texts are just as unstable, "canonical" or not: every text is subject to shifting perceptions of what it "is", may have different "identities" for different groups, may exist in several versions differently edited and presented, and is always subject to different (perhaps successive) appropriations: think of all the Shakespeares we have seen in theory's lifetime: the "sexually dissident" and "postcolonial" Shakespeares of 1980s cultural materialism, the "Catholic" and "republican" Shakespeares of the 1990s, to name only a few. Third, we are aware of the instability of language itself, its tendency to slip out of the nets of definition and strict delimitation: not only the post-Freudian alertness to "slips" and slippage as the very texture of language; we are also keenly aware of the "dream life" of metaphor and rhetoric in language, which sometimes disturbs the flattest, most instrumental discourse. Fourth, theory is everywhere: it is impossible to opt out of taking positions, since every stance is a perspective, so all our assertions are improvised, contingent, provisional, like speculative cheques drawn on the bank of thought and culture, never knowing for sure how much is in the account to back them. **Unstable identities, unstable texts, unstable linguistic structures and an uncertain bank of truth: these are the four mindsets that "after theory" has left with many people.** We do not sign up to them as a creed (almost by definition, our belief in the four instabilities is itself unstable), but they are always there, forming the climate of our thinking and feeling, not just the weather.

*Comparing the four mindsets with the five sentences of P1 shows the precise shape of theory's legacy: "human nature is a myth" has become unstable identity, "meaning is contingent" unstable texts, "language is constitutive" unstable language, while "truth is provisional" and "politics is everywhere" have merged into the uncertain bank of truth: there is no neutral standpoint. In P1 the five sentences were fighting propositions; here they have become background assumptions. They were not refuted but absorbed, at the cost of losing their edge.*

**Mechanism: four turns.** The intellectual landscape of theory itself has also undergone four general shifts, or reached four "settlements". First, **more empirical**: theory is less willing than before to suspend disbelief in the face of grand speculative claims, and more committed to dealing with material at the empirical level, so that conclusions are more likely to be proved, or at least argued in more detail, rather than majestically pronounced. The old Gallic disdain for "mere" empiricism now seems as dated as the assumption that French cuisine and French fashion are inherently superior; clarity is now expected of literary theorists, and the "poetic licence" generously issued to French theorists in the 1970s and 1980s is no longer valid (at least abroad). Theory's present "afterlife" therefore involves a kind of strategic "downsizing": the old intellectual "superzones" have shrunk; structuralism has been replaced by narratology, originally one of its own specialist branches (P4); and the abstractions of "ideology" and "politics" handled by Marxist materialism have been replaced by detailed attention to the cultural logistics of particular periods, especially the early modern, Romantic and Victorian.

Second, **less materialist**: theory has moved away from the dominant materialisms represented by British cultural materialism and American New Historicism, and even drifted towards aspects of the "spiritual", whether conceived as various metaphorical figurations of reading, writing and textuality (as in Julian Wolfreys's *Victorian Hauntings*, 2001), or as metonymic figurations of a world more real (that is, deeper, more fundamental) than material reality. A religious turn was especially evident in literary studies around the millennium, more so than for decades; the sustained and widespread interest in Shakespeare's religious beliefs may be a symptom of this "turn" (E. A. J. Honigmann's *Shakespeare: The "Lost Years"*, 1988; Richard Wilson's *Secret Shakespeare*, 2004).

Third, **away from "the linguistic sublime"**: what Barry calls `the linguistic sublime` is the "constructionist" view of language as constructing or forming our world, according to which in effect everything is language, or language is everything, depending on which way you look at it. The theorist and philosopher Norris (*who attacked Baudrillard in P8*) has long been a major force in countering and dismantling the prestige of thoroughgoing linguistic constructionism. He doubts (and more than doubts) the view that "language speaks us, not we language", holding that it (thinking presumably of Heidegger and de Man) too easily lets us deny responsibility for what we say; he vigorously attacks the "anti-realists" in philosophy (those who deny a "mind-independent" reality and tend to see everything as "mind-dependent"), and even tends to see the much-discussed "third way" between the poles of "realism" and "anti-realism" as another form of the latter; and he opposes the endless, playful, polysemic interpretation offered at the expense of systematic argument by theorists such as Baudrillard, Fish, Rorty and Lyotard, as typical of postmodern relativism. *Here one can see the theoretical consequences of the de Man affair: Norris's critique of "language speaks us" is the philosophical version of Barry's critique of Derrida's defence of de Man: a theory of language that denies the subject will, ethically, be read as denying responsibility.*

Fourth, **"crisis critique"**: a new cultural critique responds to extreme events like 9/11, and to the global pessimism produced by seemingly intractable problems such as the Arab–Israeli conflict, Iraq, Afghanistan, the spread of religious fundamentalism and the continuing deterioration of the environment. The sense that the world situation is growing ever more desperate, and that cultural critique itself looks like a foolish luxury in its shadow, runs through many of Eagleton's post-millennial books (*Sweet Violence*, 2003; *After Theory*, 2003; *Holy Terror*, 2005). His cultural critique increasingly concerns violence, terror and evil, and might be called `crisis critique`; **ecocriticism can reasonably be seen as one branch of it** (P16); such writing carries a sense of catastrophe as both pervasive and imminent, making the usual concerns of literary and cultural criticism seem secretly complicit with the forces about to destroy us. Eagleton's growing concern with moral, religious and ethical questions, and his gradual move away from Marxism, can also be seen as a symptom of the "religious turn" mentioned above. *This answers exactly the remark about the "better person" at the end of event 5: the seed of the ethical turn of twenty years later was already buried in the Marxist textbook of 1983.*

**Conclusion:** Theory in recent years has become more empiricist, less exclusively materialist, less easily impressed by "the linguistic sublime", more steeped in awareness of encroaching global crisis. **But it has not shut up shop; it remains open for business, and has even developed several new product lines.** Since people began generally saying around 1995 that theory was over, in what specific ways has theory been supplemented and developed? Without aiming at completeness, Barry examines five areas: presentism, the new aestheticism, cognitive poetics, consilience and posthumanism. *The five areas can be arranged by their relation to the legacy of theory: presentism revises historicism's (P10) choice of context; the new aestheticism revises the attitude of the "hermeneutics of suspicion" to texts; cognitive poetics and consilience respond to the empirical turn and to the scientific question left by Sokal; and posthumanism pushes theory's decentring as far as "the human" itself. The first two argue on the boundary of text and context, the middle two on the boundary of essence and construction, and the last takes constructionism to its limit.*

### Presentism: The Present as Context

**Definition:** As **Hugh Grady** defines it, `presentism` is an approach to literary study oriented towards the meaning of texts in the present rather than, as "historicist" approaches are, towards their meaning in the past. It was first concerned with early modern literature, especially Shakespeare, and has more recently appeared in Romantic studies under the name of "critical presentism"; its practitioners include **Terence Hawkes**, Grady and **Ewan Fernie**.

**Background: the historicist charter.** Presentism can be seen as a reaction against the history-centred approaches dominant since the 1980s (New Historicism and cultural materialism, P10). The emphasis on history rests on the work of Foucault, who stipulated in the first chapter of *The Archaeology of Knowledge* (English translation 1972) that in analysing a discursive field "we must grasp the statement in the *exact specificity* of its occurrence" (emphasis added by Barry). So it is not enough to analyse the "statement" (a literary text is a statement); it must be "situated" within a laboriously reconstructed historical specificity: determining the conditions of its existence, fixing at least its limits, establishing its correlations with other statements that may be connected with it, and showing what other forms of statement it excludes. This is the method of inquiry Foucault advocated, and its implications for literary study could be devastating. Barry says that this "statement" of Foucault's could be called a **historicist charter**; if we sign it (and many did), we commit ourselves to a lifetime of endless historical archaeology. Historicism also rests on Raymond Williams's emphasis (*Marxism and Literature*, 1977) on understanding "the *whole* lived social process as practically organized by specific and dominant meanings and values" (emphasis again added by Barry). The intimidating use of words like "specific", "exact" and "whole" in such manifestos drove many towards exhaustive historicist research, literary scholars being taken over by historical methods; by the late 1990s it seemed taken for granted that only amateur readers would deny that literature is best understood through history.

**Distinction: two presentisms.** This is the situation presentism opposes. The term "presentism" goes back to the early twentieth century, originally meaning a naive tendency to read the past entirely in terms of the present, treating today as the culmination and completion towards which the past was always striving. For a presentist in this naive sense, the past is interesting only insofar as its concerns bear directly on ours, so we search history for what is "relevant" to us and discard the rest. For a historian this is a serious fault, but for a literary scholar? It could be argued that a literary scholar who is not a presentist is no literary scholar at all, since if literature does not speak to our present concerns there is no point in reading it. So since about 2000 a group of literary scholars has called itself "presentist", partly to mark its position as opposed to the historicists. Hawkes is the main practitioner of presentism, and the Routledge "Accents on Shakespeare" series he edited is its main publishing base. **Hawkes was also a leading figure in promoting literary theory in the 1970s: it was the Methuen "New Accents" series he edited that did the groundwork of popularising and mediating the work of the major figures of the theory movement (event 5).** The new series continues the mission of the original "New Accents", its aim being to apply theory, or to extend and adapt it so as to connect it with specific pedagogical concerns. *Thus the "textbook era" of theory and one new direction "after theory" are linked by the same person.*

**Argument:** Several defining positions of presentism are found in Hawkes's own volume in the series, *Shakespeare in the Present* (2002). First, genuinely capturing or repeating the past is fundamentally impossible: the past is past, and we can never reconstruct or recapture its "identity" (*which Barry thinks is precisely the fundamental aim of most historicist approaches*), so neither historian nor literary scholar can engage with a past not shaped by their own concerns. Hawkes cites the Italian critic and philosopher **Benedetto Croce**: "All history is contemporary history." So the presentist literary scholar actively seeks "the present in the past", explicitly aiming to converse and negotiate with the living; historians and historicists seek "to speak with the dead", often said to be one of the historian's main aims and satisfactions. Greenblatt's *Shakespearean Negotiations* (1988), a founding work of New Historicism, opens with just such words: "I began with the desire to speak with the dead … It is true that I could hear only my own voice, but my own voice was the voice of the dead." **So the basic difference between the two is that presentists speak first to the living and historicists first to the dead, though both may be aware that they are in fact often negotiating with themselves** (Greenblatt's opening seems to admit as much).

Second, historicism aims to study literature in its "embeddedness" in the time and place of the work (Foucault's "exact specificity of its occurrence" again), which at first seems the obvious method; presentism simply asks what, for instance, the "time and place" of a Shakespeare play actually is. Fernie argues, in effect, that Shakespeare in particular is first and foremost a contemporary dramatist and writer, since he is currently taught, read and performed worldwide on a scale no one else can match, so that he is more embedded in our modern world than he ever was in the Renaissance. Third, historicism could be said to rest on a logical contradiction: **if identity really is historically constructed, we can never step outside our own historically constructed identities to discern the identities of another age.** *This is the third formulation of the dispute between Montrose and Barry above: Montrose admits that the critic's own discourse is also a practice participating in its object of analysis, and presentism draws the conclusion from this admission: in that case, make the present explicitly the starting point.*

Hawkes also mentions two areas of presentist emphasis in Shakespeare studies. One is devolution in British politics: the establishment in the late 1990s of a parliament or assemblies for Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, and the consequent redefinition of what the "United Kingdom" means. His sense of the tensions and ambiguities within British "union" runs through a chapter on *Cymbeline* titled "Aberdaugleddyf", the Welsh name for Milford Haven (literally "the mouth of the two rivers"), an "English" port in Wales long of great strategic importance for the defence of the "kingdom" (an aptly ambiguous word), and prominent in the play. In British history the Welsh Tudors and the Scottish Stuarts successively took the "British" throne, while the national status of Ireland, Scotland and Wales remained ambiguous (were they nations in their own right?); the project was to forge Englishness, Welshness, Scottishness and Irishness into a single "Britishness", without adopting a federal model. Hawkes reads the play knowing that the two streams of Welshness and Englishness never merged, and that today's devolution is making them diverge further. The other is a series of strategic reversals of established priorities, including apparently immutable conceptual hierarchies such as primary/secondary and past/present: Shakespeare's influence on Marx and Freud will be seen as just as interesting and important as Marxist and Freudian readings of Shakespeare; a Shakespeare play's "performance" will be seen as just as important as its "reference", what it *does* as important as what it *says*. Hawkes later gives a fuller definition, to the effect that presentist criticism actively and fully seeks its roots and connections in the here and now, deliberately foregrounds them and exploits them as a first principle, its engagement with the text conditioned precisely by those dimensions of the modern world that resonate most loudly with past events, perhaps as the endings of those beginnings. Presentism thus sees itself as in some measure reversing the strategy of New Historicism, starting from the "material present" and letting it set the agenda of the inquiry. *The reversal of the "primary/secondary" hierarchy is a direct application of the deconstructive operation of P7: presentism enters historicism's territory with deconstruction's tools.*

**Operations: presentism in practice.** The crux of the theoretical position may lie in this idea: **every ending, as it arrives, shapes the beginnings that preceded it.** Despite such different premises, the method of presentism, judging by *Shakespeare in the Present*, is quite similar to that of New Historicism. Essays often open with a vivid "cultural snapshot", much like the New Historicist "anecdote" (P10), except that the snapshot is taken from the present or the recent past. Hawkes's essay on *Hamlet* is titled "The Old Bill" (British slang for the police); it sees *Hamlet* as a play about policing, detection and "picking up", in which many characters are constantly under surveillance and constantly watching others. The opening "snapshot": in Berlin in 1945 the American occupying forces drew up lists of plays approved and not approved for performance; *Hamlet* was approved for its treatment of "corruption and justice", while *Julius Caesar* and *Coriolanus* were not, supposedly for "glorifying dictatorship", so that drama itself became an element in the processes of surveillance in the specific situation just after the Second World War. Hawkes then discusses the play's use of stage and performance, and weaves in the true story of the Jewish actor Mauriz Leon Reiss, who in the 1930s constructed an entirely new non-Jewish identity for himself in Nazi Germany and "performed" it in real life, came to America and Hollywood in the 1940s, and, cruelly and ironically, ended up playing Nazis in propaganda films. In the essay these elements are woven into what Barry calls a `critical plot`, **and it is precisely this element of "plotting" (more familiar in creative than in critical writing) that characterises presentist writing.** There is close-up textual work in presentist essays, but it is highly "thematised", drawing out countless aspects of key themes such as surveillance and performance from the text. In sum, a presentist "emplotment" or "performance" of a play has four key elements: a vivid opening "snapshot", a highly plotted structure of argument in which key motifs recur, a highly thematised engagement with the text, and an overriding present concern, usually political, as the driving force.

**Conclusion: the dispute over context.** In the end, the dispute between historicism and presentism is a dispute about the **choice of context**: one can read *Hamlet* in the context of the past (as Greenblatt, in *Hamlet in Purgatory*, places the play amid early modern religious beliefs and conflicts), or in the context of the present (or at least the more recent past), as Hawkes does. Fernie's essay on *Hamlet* also gives a "presentist" reading, placing the play's abundant random violence in the context of today's terrorist threat. But, as Fernie says, this can also be seen as a kind of agreement: historicists and presentists alike seem to be saying, in effect, **anything but the text**, since both see the choice of context as the decisive act of reading strategy, as if Hamlet had said not "the play's the thing" but "the context's the thing" (*"The play's the thing" comes from* Hamlet, *Act 2, Scene 2*). **Objection:** *Presentism revises the temporal direction of context but does not change the basic tendency of the fifth mechanism: meaning is still sought outside the text. It replaces the "historicist charter" with a "presentist charter", which can become just as "intimidating": only amateur readers would deny that literature is best understood through the present.* This question is taken up by the new aestheticism.

### The New Aestheticism: The Return of Textual Particularity

**Definition:** The `new aestheticism` is an emerging movement in literary criticism and theory, originating in philosophical debates in the 1990s about the status of the aesthetic, and becoming a distinct literary practice around the millennium. It stresses the "singularity" and "particularity" of literary texts, seeks *dialogue* with the text rather than *mastery* over it, and sees the text as an ongoing debate (within itself, and between it and its readers) rather than the representative of a fixed position or the predetermined expression of socially conservative views. Its practitioners include **Isobel Armstrong**, **John Joughin** and **Simon Malpas** of Birkbeck College, London.

**Background: the hermeneutics of suspicion.** The new aestheticism runs counter to the major literary theories prominent since the 1970s, since almost all of them increasingly challenged and denied the autonomy of literature: Marxist critics saw literature as the expression of social forces (P9), psychoanalytic critics as the voicing of psychic drives and instinctual conflicts (P6), poststructuralists saw every literary act as a demonstration of the instability of language itself (P7). The consensus of theory was that whatever writers thought they were doing or saying, they were always doing or saying something else: literature never really speaks, but is spoken by various combinations of social, psychological or linguistic forces, and the critic/theorist always knows better than the writer what those forces are. Literature thus lost its autonomy, its strangeness, its particularity, always being stopped and questioned by critics and theorists, even when it seemed to be behaving well: speaking up for the weak, supporting self-determination and equality, pleading for tolerance and understanding of the claims of others. Jane Austen, for instance, may have thought she was doing all this in her novels, but the critical-theoretical thought police always knew better: they could see that she was really covering up the French Revolution, condoning the brutalities rife in the British navy, whitewashing knowledge of the links between the gentry and slavery, or recommending sexual repression, and all this in a single novel, *Mansfield Park*! *Said's reading of this novel in P15 is one item on this list. Barry does not deny the insight of that reading here; he points out what such readings, added together, do to the text.* This instinctive distrust of writers is part of what the French philosopher **Paul Ricoeur** called the `hermeneutics of suspicion`; the definition Barry cites describes it as a method of interpretation that assumes the literal or surface meaning of a text to be an attempt to conceal the political interests the text serves, the aim of interpretation being to strip off the concealment and expose those interests. *This is the general form of the second mechanism, the "manifest/latent double reading": from Freud in P6 and deconstruction in P7 to Macherey in P9, each theory has its own "latent" layer.*

**Argument: an anomaly.** For twenty-five years theorists and critics have been literature's strippers and exposers, largely unchallenged since the defeat of the liberal humanists in the early 1980s. The unique qualities of each text were almost disregarded, since whatever its particular qualities, a work would be found guilty of the broad generic crimes each school of theory specialises in detecting: feminist critics look for sexism and phallocentrism, postcolonialists for Orientalism, deconstructionists for logocentrism, and so on. After decades of relentless attack, literature was bound to reassert itself. The rejoinder of literary texts (if they were allowed to speak) would be simple: all literary texts are different, and should not be stereotyped as sharing socially conservative tendencies. Postcolonialists are quite right to say that all Arabs, "Asians" or Muslims are different and particular, and should not be represented by collective negative stereotypes, which is what happens when harmful "Orientalist" thinking lumps them together; but this resistance to unthinking homogenisation has not carried over into the way we treat literary works. **Literary theory defends difference, otherness, agency and particularity in every field except its own specialism, literature, which it treats as a whole as a socially regressive formation of thought: this is a serious anomaly.** The new aestheticism can be seen as part of literature's inevitable fight-back after thirty years of interrogation by the hermeneutics of suspicion. *The form of this argument is worth noting: it does not attack theory from outside, but uses theory's own principles (P15's critique of homogenisation) to demand that theory be consistent: an immanent critique.*

**Objection: this is not a return to the old close reading.** Is the new aestheticism's reassertion of the power of literary texts simply a return to the old "close reading" long since superseded by theory? Barry thinks not, because its grounds are not a return to Richards's *Practical Criticism* (1929) and Empson's *Seven Types of Ambiguity* (1930), the founding works of close reading (P1), but a return to the philosophy of Kant and Hegel, rereading them *again* after their rereading by Derrida and others. The theorists of the 1970s and 1980s always seemed to assume that their own "rereadings" were permanent and definitive, when in fact they were only moments in a continuing cycle, as open to rereading as any other. In other words, the new aestheticism does not seek to reverse the reversal (by which the *Practical Criticism* of 1929 became, in 1980, *Critical Practice*, the title of Catherine Belsey's influential book), but makes a series of interventions aimed at changing the trajectory of theory itself. Further, the "new" aestheticism revives the interest in and attitude towards the aesthetic of the "Aesthetic Movement" of the late nineteenth century, found in the work of the poet Swinburne, the poet-painter Dante Gabriel Rossetti, Wilde, and the essayist and critic Walter Pater, attitudes often summed up in the slogan "art for art's sake", asserting the autonomy of art and literature, free of considerations of moral correctness or social usefulness. The wish to put the literary text back at the centre of literary study, but in a new "holistic" form, is in Barry's view a welcome reaction against historicism and against the tradition of hermeneutic suspicion towards literary texts. *In a note Barry recommends Rita Felski's* The Limits of Critique *(2015), calling it a lively and sustained counter-interrogation of the hermeneutics of suspicion; this line is often called "postcritique" in subsequent literary studies.*

So the new aestheticism can be seen from four angles: as a revival of the late-nineteenth-century interest in aestheticism; as the reopening of aesthetic debates rooted in the philosophy of Kant and Hegel; as (through the idea of a continuing "dialogue" between reader and text) a new ethical criticism; and as a "new formalism", foregrounding the formal features of texts and their effects on readers. It often confronts the dominant critical and theoretical consensus with an exasperated impatience, insisting on the importance of a long-excluded, long-disparaged aspect of literary study; as if suddenly tired of always being on the defensive, it blurts out the unaskable questions: "What's wrong with the aesthetic?", "What's wrong with Kant?", "How close is close?", all titles of sections or chapters in Armstrong's book.

**Example: two readings of a sonnet.** The book that marks the beginning of the new aestheticism is Armstrong's *The Radical Aesthetic* (2000). In its introduction, discussing the rejection of the idea of the aesthetic by recent schools of literary theory, she argues that developing an alternative poetics means challenging the politics of the anti-aesthetic by remaking its theoretical foundations and changing the terms of the argument. This means restoring the standing of Kant and Hegel, the founding philosophers from whom the most workable notions of the aesthetic derive. She identifies Eagleton's *The Ideology of the Aesthetic* (1990) as an influential statement of "anti-aesthetic politics", and *The Radical Aesthetic*, published ten years later, can be seen as a direct challenge to it; she also sees Eagleton's book as a high point of the hermeneutics of suspicion; we might describe the new aestheticism as an approach to literary study that **begins by being suspicious of the "hermeneutics of suspicion"**. For Eagleton, all the text-specific effects of a sonnet are always "already" explained: the rhyme scheme; the "turn" of thought between octave and sestet; the compression of a large tract of thought into a few images and the frame of fourteen lines; the deft fusing of two meanings into one paradoxical expression; the use of verbal dexterity to "lighten" heavy themes (love, death, religion and so on); and the "drama" peculiar to the sonnet form, in which the poet drives himself into a conceptual or metaphorical dead end only to escape with a deft phrase in the final lines. All this gives the reader aesthetic and intellectual pleasure, and is both the fuel and the engine of the sonnet form. But the "suspicious" theorist sees them as "mere" devices whose primary effect is ideological: the verbal skills displayed in the sonnet are class-linked and elitist, a superfluous luxury decorating thought with intricate filigree patterns; acquiring these skills requires much leisure, available only to the sufficiently privileged, so every display of them reinforces class boundaries. Further, when apparent contradictions or oppositions are "staged" in a sonnet and then reconciled at the end by verbal sleight of hand, literary form itself conveys an implicit message or ideology: all conflicts are like this; conflict is only apparent, social differences can always be resolved by sitting down and agreeing a little incremental tinkering, and no contradiction is so fundamental as to require radical renewal of the system that contains it. *This is the mirror image, in the ideology critique of P9, of the New Critical "paradox resolved in a higher unity" of P2: the same formal fact is the poem's value for New Criticism and the poem's incriminating evidence for the hermeneutics of suspicion.* How, then, does the new aestheticist version differ?

**Operations: how close is close?** Armstrong gives a brilliant demonstration at the end of her third chapter, titled "Textual Harassment: The Ideology of Close Reading, or How Close Is Close?", which discusses Wordsworth's "Tintern Abbey", a poem long a battlefield of criticism and theory, a veritable "site of struggle". Her answer to the question of the title is "not close enough": traditional close reading actually maintains a distance between reader and poem by harbouring sexual/textual fantasies of "mastery"; the (usually male) critic practises on the text the customary anatomising erotics, "exposing" its physique, "uncovering" its fireworks, "savouring" the fleshly taste of its language, all expressions drawn from a rather unfortunate passage she places at the head of the chapter, in which Stanley Fish describes his feelings in textual analysis (*the Fish of interpretive communities in P5*). Armstrong says that this "mastery" approach is an evasion of the text's `affect`, its emotional effect on the reader, which is precisely what generations of male critics feared and kept trying to exorcise: Richards condemned messy-sounding things like "stock responses" and "doctrinal adhesions", Wimsatt and Beardsley the "affective fallacy" (P2), and Empson, writing on this poem as a vehicle for finely distinguishing and defining his various kinds of verbal ambiguity, grew quite agitated about the reprehensible vagueness of the "something" in Wordsworth's "something far more deeply interfused". **Armstrong's point is that in describing feelings and sensations a certain vagueness is unavoidable, and may even be the only way of saying anything at all.** *This critique almost coincides with the image on the cover of the anthology (P1): "analysis is dissection, and dissection is killing"; the phrase "murder to dissect" used by the editors in their preface comes from Wordsworth's own "The Tables Turned" (1798): "We murder to dissect".*

Armstrong's response is to go "closer than close": of the seven pages she writes on "Tintern Abbey", two are on the word *of*. So one aspect of new aestheticist technique is "ultra close-up", attending to "form words" like *of*, whereas more traditional close reading usually concentrates on "content words": nouns and adjectives, verbs and adverbs. Secondly, she uses the paired concepts of `bifurcation` and `erasure`, taken via the philosopher **Emmanuel Levinas** from the French writer and ethnographer Michel Leiris: in "bifurcation", choosing one path rather than another brings both paths into play; "erasure" means "overwriting", as in a palimpsest, where erasing is done by rewriting, writing a new word over an old one. Both terms suggest that poems contain an undecided element, that they argue internally and invite us to join the argument; perhaps they have something to *ask* us rather than to *tell* us. Quite possibly Wordsworth himself did not fully know what that "something" was, and, not being a philosopher, he did not have to decide before putting pen to paper. Armstrong shows that "Tintern Abbey" is full of bifurcations and erasures: Wordsworth writes "hedge-rows", and immediately corrects and rewrites himself: "hardly hedge-rows, little lines / Of sportive wood run wild"; likewise, the smoke rising above the trees gives "uncertain notice, as might seem / Of vagrant dwellers in the houseless woods". "As might seem" makes the reader ask impatiently: was it like that or not? And the oxymoronic "vagrant dwellers" makes those people (who may or may not be there, since Wordsworth does not see them) seem both settled and nomadic. *Note that both passages happen to begin their second line with "Of": in both, it is this very form word that links a self-correction, or an inference, to the next line.*

On a larger scale, the poem also constantly repeats and rewrites itself: the visit described in the poem's "present" repeats one made five years earlier; and the poem Wordsworth is writing echoes and challenges another (unmentioned) poem of the same kind by his friend and rival Coleridge, "Frost at Midnight". So, Armstrong says, the poem is anxious on many levels, as its tonal and structural tensions reflect; the reader should not try to "master" it and evade its anxious "affect", but should enter the emotional turbulence it presents, **getting closer not only to its words but to its feelings**: this closeness to affect is another major component of new aestheticist practice. Her reading thus brings out the text's "protean" quality: it is not a static target of critical attention but a dynamic vortex of thought and feeling, the two almost indistinguishable, perhaps describable as a distinctive affective intensity. The text seems to call out its need to "enter into relationship with someone". Readers, she suggests, may well find in the "body" of the text what they fear, hate and desire; a moment of "narcissistic" identification may be a necessary response, since it escapes the master/slave mode of reading dominant in our culture (*the master/slave terminology derives from Hegel, one of the philosophers to whom the new aestheticism returns*). We need, Armstrong says, to face the fear of intimacy rather than retreat into the safe territory of skilful dissection of the textual corpse. **In fact, as theory after "theory" knows, the text is not a corpse and is not dead at all: while "theory" was holding its wake, it got up and danced.**

**Argument: keeping the conversation going.** Another key work, the introduction to *The New Aestheticism* (2003), edited by Joughin and Malpas, agrees with Armstrong's emphasis, holding that certain literary texts from distant periods survive not because they have "timeless" meanings but because they can withstand often contested or politically opposed interpretations. This suggests that the key quality literary texts need in order to outlive the period of their production is to leave readers room to "join in", to respond to them, to talk with them, to enter into relationship with them. By contrast, a work that is merely pious, merely propagandist or merely "politically correct" leaves no such room: it tells us what it thinks we should think, take it or leave it. So the mark of a surviving work is that it is still in progress, still in the process of thinking things through. It is this quality of the work, keeping questions open and never quite reaching a conclusion, that the new aestheticist responds to and seeks to engage; he seeks to keep the conversation with the work going, rather than seeking closure, completion or termination as other critical methods do when they make showing how Orientalist, phallocentric or self-deconstructing a work is their main aim. This "keep talking" approach does in a sense "privilege" the literary work itself, but other approaches privilege the critic or theorist, whereas the never-ending conversation with the work envisaged by the new aestheticist seems fundamentally "democratic" in nature, since it is a conversation that can never be finally completed. So it accepts that the aim of critical inquiry can never be to arrive at definitive scientific truth (*on this point its premise differs sharply from that of the cognitivists below*): for instance, one can never finally determine whether Conrad's *Heart of Darkness* is a "racist" book by a racist author (the subject of Robert Eaglestone's chapter in the Joughin and Malpas volume), or whether Hamlet is "mad", because neither text contains that kind of "is" (whether affirmative or negative). One can only discuss the question of racism in *Heart of Darkness* and the question of madness in *Hamlet*; and it is hard to imagine what good would come of settling either question, whereas much good can come of discussing them. **This emphasis on open dialogue with the literary text is the nearest Barry can come to an account of what the new aestheticism ultimately is.**

**Distinction: the new aestheticism and the New Criticism.** *Set beside P2, the similarities and differences are clear. What they share is the insistence on the particularity of the text, trust in close reading, and refusal to reduce literature to something else. They differ in three ways. First, in their grounds: the New Criticism's ground is the organic unity of the poem as a self-sufficient object, the new aestheticism's is Kant and Hegel as reread through Derrida. Second, in their attitude to affect, which is opposite: the New Criticism excludes the reader's emotions from analysis as the "affective fallacy", while the new aestheticism precisely seeks to enter affect. Third, in their aims, which are also opposite: the New Criticism has paradox resolved in a higher unity, while the new aestheticism keeps the argument in the poem open and invites the reader to join it. On the third point it is closer to the deconstruction of P7 than to the New Criticism of P2, except that it turns deconstruction's "undecidability" from a linguistic predicament into an ethical invitation.*

**Limitation:** *Barry calls the new aestheticism an "emerging" movement, and its risks are already perceptible: if every surviving work is described as "keeping questions open", that description may itself become a new homogenisation. Barry's criticism in P7 that close reading and deconstruction alike "make all poems look alike" could equally be applied to it.*

### Cognitive Poetics and Consilience: Science Re-enters Literary Study

**Definition:** `Cognitive poetics` is an approach to reading literature that combines linguistics and psychology, aiming at a better understanding of basic cognitive processes. Important practitioners include **Reuven Tsur** of Tel Aviv University, **Peter Stockwell** of the University of Nottingham, **Alan Richardson** of Boston College, Joseph Tabbi of the University of Illinois at Chicago and **Ellen Spolsky** of Bar-Ilan University. The Latin verb *cognoscere* means "to get to know", whence the English *cognition*, defined by the *Concise Oxford Dictionary* as "the mental action or process of acquiring knowledge through thought, experience, and the senses". "Cognitive science" studies how the mind is organised, the processes of thinking themselves, and the mind as the interface between inner and outer worlds.

**Background: the cognitive revolution and the return of "nature".** A "revolution" in this field began in the 1950s, closely bound up with the interdisciplinary current seen in event 1, as anthropology, psychology and linguistics began talking to one another; it was also partly a product of developments in computer technology, as computers began to offer possible models for the mechanisms of mental processing. Another important factor was Chomsky's challenge to the "behaviourist" view of mind associated with the psychologist B. F. Skinner: his famous review of Skinner's *Verbal Behavior* (1959) opposed explaining language acquisition as a cumulative response to external cues and stimuli, arguing that it is a creative, internalised process for which the human mind is uniquely equipped. It was natural to suppose that studying language would help explain how the mind works, since language use seems the most complex and characteristic of human cognitive processes; the basic figures of metaphor and metonymy, for example, seem to correspond to fundamental modes of apprehension and understanding: the former fusing two or more concepts into a new whole, the latter letting a part of something stand for the whole (*these are exactly Jakobson's two poles in P3, here reread from rhetoric as cognitive psychology*). The cognitivists say that if we are talking about mental processes and linking them to rhetorical figures such as metaphor, we have already entered the territory of literary criticism, so a form of criticism fusing literary criticism, philosophy of mind and even evolutionary biology and neuroscience no longer seems so strange.

In the early 1990s the work of Tsur (*Toward a Theory of Cognitive Poetics*) and Spolsky (*Gaps in Nature: Literary Interpretation and the Modular Mind*, 1993) laid the foundations for this combination. Literary theory was then dominated partly by poststructuralism, which allowed no one to dispute its view of language as nothing but "instability" and "relativity", and partly by historicism, whose bottom line was that "everything is socially and historically constructed". Any notion of "nature" was viewed with extreme suspicion, the word itself being taboo: as P16 showed, precisely the intellectual taboo ecocriticism had to challenge. In a sense Chomsky's theory of language brought "nature" back into play: language acquisition cannot be wholly explained by notions such as stimulus, reinforcement and deprivation; that is, "social" factors (encouragement, reward and approval, modelling and tutoring) cannot fully explain children's acquisition of language, and the capacity to learn language must in some way be "built in" or innate.
